lessons.title: Durable Agent Execution
lessons.summary: Durable Agent Execution is a core topic in modern system design. This lesson builds a first-principles model around tools, memory, and orchestration, then connects that model to capacity, failure modes, and operational practice so you can use it in real architectures.

sections.title: What Durable Agent Execution is solving
paragraphs: Durable Agent Execution exists because naive designs around tools, memory, and orchestration break under scale, partial failure, or changing requirements. Before choosing tools, name the problem: which resource is scarce, which invariant must hold, and which user-visible failures are unacceptable.
In interviews and production reviews, strong answers start with constraints (QPS, data size, latency budget, consistency needs) and only then map Durable Agent Execution onto those constraints.

A useful mental model separates the control plane (how you configure and observe Durable Agent Execution) from the data plane (the per-request/per-event path). Confusing the two leads to architectures that look neat and operate poorly.

sections.title: Core mechanics
paragraphs: Mechanically, Durable Agent Execution involves a small set of moving parts: inputs, state, an algorithm or protocol, and outputs/side effects. Draw those parts explicitly. If state is replicated, write down the replication/consistency rule. If work is asynchronous, write down delivery semantics.

Performance characteristics usually come from amplification (how much internal work per external request), locality (whether work stays on one node), and contention (locks, hot keys, leader bottlenecks).

Correctness characteristics usually come from failure handling: retries, timeouts, idempotency, and what clients observe during failover. If you cannot explain the failure story, you do not yet understand Durable Agent Execution.
bullets: Inputs → state/protocol → outputs/side effects
Name consistency and delivery guarantees
Identify the bottleneck resource early

sections.title: Designing with it
paragraphs: When incorporating Durable Agent Execution into a system, decide the API boundary first: what does a client call, what can fail, and what is retried. Keep the happy path boring and push complexity into well-tested libraries or platform components.

Capacity plan with numbers: estimate peak load, working set, and headroom. Convert that into shard counts, cache sizes, thread/connection pools, or GPU/memory budgets as relevant to Durable Agent Execution.
Prefer reversible rollout: feature flags, dual-running, shadow traffic, and clear dashboards. New uses of Durable Agent Execution should be observable on day one.

sections.title: Operations and failure modes
paragraphs: Operate Durable Agent Execution with SLIs that match user pain (availability, latency, lag, error rate, cost). Alert on burn rates and queue/lag growth, not only host CPU.
Common failures include overload without admission control, retry amplification, silent staleness, schema mismatches, and dependency brownouts. Write a runbook for the top three.
Chaos and game days should include slow dependencies and network delay, not only hard kills. Durable Agent Execution often fails in the gray area.

paragraphs: Under the hood, Durable Agent Execution typically exposes knobs for batching, buffering, concurrency, retention, and timeouts. Each knob trades latency, throughput, and cost. Change one at a time and measure.

Instrumentation should include high-signal histograms and exemplars that jump to traces. For data systems, watch amplification and compaction/GC; for RPC systems, watch queue time and saturation; for ML systems, watch memory and tokens/s.

paragraphs: Integrate via stable contracts: schemas, idempotency keys, and versioned APIs. Dual-write carefully or prefer CDC/outbox patterns when crossing storage and messaging.
Boundary tests should prove behavior under duplicate delivery, reordering, and clock skew where relevant to Durable Agent Execution.

paragraphs: Across regions, RTT and quorum placement dominate. Keep user-critical paths region-local when invariants allow; replicate asynchronously otherwise. Spell out the conflict/staleness model.
Track unit economics for Durable Agent Execution: cost per million requests, per GB stored, or per million tokens. Many scalability projects are cost projects — make the objective explicit.

lessons.title: Agent Memory Architectures
lessons.summary: Agents need short-term working memory (context window) and long-term memory (stores retrieved across sessions). Designing memory poorly causes loops, leaks of private data, and unbounded cost.

sections.title: Layers of memory
paragraphs: Working memory: the prompt/context. Summary memory: compressed history. Episodic stores: past tasks. Semantic stores: facts via RAG. Procedural: tools and skills.
Each layer has different consistency, privacy, and TTL requirements. Do not dump everything into the prompt.

sections.title: Write paths and trust
paragraphs: Decide what the agent may write to long-term memory. User-private vs tenant-shared vs global. Poisoned memory is a real attack (indirect prompt injection via stored text).
Prefer structured memories with provenance and expiry over free-form append-only blobs.

sections.title: Retrieval and compaction
paragraphs: Retrieve top-k memories with hybrid search; compact old threads with summaries that preserve decisions and open questions.
Track tokens spent on memory vs new reasoning — memory can starve the model of room to think.

sections.title: Durability for long jobs
paragraphs: Long-running agents should checkpoint state in a workflow store (step, tool results, approvals) separate from LLM chat logs.

deepDive.title: Agent Memory Architectures — Operations
paragraphs: Operating Agent Memory Architectures in production means defining SLIs before tuning knobs, knowing amplification costs, and rehearsing failure modes.
Prefer reversible changes, feature flags, and canaries. Measure p50/p99 and error rate under load that matches production skew.
bullets: Define capacity from the scarcest resource
Document blast radius per dependency
Keep rollback cheaper than forward repair when possible

deepDive.title: Agent Memory Architectures — Failure modes
paragraphs: Common failures around Agent Memory Architectures include overload, partial dependency outages, and silent correctness bugs that pass happy-path tests.
Inject faults in staging: latency, loss, clock skew, and disk full. Verify alerts fire and degradation is intentional.

expert.title: Agent Memory Architectures — Expert notes
paragraphs: At the expert level, Agent Memory Architectures intersects multi-region consistency, cost envelopes, and organizational constraints (team ownership, on-call load).
Write down the non-goals. Many outages come from optimizing a metric that was never the product requirement.

practices: ACL every memory write/read

lessons.title: Tool Calling & Planner/Executor

sections.title: Tools as APIs

sections.title: Planner vs executor

sections.title: Safety
paragraphs: Least privilege tools. Human approval for irreversible actions. Sandbox code execution. Log every call for audit.

sections.title: Reliability
paragraphs: Tool failures need retries with budgets. Partial success in multi-tool plans needs compensating actions — sagas again.

lessons.title: MCP & Agent Protocols
lessons.summary: MCP & Agent Protocols is a core topic in modern system design. This lesson builds a first-principles model around interoperability and sandboxing, then connects that model to capacity, failure modes, and operational practice so you can use it in real architectures.

sections.title: What MCP & Agent Protocols is solving
paragraphs: MCP & Agent Protocols exists because naive designs around interoperability and sandboxing break under scale, partial failure, or changing requirements. Before choosing tools, name the problem: which resource is scarce, which invariant must hold, and which user-visible failures are unacceptable.
In interviews and production reviews, strong answers start with constraints (QPS, data size, latency budget, consistency needs) and only then map MCP & Agent Protocols onto those constraints.

A useful mental model separates the control plane (how you configure and observe MCP & Agent Protocols) from the data plane (the per-request/per-event path). Confusing the two leads to architectures that look neat and operate poorly.

sections.title: Core mechanics
paragraphs: Mechanically, MCP & Agent Protocols involves a small set of moving parts: inputs, state, an algorithm or protocol, and outputs/side effects. Draw those parts explicitly. If state is replicated, write down the replication/consistency rule. If work is asynchronous, write down delivery semantics.

Performance characteristics usually come from amplification (how much internal work per external request), locality (whether work stays on one node), and contention (locks, hot keys, leader bottlenecks).

Correctness characteristics usually come from failure handling: retries, timeouts, idempotency, and what clients observe during failover. If you cannot explain the failure story, you do not yet understand MCP & Agent Protocols.
bullets: Inputs → state/protocol → outputs/side effects
Name consistency and delivery guarantees
Identify the bottleneck resource early

sections.title: Designing with it
paragraphs: When incorporating MCP & Agent Protocols into a system, decide the API boundary first: what does a client call, what can fail, and what is retried. Keep the happy path boring and push complexity into well-tested libraries or platform components.

Capacity plan with numbers: estimate peak load, working set, and headroom. Convert that into shard counts, cache sizes, thread/connection pools, or GPU/memory budgets as relevant to MCP & Agent Protocols.
Prefer reversible rollout: feature flags, dual-running, shadow traffic, and clear dashboards. New uses of MCP & Agent Protocols should be observable on day one.

sections.title: Operations and failure modes
paragraphs: Operate MCP & Agent Protocols with SLIs that match user pain (availability, latency, lag, error rate, cost). Alert on burn rates and queue/lag growth, not only host CPU.
Common failures include overload without admission control, retry amplification, silent staleness, schema mismatches, and dependency brownouts. Write a runbook for the top three.
Chaos and game days should include slow dependencies and network delay, not only hard kills. MCP & Agent Protocols often fails in the gray area.

lessons.title: Prompt Injection Defense
lessons.summary: Prompt Injection Defense is a core topic in modern system design. This lesson builds a first-principles model around evals, safety, and budgets, then connects that model to capacity, failure modes, and operational practice so you can use it in real architectures.

sections.title: What Prompt Injection Defense is solving
paragraphs: Prompt Injection Defense exists because naive designs around evals, safety, and budgets break under scale, partial failure, or changing requirements. Before choosing tools, name the problem: which resource is scarce, which invariant must hold, and which user-visible failures are unacceptable.
In interviews and production reviews, strong answers start with constraints (QPS, data size, latency budget, consistency needs) and only then map Prompt Injection Defense onto those constraints.

A useful mental model separates the control plane (how you configure and observe Prompt Injection Defense) from the data plane (the per-request/per-event path). Confusing the two leads to architectures that look neat and operate poorly.

sections.title: Core mechanics
paragraphs: Mechanically, Prompt Injection Defense involves a small set of moving parts: inputs, state, an algorithm or protocol, and outputs/side effects. Draw those parts explicitly. If state is replicated, write down the replication/consistency rule. If work is asynchronous, write down delivery semantics.

Performance characteristics usually come from amplification (how much internal work per external request), locality (whether work stays on one node), and contention (locks, hot keys, leader bottlenecks).

Correctness characteristics usually come from failure handling: retries, timeouts, idempotency, and what clients observe during failover. If you cannot explain the failure story, you do not yet understand Prompt Injection Defense.
bullets: Inputs → state/protocol → outputs/side effects
Name consistency and delivery guarantees
Identify the bottleneck resource early

sections.title: Designing with it
paragraphs: When incorporating Prompt Injection Defense into a system, decide the API boundary first: what does a client call, what can fail, and what is retried. Keep the happy path boring and push complexity into well-tested libraries or platform components.

Capacity plan with numbers: estimate peak load, working set, and headroom. Convert that into shard counts, cache sizes, thread/connection pools, or GPU/memory budgets as relevant to Prompt Injection Defense.
Prefer reversible rollout: feature flags, dual-running, shadow traffic, and clear dashboards. New uses of Prompt Injection Defense should be observable on day one.

sections.title: Operations and failure modes
paragraphs: Operate Prompt Injection Defense with SLIs that match user pain (availability, latency, lag, error rate, cost). Alert on burn rates and queue/lag growth, not only host CPU.
Common failures include overload without admission control, retry amplification, silent staleness, schema mismatches, and dependency brownouts. Write a runbook for the top three.
Chaos and game days should include slow dependencies and network delay, not only hard kills. Prompt Injection Defense often fails in the gray area.

lessons.title: REST, GraphQL, gRPC & Streaming
lessons.summary: API style shapes client flexibility, performance, team velocity, and operational complexity. REST dominates public HTTP APIs; GraphQL optimizes client-driven data fetching; gRPC excels at internal service-to-service RPC; streaming protocols handle real-time and high-throughput data flows.

sections.title: REST: Resource-Oriented HTTP
paragraphs: REST (Representational State Transfer) models APIs as resources identified by URLs, manipulated with HTTP verbs (GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE), and described by standard status codes and headers. It leverages HTTP caching, CDN compatibility, and universal tooling.

REST shines for public APIs, CRUD operations, and teams wanting simplicity and broad client support. Hypermedia (HATEOAS) is rarely implemented in practice; most REST APIs are pragmatic resource endpoints with JSON bodies.

Challenges include over-fetching (returning entire objects when clients need one field), under-fetching (requiring multiple round trips), and inconsistent conventions across teams without strict API governance.

sections.title: GraphQL: Client-Specified Queries
paragraphs: GraphQL provides a single endpoint where clients send queries specifying exactly the fields they need. The server resolves a graph of types — reducing over-fetching and enabling rapid frontend iteration without backend changes for every UI tweak.

GraphQL supports mutations (writes), subscriptions (real-time via WebSocket), and introspection for schema discovery. Tools like Apollo and Relay manage caching, batching, and optimistic updates on the client.

Risks include N+1 query problems (mitigated by DataLoader batching), complex server-side resolvers, query depth/complexity attacks, and caching difficulty at the HTTP layer — POST requests bypass CDN caches by default.

sections.title: gRPC: High-Performance RPC
paragraphs: gRPC uses Protocol Buffers for compact binary serialization and HTTP/2 for multiplexed, bidirectional streaming. Service contracts are defined in .proto files, generating typed client and server stubs in multiple languages.

gRPC supports unary (request-response), server streaming, client streaming, and bidirectional streaming. It is ideal for internal microservice communication where performance, type safety, and streaming matter more than browser compatibility.

gRPC requires gRPC-Web or a proxy (Envoy) for browser clients. Debugging is harder than JSON REST — tools like grpcurl and reflection help. Load balancing uses client-side or proxy-based approaches (xDS, lookaside LB).

sections.title: Streaming: WebSockets, SSE, and Webhooks
paragraphs: Server-Sent Events (SSE) push server-to-client updates over a persistent HTTP connection — simpler than WebSockets, unidirectional, auto-reconnect built in. Ideal for live feeds, progress updates, and notifications.
WebSockets provide full-duplex communication — chat, collaborative editing, gaming. Scaling WebSockets requires sticky connections or a pub/sub backplane to broadcast across server instances.

Webhooks are server-to-server HTTP callbacks — event producers POST to consumer URLs when something happens. Simple to integrate but require retry logic, signature verification, and idempotent handlers on the receiving side.

sections.title: Choosing and Versioning APIs
paragraphs: Public mobile and web clients: REST or GraphQL depending on client diversity and data-fetching complexity. Internal service mesh: gRPC for performance. Real-time features: WebSockets or SSE. Third-party integrations: REST webhooks.

Many organizations use REST/GraphQL at the edge and gRPC internally — an API gateway translates between them. Version APIs explicitly: URL path (/v2/users), header (Accept-Version), or schema evolution with backward compatibility.
Document APIs with OpenAPI (REST), GraphQL schema SDL, or proto files. Contract testing (Pact, Buf) catches breaking changes before deployment.

deepDive.title: REST, GraphQL, gRPC & Streaming — Operational deep dive
paragraphs: Operating REST, GraphQL, gRPC & Streaming well means defining the scarce resource (CPU, memory, disk, network, or tokens), the SLIs that reflect user pain, and the knobs that trade cost for latency.
Under load, measure amplification: how many bytes, RPCs, or disk writes you pay per user request. Prefetch and batch only when measurements show benefit — premature batching adds tail latency.
Failure drills should include dependency slowdown (not only hard down), clock skew, and disk full. Verify alerts, dashboards, and runbooks against those drills.
bullets: Name the scarcest resource and budget it
Track p50/p99 and error rate for the user journey
Rehearse partial dependency failure

deepDive.title: REST, GraphQL, gRPC & Streaming — Correctness edges
paragraphs: Correctness edges around REST, GraphQL, gRPC & Streaming often appear at retries, partial writes, and schema evolution. Make handlers idempotent and state transitions explicit.

Document what clients may observe during failover: stale reads, duplicate messages, or delayed visibility. If the product cannot tolerate an anomaly, enforce a stronger consistency boundary — and pay for it knowingly.

expert.title: REST, GraphQL, gRPC & Streaming — Expert / multi-region notes
paragraphs: At multi-region scale, REST, GraphQL, gRPC & Streaming interacts with RTT, quorum placement, and cost of cross-region replication. Prefer region-local user paths with asynchronous global state when invariants allow.
Cost envelopes matter: chart unit cost vs QPS and vs data size. Many 'performance' projects are actually cost projects in disguise — make the objective explicit.

concepts: REST: resources, HTTP verbs, status codes, cacheable GET
GraphQL: schema, queries, mutations, subscriptions, resolver graph
gRPC: Protocol Buffers, HTTP/2, four streaming modes
SSE: unidirectional server push over HTTP
WebSockets: bidirectional persistent connection
Webhooks: server-to-server event callbacks
API versioning: URL, header, schema evolution
Over-fetching vs under-fetching trade-offs
DataLoader pattern for GraphQL N+1 prevention
gRPC-Web for browser compatibility
practices: Use REST for public CRUD APIs with good HTTP semantics and caching
Use GraphQL when many client types need different field subsets
Use gRPC for internal services with high throughput requirements
Define API contracts in OpenAPI, GraphQL SDL, or proto files — generate code
Implement rate limiting and query complexity limits on GraphQL endpoints
Verify webhook signatures (HMAC) and make handlers idempotent
Version APIs before external consumers depend on them
pitfalls: GraphQL exposing entire database schema without authorization per field
gRPC without deadlines/timeouts — cascading hangs across services
REST APIs that ignore HTTP caching semantics (no ETag, no Cache-Control)
WebSockets without a scale-out strategy — connections stuck on one node
Breaking API changes without versioning or deprecation period
Using POST for all GraphQL queries without complexity analysis — DoS vector

examples.title: Netflix-style API layering
examples.description: Mobile and web clients hit a GraphQL BFF (Backend for Frontend) that aggregates data from internal gRPC microservices. The BFF handles auth, field resolution, and caching. Internal services communicate via gRPC with mTLS — never exposed publicly.

examples.title: Stripe-style webhooks
examples.description: Stripe POSTs signed webhook events to merchant endpoints on payment success. Merchants verify HMAC signatures, return 200 quickly, and process asynchronously via a queue. Idempotency keys prevent duplicate order fulfillment on webhook retry.

keyTakeaways: REST is the default for public HTTP APIs — simple, cacheable, universal
GraphQL gives clients query flexibility at the cost of server complexity
gRPC is the internal workhorse for typed, high-performance RPC
Streaming protocols (SSE, WebSockets) serve real-time use cases
Version and document APIs from day one — contract tests prevent breakage
Hybrid architectures (GraphQL edge + gRPC internal) are common at scale
lessons.whyItMatters: API choices affect latency budgets, developer experience, security surface, and deployment coupling. Wrong choices create frontend bottlenecks (REST over-fetching), operational nightmares (unbounded GraphQL queries), or integration friction (gRPC exposed to browsers). Interviewers expect nuanced comparisons, not 'always use REST.'
reflectionQuestions: When does GraphQL's flexibility become a performance or security problem?
Why do large companies use gRPC internally but REST or GraphQL externally?
How would you scale WebSocket connections across a cluster of servers?
What versioning strategy would you use for a public API with mobile clients?

lessons.title: API Versioning & Compatibility
lessons.summary: API Versioning & Compatibility is a core topic in modern system design. This lesson builds a first-principles model around contracts, evolution, and client ergonomics, then connects that model to capacity, failure modes, and operational practice so you can use it in real architectures.

sections.title: What API Versioning & Compatibility is solving
paragraphs: API Versioning & Compatibility exists because naive designs around contracts, evolution, and client ergonomics break under scale, partial failure, or changing requirements. Before choosing tools, name the problem: which resource is scarce, which invariant must hold, and which user-visible failures are unacceptable.

In interviews and production reviews, strong answers start with constraints (QPS, data size, latency budget, consistency needs) and only then map API Versioning & Compatibility onto those constraints.

A useful mental model separates the control plane (how you configure and observe API Versioning & Compatibility) from the data plane (the per-request/per-event path). Confusing the two leads to architectures that look neat and operate poorly.

sections.title: Core mechanics
paragraphs: Mechanically, API Versioning & Compatibility involves a small set of moving parts: inputs, state, an algorithm or protocol, and outputs/side effects. Draw those parts explicitly. If state is replicated, write down the replication/consistency rule. If work is asynchronous, write down delivery semantics.

Performance characteristics usually come from amplification (how much internal work per external request), locality (whether work stays on one node), and contention (locks, hot keys, leader bottlenecks).

Correctness characteristics usually come from failure handling: retries, timeouts, idempotency, and what clients observe during failover. If you cannot explain the failure story, you do not yet understand API Versioning & Compatibility.
bullets: Inputs → state/protocol → outputs/side effects
Name consistency and delivery guarantees
Identify the bottleneck resource early

sections.title: Designing with it
paragraphs: When incorporating API Versioning & Compatibility into a system, decide the API boundary first: what does a client call, what can fail, and what is retried. Keep the happy path boring and push complexity into well-tested libraries or platform components.

Capacity plan with numbers: estimate peak load, working set, and headroom. Convert that into shard counts, cache sizes, thread/connection pools, or GPU/memory budgets as relevant to API Versioning & Compatibility.
Prefer reversible rollout: feature flags, dual-running, shadow traffic, and clear dashboards. New uses of API Versioning & Compatibility should be observable on day one.

sections.title: Operations and failure modes
paragraphs: Operate API Versioning & Compatibility with SLIs that match user pain (availability, latency, lag, error rate, cost). Alert on burn rates and queue/lag growth, not only host CPU.
Common failures include overload without admission control, retry amplification, silent staleness, schema mismatches, and dependency brownouts. Write a runbook for the top three.
Chaos and game days should include slow dependencies and network delay, not only hard kills. API Versioning & Compatibility often fails in the gray area.

deepDive.title: API Versioning & Compatibility — deeper internals
paragraphs: Under the hood, API Versioning & Compatibility typically exposes knobs for batching, buffering, concurrency, retention, and timeouts. Each knob trades latency, throughput, and cost. Change one at a time and measure.

Instrumentation should include high-signal histograms and exemplars that jump to traces. For data systems, watch amplification and compaction/GC; for RPC systems, watch queue time and saturation; for ML systems, watch memory and tokens/s.
bullets: One knob at a time with a hypothesis
Histograms > averages
Tie dashboards to runbooks

deepDive.title: API Versioning & Compatibility — integration patterns
paragraphs: Integrate via stable contracts: schemas, idempotency keys, and versioned APIs. Dual-write carefully or prefer CDC/outbox patterns when crossing storage and messaging.
Boundary tests should prove behavior under duplicate delivery, reordering, and clock skew where relevant to API Versioning & Compatibility.

expert.title: API Versioning & Compatibility — multi-region and cost
paragraphs: Across regions, RTT and quorum placement dominate. Keep user-critical paths region-local when invariants allow; replicate asynchronously otherwise. Spell out the conflict/staleness model.
Track unit economics for API Versioning & Compatibility: cost per million requests, per GB stored, or per million tokens. Many scalability projects are cost projects — make the objective explicit.

Mechanics + failure model + capacity math are the core
Operations and contracts decide long-term success

lessons.title: BFF & Experience APIs
lessons.summary: BFF & Experience APIs is a core topic in modern system design. This lesson builds a first-principles model around structure, boundaries, and change management, then connects that model to capacity, failure modes, and operational practice so you can use it in real architectures.

sections.title: What BFF & Experience APIs is solving
paragraphs: BFF & Experience APIs exists because naive designs around structure, boundaries, and change management break under scale, partial failure, or changing requirements. Before choosing tools, name the problem: which resource is scarce, which invariant must hold, and which user-visible failures are unacceptable.
In interviews and production reviews, strong answers start with constraints (QPS, data size, latency budget, consistency needs) and only then map BFF & Experience APIs onto those constraints.

A useful mental model separates the control plane (how you configure and observe BFF & Experience APIs) from the data plane (the per-request/per-event path). Confusing the two leads to architectures that look neat and operate poorly.

sections.title: Core mechanics
paragraphs: Mechanically, BFF & Experience APIs involves a small set of moving parts: inputs, state, an algorithm or protocol, and outputs/side effects. Draw those parts explicitly. If state is replicated, write down the replication/consistency rule. If work is asynchronous, write down delivery semantics.

Performance characteristics usually come from amplification (how much internal work per external request), locality (whether work stays on one node), and contention (locks, hot keys, leader bottlenecks).

Correctness characteristics usually come from failure handling: retries, timeouts, idempotency, and what clients observe during failover. If you cannot explain the failure story, you do not yet understand BFF & Experience APIs.
bullets: Inputs → state/protocol → outputs/side effects
Name consistency and delivery guarantees
Identify the bottleneck resource early

sections.title: Designing with it
paragraphs: When incorporating BFF & Experience APIs into a system, decide the API boundary first: what does a client call, what can fail, and what is retried. Keep the happy path boring and push complexity into well-tested libraries or platform components.

Capacity plan with numbers: estimate peak load, working set, and headroom. Convert that into shard counts, cache sizes, thread/connection pools, or GPU/memory budgets as relevant to BFF & Experience APIs.
Prefer reversible rollout: feature flags, dual-running, shadow traffic, and clear dashboards. New uses of BFF & Experience APIs should be observable on day one.

sections.title: Operations and failure modes
paragraphs: Operate BFF & Experience APIs with SLIs that match user pain (availability, latency, lag, error rate, cost). Alert on burn rates and queue/lag growth, not only host CPU.
Common failures include overload without admission control, retry amplification, silent staleness, schema mismatches, and dependency brownouts. Write a runbook for the top three.
Chaos and game days should include slow dependencies and network delay, not only hard kills. BFF & Experience APIs often fails in the gray area.

lessons.title: Clean Architecture & DDD
lessons.summary: Clean Architecture and Domain-Driven Design (DDD) organize code around business domains rather than technical frameworks. This lesson covers hexagonal architecture, dependency inversion, bounded contexts, aggregates, and the tactical patterns that keep core business logic testable, framework-independent, and aligned with how the business actually works.

sections.title: Clean Architecture: Dependencies Point Inward
paragraphs: Robert Martin's Clean Architecture organizes code into concentric rings. The innermost ring is the domain — entities and business rules that would exist even if you had no database, no web framework, and no UI. Each outer ring depends on the inner rings, never the reverse. Frameworks, databases, and UI are details that belong on the outside.

The Dependency Inversion Principle makes this work: high-level modules (business logic) define interfaces (ports); low-level modules (database adapters, HTTP handlers) implement them. Your OrderService depends on an IOrderRepository interface defined in the domain layer; PostgreSQLOrderRepository in the infrastructure layer implements it.

The payoff is testability and longevity. You can unit-test business rules without spinning up a database. You can swap PostgreSQL for MongoDB by writing a new adapter. When your web framework releases a breaking version, the domain layer doesn't change.
bullets: Entities: core business objects with identity and lifecycle (Order, Customer, Account)
Use cases / application services: orchestrate domain logic for a specific user action
Interface adapters: controllers, presenters, gateways that translate between layers
Frameworks & drivers: web framework, ORM, message broker — outermost, most replaceable

sections.title: Hexagonal Architecture: Ports and Adapters
paragraphs: Alistair Cockburn's Hexagonal Architecture (Ports and Adapters) expresses the same idea with a vivid metaphor: the application core is a hexagon with ports (interfaces) on each side. Adapters plug into those ports — a REST controller adapter on one side, a PostgreSQL repository adapter on another, a Kafka event publisher on a third.

Primary (driving) adapters initiate interaction: HTTP controllers, CLI commands, message consumers. Secondary (driven) adapters respond to the core's needs: database repositories, email senders, external API clients. The core knows nothing about HTTP status codes or SQL syntax.

This symmetry makes the architecture explicit in your folder structure: domain/ contains entities and ports; application/ contains use cases; adapters/inbound/ and adapters/outbound/ contain framework-specific code. New team members can navigate by business concept, not by technology.
bullets: Port: an interface the core defines (OrderRepository, PaymentGateway, EventPublisher)
Adapter: a concrete implementation for a specific technology (PostgresOrderRepository, StripePaymentGateway)
Primary adapter: drives the application (HTTP handler calls CreateOrderUseCase)
Secondary adapter: driven by the application (use case calls repository.save())

sections.title: Domain-Driven Design: Strategic Patterns
paragraphs: Eric Evans' Domain-Driven Design distinguishes strategic design (how large systems are divided) from tactical design (how code is structured within a boundary). The strategic cornerstone is the bounded context: a explicit boundary within which a particular domain model is defined and consistent.

In an e-commerce platform, 'Product' means different things in different contexts: the Catalog context cares about descriptions and images; the Inventory context cares about stock counts and warehouse locations; the Pricing context cares about cost, margin, and discounts. Forcing one Product model across all three creates confusion and coupling.

Context maps document relationships between bounded contexts: Shared Kernel (shared code), Customer-Supplier (upstream/downstream), Conformist (downstream adopts upstream model), Anti-Corruption Layer (translates foreign models). These relationships guide integration decisions when building microservices or modular monoliths.
bullets: Ubiquitous language: developers and business stakeholders use the same terms in code and conversation
Bounded context: scope where a domain model is internally consistent
Context map: visual diagram of how bounded contexts relate and integrate
Anti-corruption layer: translation layer preventing foreign domain models from leaking in

sections.title: Domain-Driven Design: Tactical Patterns
paragraphs: Within a bounded context, tactical patterns structure the domain model. Entities have identity that persists over time (Order #12345). Value objects are defined by their attributes, not identity — Money($10, USD), Address, DateRange. They are immutable and interchangeable.

Aggregates are clusters of entities and value objects treated as a single consistency boundary. An Order aggregate contains OrderLineItems; you never modify a line item directly — you load the Order, call order.addItem(), and save the whole aggregate. This ensures invariants (total price matches sum of items) are always enforced.

Domain events capture something meaningful that happened in the domain: OrderPlaced, PaymentFailed, InventoryReserved. They enable loose coupling between aggregates and bounded contexts. Domain services handle operations that don't naturally belong to a single entity (e.g., transferring funds between two Accounts).
bullets: Entity: object with unique identity (Customer, Order, Shipment)
Value object: immutable, defined by attributes (Email, Money, GeoCoordinate)
Aggregate root: the single entry point for modifying an aggregate (Order is root; LineItem is not accessed directly)
Repository: persistence abstraction that retrieves and saves aggregates as whole units
Domain event: record of a significant state change within the domain

sections.title: Applying Clean Architecture and DDD in Practice
paragraphs: These patterns are not all-or-nothing. A CRUD admin panel doesn't need aggregates and domain events. A payment processing core benefits enormously from them. Apply DDD tactically where business complexity is highest — the domain experts care deeply about correctness there.

Common project structure: src/domain/ (entities, value objects, repository interfaces, domain events), src/application/ (use cases, DTOs, application services), src/infrastructure/ (database adapters, message broker adapters, external API clients), src/interfaces/ (HTTP controllers, GraphQL resolvers, CLI).

Testing strategy follows naturally: unit tests for domain logic (fast, no I/O), integration tests for adapters (real database in test container), end-to-end tests for critical user flows. Most tests should live at the unit level because the domain layer contains the business rules that matter most.

deepDive.title: Clean Architecture & DDD — Operational deep dive
paragraphs: Operating Clean Architecture & DDD well means defining the scarce resource (CPU, memory, disk, network, or tokens), the SLIs that reflect user pain, and the knobs that trade cost for latency.
Under load, measure amplification: how many bytes, RPCs, or disk writes you pay per user request. Prefetch and batch only when measurements show benefit — premature batching adds tail latency.
Failure drills should include dependency slowdown (not only hard down), clock skew, and disk full. Verify alerts, dashboards, and runbooks against those drills.
bullets: Name the scarcest resource and budget it
Track p50/p99 and error rate for the user journey
Rehearse partial dependency failure

deepDive.title: Clean Architecture & DDD — Correctness edges
paragraphs: Correctness edges around Clean Architecture & DDD often appear at retries, partial writes, and schema evolution. Make handlers idempotent and state transitions explicit.

Document what clients may observe during failover: stale reads, duplicate messages, or delayed visibility. If the product cannot tolerate an anomaly, enforce a stronger consistency boundary — and pay for it knowingly.

paragraphs: At multi-region scale, Clean Architecture & DDD interacts with RTT, quorum placement, and cost of cross-region replication. Prefer region-local user paths with asynchronous global state when invariants allow.
Cost envelopes matter: chart unit cost vs QPS and vs data size. Many 'performance' projects are actually cost projects in disguise — make the objective explicit.

examples.title: Amazon's Bounded Contexts
examples.description: Amazon's platform spans dozens of bounded contexts — Catalog, Ordering, Fulfillment, Payments, Recommendations — each with its own model of core concepts. 'Product' in Catalog (marketing copy, images) differs from 'Product' in Fulfillment (weight, dimensions, hazmat flags). Anti-corruption layers translate between them at integration points.

examples.title: Clean Architecture in a Payment Service
examples.description: A payment service's domain layer defines Payment (entity), Money (value object), and PaymentGateway (port). The application layer has ProcessPaymentUseCase. Dependencies must point inward — the domain never imports infrastructure
Bounded contexts prevent a single overloaded model from serving every use case
Aggregates enforce consistency boundaries — always modify through the root

Ubiquitous language bridges the gap between code and business stakeholders
lessons.whyItMatters: Systems outlive frameworks. The average web framework has a 5–10 year dominance cycle; business rules persist for decades. Clean Architecture and DDD protect your most valuable asset — business logic — from being entangled with replaceable infrastructure. In system design interviews and real projects, demonstrating domain-centric thinking signals senior-level engineering judgment.

lessons.summary: Event-driven architectures communicate via events. CQRS separates write and read models. Event sourcing stores state as an append-only event log. Powerful patterns — easy to overcomplicate.

sections.title: Event-driven integration

sections.title: Event sourcing
paragraphs: State = fold(events). Auditing and replay shine; schema evolution and snapshots become mandatory ops. Not every domain wants this complexity.

sections.title: When not to
paragraphs: CRUD with modest scale often needs a modular monolith first. Introduce events at real integration boundaries.

lessons.title: Hexagonal Architecture & Domain-Driven Design
lessons.summary: Hexagonal Architecture (Ports and Adapters) isolates business logic from infrastructure concerns through explicit boundaries. Domain-Driven Design provides the vocabulary and modeling tools—bounded contexts, aggregates, value objects, and ubiquitous language—to build software that accurately reflects complex business domains. Together they produce codebases that are testable, evolvable, and aligned with business reality.

sections.title: Hexagonal Architecture: Ports and Adapters
paragraphs: Hexagonal Architecture, coined by Alistair Cockburn in 2005, structures an application around a core domain that is completely ignorant of its surroundings. The core—containing business logic and domain model—communicates with the outside world only through ports: interfaces defined by the domain. Adapters implement those interfaces, translating between the domain's language and external technologies (HTTP, databases, message queues, file systems). The 'hexagon' shape is symbolic; the key insight is symmetric treatment of all external actors—a database adapter and an HTTP adapter are equally external.

Ports come in two directions. Driving ports (primary/inbound) are interfaces through which external actors drive the application—the application's API as far as the outside world is concerned. A REST adapter, a CLI adapter, and a Kafka consumer adapter all call driving ports. Driven ports (secondary/outbound) are interfaces the application uses to reach external systems—a repository interface, a notification service interface, an event publisher interface. The domain defines these interfaces; infrastructure implements them. This inversion of control is the dependency inversion principle applied architecturally.

The concrete benefit is testability. The domain core can be tested without any infrastructure: in-memory implementations of repositories, mock event publishers, and fake clocks replace real adapters. A fast unit test suite covering the full domain logic runs in milliseconds. Integration tests swap in real adapters to verify the adapters work correctly with real infrastructure. This separation collapses the feedback loop dramatically compared to architectures where business logic is entangled with SQL queries and HTTP calls.

Common implementation pitfalls undermine the architecture. Leaking domain model into adapters (returning JPA entities from repository ports) couples the domain to persistence technology. Anemic domain models—where domain objects are just DTOs and all logic lives in services—forfeit the testability benefit. Infrastructure dependencies in the domain package (importing Spring annotations, Hibernate annotations) couple the core to frameworks it shouldn't know about. The discipline of hexagonal architecture requires consistent enforcement of the dependency rule: domain depends on nothing external.
bullets: Application core: entities, value objects, domain services, use cases—zero infrastructure imports
Driving adapters: REST controllers, CLI, message consumers—translate external inputs to domain calls
Driven adapters: JPA repositories, Redis clients, email senders—implement domain-defined interfaces
The dependency rule: outer layers depend on inner; inner layers define interfaces the outer layers implement

sections.title: Domain-Driven Design: Modeling the Business
paragraphs: Domain-Driven Design (DDD) is a software development approach that centers domain complexity as the primary challenge and positions the domain model as the most important artifact. Eric Evans codified DDD in his 2003 Blue Book with a set of patterns for expressing complex business domains in code. DDD is not primarily about technical patterns—it's about collaboration between domain experts and developers to build a shared mental model expressed in code.

Ubiquitous language is the foundational practice: a shared vocabulary used consistently by developers, domain experts, product managers, and the code itself. The same words should appear in requirements, design discussions, variable names, class names, and database tables. When code names diverge from business names, the translation overhead causes bugs and miscommunication. Building ubiquitous language requires sustained collaboration—event storming workshops, regular domain expert interviews, and constant vigilance against technical terminology contaminating the domain model.

The strategic patterns—bounded contexts and context maps—address the reality that large domains cannot have a single consistent model. A product may mean different things to inventory (SKU, quantity, location), pricing (price tiers, discounts), and marketing (descriptions, images). Each context has its own model of Product that is correct within its boundaries. Context maps make explicit how bounded contexts integrate: shared kernel (shared model maintained by both teams), customer/supplier (downstream depends on upstream's model), anti-corruption layer (downstream translates upstream model to its own), or published language (upstream publishes a stable schema for all consumers).

Tactical DDD patterns—entities, value objects, aggregates, domain services, domain events, repositories, factories—provide the building blocks for the domain model. Entities have identity and lifecycle ('Customer' persists over time). Value objects are immutable descriptors with no identity ('Money', 'Address'). Aggregates group entities and value objects into consistency boundaries, enforcing invariants. The aggregate root is the only entry point—external code cannot directly manipulate internal entities, ensuring business rules are always enforced.
bullets: Bounded context: the boundary within which a model is consistent and terms have single meaning
Aggregate: a cluster of objects treated as a unit for data changes; root enforces all invariants
Value object: immutable, defined by attributes not identity; freely interchangeable (Money(10, USD) == Money(10, USD))
Repository: a collection-oriented interface for retrieving aggregates; hides persistence technology

sections.title: Aggregates: Designing Consistency Boundaries
paragraphs: Aggregates are the most consequential and most frequently misapplied tactical DDD pattern. An aggregate is a cluster of domain objects—entities and value objects—that must be changed together to maintain consistency. The aggregate root enforces all invariants: business rules that must hold after any state change. The rule is simple but profound: within a transaction, only one aggregate root should be modified. Cross-aggregate changes require eventual consistency via domain events.

Aggregate size is a critical design decision. Large aggregates (Order with all line items, shipping address, payment details, customer reference) are easy to model but create contention: any concurrent modification locks the entire aggregate. Small aggregates minimize contention and distribute load better, but push coordination to the application layer or domain events. The heuristic: start small. If two objects must be consistent within a single transaction, they belong in the same aggregate. If eventual consistency is acceptable, separate them.

Aggregate invariants deserve explicit representation. Rather than scattered null checks and conditional logic in service classes, invariants should be enforced by the aggregate root through private setters, factory methods, and domain methods. Example: Order.addLineItem() checks that the order is in DRAFT status, that the product exists and is available, and that the total doesn't exceed the customer's credit limit—all in one domain method that throws a domain exception on violation. This is the essence of a rich domain model.

References between aggregates should use identity, not direct object references. If OrderItem references Product, store the productId (a value object), not the Product entity. This enforces the aggregate boundary at the code level and makes it clear that loading a product requires a separate repository call. It also enables independent lifecycle management: products can be archived without cascading effects into every order that referenced them.
bullets: Only one aggregate per transaction—cross-aggregate coordination via eventual consistency
Aggregate boundaries emerge from business invariants, not data relationships
Reference aggregates by identity only—no direct object references across boundaries
Lock contention increases with aggregate size—prefer small aggregates with eventual consistency

sections.title: Bounded Contexts and Context Maps in Practice
paragraphs: Bounded contexts are the most strategic and least understood DDD concept. In practice, they define team and service ownership boundaries. Each bounded context is owned by one team, has its own domain model, ubiquitous language, and data store. This mapping—one team, one bounded context, one service or small group of services—is the organizational pattern behind successful microservices architecture. Conway's Law in reverse: design your context boundaries to match the team structure you want.

Context maps describe integration patterns between bounded contexts. The anticorruption layer (ACL) is the most important for maintaining model integrity: it translates the upstream context's model into the downstream context's own terms. When integrating with a legacy system or a third-party API, the ACL prevents the foreign model from leaking into your domain. The ACL might map between an external 'Account' (with 40 fields, most irrelevant) and your domain's 'Customer' (with 5 fields you actually need).

Shared kernel is the riskiest integration pattern—both contexts share a subset of the domain model maintained jointly. It's tempting (reduces duplication) but creates coupling: changes to the shared kernel require coordination between teams. Use it only for genuinely stable, shared concepts (like a common identity model across a platform) with explicit governance. In practice, most integration should use published language (stable schemas with explicit versioning) or customer/supplier (the upstream publishes what downstream needs, with explicit feedback loops).

Event Storming is the most effective technique for discovering bounded contexts. In a workshop with domain experts and developers, model the business process by placing domain events on a timeline, then clustering related events, commands, and policies. Natural seams emerge where events cross from one business capability to another—these seams suggest bounded context boundaries. The resulting context map is the foundation for service decomposition.
bullets: One team owns one bounded context—cross-context dependencies should be explicit and minimal
Anticorruption layer: translate between contexts, preventing foreign models from polluting yours
Published language: a stable, versioned integration schema used by multiple consuming contexts
Event Storming: collaborative domain discovery that reveals bounded context seams

sections.title: Combining Hexagonal Architecture with DDD
paragraphs: Hexagonal architecture and DDD complement each other naturally. DDD provides the content of the application core: aggregates, value objects, domain services, and domain events. Hexagonal architecture provides the structure that protects the core from infrastructure. Together they produce a layered structure: Domain layer (aggregates, value objects, domain events, repository interfaces), Application layer (use cases/application services that orchestrate domain objects), Infrastructure layer (adapter implementations: JPA repositories, REST controllers, Kafka producers).

The application service is the entry point to the use case. It loads aggregates via repository ports, invokes domain methods, persists changes via repository ports, and publishes domain events via event publisher ports. The application service is thin—it orchestrates, doesn't contain business logic. Business rules live in the domain. This separation means the application service can be tested with mock ports, and the domain can be tested without any infrastructure at all.

Modular monolith is an underappreciated architectural style that uses these patterns without the operational complexity of microservices. Bounded contexts become modules with strict visibility rules (each module's domain is package-private; only application services and ports are public). The modules communicate via well-defined application service calls or domain events, maintaining the same loose coupling as microservices but with in-process performance and deployment simplicity. Many teams successfully operate at scale on modular monoliths before the organizational or performance pressures that justify microservices extraction arise.
bullets: Domain layer: aggregates, value objects, domain events, repository/service interfaces only
Application layer: use cases, application services, orchestration—thin, no business logic
Infrastructure layer: adapter implementations—the only layer with framework/library imports
Modular monolith: DDD + hexagonal architecture without microservices operational complexity

sections.title: When DDD and Hexagonal Architecture Pay Off
paragraphs: DDD and hexagonal architecture have a real cost: more files, more abstraction, more indirection, and a steeper learning curve than a simple CRUD application. This investment pays off in domains with complex business rules that change frequently, with multiple delivery channels (REST API, CLI, message consumers) that share the same business logic, with large teams where clear boundaries prevent stepping on each other, and in contexts where long-term maintainability trumps initial delivery speed.

They're poor fits for simple CRUD applications, throwaway prototypes, data pipelines with no business logic, or small teams with shallow domain complexity. Applying full DDD to a blog or a simple inventory tracker is overengineering that creates complexity without benefit. The key diagnostic: if the domain has fewer than five meaningful business rules, if data mostly flows through without transformation, or if the team is fewer than four engineers, start simpler and introduce patterns as genuine complexity demands them.

Evolutionary design is the pragmatic path: start with a layered architecture, extract value objects when you notice primitive obsession, introduce aggregates when invariant violations become a source of bugs, draw explicit bounded context boundaries when teams begin to step on each other, and add anticorruption layers when integrating with legacy systems. DDD is a destination you approach incrementally, not a foundation you build completely before writing any features.
bullets: DDD pays off: complex rules that change, multiple delivery channels, large teams, long maintenance horizon
Skip DDD for: simple CRUD, prototypes, pipelines, small teams with shallow domain
Start simple: introduce DDD patterns incrementally as genuine complexity demands them
Architecture Fitness Functions: automated tests that enforce architectural boundaries (e.g., no infrastructure imports in domain package)

core.title: Hexagonal Architecture: Ports and Adapters
paragraphs: Hexagonal architecture structures an application around a domain core isolated from infrastructure via ports (interfaces) and adapters (implementations). Driving adapters call domain code through driving ports; driven adapters implement driven ports the domain calls.
The dependency rule is absolute: domain depends on nothing external. Framework annotations, database imports, and HTTP libraries never appear in the domain package.
The payoff is testability: in-memory adapters replace real infrastructure in unit tests, enabling a fast feedback loop over the full domain logic.
bullets: Ports: interfaces defined by the domain; adapters implement them
Driving ports: application's API (inbound); Driven ports: application's dependencies (outbound)
Dependency inversion: domain defines interfaces; infrastructure depends on domain, not vice versa

core.title: Domain-Driven Design: Strategic and Tactical Patterns
paragraphs: Strategic DDD: bounded contexts define consistent model boundaries; context maps describe integration patterns between them. Each bounded context owns its model and language.

Tactical DDD: entities (identity + lifecycle), value objects (immutable descriptors), aggregates (consistency boundary), repositories (collection interface), domain services (stateless domain logic), domain events (facts broadcast to other contexts).
Ubiquitous language bridges code and business: the same terms in requirements, conversations, variable names, and table names eliminate translation overhead and reduce bugs.
bullets: Bounded context = team boundary + model boundary + deployment boundary
Aggregate enforces invariants; only root is accessible from outside
Value objects: immutable, equality by value, no identity

core.title: Aggregates: Designing Consistency Boundaries
paragraphs: Aggregates group entities into consistency units. Only one aggregate is modified per transaction; cross-aggregate coordination uses domain events and eventual consistency.
Aggregate size matters: large aggregates reduce contention at the cost of concurrency. Start small; expand only when the invariant requires it.
Reference aggregates by identity only—no object references across boundaries. This enforces the boundary at the code level.
bullets: One transaction = one aggregate root mutation
Reference across aggregates by ID, not object reference
Rich domain model: logic inside aggregates, not in service classes

core.title: Combining Hexagonal Architecture with DDD
paragraphs: Domain layer contains aggregates, value objects, domain events, and interface definitions. Application layer contains thin use cases that orchestrate domain objects. Infrastructure layer contains adapter implementations with framework imports.
Modular monolith: apply hexagonal + DDD within a single deployable, with strict module visibility—same loose coupling as microservices without operational overhead.
Application services are thin: load aggregate, invoke domain method, persist, publish events. Business logic belongs in the domain, not the service.
bullets: Three layers: Domain, Application, Infrastructure
Application service = orchestration only; domain = business rules
Modular monolith as a valid long-term architecture, not just a stepping stone

deepDive.title: Event Storming and Bounded Context Discovery
paragraphs: Event Storming (Alberto Brandolini) is a lightweight workshop technique for rapid domain modeling. In Big Picture Event Storming, all stakeholders gather, and everyone writes domain events on orange sticky notes placed on a timeline. No structure is imposed initially—the goal is to surface all significant business events chaotically, then organize. After an hour of divergent thinking, patterns emerge: clusters of events that belong together, hotspots of confusion or disagreement, and 'pivotal events' that mark transitions between business capabilities.

Bounded context seams appear naturally at pivotal events: 'OrderPlaced' might be the hand-off between the Shopping bounded context and the Fulfillment bounded context. Each context has different actors, commands, policies, and terminology. The seams suggest team and service boundaries. Following Big Picture, Process-Level Event Storming zooms in on a specific bounded context, adding commands (blue), actors (yellow), policies (lilac), read models (green), and external systems to fully specify a business process.

Design-Level Event Storming maps the process model to aggregate design: group commands, events, and policies around aggregates; identify the aggregate roots; name the domain events. The output is a detailed spec that maps directly to code: aggregate classes, command methods, event types, and saga/process manager structures. Teams that practice Event Storming consistently report fewer requirement gaps and significantly faster alignment between business and engineering.
bullets: Orange: domain events; Blue: commands; Yellow: actors; Lilac: policies; Green: read models
Hotspot: a point of confusion or disagreement—prioritize for domain expert clarification
Pivotal event: marks a business transition; often a bounded context boundary
Event Storming output maps directly to aggregate, command, and event code structures

deepDive.title: Anti-Corruption Layer Implementation Patterns
paragraphs: The Anti-Corruption Layer (ACL) is the defensive shield that prevents an upstream context's model from infecting your domain. At its simplest, an ACL is a translation service: it accepts external representations (a third-party API response, a legacy database schema, an upstream context's integration event) and maps them to your domain's vocabulary. The ACL is part of the infrastructure layer—your domain defines what it needs through driven port interfaces; the ACL implements those interfaces and handles the translation.

Practical ACL patterns: Facade wraps a complex external API with a simplified interface aligned with your domain; Translator maps between external and internal models; Gateway handles authentication, retry, and error normalization before the domain ever sees external data. For high-change external integrations, an ACL with a schema version map (a lookup table of external model versions to internal translations) handles upstream schema evolution without domain model changes.

The cost of not having an ACL is subtle and cumulative. Each external type that leaks into the domain (a Stripe Charge object used as a domain Payment, a Salesforce Account used as a domain Customer) adds a dependency that makes the domain harder to test, harder to understand, and harder to change. When Stripe changes their API or Salesforce changes their data model, you're forced to change your domain model—a violation of the principle that domain logic should change only when business rules change, not when vendors change their APIs.
bullets: ACL is in the infrastructure layer—implements domain-defined driven ports
Facade, Translator, Gateway: common ACL structural patterns
Without ACL: vendor model leaks into domain, creating tight external coupling
ACL is especially critical when integrating legacy systems or third-party APIs

expert.title: DDD in Microservices: Team Topologies and Context Mapping at Scale
paragraphs: At scale, DDD bounded contexts and Team Topologies (Skelton & Pais) converge. Stream-aligned teams own end-to-end bounded contexts, including their own data stores and deployment pipelines. Platform teams provide enabling capabilities (observability, CI/CD, shared infrastructure) that stream-aligned teams consume through self-service interfaces—these platform interfaces are themselves bounded contexts with published languages. Enabling teams provide temporary expertise transfer; complicated-subsystem teams own contexts with unusual technical depth (ML models, real-time trading engines).

Context Map governance at scale requires explicit contracts between contexts. This means: schema registries for event-based integration, API versioning policies for HTTP-based integration, formal consumer-driven contract tests (Pact) to prevent breaking changes, and regular context mapping reviews as business domains evolve. The most common failure mode in large organizations is context boundary drift: teams add fields to shared schemas, teams develop direct database dependencies to other teams' stores, and the clean bounded context boundaries erode until the system is effectively a distributed monolith.

Strategic refactoring of legacy bounded contexts requires the Strangler Fig pattern: build new bounded contexts alongside the legacy, incrementally route traffic from legacy to new, and retire legacy pieces one by one. This requires a facade or proxy layer (the strangler fig's vine) that intercepts calls and routes based on the migration state. The bounded context map guides which legacy capabilities to strangle first (highest business value, highest coupling cost) and what integration patterns to use during the transition.

concepts: Hexagonal architecture: domain core + ports (interfaces) + adapters (infrastructure implementations)
Driving port: interface through which external actors call the domain (inbound API)
Driven port: interface the domain calls for external services (repository, notification, event publisher)
Bounded context: a business domain boundary within which a model is consistent and terms have single meaning
Ubiquitous language: shared vocabulary used identically in conversation, requirements, and code
Aggregate: consistency boundary; root enforces invariants; one aggregate per transaction
Value object: immutable, equality by attributes, no identity, freely replaceable
Entity: has identity, persists over lifecycle, can change state while maintaining identity
Domain event: an immutable fact emitted by an aggregate that other contexts can react to
Anti-corruption layer: a translation layer that prevents external models from polluting the domain
Context map: explicit description of integration patterns between bounded contexts
Event Storming: collaborative workshop technique for domain discovery and bounded context identification
practices: Enforce the dependency rule with architecture tests (ArchUnit, Dependency Cruiser) in CI
Name domain classes using ubiquitous language—if business calls it 'claim', don't name it 'transaction'
Make aggregates small by default; only expand when a business invariant demands co-location
Use value objects aggressively to eliminate primitive obsession (Money, EmailAddress, OrderId)
Create in-memory adapter implementations for all driven ports; use them as the default in unit tests
Conduct Event Storming workshops before designing new bounded contexts, not after
Document your context map explicitly—which contexts integrate how—and review it quarterly
pitfalls: Anemic domain model: putting all logic in services and treating domain objects as data bags defeats the purpose
Leaking infrastructure types into the domain (JPA annotations, Hibernate entities as domain objects)
God aggregates that model an entire entity relationship diagram as one aggregate, creating contention
Sharing a database between bounded contexts, coupling them despite separate domain models
Applying tactical DDD patterns without strategic patterns—aggregates without bounded contexts create a local-optima trap
Using 'microservices' as synonymous with 'bounded contexts'—service granularity and context boundaries are different concerns
Skipping the ubiquitous language discipline: code that uses different names from the business erodes model accuracy over time

examples.title: E-commerce Platform Bounded Context Map
examples.description: An e-commerce platform has distinct bounded contexts: Catalog (products, categories, search), Ordering (cart, order placement, order lifecycle), Fulfillment (warehouse, picking, shipping), Payments (payment processing, refunds), and Customer (account, preferences, address book). Each context owns its model of 'Product' and 'Customer'—the Fulfillment context needs SKU, weight, and location; the Catalog context needs description, images, and attributes. An anticorruption layer translates between contexts at integration points. Teams are aligned to contexts, enabling independent deployment.

examples.title: Insurance Claims Processing System
examples.description: An insurance domain uses full hexagonal architecture + DDD. The Claims bounded context has a Claim aggregate enforcing complex rules: a claim cannot be approved if the policy is lapsed, the claim amount cannot exceed policy coverage, and re-submissions require a 30-day waiting period. These invariants live in the aggregate, enforced by domain methods. The application core has zero framework imports—it's pure Java. REST adapters, event adapters, and JPA adapters are infrastructure. The result: 95% of business logic is covered by unit tests that run in 200ms.

examples.title: Modular Monolith at Shopify-Scale
examples.description: Shopify built their core platform as a modular Rails monolith with ~20 bounded contexts (Orders, Billing, Merchants, Products, Shipping) each with strict visibility rules enforced by Ruby's module system. This architecture supported >$5B GMV per day before they began extracting microservices for specific scaling bottlenecks. The modular monolith provided team independence, strong domain model coherence, and deployment simplicity. DDD + hexagonal architecture doesn't require microservices—it enables them when they're genuinely needed.

keyTakeaways: Hexagonal architecture's core value is testability: the domain can be fully tested without any infrastructure
DDD's core value is alignment: code that uses business language and enforces business rules explicitly
Aggregates are consistency boundaries, not data models—design them around invariants, not relationships
Bounded contexts should match team boundaries—Conway's Law is a tool, not just an observation
The anti-corruption layer is essential when integrating with external or legacy systems to preserve model integrity
Modular monolith using these patterns can scale further than many teams expect before requiring microservices
Event Storming is the most effective technique for discovering bounded context boundaries collaboratively
lessons.whyItMatters: Hexagonal architecture and DDD are the foundations of maintainable software at scale. Without them, complex business logic leaks into infrastructure layers, test coverage is impossible without spinning up databases, and teams step on each other because there are no clear ownership boundaries. With them, you can build systems where business rules are explicit and testable, where teams deploy independently, and where the code is comprehensible to both engineers and domain experts—a rare and valuable property in production systems.
reflectionQuestions: You're designing a new insurance claims system. Walk through how you'd use Event Storming to discover bounded contexts, then how you'd design the Claims aggregate with its key invariants.
Your team notices that the Order domain object is imported by 12 different services, each adding their own fields. How do you apply DDD to fix this model soup?
A teammate argues that hexagonal architecture is overengineering for a 5-person startup. Under what conditions would you agree, and when would you push back?
How does the anti-corruption layer pattern help when migrating from a legacy monolith that has a different data model and language than your new microservice?
numbersToKnow: Aggregate transaction scope: 1 aggregate per transaction is the strict rule; >1 aggregates = eventual consistency required
Modular monolith sweet spot: 5-50 engineers, 1-20 bounded contexts before microservices extraction pressure
Event Storming workshop: 4-8 hours for a Big Picture session covering a core business domain
Architecture test execution: ArchUnit rules run in <1 second in CI, enforcing boundary rules on every commit
Unit test speed target: domain unit tests should run in <500ms for the entire domain suite (no infrastructure)
Bounded context team size: 5-12 engineers per context (two-pizza team rule applies)
