lessons.title: Caching Fundamentals
lessons.summary: Caching is the most impactful performance optimization available to distributed systems engineers. A cache hit at 0.1ms versus a database query at 10ms is a 100x improvement. Understanding cache placement, eviction policies, invalidation, and consistency trade-offs separates engineers who apply caching effectively from those who create cache-related bugs.

sections.title: Why Caching Works: Locality and Skew
paragraphs: Caching is effective because of two universal properties of real-world workloads: temporal locality (recently accessed data is likely to be accessed again soon) and skew (a small fraction of data accounts for a large fraction of access). The Pareto principle applies broadly: 20% of content drives 80% of reads. For a news site, the top 1000 articles out of 10 million receive 90% of traffic. If those 1000 articles fit in cache, you serve 90% of reads from memory at sub-millisecond latency, reducing database load by 10x.

Cache hit rate is the fundamental metric. A hit rate of 90% means 90% of reads are served from cache; 10% miss and hit the database. If your database can handle 10,000 QPS and your cache delivers 90% hit rate, your effective capacity is 100,000 QPS. At 99% hit rate, it is 1,000,000 QPS—a 100x multiplier. This nonlinear relationship between hit rate and effective capacity is why investing in higher hit rates pays compounding dividends.

Caches are only beneficial when reads outweigh writes and when the same data is read multiple times after each write. For write-heavy workloads with low read amplification (each record is written once and read once), caching adds memory cost and coherence complexity without benefit. Always profile your read-to-write ratio and access frequency before adding a cache layer—cache the top-N most frequently accessed keys and nothing else.
bullets: Temporal locality + skew: small data subset accounts for large read fraction
Hit rate multiplier: 90% hit -> 10x capacity; 99% hit -> 100x capacity
Effective for: read-heavy, repeated reads of same data
Measure hit rate, miss rate, and eviction rate before tuning

sections.title: Cache Placement: Where to Cache
paragraphs: Client-side cache (browser cache, in-process application cache): fastest possible access with no network hop, but each client has its own copy. Changes to the underlying data are not propagated until TTL expires or the client explicitly invalidates. Appropriate for: user preferences, static config, reference data that changes rarely. The in-process application cache is powerful but creates consistency risks in multi-instance deployments—each instance's cache diverges after writes.

Distributed cache (Redis, Memcached): a shared external cache accessible to all application instances. Adds 0.5–2ms per lookup (network hop) but ensures all instances see the same cached values. Redis is the industry default: it supports rich data structures (strings, hashes, sorted sets, lists, streams), atomic operations, pub/sub, and optional persistence. Memcached is simpler and uses slightly less memory per key; prefer Redis unless you have a specific reason not to.

CDN edge cache (Cloudflare, Akamai, Fastly): caches responses geographically close to users. A CDN PoP (Point of Presence) in Frankfurt serves European users 150ms faster than an origin in US-East. CDNs primarily cache static assets (images, CSS, JS) and cacheable API responses. Cache-Control headers control CDN behavior. CDN placement is the highest-leverage cache for globally-distributed user-facing systems.
bullets: In-process: zero network hops; risk of divergence across instances; best for static reference data
Distributed (Redis): 0.5–2ms; shared across all instances; industry standard
CDN: nearest edge PoP; 150ms faster for global users; best for static and cacheable responses
L1/L2 pattern: in-process (L1) backed by Redis (L2) for ultra-low latency hot path

sections.title: Cache Strategies: Aside, Write-Through, Write-Behind
paragraphs: Cache-aside (lazy loading) is the most common pattern. The application checks the cache first; on a miss, it loads from the database, populates the cache, and returns the result. On write, the application writes to the database and invalidates (or updates) the cache. Cache-aside is resilient: a cache failure falls back gracefully to the database. The main trade-off is the thundering herd on cold start—after cache restart, every request misses until warm-up completes.

Write-through cache: every write goes to both the cache and the database synchronously. Reads are always served from cache (near 100% hit rate for recent data). No stale reads after a write. The cost: every write is slower (must write to both) and the cache fills with data that may never be read (write-once, read-never entries). Best for read-heavy workloads where read latency is paramount.

Write-behind (write-back): writes go to cache immediately, with asynchronous write to the database. Very low write latency; batching reduces database write amplification. Significant risk: if the cache node fails before the async flush, data is lost. Use only for data where some loss is acceptable (view counts, analytics counters) and always with persistence and replication enabled.
bullets: Cache-aside: app checks cache, misses go to DB, then populate cache; most common pattern
Write-through: writes go to cache + DB synchronously; consistent; slower writes
Write-behind: writes to cache, async flush to DB; risk of data loss on node failure
Read-through: cache fetches from DB on miss automatically; app only talks to cache

sections.title: Eviction Policies and TTLs
paragraphs: When a cache fills up, it must evict entries. LRU (Least Recently Used) evicts the entry that was accessed longest ago—effective for temporal locality. LFU (Least Frequently Used) evicts the entry accessed fewest times—better for skewed workloads where viral content should stay cached even if not recently accessed. Redis supports approximated LRU and LFU (allkeys-lfu policy). For most applications, LRU is correct; use LFU when access patterns are highly skewed.

TTL (Time to Live) is a mandatory expiry time on cached entries. Without TTL, stale data lives forever after updates. Setting TTL requires balancing two risks: too short and you evict entries before they are read again (unnecessary DB hits); too long and you serve stale data for extended periods. Rule of thumb: set TTL to the maximum staleness your application can tolerate. User preferences (acceptable 5 minutes stale): TTL=300s. Product prices (must be fresh for checkout): TTL=10–30s or use event-driven invalidation.

Cache stampede (thundering herd) occurs when a popular entry expires and thousands of concurrent requests simultaneously miss the cache, all querying the database at once. The database, designed for cache-assisted load, may be overwhelmed. Mitigations: probabilistic early expiration (re-fetch the entry slightly before TTL expires with probability proportional to remaining TTL), mutex-based locking (only one request rebuilds the entry; others wait or serve stale), and jitter in TTL values (spread expiration times to avoid synchronized stampedes).
bullets: LRU: evict least recently used; good for temporal locality
LFU: evict least frequently used; good for skewed access patterns
TTL = maximum acceptable staleness; set mandatory TTL on every cache entry
Stampede prevention: probabilistic early expiry, mutex lock on rebuild, jitter in TTL

sections.title: Cache Invalidation: The Hardest Problem
paragraphs: Phil Karlton's quip holds: 'There are only two hard things in Computer Science: cache invalidation and naming things.' When underlying data changes, cached versions must be invalidated or updated. The simplest approach is TTL-based expiry: accept that the cache may serve up to TTL-seconds of stale data. For most use cases this is sufficient. When you need fresher data, you must implement active invalidation.

Event-driven invalidation: when a write occurs, publish an invalidation event (to Redis pub/sub, Kafka, or an internal event bus) and all cache instances that hold the affected key invalidate it. This requires knowing which cache keys correspond to which data entities. The key design challenge: a single database write may affect many cache keys. Updating a user's profile might invalidate the user object cache, any feed caches that display this user's name, and any search result caches containing this user. Mapping writes to affected cache keys is the core complexity of invalidation systems.

Cache versioning (namespace invalidation): add a version number to all cache keys for a given entity. user:v3:12345 instead of user:12345. To invalidate all cached data for a user, increment the version counter. The old keys will naturally expire via TTL (they just become orphaned with the wrong version prefix). This avoids expensive enumeration of cache keys to invalidate and works well for group invalidation (invalidate all entries in a namespace by incrementing the namespace version).
bullets: TTL-based: accept up to N seconds of staleness; simple; sufficient for most use cases
Active invalidation: publish event on write; subscribers delete affected keys
Versioned keys: user:v3:12345; increment version to atomically orphan all old keys
Mapping challenge: one DB write may affect many cache keys; design this mapping explicitly

core.title: Why Caching Works
paragraphs: Temporal locality and access skew make caching effective: the top 20% of data drives 80% of reads. 90% hit rate gives 10x capacity multiplier; 99% gives 100x.
Profile read-to-write ratio and access frequency before adding cache. Caching write-heavy data with low read amplification adds complexity without benefit.
Measure: hit rate, miss rate, eviction rate. Alert when hit rate drops below threshold.

core.title: Cache Strategies
paragraphs: Cache-aside: check cache on read, miss -> fetch DB -> populate; write -> DB + invalidate cache. Most common. Falls back gracefully on cache failure.
Write-through: writes go to cache and DB synchronously. No stale reads; slower writes.
TTL is mandatory on every entry. Set TTL to maximum acceptable staleness. Use jitter to spread expiry times and prevent stampedes.

core.title: Cache Invalidation
paragraphs: TTL-based expiry is the simplest and usually sufficient. For fresher data, use event-driven invalidation via Redis pub/sub or Kafka.
Versioned keys (user:v3:12345) enable atomic group invalidation by incrementing the version counter.
Map each write to its affected cache keys explicitly; untracked dependencies cause silent stale data bugs.

deepDive.title: Redis Deep Dive: Data Structures and Persistence
paragraphs: Redis is not just a simple key-value store. Sorted sets (ZADD/ZRANGE) implement leaderboards and rate-limiting windows efficiently. HyperLogLog provides O(1)-space cardinality estimation. Streams (XADD/XREAD) implement event sourcing and message queues. BITFIELD supports compact bit-packing for feature flags and counters. Using the right Redis data structure reduces memory usage by 2–10x compared to naively serializing everything as JSON strings.

Redis persistence: RDB snapshots create point-in-time backups at configurable intervals (every N seconds if M keys changed). AOF (Append-Only File) logs every write operation; replaying the AOF reconstructs the dataset. AOF with appendfsync=everysec provides at-most-1-second data loss with minimal performance impact. For caching use cases, disable persistence (save '') for maximum throughput; for primary data store use cases, enable AOF. Redis Sentinel provides automatic failover for standalone deployments; Redis Cluster provides horizontal sharding.

Redis Cluster partitions keys across 16384 hash slots assigned to nodes. Keys are assigned to a slot by CRC16(key) mod 16384. Hash tags ({user}:profile and {user}:permissions map to the same slot if key contains {user}) allow related keys to be colocated, enabling atomic MULTI/EXEC transactions across those keys. Avoid hot slots (all traffic going to one shard) by designing key schemas with entropy.
bullets: Sorted sets: O(log n) rank operations; perfect for leaderboards and sliding-window rate limits
HyperLogLog: estimate cardinality with 12KB of memory; <1% error
RDB vs AOF: RDB for compact snapshots; AOF for durability; use both in production
Redis Cluster: 16384 hash slots; hash tags colocate related keys to the same shard

deepDive.title: Cache Coherence in Distributed Systems
paragraphs: In a multi-instance deployment, each application instance may have an in-process (L1) cache. When instance A updates a record and invalidates its L1 cache, instances B and C still hold the stale value. Solutions: (1) Skip in-process cache entirely; use only the distributed Redis cache (adds 1–2ms but all instances converge quickly). (2) Broadcast invalidation messages via Redis pub/sub; each instance subscribes and deletes its local copy. (3) Short TTL (1–5 seconds) on in-process cache; accept brief window of inconsistency.

Read-your-own-writes consistency is a common requirement: after a user updates their profile, the next page load should show the updated value. With async replication to Redis replicas, the write may not yet be visible if the read hits a replica. Solutions: route writes to Redis primary and reads for the writing user to the same primary (sticky primary), or add a small delay before redirecting to the profile page, or implement read-your-own-writes by consulting a local version vector. This edge case trips up many caching implementations.

expert.title: Expert: Hot Key Problem and Cache Sharding
paragraphs: A viral post, popular product, or celebrity profile creates a hot key: millions of requests all targeting the same Redis key per second. A single Redis instance handles ~100K simple ops/second; a hot key generating 500K req/s overwhelms it. Mitigations: local replication (read the value once and cache locally for a very short TTL, 10–50ms, in the application tier—this caps Redis load at application-tier instance count × 1 request per 50ms per key), key spreading (append a random suffix hot_key:rand(0,99) and query a random shard, requiring reads to query all 100 shards for writes—acceptable for read-heavy hot keys), and Redis replica routing (direct all reads for hot keys to dedicated replicas).

Cache-on-write for social media fan-out: when a celebrity with 10M followers posts a tweet, eagerly populating 10M follower caches synchronously is too slow. Twitter's solution: use a hybrid fan-out model. Celebrities above a follower threshold write to a single timeline object; each follower's feed query fetches and merges this object on read. Users below the threshold use push fan-out (populate each follower's cache). This avoids the write amplification of pure push fan-out while still delivering good feed read latency.

concepts: Cache hit rate: fraction of reads served from cache; determines effective capacity multiplier
Temporal locality: recently accessed data likely to be accessed again; justifies caching
Cache-aside: application-managed cache; most common pattern; resilient to cache failure
Write-through: synchronous write to cache and DB; consistent; slower writes
Write-behind: async flush from cache to DB; low write latency; risk of data loss
LRU (Least Recently Used): evict least recently accessed entry; best for temporal locality
LFU (Least Frequently Used): evict least frequently accessed; best for skewed workloads
TTL (Time to Live): mandatory expiry; set to maximum acceptable staleness
Cache stampede: expired popular key causes thundering herd to database
Cache versioning: versioned keys (user:v3:key) enable atomic group invalidation
practices: Profile access patterns before adding cache—identify top-N most accessed keys
Set mandatory TTL on every cache entry; never store without expiry
Add jitter to TTL values to prevent synchronized expiration and stampedes
Use Redis Cluster or consistent hashing to avoid hot key problems at scale
Implement probabilistic early expiration for critical high-traffic keys to prevent stampedes
Monitor hit rate; alert when it drops below target threshold (typically 85–95%)
Use read-your-own-writes routing (write to primary, read from primary for the writing user)
pitfalls: Forgetting TTL on cache entries—stale data lives forever after underlying data changes
Storing everything in cache regardless of access frequency—wasting memory on cold data
Cache stampede: popular entry expires, thousands of concurrent misses overwhelm the database
Hot key: viral content generates more ops/second than a single Redis instance can handle
In-process cache divergence: instances hold different stale values; invalidation requires broadcast
Cache as primary store: using cache without a persistent backing store risks data loss on restart

examples.title: Facebook's Memcached at Scale
examples.description: Facebook famously ran the world's largest Memcached deployment to serve social graph queries. Each user profile read hit Memcached first; misses populated the cache from MySQL. Lease tokens solved the thundering herd problem: the first miss for an expired key gets a lease token and fetches from DB; subsequent misses for the same key wait for the token holder to repopulate. This one mechanism eliminated most cache stampede incidents.

examples.title: Redis Rate Limiting with Sorted Sets
examples.description: API rate limiting using Redis sorted sets implements a sliding window counter: each request adds (timestamp, request_id) to a sorted set keyed by user_id; remove entries older than the window (60 seconds); count remaining entries; allow if below limit. This is atomic, accurate, and handles distributed rate limiting across any number of API servers without server-side coordination.

keyTakeaways: 90% cache hit rate = 10x capacity multiplier; 99% = 100x; invest in higher hit rates
Cache-aside is the most common and resilient pattern; use it as your default
TTL is mandatory on every cache entry; set it to maximum acceptable staleness
Cache invalidation is the hard problem; prefer TTL + event-driven invalidation over complex dependency tracking
Hot keys require special treatment: local short-TTL caching or key spreading
Redis sorted sets, HyperLogLog, and streams enable patterns beyond simple key-value caching
lessons.whyItMatters: Caching appears in virtually every system design interview and every high-performance production system. The ability to reason about where to cache (in-process vs. distributed vs. CDN), how to invalidate (TTL vs. event-driven), and how to handle edge cases (stampede, hot keys, stale reads) demonstrates mastery of one of the highest-leverage techniques in distributed systems.
reflectionQuestions: Your API hit rate dropped from 95% to 70% after a deployment. What might have caused this, and how do you investigate?
Design a caching strategy for a product page that shows real-time inventory (must be fresh) and product description (can be stale for 1 hour).
A popular Redis key is receiving 500K requests/second, overwhelming a single shard. What are your options?
When would you choose write-through over cache-aside, and what consistency guarantees does each provide?
numbersToKnow: Redis in-process latency: 0.1–0.3ms; network round-trip to Redis: 0.5–2ms
Redis throughput: 100K–1M ops/sec per instance depending on operation type
Memcached max value size: 1MB; Redis max value size: 512MB
Redis Cluster: up to 1000 nodes; 16384 hash slots distributed across nodes
In-process LRU cache (Caffeine/Guava): sub-microsecond; holds up to available heap

  Cache -->|hit: return value| App

lessons.title: Content Delivery Networks
lessons.summary: A CDN (Content Delivery Network) is a globally distributed network of edge servers that cache and serve content close to end users, reducing latency, offloading origin bandwidth, and improving availability. CDNs are non-negotiable infrastructure for any globally-accessed web service, handling static assets, dynamic API responses, video streaming, and DDoS mitigation.

sections.title: How CDNs Work: Anycast, PoPs, and Cache Hierarchies
paragraphs: A CDN operator (Cloudflare, Akamai, Fastly, AWS CloudFront) maintains hundreds to thousands of Points of Presence (PoPs) globally—data centers near major population centers. When a user requests your website, Anycast DNS routing directs them to the nearest PoP. Instead of your request crossing the Atlantic to reach a US-East origin server (100–300ms round-trip), it hits a Frankfurt PoP 20ms away. The PoP checks its local cache; on a hit, it responds immediately. On a miss, it fetches from origin, caches the response, and returns it.

CDNs use a hierarchical cache architecture. Edge nodes (closest to users) are backed by regional shield nodes, which are backed by origin. A cache miss at the edge first checks the regional shield (another cache layer), reducing direct origin hits. This hierarchy dramatically reduces origin load: even with a 70% edge hit rate, the shield may serve 80% of the remaining misses, reducing origin traffic by 94%. Shield caching is particularly important for large-object delivery (video, large file downloads) where repeated origin fetches would be expensive.

Anycast works by advertising the same IP address from multiple PoPs via BGP. When a user sends a packet to that IP, the internet's routing protocol naturally directs it to the topologically nearest PoP. This is different from DNS-based load balancing (which requires TTL expiry to redirect) and provides true per-packet routing. Anycast is also the mechanism behind DDoS mitigation: attack traffic from thousands of sources is absorbed across hundreds of PoPs, each handling a fraction of the total attack volume rather than concentrating it at a single origin.
bullets: PoPs: hundreds to thousands of globally distributed edge data centers
Anycast DNS: routes user to nearest PoP via BGP topology; per-packet routing
Cache hierarchy: edge -> regional shield -> origin; shield cuts origin traffic 80–90%
DDoS mitigation: attack traffic distributed across all PoPs rather than concentrated at origin

sections.title: Cache-Control Headers: Directing CDN Behavior
paragraphs: Cache-Control headers are the primary interface between your application and CDN caching behavior. The key directives: max-age=N tells the browser to cache for N seconds. s-maxage=N tells CDNs (shared caches) to cache for N seconds, overriding max-age. public indicates the response may be cached by any cache (CDN, proxy). private indicates the response is user-specific and must not be cached by shared caches—CDNs honor this and do not cache the response. no-cache means validate with origin before serving (not 'do not cache'; use no-store for truly no caching).

Combining s-maxage and stale-while-revalidate creates a powerful pattern: Cache-Control: s-maxage=300, stale-while-revalidate=60. The CDN serves the cached response for 300 seconds. After expiry, for the next 60 seconds it serves the stale response while asynchronously refreshing from origin in the background. The user never sees a slow cache-miss response; they get immediate responses, with staleness bounded at 360 seconds. This is ideal for content that changes periodically but where brief staleness is tolerable.

Surrogate keys (also called cache tags) are a CDN feature for targeted bulk invalidation. Tag responses with headers like Surrogate-Key: product-123 or Cache-Tag: category-electronics. When a product is updated, issue an API call to invalidate all responses tagged product-123—potentially thousands of cached URLs purged with one API call. Fastly, Cloudflare, and Varnish all support surrogate key invalidation. Without this, purging all cached pages for a product requires knowing and enumerating every URL that shows that product.
bullets: s-maxage: CDN-specific max age; overrides max-age for shared caches
stale-while-revalidate: serve stale while refreshing in background; zero-latency on expiry
private: CDN must not cache; use for user-specific responses
Surrogate keys / cache tags: tag responses; bulk invalidate by tag with one API call

sections.title: What to Cache: Static vs Dynamic Content
paragraphs: Static assets (JS, CSS, images, fonts, videos) are the ideal CDN candidates: they are identical for all users, rarely change, and can be cached for hours to years. Use content-addressed URLs (include a hash of the file content in the URL: /main.a3f9c2.js) with Cache-Control: max-age=31536000, immutable. When you deploy new code, the URL changes, forcing a cache miss and serving the new file. Old URLs continue to be served from CDN cache until TTL expires—a natural, safe rollout mechanism.

Dynamic API responses can also be cached at the CDN if they are shared across users. 'Top 10 products this week,' 'current weather for London,' and 'homepage content' are the same for every user requesting them and change infrequently. Cache these at the CDN with appropriate TTLs. The cache key must exclude user-specific headers (cookies, Authorization headers) to avoid caching personalized responses. CDNs allow cache key configuration to include/exclude specific headers and query parameters.

User-specific content must not be cached by the CDN. User dashboards, shopping carts, and authenticated API responses that differ per user: either serve these from origin (CDN passes through) or use edge-side includes (ESIs) to assemble the page at the CDN from a mix of cached and uncached fragments. Edge computing (Cloudflare Workers, Fastly Compute@Edge) enables user-specific logic at the CDN edge—authentication, A/B testing, personalization—without round-tripping to origin.
bullets: Static assets: content-addressed URLs + immutable TTL; ideal CDN use case
Public dynamic responses: same for all users; cache with TTL; exclude auth headers from cache key
Private responses: set Cache-Control: private; CDN passes through to origin
Edge computing (Cloudflare Workers): run auth/personalization logic at CDN without origin round-trip

sections.title: CDN Invalidation and Cache Purge Strategies
paragraphs: CDN cache purge: when you deploy a critical bug fix or update content, waiting for TTL expiry is unacceptable. All major CDNs provide an API to purge cached objects by URL, path pattern, or surrogate key. Cloudflare's purge API clears a URL from all PoPs within 150ms globally. The challenge: purge by URL requires knowing every cached URL—for parameterized URLs (search results, product pages with query parameters), the number of cached variants can be enormous. Surrogate keys solve this by grouping related URLs under a single tag.

Versioned deployments are the alternative to cache purging. By using content-addressed URLs for all assets, there is nothing to purge—the new version has a new URL, and old users on the old version continue working until they reload (at which point they get the new URL). This zero-invalidation approach requires your build tooling to generate hashed URLs (webpack, Vite, and other modern bundlers do this automatically). For CDN-cached HTML pages, a short TTL (60–300 seconds) combined with stale-while-revalidate provides a good balance.

Instant purge is not always instant. Even 150ms global propagation means thousands of requests in-flight during propagation. Design your application to tolerate brief periods of mixed old/new content after a purge. Semantic versioning in API responses (include a version field) allows clients to detect and handle version mismatches gracefully.
bullets: CDN purge API: clears URL/path/tag from all PoPs within seconds
Surrogate keys: group related URLs under a tag; bulk purge with one API call
Content-addressed URLs: new deploy = new URL; no purge needed; best practice for static assets
Design for brief mixed-version windows; purge is not instantaneous at all PoPs

sections.title: CDN for Video, Security, and Advanced Use Cases
paragraphs: Video streaming over CDN uses HTTP streaming protocols (HLS, MPEG-DASH). Video is segmented into 2–10 second chunks; each chunk is a separate cacheable HTTP object. The CDN caches each segment independently; different users watching the same video at different points are served from cache. For live streaming, the latest segments may not be cached (or cached with TTL=0), requiring origin fetches, while older segments of the same livestream are heavily cached. At Netflix and YouTube scale, CDN is the entire delivery backbone, with ISPs hosting CDN nodes for maximum proximity.

CDN as security perimeter: CDNs terminate user connections at the edge, keeping your origin's IP secret. Without a CDN, a DDoS attacker targeting your origin IP can bypass your CDN entirely. With a CDN, your origin only accepts connections from CDN IP ranges (enforced by firewall rules). The CDN absorbs DDoS traffic distributed across its PoPs, while your origin remains unreachable from the public internet. Cloudflare Spectrum, Akamai Prolexic, and similar products extend this model to protect non-HTTP TCP/UDP services.

Edge functions (Cloudflare Workers, Lambda@Edge, Fastly Compute) allow running arbitrary code at CDN PoPs. Use cases: A/B testing (split traffic at the edge without origin involvement), authentication (validate JWT at edge, reject unauthenticated requests before they reach origin), URL rewriting and redirects, geographic content customization, and request coalescing. The key constraint: edge functions must run in a few milliseconds; they have limited CPU and memory. For complex logic, use edge functions for fast path decisions and origin for complex processing.
bullets: HLS/DASH: video segmented into cacheable chunks; each segment cached independently
Security: CDN IP allowlist at origin prevents origin IP exposure; absorbs DDoS
Edge functions: run auth, A/B testing, redirects at CDN; must complete in <10ms
Origin shield: single PoP designated as the CDN-to-origin gateway; reduces origin fan-out

core.title: CDN Fundamentals
paragraphs: CDNs cache content at globally distributed PoPs near users. Anycast DNS routes requests to nearest PoP. Cache hits serve in 20ms vs 300ms round-trip to origin.
Cache hierarchy: edge -> regional shield -> origin. Shield absorbs 80–90% of edge misses, dramatically reducing origin load.
Cache-Control headers direct behavior: s-maxage for CDN TTL, private to prevent CDN caching, stale-while-revalidate for zero-latency background refresh.

core.title: What to Cache and How to Invalidate
paragraphs: Static assets: content-addressed URLs (hashed filename) + max-age=31536000 immutable. No purge needed; new deploy = new URL.
Public dynamic responses: cache with TTL; exclude auth/session headers from cache key.
Surrogate keys: tag responses; bulk invalidate by tag. Use for product/article updates affecting many cached URLs.

core.title: CDN Security
paragraphs: CDN terminates user connections at edge; origin IP hidden behind CDN. Restrict origin to CDN IP ranges via firewall.
DDoS absorption: attack traffic distributed across hundreds of PoPs; each handles a fraction.
Edge functions: run JWT validation, redirects, A/B testing at edge without origin round-trip.

deepDive.title: CDN Architecture for Dynamic Sites
paragraphs: Full-site delivery CDN (Cloudflare full-proxy) routes all traffic through the CDN, including dynamic requests. The CDN terminates TLS, routes to origin via optimized backbone, and applies WAF rules. Even uncacheable dynamic requests benefit: Cloudflare's private backbone between PoP and origin is faster than the public internet (Argo Smart Routing reports 30–60% latency improvement for dynamic content via backbone routing versus public internet routing).

API acceleration: CDNs can cache API responses with fine-grained cache key control. Cache by URL path + specific query parameters, excluding user identity parameters. Vary headers specify which request headers affect caching: Vary: Accept-Language causes separate caches per language. Excessive Vary headers fragment the cache and reduce hit rate. Normalize headers at the edge (lowercase Accept-Language value, map regional variants to canonical codes) before using them as cache dimensions.

Real-time cache telemetry: CDNs expose cache metrics via API (hit rate, bytes transferred, requests by cache status: HIT, MISS, STALE, REVALIDATING, EXPIRED). Monitor hit rate per URL pattern; a drop in hit rate for a critical URL often indicates a misconfigured Cache-Control header or an inadvertent cache-busting header added to responses.

deepDive.title: CDN Cost Optimization
paragraphs: CDN pricing models vary: Cloudflare charges flat-rate per plan tier (unlimited bandwidth for most plans); Akamai and AWS CloudFront charge per GB transferred and per 10K HTTP requests. For high-bandwidth workloads (video, large file distribution), flat-rate CDN pricing is dramatically cheaper. For low-bandwidth, high-request-count workloads (API acceleration), per-GB pricing is more economical.

Cache warming: after a cache purge or new PoP addition, the cache is cold and traffic flows to origin until the cache warms up. Proactive cache warming (pre-fetching popular URLs to new PoP caches before serving live traffic) reduces origin load spikes. For large static assets, use CDN pre-positioning: push content to CDN PoPs before launch (CDN vendors offer this via API). For critical events (product launches, sports finals), coordinate with your CDN vendor—they can pre-stage content.

expert.title: Expert: Multi-CDN Strategies
paragraphs: Large-scale platforms (Netflix, Apple, Facebook) run multi-CDN: routing traffic across multiple CDN providers simultaneously. Benefits: resilience (CDN outage redirects to another provider), performance (route each user to whichever CDN PoP has lower latency for them at that moment), and negotiating leverage (competition keeps pricing competitive). Real-time CDN selection uses performance probing (each provider is probed periodically; the fastest one for a given user gets traffic) or steering based on CDN telemetry APIs.

CDN failover: a CDN provider outage (Fastly June 2021, Cloudflare July 2020) can take down thousands of customers simultaneously. Multi-CDN with DNS-based or anycast-based failover provides resilience. The challenge is cache state: if CDN A has a warmed cache and CDN B doesn't, failing over to CDN B causes a cold cache and origin overload. Solutions: origin shield with pre-warmed cache shared between CDN providers, or accept temporary origin overload during failover with origin auto-scaling.

concepts: CDN PoP (Point of Presence): edge data center near users; serves cached content
Anycast: same IP advertised from multiple PoPs; BGP routes to nearest
Cache-Control: s-maxage, private, stale-while-revalidate, immutable directives
Content-addressed URLs: hash of file content in URL; enables immutable caching
Surrogate keys (cache tags): tag responses for targeted bulk invalidation
Origin shield: designated CDN-to-origin gateway; prevents fan-out to origin
Edge functions (Workers): code running at CDN PoP; auth, A/B testing, redirects
Vary header: specifies which request headers create separate cache entries
Multi-CDN: routing across multiple CDN providers for resilience and performance
Cache warming: proactively pre-fetching content to cold caches before serving live traffic
practices: Use content-addressed URLs for all static assets; enables immutable long TTLs
Set s-maxage on public API responses; set Cache-Control: private on user-specific responses
Implement surrogate keys on all cacheable content types for targeted invalidation
Restrict origin to CDN IP ranges; never expose origin IP publicly
Monitor CDN hit rate per path; alert on drops that indicate misconfigured Cache-Control
Use stale-while-revalidate for content where brief staleness is acceptable; eliminates miss latency
Pre-warm caches before major launches; coordinate with CDN vendor for traffic spikes
pitfalls: Caching user-specific responses at the CDN by not setting Cache-Control: private—leaks user data
Forgetting to exclude Authorization or Cookie headers from CDN cache key—serves one user's data to another
Excessive Vary headers fragment the cache; every unique header value creates a separate cache entry
No origin IP protection—attackers can bypass CDN by targeting the origin IP directly
Assuming CDN purge is instant everywhere—design for brief mixed-version windows post-purge
Cold cache overload: CDN outage or mass purge causes all traffic to hit origin simultaneously

examples.title: Netflix's CDN: Open Connect
examples.description: Netflix operates Open Connect, its own CDN, by deploying proprietary appliances inside ISPs worldwide. These appliances store the most popular Netflix titles for that ISP's subscriber base, pre-positioned during off-peak hours. During peak evening viewing, 95%+ of Netflix traffic is served from these ISP-embedded appliances, never touching Netflix's AWS infrastructure. This radical proximity to end users provides consistent low-latency streaming while dramatically reducing Netflix's transit costs.

examples.title: Cloudflare Blocking DDoS for Krebs on Security
examples.description: In 2016, security journalist Brian Krebs's website was targeted by a 620 Gbps DDoS attack—then the largest recorded. Cloudflare's global network distributed the attack traffic across its PoPs, absorbing it without origin disruption. Each PoP received a fraction of the total attack volume, within its capacity. This demonstrated that Anycast DDoS absorption scales with PoP count and capacity, making it effectively unbounded for distributed volumetric attacks.

keyTakeaways: CDN Anycast routes users to the nearest PoP; cache hits serve at 20ms vs 300ms origin round-trip
s-maxage controls CDN TTL; stale-while-revalidate enables zero-latency background refresh
Content-addressed URLs with immutable TTL are the best practice for static assets—zero purge complexity
Surrogate keys enable bulk invalidation by tag, solving the many-URL-per-entity purge problem
CDN hides origin IP; restrict origin to CDN IP ranges for security and DDoS protection
Edge functions at the CDN enable auth, redirects, and A/B testing without origin round-trips
lessons.whyItMatters: CDN is table-stakes infrastructure for any user-facing web service. Without it, global users experience unacceptable latency, origin bandwidth is exhausted by repeated static file delivery, and DDoS attacks can take down the service. Understanding how to configure Cache-Control headers, design cacheable URL structures, and implement invalidation strategies is a practical skill every infrastructure engineer needs.

Cloudflare purge propagation: ~150ms globally
CloudFront pricing: $0.0085/GB (Americas/Europe), $0.012/GB (Asia); $0.0075/10K HTTP requests
CDN DDoS capacity: Cloudflare >320 Tbps, Akamai >325 Tbps network capacity
Typical CDN offload for media sites: 70–95% of bytes; 50–90% of requests

lessons.title: Capacity Planning
lessons.summary: Capacity Planning is a core topic in modern system design. This lesson builds a first-principles model around resource budgets and unit economics, then connects that model to capacity, failure modes, and operational practice so you can use it in real architectures.

sections.title: What Capacity Planning is solving
paragraphs: Capacity Planning exists because naive designs around resource budgets and unit economics break under scale, partial failure, or changing requirements. Before choosing tools, name the problem: which resource is scarce, which invariant must hold, and which user-visible failures are unacceptable.
In interviews and production reviews, strong answers start with constraints (QPS, data size, latency budget, consistency needs) and only then map Capacity Planning onto those constraints.

A useful mental model separates the control plane (how you configure and observe Capacity Planning) from the data plane (the per-request/per-event path). Confusing the two leads to architectures that look neat and operate poorly.

sections.title: Core mechanics
paragraphs: Mechanically, Capacity Planning involves a small set of moving parts: inputs, state, an algorithm or protocol, and outputs/side effects. Draw those parts explicitly. If state is replicated, write down the replication/consistency rule. If work is asynchronous, write down delivery semantics.

Performance characteristics usually come from amplification (how much internal work per external request), locality (whether work stays on one node), and contention (locks, hot keys, leader bottlenecks).

Correctness characteristics usually come from failure handling: retries, timeouts, idempotency, and what clients observe during failover. If you cannot explain the failure story, you do not yet understand Capacity Planning.
bullets: Inputs → state/protocol → outputs/side effects
Name consistency and delivery guarantees
Identify the bottleneck resource early

sections.title: Designing with it
paragraphs: When incorporating Capacity Planning into a system, decide the API boundary first: what does a client call, what can fail, and what is retried. Keep the happy path boring and push complexity into well-tested libraries or platform components.

Capacity plan with numbers: estimate peak load, working set, and headroom. Convert that into shard counts, cache sizes, thread/connection pools, or GPU/memory budgets as relevant to Capacity Planning.
Prefer reversible rollout: feature flags, dual-running, shadow traffic, and clear dashboards. New uses of Capacity Planning should be observable on day one.

sections.title: Operations and failure modes
paragraphs: Operate Capacity Planning with SLIs that match user pain (availability, latency, lag, error rate, cost). Alert on burn rates and queue/lag growth, not only host CPU.
Common failures include overload without admission control, retry amplification, silent staleness, schema mismatches, and dependency brownouts. Write a runbook for the top three.
Chaos and game days should include slow dependencies and network delay, not only hard kills. Capacity Planning often fails in the gray area.

sections.title: What FinOps & Cost Optimization is solving

sections.title: Core mechanics

lessons.title: Change Data Capture
lessons.summary: CDC streams database changes from WAL/binlog into downstream systems without dual writes. It powers caches, search indexes, analytics, and event-driven integrations — with ordering, schema, and backfill challenges.

sections.title: Why CDC beats dual writes
paragraphs: Application dual writes to DB and queue fail partially. CDC treats the database transaction log as the source of truth and emits ordered change events.
Debezium, AWS DMS, and native logical decoding plug into WAL/binlog/oplog. Consumers rebuild read models asynchronously.

sections.title: Semantics and ordering
paragraphs: Events usually carry before/after images, transaction ids, and log coordinates (LSN). Ordering is per partition/key — not global across shards.
Deletes, schema changes, and toasted/large values need explicit handling. Snapshot + streaming backfill must be coordinated to avoid gaps/duplicates.

sections.title: Operational concerns
paragraphs: Log retention must exceed consumer lag. Long downtime means re-snapshot. Privileges for replication slots are sensitive.
Downstream must be idempotent; at-least-once is the common delivery mode.

sections.title: Design patterns
paragraphs: Use CDC for search indexing, cache hydration, and analytics lakes. Avoid using CDC as a hidden microservice choreography bus without schema contracts.

lessons.title: Indexes, Replication & Sharding
lessons.summary: Indexes accelerate queries at the cost of write overhead and storage. Replication provides availability, fault tolerance, and read scaling. Sharding partitions data across nodes for write scaling — but introduces cross-shard query complexity and hot spot risk. These three mechanisms are the primary toolkit for scaling databases.

sections.title: Indexes: How Queries Find Data Fast
paragraphs: Without an index, finding a row by email requires a full table scan — O(n) pages read. A B+ tree index on email reduces this to O(log n) — typically 3–4 page reads for billions of rows. Indexes are separate data structures (usually B+ trees) storing indexed columns plus a pointer to the row (primary key or physical location).

Composite indexes (a, b, c) support queries filtering on prefix columns — useful for WHERE a = ? AND b = ? but not WHERE b = ? alone (left-prefix rule). Column order matters: put equality filters first, range filters last.

Covering index: the index contains all columns needed by the query — the engine satisfies the query from the index alone (index-only scan), avoiding heap/table lookups. CREATE INDEX ... INCLUDE (col) in PostgreSQL adds non-key columns to leaf pages.

Index trade-offs: every INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE must update affected indexes — more indexes = slower writes and more storage. Partial indexes (WHERE active = true) and expression indexes (LOWER(email)) target specific query patterns efficiently.
bullets: Primary key index: unique, often clustered (InnoDB) or separate (PostgreSQL)
Secondary index: non-unique, points to PK or row location
Hash index: O(1) equality only, no range scans (PostgreSQL hash, Redis)
GIN/GiST: specialized indexes for full-text, JSON, geospatial (PostgreSQL)

sections.title: Query Planning and Index Selection
paragraphs: The query optimizer (planner) estimates cost of execution plans — seq scan vs index scan vs bitmap scan — using statistics (row counts, value distribution, index correlation). Outdated statistics cause bad plans; ANALYZE (PostgreSQL) or AUTO ANALYZE keeps them fresh.

Index scan: walk B+ tree to find matching keys, fetch rows. Bitmap index scan: collect TID bitmap from index, sort by physical location, fetch in batch — reduces random I/O for moderate selectivity. Seq scan: read all pages — often faster for large fraction of table (optimizer threshold ~5–30% depending on config).

EXPLAIN ANALYZE is your diagnostic tool — shows actual vs estimated rows, index usage, and sort methods. 'Seq Scan on users' on a 10M row table for a high-selectivity query means missing or unused index.

Anti-patterns: indexing every column, redundant indexes (a,b) when (a,b,c) suffices for prefix queries, functions on indexed columns without expression index (WHERE LOWER(email) = ? bypasses index on email).

sections.title: Replication: Availability and Read Scaling
paragraphs: Replication copies data from a leader (primary) to followers (replicas). Purposes: failover when leader dies, read scaling by routing SELECTs to replicas, geographic distribution for low-latency reads.

Synchronous replication: leader waits for follower acknowledgment before commit — no data loss on failover but higher write latency and availability risk if follower is slow. Asynchronous: leader commits immediately, replicates in background — lower latency but possible data loss if leader fails before replication (RPO > 0).

Leader-follower (primary-replica) is most common: PostgreSQL streaming replication, MySQL binlog replication, Redis replication. Multi-leader: writes to any node, conflict resolution needed — rare, used in multi-datacenter (CouchDB, some CRDT systems). Leaderless (Dynamo-style): write to W of N nodes, read from R of N; R + W > N gives read-your-writes consistency.

Replication lag: async replicas fall behind under write load. Reading stale data from replica causes 'post redirect GET shows old profile' bugs. Monitor lag (seconds behind primary); route consistency-sensitive reads to primary or use quorum reads.
bullets: Failover: promote replica to leader — manual or automatic (Patroni, Orchestrator)
Split-brain: two nodes think they are leader — use fencing, quorum, or STONITH
Read replica: scale reads, not writes — all writes still go to leader
Chain replication: A → B → C reduces leader fan-out

sections.title: Sharding: Horizontal Partitioning for Write Scale
paragraphs: When a single node cannot handle write throughput or storage, partition data across shards — each shard is an independent database holding a subset of keys. Application or proxy layer routes queries by shard key.

Shard key choice is the most critical decision. Good key: high cardinality, even distribution, aligns with query patterns (most queries filter by shard key). Bad key: low cardinality (country=US for 95% of users), monotonically increasing (timestamp — all writes hit last shard), or unrelated to access pattern (causes cross-shard joins).

Cross-shard queries are expensive: aggregating across all shards, JOINs between sharded tables, global secondary indexes (maintained asynchronously). Design schemas so co-located data shares a shard key — user_id shards user profile, orders, and settings together.

Resharding: when adding nodes, remapping keys requires moving data. Consistent hashing minimizes remapping — only K/n keys move when adding K nodes to n existing. Virtual nodes improve balance. Tools: Vitess, Citus, MongoDB sharding, application-level routing.

sections.title: Putting It Together in Production
paragraphs: Typical evolution: single PostgreSQL with indexes → add read replicas for analytics and read-heavy endpoints → cache hot data in Redis → shard when write/storage limits hit. Each step adds operational complexity — do not shard prematurely.

Hot spots: even with good shard key, celebrity users or viral content concentrate load on one shard. Mitigations: sub-sharding hot keys, read replicas for hot shard, application-level fan-out, or splitting hot entity across synthetic keys.

Global systems combine replication (availability, geo-reads) and sharding (write scale). CockroachDB and Spanner shard automatically with distributed consensus. Application-level sharding (Vitess, custom) offers control at the cost of routing logic.

For interviews: articulate index strategy for access patterns, replication mode for RPO/RTO requirements, and shard key with awareness of hot spots and cross-shard query cost. Draw the data flow: write → leader → async replica → cache invalidation.

Chain replication: A → B → C reduces leader fan-out

core.title: Sharding: Horizontal Partitioning for Write Scale
paragraphs: When a single node cannot handle write throughput or storage, partition data across shards — each shard is an independent database holding a subset of keys. Application or proxy layer routes queries by shard key.

Shard key choice is the most critical decision. Good key: high cardinality, even distribution, aligns with query patterns (most queries filter by shard key). Bad key: low cardinality (country=US for 95% of users), monotonically increasing (timestamp — all writes hit last shard), or unrelated to access pattern (causes cross-shard joins).

Cross-shard queries are expensive: aggregating across all shards, JOINs between sharded tables, global secondary indexes (maintained asynchronously). Design schemas so co-located data shares a shard key — user_id shards user profile, orders, and settings together.

Resharding: when adding nodes, remapping keys requires moving data. Consistent hashing minimizes remapping — only K/n keys move when adding K nodes to n existing. Virtual nodes improve balance. Tools: Vitess, Citus, MongoDB sharding, application-level routing.

core.title: Putting It Together in Production
paragraphs: Typical evolution: single PostgreSQL with indexes → add read replicas for analytics and read-heavy endpoints → cache hot data in Redis → shard when write/storage limits hit. Each step adds operational complexity — do not shard prematurely.

Hot spots: even with good shard key, celebrity users or viral content concentrate load on one shard. Mitigations: sub-sharding hot keys, read replicas for hot shard, application-level fan-out, or splitting hot entity across synthetic keys.

Global systems combine replication (availability, geo-reads) and sharding (write scale). CockroachDB and Spanner shard automatically with distributed consensus. Application-level sharding (Vitess, custom) offers control at the cost of routing logic.

For interviews: articulate index strategy for access patterns, replication mode for RPO/RTO requirements, and shard key with awareness of hot spots and cross-shard query cost. Draw the data flow: write → leader → async replica → cache invalidation.

deepDive.title: Indexes, Replication & Sharding — Operational deep dive
paragraphs: Operating Indexes, Replication & Sharding well means defining the scarce resource (CPU, memory, disk, network, or tokens), the SLIs that reflect user pain, and the knobs that trade cost for latency.
Under load, measure amplification: how many bytes, RPCs, or disk writes you pay per user request. Prefetch and batch only when measurements show benefit — premature batching adds tail latency.
Failure drills should include dependency slowdown (not only hard down), clock skew, and disk full. Verify alerts, dashboards, and runbooks against those drills.
bullets: Name the scarcest resource and budget it
Track p50/p99 and error rate for the user journey
Rehearse partial dependency failure

deepDive.title: Indexes, Replication & Sharding — Correctness edges
paragraphs: Correctness edges around Indexes, Replication & Sharding often appear at retries, partial writes, and schema evolution. Make handlers idempotent and state transitions explicit.

Document what clients may observe during failover: stale reads, duplicate messages, or delayed visibility. If the product cannot tolerate an anomaly, enforce a stronger consistency boundary — and pay for it knowingly.

expert.title: Indexes, Replication & Sharding — Expert / multi-region notes
paragraphs: At multi-region scale, Indexes, Replication & Sharding interacts with RTT, quorum placement, and cost of cross-region replication. Prefer region-local user paths with asynchronous global state when invariants allow.
Cost envelopes matter: chart unit cost vs QPS and vs data size. Many 'performance' projects are actually cost projects in disguise — make the objective explicit.

examples.title: Twitter/X user timeline shard key

lessons.title: Isolation Levels & Anomalies
lessons.summary: Isolation Levels & Anomalies is a core topic in modern system design. This lesson builds a first-principles model around storage engines, transactions, and query access paths, then connects that model to capacity, failure modes, and operational practice so you can use it in real architectures.

sections.title: What Isolation Levels & Anomalies is solving
paragraphs: Isolation Levels & Anomalies exists because naive designs around storage engines, transactions, and query access paths break under scale, partial failure, or changing requirements. Before choosing tools, name the problem: which resource is scarce, which invariant must hold, and which user-visible failures are unacceptable.
In interviews and production reviews, strong answers start with constraints (QPS, data size, latency budget, consistency needs) and only then map Isolation Levels & Anomalies onto those constraints.

A useful mental model separates the control plane (how you configure and observe Isolation Levels & Anomalies) from the data plane (the per-request/per-event path). Confusing the two leads to architectures that look neat and operate poorly.

sections.title: Core mechanics
paragraphs: Mechanically, Isolation Levels & Anomalies involves a small set of moving parts: inputs, state, an algorithm or protocol, and outputs/side effects. Draw those parts explicitly. If state is replicated, write down the replication/consistency rule. If work is asynchronous, write down delivery semantics.

Performance characteristics usually come from amplification (how much internal work per external request), locality (whether work stays on one node), and contention (locks, hot keys, leader bottlenecks).

Correctness characteristics usually come from failure handling: retries, timeouts, idempotency, and what clients observe during failover. If you cannot explain the failure story, you do not yet understand Isolation Levels & Anomalies.
bullets: Inputs → state/protocol → outputs/side effects
Name consistency and delivery guarantees
Identify the bottleneck resource early

sections.title: Designing with it
paragraphs: When incorporating Isolation Levels & Anomalies into a system, decide the API boundary first: what does a client call, what can fail, and what is retried. Keep the happy path boring and push complexity into well-tested libraries or platform components.

Capacity plan with numbers: estimate peak load, working set, and headroom. Convert that into shard counts, cache sizes, thread/connection pools, or GPU/memory budgets as relevant to Isolation Levels & Anomalies.
Prefer reversible rollout: feature flags, dual-running, shadow traffic, and clear dashboards. New uses of Isolation Levels & Anomalies should be observable on day one.

sections.title: Operations and failure modes
paragraphs: Operate Isolation Levels & Anomalies with SLIs that match user pain (availability, latency, lag, error rate, cost). Alert on burn rates and queue/lag growth, not only host CPU.
Common failures include overload without admission control, retry amplification, silent staleness, schema mismatches, and dependency brownouts. Write a runbook for the top three.
Chaos and game days should include slow dependencies and network delay, not only hard kills. Isolation Levels & Anomalies often fails in the gray area.

lessons.title: Data Modeling for Scale
lessons.summary: At scale, data models optimize for access patterns and partition keys, not only normalization purity. Good models make hot queries local and cheap; bad models force scatter-gather forever.

sections.title: Access patterns first
paragraphs: List reads/writes with QPS and latency. Model around those paths. In partitioned stores, the partition key is the most important decision.

sections.title: Normalization vs denormalization
paragraphs: Normalize to protect write integrity; denormalize to protect read latency. Duplication requires clear update rules — CDC and application dual updates are options with different failure modes.

sections.title: Keys and hotspots
paragraphs: Monotonic keys create write hotspots. High cardinality + even access is ideal. Tenant+time composites need care to avoid skew.

sections.title: Evolving schemas
paragraphs: Expand/contract migrations, dual writes, and backfills. Avoid locking migrations on huge tables without a plan.

lessons.title: Replication & Sharding
lessons.summary: Replication copies data for durability and read scale; sharding splits data for write/storage scale. Together they define how databases grow — and how consistency and operational complexity grow with them.

sections.title: Replication topologies
paragraphs: Primary-replica async replication is common: fast writes, possible loss on failover. Semi-sync and quorum replication reduce loss windows. Multi-primary increases conflict complexity.

sections.title: Sharding strategies
paragraphs: Hash, range, and directory-based sharding. Resharding is the expensive part — plan early. Cross-shard transactions should be rare.

sections.title: Read your writes
paragraphs: Async replicas cause stale reads. Session stickiness, primary reads for critical paths, or causal tokens mitigate.

sections.title: Ops realities
paragraphs: Failover automation, replica lag alerts, backup per shard, and schema change coordination dominate real-world success.

core.title: Replication topologies
paragraphs: Primary-replica async replication is common: fast writes, possible loss on failover. Semi-sync and quorum replication reduce loss windows. Multi-primary increases conflict complexity.

core.title: Sharding strategies

lessons.title: B+ Trees & LSM Trees
lessons.summary: Storage engines define how databases organize data on disk and in memory. B+ trees optimize for read-heavy, in-place update workloads (PostgreSQL, MySQL InnoDB). LSM trees optimize for write-heavy, append-only workloads (RocksDB, Cassandra, LevelDB). Choosing the wrong engine shape for your access pattern is one of the costliest architectural mistakes.

sections.title: Why Storage Engine Design Matters
paragraphs: A database is not a monolith — at its core sits a storage engine responsible for persisting rows or key-value pairs, maintaining indexes, and recovering after crashes. The engine's on-disk layout determines read latency, write throughput, compression efficiency, and how the system behaves under compaction or vacuum.

Two families dominate modern systems: update-in-place B+ trees and append-only LSM (Log-Structured Merge) trees. Neither is universally superior. PostgreSQL's B+ tree excels at complex queries with range scans and secondary indexes. Cassandra's LSM tree excels at high-volume sequential writes and horizontal scaling — but range queries and updates are expensive.

Every storage engine also implements a WAL (Write-Ahead Log): before applying changes to data structures, append an durable log record. On crash, replay the WAL to recover. The WAL is sequential write — fast on both HDD and SSD — and is the foundation of durability (the D in ACID).

When designing a system, your read/write ratio, update frequency, range query needs, and tolerance for write amplification during compaction should drive engine selection — not brand familiarity or what your team used last project.

sections.title: B+ Trees: Read-Optimized, Update-in-Place
paragraphs: A B+ tree is a balanced tree where data lives only in leaf nodes; internal nodes store keys for navigation. Leaves are linked for efficient range scans. Each node typically matches a disk page (4–16 KB), so a tree of height 3–4 can index billions of keys with only 3–4 disk reads.

To insert or update, the engine finds the leaf, modifies it in place (or splits the page if full), and propagates splits upward. Reads follow the root-to-leaf path — predictable latency, excellent for point lookups and ORDER BY on indexed columns. Secondary indexes in PostgreSQL and MySQL are separate B+ trees pointing to primary key tuples.

Random writes to B+ tree pages cause write amplification at the filesystem level — updating one row may dirty an entire page. SSDs handle this better than HDDs, but sustained random write loads still wear flash and trigger garbage collection in the FTL. Buffer pools cache hot pages in RAM, minimizing disk reads.

PostgreSQL stores rows in heap files (unordered) with B+ tree indexes on top. MySQL InnoDB clusters the primary key — data rows live in the PK B+ tree leaf pages, making PK lookups very fast but secondary index lookups require two tree traversals (secondary index → PK → row).
bullets: Page-oriented: one node = one disk page, fits in buffer pool
Range scan: follow leaf sibling pointers left to right
Page split: insert into full page splits node, may cascade upward
Clustered vs non-clustered index: row data in PK tree (InnoDB) vs separate heap (PostgreSQL)

sections.title: LSM Trees: Write-Optimized, Append-Only
paragraphs: LSM trees invert the B+ tree trade-off. Writes go to an in-memory sorted structure (memtable, often a skip list or red-black tree) and an append-only WAL on disk. When the memtable fills, it is flushed as an immutable sorted SSTable (Sorted String Table) file on disk.

Reads check memtable, then search SSTables newest-to-oldest, often using Bloom filters to skip SSTables that definitely do not contain the key. Without compaction, read amplification grows linearly with the number of SSTables — unacceptable for production.

Compaction merges SSTables in the background — rewriting data to reduce duplicates (updates and deletes become tombstones), remove expired tombstones, and organize data into fewer, larger files. Compaction strategies (leveled, tiered, size-tiered) trade write amplification, read amplification, and space amplification differently.

Cassandra, RocksDB, LevelDB, and ScyllaDB use LSM variants. They shine when writes are inserts or append-only events, when you partition data so each node handles a subset of keys, and when you can tolerate eventual visibility of data during compactions.

SSTable: immutable on-disk sorted file, never modified in place
Bloom filter: probabilistic 'key definitely not here' to skip SSTables
Tombstone: deletion marker removed only after compaction

sections.title: Amplification and Compaction Trade-offs
paragraphs: Write amplification: bytes written to disk per byte of application data. LSM compaction rewrites the same key multiple times as it moves through levels — 10–30× write amplification is common in leveled compaction. SSD endurance and cloud IOPS billing make this a real cost.

Read amplification: disk reads per logical read. B+ tree is typically 1–3 page reads. LSM may check memtable + multiple SSTable levels + Bloom filter false positives. Read-heavy workloads on LSM without sufficient RAM for block cache suffer.
Space amplification: disk usage vs logical data size. Tombstones, duplicate versions during compaction, and snapshot isolation retain old versions until compaction cleans them.

Leveled compaction (LevelDB, RocksDB default): SSTables in level L are ~10× larger than L-1; each key appears in at most one SSTable per level — bounded read amplification, higher write amplification. Size-tiered compaction (Cassandra STCS): merge similar-sized SSTables — lower write amp, higher read amp and space amp. Incremental strategies (DTCS, ICS) target time-series data.

sections.title: Choosing and Operating Storage Engines
paragraphs: Choose B+ tree engines when: complex queries with joins and range scans dominate, updates modify existing rows frequently, strong single-node consistency is required, and working set fits mostly in buffer pool. PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server fit this profile.

Choose LSM engines when: write throughput is the bottleneck, data is naturally partitioned by key, access is mostly primary-key get/put, or you need embedded storage (RocksDB inside Kafka Streams, Cockroach's Pebble). Cassandra, DynamoDB (conceptually), TiKV/RocksDB fit here.

Hybrid systems exist: MyRocks (MySQL on RocksDB) for write-heavy MySQL workloads. CockroachDB and TiDB use LSM (Pebble/RocksDB) with distributed SQL layers. ClickHouse uses merge-tree structures optimized for analytics — yet another design point.

Operational implications: B+ trees need VACUUM (PostgreSQL) or purge (InnoDB) to reclaim space from dead tuples. LSM trees need compaction tuning — stalled compaction causes read degradation and disk fill. Monitor compaction pending bytes, SSTable count, and write stall events in RocksDB.

paragraphs: Correctness edges around B+ Trees & LSM Trees often appear at retries, partial writes, and schema evolution. Make handlers idempotent and state transitions explicit.

examples.title: PostgreSQL heap + B+ tree index
examples.description: An UPDATE in PostgreSQL creates a new row version (MVCC) in the heap and updates index entries pointing to the new tuple. Old versions remain until VACUUM reclaims them. Heavy UPDATE workloads cause bloat — autovacuum must keep pace. Index-only scans avoid heap fetches when visibility map confirms all tuples on a page are visible — a B+ tree optimization for read-heavy analytics.

examples.title: Cassandra write path
examples.description: A write goes to commit log (WAL) + memtable. When memtable exceeds memtable_flush_after, it flushes to SSTable on disk. Reads merge memtable + SSTables. With size-tiered compaction, many SSTables accumulate; read latency grows until compaction merges them. Production clusters tune compaction strategy, gc_grace_seconds, and concurrent_compactors based on write rate and read SLA.

examples.title: RocksDB in Kafka Streams state store
examples.description: Kafka Streams embeds RocksDB for local state (aggregations, joins). Changelog topics provide durability — RocksDB can rebuild from Kafka on restore. Compaction and block cache sizing directly affect stream processing latency during repartitioning or recovery. This shows LSM as an embedded component, not just a standalone database.

WAL provides durability for both engine families — sequential append before data structure change
Write/read/space amplification quantify engine trade-offs — measure at production scale
Compaction is the defining operational concern for LSM; VACUUM/bloat for B+ tree heaps
Engine choice follows access patterns — not SQL vs NoSQL labels
Hybrid and specialized engines (ClickHouse merge-tree) exist for analytics workloads

lessons.title: Transactions & Isolation Levels
lessons.summary: Transactions group operations into atomic units that succeed or fail together. Isolation levels control what concurrent transactions can observe — trading consistency guarantees for performance. Understanding ACID, anomalies, MVCC, and locking strategies is essential for payment systems, inventory, and any shared mutable state.

sections.title: ACID: The Contract Transactions Provide
paragraphs: Atomicity: all operations in a transaction commit or none do. If transferring money debits account A but crashes before crediting B, the database rolls back the debit. Implemented via WAL and undo logs — on failure, replay undo records to restore prior state.

Consistency: transactions take the database from one valid state to another — constraints, foreign keys, and triggers hold. Note: 'C' is partly application responsibility; the DB enforces declared constraints, not all business rules.

Isolation: concurrent transactions behave as if they ran serially (in some level of approximation). The real world runs transactions in parallel for performance — isolation levels define acceptable anomalies.

Durability: once committed, data survives crashes. WAL fsync before commit acknowledgment ensures log records reach stable storage. Replication adds another durability dimension — a commit on the leader may not yet be on followers.
bullets: BEGIN / COMMIT / ROLLBACK: transaction boundaries
Single-statement auto-commit: each statement is its own transaction by default
Distributed transactions (2PC): atomicity across nodes — costly, avoided in modern microservices
Saga pattern: application-level compensation instead of 2PC across services

sections.title: Isolation Levels and Anomalies
paragraphs: SQL standard defines four isolation levels, from weakest to strongest: Read Uncommitted, Read Committed, Repeatable Read, Serializable. Each prevents some anomalies but not others, with increasing locking or versioning overhead.
Dirty read: transaction T2 reads data written by T1 that T1 has not committed. If T1 rolls back, T2 acted on garbage. Prevented by Read Committed and above.
Non-repeatable read: T1 reads a row, T2 updates and commits it, T1 reads again and gets a different value. Prevented by Repeatable Read and above.

Phantom read: T1 runs a range query, T2 inserts a new row matching the range and commits, T1 re-runs the query and sees new rows. Prevented by Serializable (or snapshot isolation with careful handling in PostgreSQL).

Lost update: two transactions read-modify-write the same row; one overwrites the other without seeing its change. Not fully solved by isolation level alone — needs optimistic locking (version column) or SELECT FOR UPDATE.

sections.title: MVCC: Multi-Version Concurrency Control
paragraphs: MVCC avoids read-write blocking by keeping multiple versions of rows. Readers see a snapshot as of transaction start; writers create new versions without overwriting visible data. PostgreSQL and Oracle use MVCC; readers never block writers and writers rarely block readers.

PostgreSQL implements this with xmin/xmax system columns and tuple visibility rules. UPDATE creates a new row version; old version remains until VACUUM. Repeatable Read uses a snapshot taken at first statement (or transaction start in PostgreSQL) — same row read twice returns the same version.

MySQL InnoDB MVCC uses undo logs to reconstruct older row versions for Read View. Repeatable Read is the default — phantoms possible on index ranges without gap locks. Gap locks and next-key locks prevent phantoms but increase deadlock risk.

Snapshot isolation (SI) is often stronger than Read Committed but weaker than full Serializable — it prevents dirty and non-repeatable reads but historically allowed write skew (two transactions read disjoint sets, make consistent-looking updates that violate an invariant together). PostgreSQL 9.1+ Serializable uses SSI (Serializable Snapshot Isolation) to detect dangerous structures.
bullets: Read snapshot: transaction sees consistent view frozen at start
Write creates new version; old version visible to older snapshots
VACUUM / purge: reclaim versions no longer visible to any transaction
Write skew: concurrent transactions pass row checks but violate global invariant

sections.title: Pessimistic vs Optimistic Locking
paragraphs: Pessimistic locking: lock rows before modifying (SELECT FOR UPDATE, SELECT FOR SHARE). Other transactions block until lock released. Prevents lost updates and ensures exclusive access — but reduces concurrency and risks deadlocks.

Optimistic locking: read without lock, check version at commit (UPDATE ... WHERE id = ? AND version = ?). If version changed, retry. Good for low-contention workloads — no blocking, but retries under high contention.

Application-level locks: Redis SETNX, ZooKeeper ephemeral nodes, or advisory locks (PostgreSQL pg_advisory_lock) coordinate across services when transaction boundaries span systems. These are not ACID with the database — design idempotency and timeout carefully.

In microservices, each service owns its database — cross-service 'transactions' use sagas (choreography or orchestration) with compensating actions (cancel reservation, refund payment) rather than distributed 2PC, which blocks on failure and does not scale.

sections.title: Transactions in System Design
paragraphs: Payment and ledger systems demand Serializable or careful serial execution per account — double-spend and negative balance are unacceptable. Inventory systems need to prevent overselling — pessimistic lock on stock row or atomic decrement with CHECK (quantity >= 0).

Read-heavy dashboards can use Read Committed or even read replicas with lag acceptance — stale analytics is tolerable. Session state and shopping carts tolerate eventual consistency; checkout does not.

Long-running transactions are dangerous: they hold locks or old snapshots, block VACUUM (PostgreSQL xact wraparound risk), and increase deadlock probability. Keep transactions short — do validation and external API calls outside the transaction when possible.

When interviewing, state your isolation choice explicitly: 'Bank transfer: Serializable or SELECT FOR UPDATE on both accounts in consistent order to prevent deadlock.' 'Social feed like count: eventual consistency, no transaction needed.' This demonstrates intentional trade-offs.

In microservices, each service owns its database — cross-service 'transactions' use sagas (choreography or orchestration) with compensating actions (cancel reservation, refund payment) rather than distributed 2PC, which blocks on failure and does not scale.

core.title: Transactions in System Design
paragraphs: Payment and ledger systems demand Serializable or careful serial execution per account — double-spend and negative balance are unacceptable. Inventory systems need to prevent overselling — pessimistic lock on stock row or atomic decrement with CHECK (quantity >= 0).

Read-heavy dashboards can use Read Committed or even read replicas with lag acceptance — stale analytics is tolerable. Session state and shopping carts tolerate eventual consistency; checkout does not.

Long-running transactions are dangerous: they hold locks or old snapshots, block VACUUM (PostgreSQL xact wraparound risk), and increase deadlock probability. Keep transactions short — do validation and external API calls outside the transaction when possible.

When interviewing, state your isolation choice explicitly: 'Bank transfer: Serializable or SELECT FOR UPDATE on both accounts in consistent order to prevent deadlock.' 'Social feed like count: eventual consistency, no transaction needed.' This demonstrates intentional trade-offs.

deepDive.title: Transactions & Isolation Levels — Operational deep dive
paragraphs: Operating Transactions & Isolation Levels well means defining the scarce resource (CPU, memory, disk, network, or tokens), the SLIs that reflect user pain, and the knobs that trade cost for latency.
Under load, measure amplification: how many bytes, RPCs, or disk writes you pay per user request. Prefetch and batch only when measurements show benefit — premature batching adds tail latency.
Failure drills should include dependency slowdown (not only hard down), clock skew, and disk full. Verify alerts, dashboards, and runbooks against those drills.

Track p50/p99 and error rate for the user journey
Rehearse partial dependency failure
