concepts: ACID: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability
Isolation levels: Read Uncommitted → Committed → Repeatable Read → Serializable
Dirty read, non-repeatable read, phantom read, lost update
MVCC: multi-version concurrency, snapshot reads without blocking writes
SELECT FOR UPDATE: pessimistic row lock
Optimistic locking: version column check at update time
WAL and undo log: atomicity and crash recovery mechanisms
Write skew: anomaly under snapshot isolation
Saga: distributed transaction alternative with compensating actions
2PC: two-phase commit for cross-node atomicity — high latency, blocking
practices: Use the weakest isolation level that meets correctness requirements — do not default to Serializable everywhere
Keep transactions short — no external HTTP calls or user think-time inside BEGIN...COMMIT
Prevent lost updates with version columns or SELECT FOR UPDATE on contested rows
Acquire locks in consistent order (account ID ascending) to prevent deadlocks
Use idempotency keys for retried operations in payment and order flows
Monitor long-running transactions and lock wait times in production
Prefer sagas over 2PC for cross-service workflows; design compensating actions
pitfalls: Assuming READ COMMITTED prevents lost updates — it does not without explicit locking
Long transactions blocking VACUUM in PostgreSQL — leads to table bloat and txid wraparound
Serializable isolation without handling serialization failures — apps must retry on 40001
Distributed transactions (2PC) across microservices — blocks, fragile, avoid in favor of sagas
Optimistic locking under high contention — retry storms degrade performance
Reading from async replica for financial balance checks — replication lag causes wrong decisions

examples.title: Bank transfer with row locks
examples.description: Transfer $100 from A to B: BEGIN; SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE id IN (A,B) ORDER BY id FOR UPDATE; validate A >= 100; UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 100 WHERE id = A; UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 100 WHERE id = B; COMMIT. Lock ordering by ID prevents deadlock when two transfers cross (A→B and B→A simultaneously). Serializable isolation would also work but may retry on conflict.

examples.title: Inventory oversell with Read Committed
examples.description: Two checkout requests read stock=1 concurrently under Read Committed. Both pass validation. Both decrement. stock=-1. Fix: UPDATE products SET stock = stock - 1 WHERE id = ? AND stock >= 1 RETURNING stock — atomic check-and-decrement, or SELECT FOR UPDATE before decrement. Isolation level alone is insufficient; the write must be conditional.

examples.title: E-commerce order saga
examples.description: Place order spans Order Service, Payment Service, Inventory Service. Instead of 2PC: Order creates pending order → Payment charges card → Inventory reserves stock → Order confirms. On payment failure: compensating cancel order. On inventory failure: refund payment, cancel order. Each step is local ACID; global consistency is eventual with defined failure paths.

keyTakeaways: ACID defines transaction guarantees — durability and atomicity rely on WAL
Weaker isolation = better performance but more anomalies — choose intentionally
MVCC enables concurrent reads and writes without blocking — PostgreSQL's core model
Lost updates require explicit locking or conditional writes, not just isolation level
Keep transactions short; long transactions harm VACUUM, locks, and throughput
Microservices use sagas with compensation, not distributed 2PC
Match isolation to business risk: payments strict, analytics relaxed

Bugs from wrong isolation level cause double charges, overselling, and data corruption that no amount of caching or load balancing fixes. lessons.title: Architecture, Failures & Trade-offs
lessons.summary: Architecture is the art of choosing trade-offs under constraints. No design optimizes everything — you balance latency vs consistency, availability vs durability, simplicity vs flexibility. This lesson provides a framework for structuring designs, reasoning about failure modes, and articulating trade-offs clearly in reviews and interviews.

sections.title: A Structured Approach to System Design
paragraphs: After requirements and estimation, proceed in layers: (1) high-level components and data flow, (2) API and data model, (3) deep dives on the hardest problems, (4) bottlenecks and scale plan, (5) failure modes and monitoring. This sequence keeps interviews organized and ensures you don't optimize details before defining scope.

Start with a simple design that meets functional requirements for moderate scale — single app server, one database, cache optional. Then evolve: 'at 10× traffic, the database becomes the bottleneck → read replicas and cache; at 100×, shard by user_id.' Iterative scaling narrative shows you won't over-engineer day one but have a credible growth path.

Draw data flow for critical paths: user action → API → business logic → storage → async side effects. Mark sync vs async boundaries, cache layers, and external dependencies. One diagram for happy path; annotate failure behavior on the same diagram.

Identify the 2–3 core entities and their relationships. Resist designing every feature — depth on timeline generation beats breadth on 15 minor endpoints. Interviewers probe where you go deep, not how many boxes you draw.
bullets: Layer 1: clients, load balancer, app tier, storage, async pipeline
Layer 2: API contracts, schema, indexes for access patterns
Layer 3: deep dive — the hardest NFR (feed, search, consistency)
Evolution narrative: what breaks at 10×, 100×, 1000×

sections.title: CAP, PACELC, and Consistency Models
paragraphs: CAP theorem: in a network partition, you choose Consistency (all nodes see same data) or Availability (every request gets a response). Partition tolerance is mandatory in distributed systems — the real choice is CP (ZooKeeper, etcd, strongly consistent DB during partition) vs AP (Cassandra, Dynamo-style, available with divergent state merged later).

PACELC extends CAP: else (even without partition), you choose Latency or Consistency. Most systems are PA/EL — available during partition, low latency when network is fine, accepting eventual consistency. This matches most user-facing products where 100ms matters more than immediate global consistency.

Consistency models in practice: strong (linearizable reads/writes), causal (see your own writes and related ordering), read-your-writes (session stickiness or version check), eventual (converge after delay). Pick per operation: inventory deduction strong; view count eventual; user profile read-your-writes.

Don't cite CAP as excuse without specifics. Say: 'like counts use eventual consistency with periodic sync — stale by seconds is acceptable; payment status uses strong consistency via synchronous DB transaction.' Tie model to user-visible behavior.
bullets: CP: consistent during partition, may reject requests (etcd, Spanner)
AP: available during partition, reconcile later (Cassandra, DynamoDB)
PACELC: without partition, latency vs consistency trade-off
Per-operation consistency — not one choice for entire system

sections.title: Designing for Failure
paragraphs: Everything fails: servers, disks, networks, deployments, humans. Design assumes failure is normal. Redundancy: N+1 or N+2 for critical tiers — multiple app instances across AZs, database with automatic failover, multi-AZ object storage. Single points of failure (one Redis node, one cron leader) must be identified and eliminated or accepted with documented risk.

Timeouts everywhere: client → service, service → database, service → external API. Without timeouts, one slow dependency blocks thread pools and cascades. Retries with exponential backoff and jitter for idempotent operations — never unbounded retry storms. Circuit breakers fail fast when downstream is unhealthy.

Idempotency keys for writes: client sends Idempotency-Key header; server deduplicates within TTL window. Essential for payment APIs and any at-least-once delivery (Kafka consumers, webhook retries). Without idempotency, retries double-charge or duplicate records.

Graceful degradation: if recommendations fail, show popular items; if search is down, browse categories. Define fallback behavior per dependency. Bulkheads isolate thread pools so one slow dependency cannot exhaust all resources. Health checks and load balancer draining remove unhealthy instances before total collapse.
bullets: Failover: automatic promotion of replica (RDS, Redis Sentinel)
Blast radius: limit impact of one failure (AZ isolation, cell architecture)
Chaos engineering: inject failures to validate assumptions (Netflix Simian Army)
Runbooks: documented response for each alert — not improvised during outage

sections.title: Common Architectural Trade-offs
paragraphs: Push vs pull for fan-out: push (write-time fan-out to follower timelines) gives fast reads but expensive writes for celebrities; pull (assemble timeline at read time) saves writes but slow reads; hybrid (push for normal users, pull for celebrities) is Twitter's approach. Trade-off: read latency vs write amplification vs implementation complexity.

SQL vs NoSQL: relational for ACID, joins, complex queries; document/wide-column for horizontal scale, flexible schema, high write throughput. Polyglot persistence is normal — Postgres for transactions, Elasticsearch for search, Redis for cache, S3 for blobs.

Sync vs async: sync simplifies client mental model (request → response includes result) but couples latency and availability; async (queue, webhook, polling) decouples and absorbs spikes but complicates UX (job status, notifications). Choose async when side effects are slow, optional, or fan out to many systems.

Build vs buy: managed services (RDS, SQS, CloudFront) reduce ops burden and accelerate MVP; self-hosted (Kafka cluster, custom CDN) offers control and cost at scale. Trade-off: engineering time vs operational ownership vs vendor lock-in.
bullets: Write amplification vs read optimization — pick based on read/write ratio
Normalization vs denormalization — joins vs duplicate data for read speed
Strong consistency cost: coordination, latency, reduced availability during partition
Operational complexity: microservices vs monolith team velocity trade-off

sections.title: Presenting and Defending Your Design
paragraphs: Lead with the core flow, then justify each major component: 'Redis cache here because 95% of reads are hot keys; 90% hit rate cuts DB load 10×.' Anticipate challenges: 'What if cache fails? DB absorbs load — we have headroom to 2×; alerts fire; degrade non-critical features.'

Name trade-offs explicitly: 'We chose eventual consistency for likes because strong consistency would require distributed locking on every click, adding 50ms latency for negligible user benefit.' Unnamed trade-offs look like oversights.

Scope management: when interviewer adds 'also support real-time notifications,' acknowledge, prioritize against MoSCoW, extend diagram incrementally rather than restarting. 'I'll add a WebSocket gateway and notification service fed by the existing event bus — deferring mobile push provider integration to phase 2.'
Close with monitoring and success criteria: metrics, alerts, SLIs/SLOs. Architecture without observability is incomplete — you cannot operate what you cannot measure.

concepts: Layered design: components → API/schema → deep dive → scale → failures
CAP / PACELC: consistency vs availability vs latency trade-offs
Idempotency: safe retries without duplicate side effects
Circuit breaker, bulkhead, timeout: fault isolation patterns
Graceful degradation: reduced functionality vs total outage

practices: Start simple; add complexity only when estimation or NFRs demand it
Assign consistency model per operation with user-visible justification
Set timeouts and retries on every external call; use circuit breakers
Require idempotency keys on all non-read APIs that mutate state
Identify single points of failure; eliminate or document accepted risk
Name trade-offs aloud in reviews — push vs pull, sync vs async, SQL vs NoSQL
Define SLIs, alerts, and runbooks alongside architecture diagrams

Golden hammer: Kafka/microservices for every problem regardless of scale
Ignoring failure modes until 'phase 2' — outages happen in phase 1
Unbounded retries causing retry storms that amplify outages
Strong consistency everywhere — unnecessary latency and availability cost
Diagram without data flow numbers — architecture disconnected from capacity

examples.title: Hybrid timeline fan-out (Twitter model)
examples.description: Normal users (< 10K followers): push tweets to follower timeline Redis lists on write — O(followers) write, O(1) read. Celebrities: pull at read time from celebrity's tweet list merged with pushed timelines. Trade-off: bounded write amplification while keeping read latency under 200ms for 99% of users.

examples.title: Payment service CP design
examples.description: During network partition, payment service rejects writes rather than risk double-spend or inconsistent balances. Strong consistency via Postgres serializable isolation + idempotency keys. Availability sacrificed for financial correctness — explicit CP choice with user-facing 'try again' messaging.

examples.title: Circuit breaker on third-party SMS
examples.description: SMS provider latency degrades from 200ms to 30s. Circuit breaker opens after 50% error rate in 10s window. Notification service queues messages locally, returns success to user ('notification pending'), drains queue when circuit half-open probes succeed. Graceful degradation — email fallback if SMS unavailable > 5 min.

keyTakeaways: Architecture is structured trade-off decisions anchored in requirements and scale
Design for failure first — timeouts, idempotency, redundancy, degradation
Consistency and availability choices apply per operation, not globally
Push vs pull, sync vs async, SQL vs NoSQL are context-dependent trade-offs
Evolve design in layers: simple first, then credible 10×/100× scaling narrative
Name trade-offs explicitly — unnamed choices look like blind spots in reviews
Observability (SLIs, alerts, runbooks) is part of architecture, not an afterthought

Frameworks for structure and trade-off vocabulary separate thoughtful designers from diagram collectors.

lessons.title: The Design → Build → Measure Loop
lessons.summary: System design does not end at deployment. The best architects treat design as a continuous loop: hypothesize, build minimally, measure against SLOs, learn, and iterate. This lesson connects design frameworks to operational reality — load testing, observability, postmortems, and evolutionary architecture that adapts as requirements and traffic change.

sections.title: From Design Doc to MVP
paragraphs: A design document captures intent: requirements, architecture diagram, data model, failure modes, and open questions. It is a proposal, not a contract. The MVP implements must-have functional requirements at modest scale with explicit non-goals — 'no multi-region, no full-text search, single AZ database with nightly backups.'

Build the simplest architecture that validates the core hypothesis: do users want this feature? Can we meet latency targets at 1K QPS? Premature optimization wastes weeks; missing critical path design (wrong data model, unshardable schema) wastes months. Focus MVP engineering on reversible decisions and hard-to-change foundations (data model, API contracts).

Feature flags decouple deployment from release — ship code dark, enable for 1% of users, measure, expand. Strangler patterns apply within monoliths: new code path behind flag, old path default, migrate traffic incrementally. Design docs should specify flag strategy and rollback plan for risky changes.
Define 'done' for MVP with measurable criteria: p99 < 300ms at 500 QPS load test, error rate < 0.1%, core user journey E2E tests pass. Without exit criteria, MVP scope creeps indefinitely.
bullets: Design doc: requirements, diagram, schema, risks, open questions
MVP: must-haves only; explicit non-goals documented
Reversible vs irreversible decisions — invest design time accordingly
Feature flags: deploy != release; enable gradual rollout

sections.title: Measuring What Matters: SLIs, SLOs, and Error Budgets
paragraphs: SLI (Service Level Indicator) is a measured metric: request latency, availability, throughput, correctness. SLO (Service Level Objective) is a target: 99.9% of requests complete in < 200ms over 30 days. SLAs are contractual SLOs with penalties — internal teams use SLOs without legal binding.

Error budget = 100% - SLO. At 99.9% availability, you have 0.1% budget (~43 minutes downtime/month). Budget exhausted → freeze features, focus on reliability. Budget healthy → take more deployment risk. This framework aligns product velocity with reliability mathematically.

Choose SLIs users feel: availability (successful responses / total), latency (p99 of server-side duration), freshness (age of data in async pipeline). Avoid vanity metrics (CPU average) as primary SLOs — correlate to user experience.

Instrument from day one: structured logs, metrics (Prometheus/Datadog), distributed tracing (OpenTelemetry). Design docs should list golden signals (latency, traffic, errors, saturation) per component before build starts — retrofitting observability is expensive.
bullets: Four golden signals: latency, traffic, errors, saturation (Google SRE)
SLO: target over rolling window (30 days common)
Error budget: remaining allowable unreliability before SLO breach
RED method: Rate, Errors, Duration for request-driven services

sections.title: Load Testing and Validation
paragraphs: Load tests validate capacity assumptions before users do. Types: smoke (minimal, CI), load (expected peak), stress (beyond peak to find breaking point), soak (sustained hours — memory leaks, connection exhaustion), spike (sudden 10× burst). Match test profile to estimated traffic shape.

Test in production-like environment — staging with 10% of prod data size often lies about query plans and cache behavior. Use anonymized production data snapshots or synthetic generators that reproduce skew (hot keys, celebrity users).

Measure during tests: p50/p95/p99 latency, error rate, resource saturation (CPU, memory, disk IOPS, connection pool usage, Kafka lag). Compare against design doc estimates. Gap analysis drives next iteration: 'estimated 10K QPS; stress test knee at 4K — database write lock contention.'

Chaos and fault injection in staging: kill a replica, inject latency to dependencies, partition network. Validate failover, circuit breakers, and degradation paths designed on paper actually work. A design untested under failure is hope, not engineering.
bullets: k6, Locust, Gatling — programmatic load test scripts in CI
Production traffic shadowing/mirroring — test new path with real traffic safely
Gradual rollout: canary 1% → 10% → 50% → 100% with automated rollback
Load test failure is success — you found the bottleneck before users did

sections.title: Learning from Production: Postmortems and Iteration
paragraphs: Blameless postmortems document incidents: timeline, root cause, contributing factors, action items. Focus on systems and processes, not individuals. 'Database failover took 15 minutes because runbook was stale' → action: automate failover + quarterly drill.

Postmortem action items feed the design loop: add cache layer, increase timeout, fix idempotency bug, shard hot table. Architecture evolves from production pain — the best designs are revised, not born perfect.

Continuous profiling (CPU, memory, lock contention) in production finds regressions invisible in averages. A deployment that adds 5ms p99 doesn't trip error alerts but erodes SLO over weeks. Compare canary metrics to baseline automatically during rollout.

Capacity review cadence: quarterly re-run estimation with growth metrics. Traffic 3× in six months? Revisit shard plan before emergency. Technical debt register tracks shortcuts taken in MVP with remediation triggers ('shard when write QPS > 5K').
bullets: Blameless culture: fix systems, not punish people
Five whys: dig from symptom to root cause
Action items: specific, owned, dated — tracked to completion
Game days: scheduled disaster recovery exercises

sections.title: Evolutionary Architecture and Knowing When to Redesign
paragraphs: Evolutionary architecture supports guided change: fitness functions (automated architecture tests) enforce rules ('domain layer cannot import infrastructure'). Modular monoliths evolve into services when metrics justify — not on a calendar.

Recognize redesign triggers: sustained SLO breach despite optimization, org structure outgrows architecture (Conway's Law), fundamental schema change needed, cost curve nonlinear. Incremental refactor (Strangler Fig) beats rewrite unless technical debt is existential.

Document architecture decision records (ADRs): context, decision, consequences, status. Future teams understand why Kafka was chosen over RabbitMQ in 2024 and when to revisit. Design loop includes revisiting ADRs when assumptions change.
The meta-skill: hold design lightly. Measure ruthlessly. Iterate quickly. Systems that survive are not the most elegant initial design — they are the ones whose teams learned fastest from reality.

core.title: From Design Doc to MVP
paragraphs: A design document captures intent: requirements, architecture diagram, data model, failure modes, and open questions. It is a proposal, not a contract. The MVP implements must-have functional requirements at modest scale with explicit non-goals — 'no multi-region, no full-text search, single AZ database with nightly backups.'

Build the simplest architecture that validates the core hypothesis: do users want this feature? Can we meet latency targets at 1K QPS? Premature optimization wastes weeks; missing critical path design (wrong data model, unshardable schema) wastes months. Focus MVP engineering on reversible decisions and hard-to-change foundations (data model, API contracts).

Feature flags decouple deployment from release — ship code dark, enable for 1% of users, measure, expand. Strangler patterns apply within monoliths: new code path behind flag, old path default, migrate traffic incrementally. Design docs should specify flag strategy and rollback plan for risky changes.
Define 'done' for MVP with measurable criteria: p99 < 300ms at 500 QPS load test, error rate < 0.1%, core user journey E2E tests pass. Without exit criteria, MVP scope creeps indefinitely.
bullets: Design doc: requirements, diagram, schema, risks, open questions
MVP: must-haves only; explicit non-goals documented
Reversible vs irreversible decisions — invest design time accordingly
Feature flags: deploy != release; enable gradual rollout

core.title: Measuring What Matters: SLIs, SLOs, and Error Budgets
paragraphs: SLI (Service Level Indicator) is a measured metric: request latency, availability, throughput, correctness. SLO (Service Level Objective) is a target: 99.9% of requests complete in < 200ms over 30 days. SLAs are contractual SLOs with penalties — internal teams use SLOs without legal binding.

Error budget = 100% - SLO. At 99.9% availability, you have 0.1% budget (~43 minutes downtime/month). Budget exhausted → freeze features, focus on reliability. Budget healthy → take more deployment risk. This framework aligns product velocity with reliability mathematically.

Choose SLIs users feel: availability (successful responses / total), latency (p99 of server-side duration), freshness (age of data in async pipeline). Avoid vanity metrics (CPU average) as primary SLOs — correlate to user experience.

Instrument from day one: structured logs, metrics (Prometheus/Datadog), distributed tracing (OpenTelemetry). Design docs should list golden signals (latency, traffic, errors, saturation) per component before build starts — retrofitting observability is expensive.
bullets: Four golden signals: latency, traffic, errors, saturation (Google SRE)
SLO: target over rolling window (30 days common)
Error budget: remaining allowable unreliability before SLO breach
RED method: Rate, Errors, Duration for request-driven services

core.title: Load Testing and Validation
paragraphs: Load tests validate capacity assumptions before users do. Types: smoke (minimal, CI), load (expected peak), stress (beyond peak to find breaking point), soak (sustained hours — memory leaks, connection exhaustion), spike (sudden 10× burst). Match test profile to estimated traffic shape.

Test in production-like environment — staging with 10% of prod data size often lies about query plans and cache behavior. Use anonymized production data snapshots or synthetic generators that reproduce skew (hot keys, celebrity users).

Measure during tests: p50/p95/p99 latency, error rate, resource saturation (CPU, memory, disk IOPS, connection pool usage, Kafka lag). Compare against design doc estimates. Gap analysis drives next iteration: 'estimated 10K QPS; stress test knee at 4K — database write lock contention.'

Chaos and fault injection in staging: kill a replica, inject latency to dependencies, partition network. Validate failover, circuit breakers, and degradation paths designed on paper actually work. A design untested under failure is hope, not engineering.
bullets: k6, Locust, Gatling — programmatic load test scripts in CI
Production traffic shadowing/mirroring — test new path with real traffic safely
Gradual rollout: canary 1% → 10% → 50% → 100% with automated rollback
Load test failure is success — you found the bottleneck before users did

deepDive.title: The Design → Build → Measure Loop — Operational deep dive
paragraphs: Operating The Design → Build → Measure Loop well means defining the scarce resource (CPU, memory, disk, network, or tokens), the SLIs that reflect user pain, and the knobs that trade cost for latency.
Under load, measure amplification: how many bytes, RPCs, or disk writes you pay per user request. Prefetch and batch only when measurements show benefit — premature batching adds tail latency.
Failure drills should include dependency slowdown (not only hard down), clock skew, and disk full. Verify alerts, dashboards, and runbooks against those drills.
bullets: Name the scarcest resource and budget it
Track p50/p99 and error rate for the user journey
Rehearse partial dependency failure

deepDive.title: The Design → Build → Measure Loop — Correctness edges
paragraphs: Correctness edges around The Design → Build → Measure Loop often appear at retries, partial writes, and schema evolution. Make handlers idempotent and state transitions explicit.

Document what clients may observe during failover: stale reads, duplicate messages, or delayed visibility. If the product cannot tolerate an anomaly, enforce a stronger consistency boundary — and pay for it knowingly.

paragraphs: At multi-region scale, The Design → Build → Measure Loop interacts with RTT, quorum placement, and cost of cross-region replication. Prefer region-local user paths with asynchronous global state when invariants allow.
Cost envelopes matter: chart unit cost vs QPS and vs data size. Many 'performance' projects are actually cost projects in disguise — make the objective explicit.

examples.title: MVP → scale iteration for a startup API
examples.description: MVP: monolith + Postgres, SLO 99.5% / 500ms p99. Month 3: p99 degrades to 800ms at 2K QPS — load test reproduces; add Redis cache for hot reads, p99 back to 200ms. Month 9: write QPS nears 3K — add read replica, async job queue for emails. Month 18: shard users table by user_id. Each step triggered by SLO breach or capacity review, not premature planning.

examples.title: Error budget freeze before holiday season
examples.description: E-commerce platform has 99.95% availability SLO. October error budget at 15% remaining before Black Friday freeze. Team defers risky database migration to January, focuses on load test remediation and runbook drills. December traffic 5× — SLO met. Budget framework prevented a risky change during critical window.

examples.title: Postmortem-driven architecture change
examples.description: Outage: payment webhook consumer fell behind, 4-hour delay in order confirmations. Root cause: single-threaded consumer, no dead letter queue, poison message blocked partition. Actions: horizontal consumer scaling, DLQ, idempotency keys, alert on consumer lag > 1 min. Design loop turned incident into durable architecture improvement.

lessons.whyItMatters: Interview designs are static; production systems are living. This mindset distinguishes staff-level ownership from feature-level implementation.

lessons.title: Requirements & Capacity Estimation
lessons.summary: Every system design begins before boxes and arrows: clarify requirements, define success metrics, and estimate scale. This lesson teaches a structured approach to functional vs non-functional requirements, back-of-the-envelope capacity math, and the assumptions you must state explicitly so your architecture stands up to scrutiny in interviews and design reviews.

sections.title: Functional vs Non-Functional Requirements
paragraphs: Functional requirements describe what the system does: users can post tweets, search products, transfer money. Non-functional requirements (NFRs) describe how well: latency under 200ms p99, 99.99% availability, GDPR compliance, support 10M DAU. Architecture is driven as much by NFRs as by features — a chat app and a batch analytics pipeline share 'store messages' but diverge radically on latency and consistency.

Explicitly categorize requirements into must-have (MVP), should-have (near-term), and could-have (future). In a 45-minute interview, scope to must-haves plus one differentiating NFR. Ask clarifying questions: Who are the users? Read vs write ratio? Geographic distribution? Durability expectations if a datacenter fails?

Constraints narrow the solution space: budget, team size, existing tech stack, regulatory environment, time to market. A startup with three engineers should not design Google-scale sharding on day one. Document constraints as actively as requirements — they explain why you chose a monolith over 50 microservices.

Success metrics translate NFRs into measurable targets: p50/p95/p99 latency, error rate, throughput (QPS), availability (nines), data durability (RPO/RTO), cost per request. Without numbers, 'fast' and 'scalable' are meaningless and impossible to validate after build.
bullets: Functional: features and behaviors
Non-functional: latency, availability, consistency, durability, compliance
MoSCoW prioritization: Must, Should, Could, Won't (this session)
RPO/RTO: acceptable data loss and recovery time on failure

sections.title: Back-of-the-Envelope Estimation
paragraphs: Capacity estimation grounds architecture in physics and economics. Start with daily active users (DAU), actions per user per day, and peak-to-average ratio (often 2–3×, higher for events like New Year's Eve). Convert to peak QPS: if 100M DAU each post 2 times/day, writes = 200M/day ≈ 2,300 avg QPS; at 3× peak ≈ 7,000 write QPS.

Know handy constants: 1 day ≈ 86,400 seconds (~100K for quick math); 1 million seconds ≈ 11.5 days; 1 GB = 10^9 bytes (or 2^30 for memory — state which). SSD random read ~100 μs; sequential ~1 GB/s; datacenter round trip ~0.5 ms same region, ~150 ms cross-continent; memory ~100 ns access.

Storage estimation: average object size × objects retained × replication factor. 500 bytes per tweet × 500M tweets/day × 365 days × 3 replicas ≈ 274 TB/year before compression. Does it fit one Postgres instance? No — partition, archive, or object storage.

Bandwidth: average response size × QPS. 10 KB response × 100K QPS = 1 GB/s egress — significant cost and CDN requirement. Estimation reveals bottlenecks early: a 1 KB write triggering 50 KB of fan-out read is a architectural red flag at scale.
bullets: Peak QPS = (DAU × actions/day × peak factor) / 86400
Storage = object_size × volume × retention × replication
Bandwidth = response_size × read_QPS (+ upload for writes)
Memory cache: working set size — what fraction of data is hot?

sections.title: Capacity Planning for Compute, Storage, and Cache
paragraphs: Compute: a single modern server handles ~1–10K simple HTTP req/s depending on work. 100K read QPS / 5K per server ≈ 20 app servers + load balancer overhead. CPU-bound workloads (video encode, ML inference) scale differently — profile per core throughput.

Database sizing: Postgres comfortable ~5–10K simple reads/s or ~1–2K writes/s on tuned hardware before sharding. Redis ~100K ops/s per node for simple commands. Disk IOPS limits random write throughput — WAL and index updates matter. Don't assume linear scale; measure knee points.

Cache hit ratio dramatically reduces backend load. If 90% of reads hit CDN/Redis, 100K read QPS becomes 10K database QPS — the difference between one cluster and ten. Estimate working set: if 20% of users are active daily and each accesses 50 keys, that's DAU × 0.2 × 50 hot keys (with skew — 80/20 rule applies).

State assumptions explicitly: 'assuming 100M DAU, 10:1 read/write, 500 byte records, 5 year retention, 99.9% availability.' Reviewers and future you can revisit when assumptions change. Wrong assumptions are fine; unstated ones cause production surprises.

sections.title: API Design and Data Model Implications
paragraphs: Requirements drive API shape. Read-heavy feeds favor cursor pagination and precomputed timelines. Write-heavy logs favor append-only ingestion and async processing. Search requirements imply inverted indexes (Elasticsearch) beyond primary storage.

Entity relationships emerge from use cases: User posts Tweet, User follows User, Tweet has Likes. Identify access patterns before schema: 'get timeline for user' (read fan-out), 'get likes for tweet' (counter or aggregate), 'search tweets by keyword' (secondary index). Each pattern maps to storage and cache choices.

Consistency requirements per operation: liking a post can be eventually consistent (count off by one briefly); bank transfer cannot. Classify operations into strong consistency, read-your-writes, or eventual — this directly determines database choice, cache invalidation, and sync vs async boundaries.

Multi-tenancy, permissions, and audit requirements add columns, row-level security, or separate schemas. Compliance (HIPAA, PCI) may mandate encryption at rest, network isolation, and retention policies — non-negotiable constraints that affect every layer.
bullets: Access patterns first: how data is read/written drives schema and indexes
Pagination: offset (small datasets) vs cursor (infinite feeds)
Consistency tier per operation — not one global setting
Audit trail: append-only event log vs mutable rows with history tables

sections.title: Documenting and Presenting Estimates
paragraphs: In interviews, spend 5–10 minutes on requirements and estimation before drawing architecture. Verbalize math aloud; round aggressively; sanity-check orders of magnitude. Interviewers care about structured thinking, not exact digits.

A one-page capacity summary for design reviews includes: traffic (peak QPS read/write), storage (GB/TB per year), bandwidth, cache working set, and growth assumptions (2× per year?). Tie each number to a component: '7K write QPS → Kafka 20 partitions, 3 brokers; 100K read QPS → CDN + 10 Redis nodes + 5 read replicas.'

Identify the first bottleneck: usually single-database writes, hot partition, or egress cost. Propose mitigation in the design: sharding key, read replicas, CDN, async pipeline. Estimation without bottleneck analysis is arithmetic, not engineering.
Re-estimate after MVP launch with real metrics. Capacity planning is continuous — load tests validate assumptions; production traffic reveals skew and long-tail behavior estimates miss.

examples.title: Twitter-like timeline (interview classic)
examples.description: 300M DAU, 200M tweet/day, 5:1 read/write for timeline fetches. Write QPS ≈ 2,300 avg, 7K peak. Timeline read: 300M DAU × 20 views/day = 6B reads/day ≈ 70K avg, 200K peak. Storage: 280 bytes/tweet × 200M/day × 365 × 3 replicas ≈ 60 TB/year. Conclusion: write path is easy; fan-out read path drives cache (Redis timelines) and CDN for media.

examples.title: URL shortener capacity
examples.description: 100:1 read/write ratio, 100M new URLs/month, 10B redirects/month. Write ≈ 40/s avg; read ≈ 4,000/s avg, 12K peak. Storage: 500 bytes/URL × 1.2B URLs/year ≈ 600 GB/year — fits one DB with sharding by hash. Cache: 20% URLs get 80% traffic — Redis working set ~120M keys × 100 bytes ≈ 12 GB. Bottleneck: read QPS → Redis + CDN redirect at edge.

examples.title: Video upload platform
examples.description: 1M uploads/day, average 500 MB file. Ingress bandwidth: 1M × 500 MB / 86400 ≈ 5.8 GB/s peak ~15 GB/s. Storage: 500 TB/day raw — object storage (S3), not database. Transcoding: async worker pool; 10 min video × 5 renditions = compute-bound pipeline. Requirements drive async upload → queue → workers architecture.

sections.title: Core mechanics

lessons.title: Bottlenecks, Failures, Trade-offs & Iteration
lessons.summary: Bottlenecks, Failures, Trade-offs & Iteration is a core topic in modern system design. This lesson builds a first-principles model around a repeatable design process, then connects that model to capacity, failure modes, and operational practice so you can use it in real architectures.

sections.title: What Bottlenecks, Failures, Trade-offs & Iteration is solving
paragraphs: Bottlenecks, Failures, Trade-offs & Iteration exists because naive designs around a repeatable design process break under scale, partial failure, or changing requirements. Before choosing tools, name the problem: which resource is scarce, which invariant must hold, and which user-visible failures are unacceptable.

In interviews and production reviews, strong answers start with constraints (QPS, data size, latency budget, consistency needs) and only then map Bottlenecks, Failures, Trade-offs & Iteration onto those constraints.

A useful mental model separates the control plane (how you configure and observe Bottlenecks, Failures, Trade-offs & Iteration) from the data plane (the per-request/per-event path). Confusing the two leads to architectures that look neat and operate poorly.

lessons.title: CAP, PACELC & Consensus
lessons.summary: Distributed systems face unavoidable trade-offs between consistency, availability, and latency. CAP and PACELC frameworks help you reason about these trade-offs consciously. Consensus algorithms like Raft keep replicas in agreement — powering everything from etcd to distributed databases.

sections.title: The Reality of Distributed Systems
paragraphs: When components run on multiple machines connected by a network, failures are normal — not exceptional. Networks partition, packets drop, nodes crash, clocks skew. A distributed system must continue operating (or fail gracefully) despite these failures.

The fundamental challenge is maintaining shared state across unreliable nodes. Should all replicas agree before responding (consistency)? Should the system keep serving requests even if some replicas are unreachable (availability)? You cannot maximize both during a network partition.

Understanding these trade-offs prevents you from choosing tools with wrong expectations — expecting strong consistency from an AP cache or five-nines availability from a CP coordination service during splits.

sections.title: CAP Theorem
paragraphs: CAP states that a distributed data store can provide at most two of three properties: Consistency (every read receives the most recent write or an error), Availability (every request receives a non-error response), and Partition tolerance (the system operates despite network partitions between nodes).

In practice, partition tolerance is non-negotiable — networks fail. So the real choice during a partition is Consistency (CP) or Availability (AP). CP systems (etcd, ZooKeeper, traditional RDBMS with sync replication) may reject writes or reads to preserve consistency. AP systems (Cassandra, DynamoDB with eventual consistency) accept writes on both sides of a partition and reconcile later.
CAP is often misunderstood as a static label. Systems can be mostly AP with tunable consistency, or mostly CP with read replicas that serve stale data. Context and configuration matter.

sections.title: PACELC Extension
paragraphs: PACELC extends CAP: if there is a Partition (P), choose between Availability (A) and Consistency (C); Else (E), choose between Latency (L) and Consistency (C). This captures the everyday trade-off even when the network is healthy.

Even without partitions, synchronous replication to all replicas adds latency. Many systems default to reading from the nearest replica (low latency, eventual consistency) and offer optional linearizable reads (high latency, strong consistency) per request.

DynamoDB is PA/EL by default (available during partition, low-latency eventually consistent reads). PostgreSQL with synchronous replication is PC/EC (consistent during partition, consistent but slower when healthy). Cassandra is PA/EL with tunable consistency per query.

sections.title: Consistency Models
paragraphs: Strong consistency (linearizability): every read sees the latest write — as if one copy exists. Eventual consistency: replicas converge over time; reads may return stale data temporarily. Causal consistency: preserves cause-effect ordering without full linearizability.
Read-your-writes: a user always sees their own updates. Monotonic reads: a user never sees time go backward. These session guarantees are often sufficient and cheaper than global strong consistency.
Choose consistency per operation: financial transfers need linearizability; social media like counts tolerate eventual consistency; shopping cart reads need read-your-writes.

sections.title: Consensus with Raft
paragraphs: Consensus algorithms ensure multiple nodes agree on a value or log sequence despite failures. Raft is the approachable standard: nodes are followers, one leader is elected, the leader replicates log entries to a majority quorum before committing.

Quorum (majority of nodes) ensures any two quorums overlap — at least one node has the latest committed entry. Leader election uses randomized timeouts to avoid split-brain. etcd, Consul, and CockroachDB use Raft variants.

Consensus is expensive — typically 3 or 5 nodes, limited write throughput compared to leaderless systems. Use it for coordination (service discovery, config, locks), not high-throughput data ingestion.

paragraphs: Operating CAP, PACELC & Consensus well means defining the scarce resource (CPU, memory, disk, network, or tokens), the SLIs that reflect user pain, and the knobs that trade cost for latency.
Under load, measure amplification: how many bytes, RPCs, or disk writes you pay per user request. Prefetch and batch only when measurements show benefit — premature batching adds tail latency.
Failure drills should include dependency slowdown (not only hard down), clock skew, and disk full. Verify alerts, dashboards, and runbooks against those drills.

paragraphs: Correctness edges around CAP, PACELC & Consensus often appear at retries, partial writes, and schema evolution. Make handlers idempotent and state transitions explicit.

Document what clients may observe during failover: stale reads, duplicate messages, or delayed visibility. If the product cannot tolerate an anomaly, enforce a stronger consistency boundary — and pay for it knowingly.

paragraphs: At multi-region scale, CAP, PACELC & Consensus interacts with RTT, quorum placement, and cost of cross-region replication. Prefer region-local user paths with asynchronous global state when invariants allow.

examples.title: Kubernetes etcd
examples.description: Kubernetes stores cluster state in etcd — a CP system using Raft. During a network partition, the minority partition becomes read-only. This is acceptable because cluster coordination demands consistency over availability. Application data lives elsewhere.

examples.title: DynamoDB global tables
examples.description: Multi-region DynamoDB global tables replicate asynchronously — AP with eventual consistency across regions. A user updating profile in US-East may see stale data in EU-West for seconds. Product accepts this for profile reads; payment uses single-region strong consistency.

examples.title: Bank transfer with quorum
examples.description: A bank uses a strongly consistent store requiring quorum writes for transfers. During partition, minority nodes reject writes — users see errors rather than double-spend. Availability is sacrificed for correctness on this critical path.

Test partition and failure scenarios — theoretical CAP choices meet reality in production
Read replicas and caches introduce staleness — monitor lag explicitly

lessons.title: Clocks (Lamport, Vector, HLC)
lessons.summary: Wall clocks lie across machines. Logical clocks (Lamport, vector) and hybrid logical clocks capture causality so distributed systems can order events without assuming synchronized time.

sections.title: The problem with wall time
paragraphs: NTP synchronizes clocks imperfectly. Under failover and heavy load, clocks jump. Ordering events by `datetime.now()` across nodes creates false histories and lost updates.
Google's Spanner uses TrueTime (GPS/atomic) to bound uncertainty — most systems do not have that. You need protocols that tolerate uncertainty or avoid wall-clock ordering.

sections.title: Lamport clocks
paragraphs: Each process keeps a counter. On send/local event, increment; on receive, set to max(local, message) + 1. If a→b causally, then L(a) < L(b). The converse is false: concurrent events can have ordered timestamps.
Lamport clocks are cheap and good for fencing tokens and monotonic versions when you only need a total order consistent with causality.

sections.title: Vector clocks
paragraphs: A vector of counters — one per replica — tracks causal history. You can detect concurrency: incomparable vectors mean conflicts. Storage systems (Riak, Dynamo-style) use them for sibling reconciliation.
Vectors grow with the number of actors. For large actor sets, dotted version vectors and other optimizations bound metadata size.

sections.title: Hybrid logical clocks
paragraphs: HLCs combine physical time with a logical component to keep causality while staying close to wall time for humans and TTL. CockroachDB and others use HLC variants.
You still must handle clock uncertainty windows when comparing timestamps for linearizability-style guarantees.

lessons.title: Consistency Models
lessons.summary: Consistency models specify what observations clients may make. From linearizability to eventual consistency, each model enables and forbids certain anomalies — learn them to pick storage and API guarantees.

sections.title: Linearizability and sequential consistency
paragraphs: Linearizability: operations appear instantaneously at a single point between invocation and response, globally. Sequential consistency allows reordering across clients but preserves each client's order.

sections.title: Causal and session models
paragraphs: Causal consistency preserves cause-before-effect. Session guarantees (read-your-writes, monotonic reads) are often what users actually need for a single device/login.

sections.title: Eventual consistency
paragraphs: If updates stop, replicas converge. During churn, stale reads and conflicts happen. Pair with conflict resolution (LWW, CRDT, app merge).

sections.title: Choosing per API
paragraphs: Payments capture may need strong guarantees; feed ranking may tolerate staleness. Document guarantees in API specs so clients do not invent them.

lessons.title: CRDTs
lessons.summary: Conflict-free Replicated Data Types merge concurrent updates without coordination. They enable local-first and multi-master designs when you can accept their semantics and metadata costs.

sections.title: Why CRDTs
paragraphs: When replicas accept writes offline, conflicts happen. CRDTs mathematically guarantee convergence with defined merge functions — G-Counter, OR-Set, LWW-Register, and richer text types.

sections.title: State vs operation based
paragraphs: State-based (CvRDT) gossip full state merges; op-based (CmRDT) reliably deliver operations. Trade bandwidth vs delivery assumptions.

sections.title: Costs and limits
paragraphs: Metadata growth (tombstones, version vectors) needs compaction. Not every business invariant is mergeable — money transfer is the classic counterexample without extra constraints.

sections.title: Fit
paragraphs: Collaborative editing, presence, feature flags, shopping carts — good fits. Banking ledgers — usually not without additional protocol.

lessons.title: Distributed Transactions (2PC, Sagas)
lessons.summary: Cross-service atomicity is hard. Two-phase commit coordinates strong atomicity at high cost; sagas use sequenced local transactions with compensations for practical workflows.

sections.title: 2PC mechanics
paragraphs: Prepare then commit. Blocking on coordinator failure is the classic weakness. XA works in narrow environments; across microservices and heterogeneous stores it is painful.

sections.title: Sagas
paragraphs: Each step commits locally; on failure, run compensations. Orchestration vs choreography styles. Idempotency is mandatory.

sections.title: Outbox pairing
paragraphs: Transactional outbox starts reliable saga messages. Without it, dual writes reopen the original consistency hole.

sections.title: Choosing
paragraphs: Prefer single-service transactions when possible. Use sagas for long business workflows. Reserve 2PC for tightly controlled homogeneous systems.

lessons.title: Distributed Systems Fundamentals
lessons.summary: Distributed systems are fundamentally different from single-machine systems: nodes fail independently, networks are unreliable, clocks drift, and there is no shared memory. The core challenge is building reliable behavior from unreliable components. Understanding the impossibility results (CAP, FLP), consensus algorithms, and practical failure modes is prerequisite knowledge for designing any system that runs on multiple machines.

sections.title: The Eight Fallacies of Distributed Computing
paragraphs: Peter Deutsch and James Gosling identified eight assumptions developers make when writing distributed systems that are invariably wrong: (1) The network is reliable. (2) Latency is zero. (3) Bandwidth is infinite. (4) The network is secure. (5) Topology doesn't change. (6) There is one administrator. (7) Transport cost is zero. (8) The network is homogeneous. Each fallacy represents a failure mode that will eventually manifest in production. The fundamental difference between a monolith and a distributed system is that the monolith calls a function and always gets a response; a distributed service call may succeed, fail, timeout, or succeed-but-the-response-is-lost.

The partial failure problem is the defining challenge. In a monolith, a crash fails everything. In a distributed system, a subset of components fail while others continue. A database write may succeed while the acknowledgment is lost in transit—the client doesn't know whether the write happened. A network partition may separate nodes that were previously coordinating, leaving each half unsure whether the other half is down or just unreachable. These partial failure scenarios require explicit handling; there is no automatic recovery mechanism.

The two generals problem (and its generalization, the Byzantine Generals Problem) proves that reliable communication over an unreliable channel is impossible without additional assumptions. Two armies must coordinate an attack, but their only communication is via messengers who may be captured. No matter how many acknowledgment rounds are exchanged, there is always uncertainty. This theoretical result has practical implications: TCP cannot guarantee delivery over an unreliable network; application protocols must design for acknowledged message loss.
bullets: Network is NOT reliable: messages are lost, delayed, duplicated, reordered
Partial failure: some nodes fail while others continue; hardest failure mode to handle
Two Generals: reliable communication over unreliable channel is impossible in theory
Design for failure, not against it: assume any component can fail at any time

sections.title: CAP Theorem: Consistency, Availability, Partition Tolerance
paragraphs: The CAP theorem (Brewer, 2000; formally proved by Gilbert and Lynch, 2002) states that a distributed data store can provide at most two of three properties: Consistency (every read receives the most recent write or an error), Availability (every request receives a non-error response, though it may not be the latest data), and Partition Tolerance (the system continues operating despite network partitions). Since network partitions are inevitable in real distributed systems, the practical choice is between CP (sacrifice availability during partitions) and AP (sacrifice consistency during partitions).

CP systems (HBase, ZooKeeper, etcd) refuse requests when they cannot guarantee consistency during a partition. ZooKeeper's read-your-own-writes guarantee requires that reads go to the leader or a majority; during a partition, minority nodes stop serving reads. This prevents serving stale data at the cost of availability. AP systems (Cassandra, DynamoDB, CouchDB) continue serving requests during partitions but may serve stale or conflicting data. When the partition heals, conflicting writes must be reconciled via last-write-wins, vector clocks, or CRDTs.

The PACELC model (Daniel Abadi, 2012) extends CAP by noting that even without partitions, there is always a trade-off between latency (L) and consistency (C). Systems optimized for consistency incur higher latency because they require coordination across replicas before responding. Systems optimized for latency respond from local state without coordination. PACELC gives a more nuanced picture: a database that is available during partitions (AP) might still offer low latency/high consistency trade-offs in the normal case.
bullets: CAP: pick 2 of Consistency, Availability, Partition Tolerance; in practice choose CP or AP
CP: refuse requests on minority partition; ZooKeeper, etcd, HBase
AP: serve potentially stale data during partition; Cassandra, DynamoDB, Riak
PACELC: even without partitions, latency vs consistency trade-off always exists

sections.title: Consensus: The Core Problem
paragraphs: Consensus is the problem of getting a group of nodes to agree on a single value—the cornerstone of distributed system correctness. Consensus is needed for leader election (which node is the primary?), distributed locks (which process holds the lock?), and replicated state machines (all nodes execute the same operations in the same order). The FLP impossibility result (Fischer, Lynch, Paterson, 1985) proves that no deterministic consensus algorithm can guarantee both safety (all nodes agree on the same value) and liveness (the algorithm always terminates) in an asynchronous system with even one faulty process.

Practical consensus algorithms resolve the FLP dilemma by weakening the liveness guarantee: they guarantee termination only when the network is stable (no ongoing failures). Paxos (Lamport, 1989) is the foundational algorithm; it is correct but notoriously difficult to implement correctly. Raft (Ongaro and Ousterhout, 2014) was designed for understandability: leader election, log replication, and cluster membership changes are separated into well-defined sub-protocols. etcd, CockroachDB, and InfluxDB use Raft. ZooKeeper uses Zab (a Paxos variant).

In practice, you rarely implement consensus yourself—you use etcd, ZooKeeper, or Consul as a consensus service. These provide distributed locks, leader election, and configuration coordination as primitives. The critical operational concern: a consensus service requires a quorum (majority of nodes) to be available. A 3-node etcd cluster can tolerate 1 failure; a 5-node cluster can tolerate 2. Never run consensus services with fewer than 3 nodes in production, and never run an even number of nodes (even N has the same fault tolerance as N-1).
bullets: Consensus: getting all nodes to agree on one value; needed for leader election, locks, replication
FLP impossibility: no deterministic consensus algorithm guarantees both safety + liveness asynchronously
Paxos/Raft: practical algorithms; guarantee termination when network is stable
Quorum: majority of N nodes; 3-node tolerates 1 failure; 5-node tolerates 2

sections.title: Replication, Consistency Models, and Leader Election
paragraphs: Replication serves two purposes: availability (data is available from multiple nodes; one failure doesn't lose data or service) and read scalability (multiple replicas can handle read load in parallel). Single-leader replication is the most common model: one primary accepts writes; replicas apply changes asynchronously (or synchronously with higher latency). The primary is elected via a consensus algorithm or external coordinator. When the primary fails, a new primary must be elected—this is a critical moment for consistency.

Split-brain is the catastrophic failure mode in leader election: two nodes both believe they are the primary and accept conflicting writes. It occurs when the network partitions and both halves elect a new leader. Prevention: fencing tokens (monotonically increasing token issued by the consensus service; the old leader's fencing token is lower than the new leader's; storage systems reject writes from holders of lower tokens). STONITH (Shoot The Other Node In The Head): when a new leader is elected, the cluster sends a fence signal (cut power, revoke network access) to the old leader, ensuring it stops writing before the new leader starts.

Linearizability (the strongest consistency model) requires that operations on a distributed system appear to execute atomically and in real-time order. If write W completes before read R starts, R must return the value written by W (or a later write). Achieving linearizability requires coordination: every read must contact a quorum or the leader. Sequential consistency is weaker: operations appear in some valid sequential order, but not necessarily in real-time order. Eventual consistency is the weakest: all replicas converge to the same value eventually if writes stop.
bullets: Single-leader: primary accepts writes; replicas apply asynchronously; leader election needed on failure
Split-brain: two nodes both think they are primary; prevents using fencing tokens or STONITH
Linearizability: strongest consistency; operations appear atomic in real-time order
Eventual consistency: weakest; replicas converge eventually; allows temporary divergence

sections.title: Practical Failure Handling: Timeouts, Retries, and Idempotency
paragraphs: In a distributed system, a timeout means you don't know what happened. The request may have never arrived (safe to retry), arrived and succeeded but the response was lost (unsafe to retry—may duplicate), or is still in progress (retrying may cause two concurrent executions). This ambiguity is fundamental and cannot be resolved without additional information. Idempotency keys are the standard solution: include a unique identifier with the request; the server deduplicates based on this key and returns the same response for a repeated request regardless of whether the original succeeded.

Retry policies must implement exponential backoff with jitter. Immediate retries (or linear backoff) on transient failures cause thundering herd: if 10,000 clients all retry at the same interval, they simultaneously hammer the recovering service. Exponential backoff with jitter (random delay in range [0, 2^n × base]) spreads retries over time. Add a circuit breaker to stop retrying when a service is clearly failing—fast failure (fail immediately without waiting for timeout) prevents cascading failures where a downstream failure causes timeouts across all upstream services.

Distributed tracing (Zipkin, Jaeger, OpenTelemetry) is the essential observability tool for distributed systems. A trace ID propagated through all service calls connects all spans in a request path, allowing you to see where latency and errors originate. Without distributed tracing, debugging a request that touches 10 services is essentially impossible. Treat distributed tracing as a day-one infrastructure requirement, not an afterthought.
bullets: Timeout ambiguity: cannot distinguish 'failed before processing' from 'succeeded but response lost'
Idempotency key: deduplicate at server; safe to retry without double-processing
Exponential backoff with jitter: prevent thundering herd on retry storms
Circuit breaker: fail fast when downstream is clearly unavailable; prevent cascading failure

core.title: Fallacies and Partial Failure
paragraphs: The 8 fallacies: network is reliable, latency is zero, bandwidth infinite, network secure, topology static. All false. Partial failure is the core challenge: some nodes fail while others continue.
Timeout ambiguity: cannot know if the request succeeded or not. Idempotency keys allow safe retries.
Design for failure: assume any component fails; build systems that degrade gracefully.

core.title: CAP Theorem and Consensus
paragraphs: CAP: pick 2 of Consistency/Availability/Partition-Tolerance. Since partitions are inevitable, choose CP or AP.
Consensus (Raft/Paxos): all nodes agree on one value. Requires quorum. FLP: cannot guarantee both safety and liveness in async systems with failures.
etcd/ZooKeeper/Consul: use consensus as a service; don't implement yourself.

core.title: Failure Handling Patterns
paragraphs: Exponential backoff with jitter for retries; prevents thundering herd. Circuit breaker stops retrying a clearly-failing dependency.
Fencing tokens prevent split-brain: storage rejects writes from holders of stale tokens.
Distributed tracing: trace ID propagated across all service calls; essential for debugging.

deepDive.title: Vector Clocks and Causal Consistency
paragraphs: Lamport timestamps assign logical timestamps to events such that if event A causally precedes event B, then timestamp(A) < timestamp(B). Useful for establishing event ordering without synchronized clocks. However, Lamport timestamps don't capture concurrent events—if timestamp(A) < timestamp(B), A may have caused B, or they may be concurrent.

Vector clocks (one counter per node) capture causality precisely. A vector clock V_A < V_B iff for all i, V_A[i] <= V_B[i] and at least one is strictly less. Incomparable vector clocks indicate concurrent events that may conflict. DynamoDB uses vector clocks (versioned objects) to detect conflicting concurrent writes. When a conflict is detected, it is surfaced to the application for resolution (shopping cart merge uses set union; balance uses read-repair).

Causal consistency guarantees that causally related operations are seen in causal order by all processes. Causal+ consistency (used in COPS, Bayou) also ensures that conflicting operations are ordered consistently across all replicas. Causal consistency is weaker than linearizability (allows different replicas to diverge temporarily) but stronger than eventual consistency (guarantees causal ordering). It achieves better availability than linearizability while providing stronger guarantees than eventual consistency.

deepDive.title: Byzantine Fault Tolerance
paragraphs: Byzantine faults are nodes that behave arbitrarily—sending contradictory messages, forging messages, or acting maliciously. Byzantine Fault Tolerant (BFT) consensus requires 3f+1 nodes to tolerate f Byzantine faults (vs 2f+1 for crash-fault-tolerant). PBFT (Practical Byzantine Fault Tolerance) is the foundational algorithm; Tendermint and HotStuff are modern BFT protocols used in blockchain systems.

BFT is rarely needed in private datacenter deployments where node compromise is unlikely and crash faults (hardware/software failures) dominate. It is essential for public blockchain networks where nodes are operated by untrusted parties. The overhead is significant: BFT requires O(n^2) message complexity vs O(n) for CFT; this limits practical BFT cluster sizes to tens of nodes. For most distributed systems, crash-fault-tolerant consensus (Raft, Paxos) is appropriate.

expert.title: Expert: Spanner's TrueTime and External Consistency
paragraphs: Google Spanner achieves external consistency (a form of linearizability across geographically distributed shards) using TrueTime, a globally synchronized clock API that provides a time interval [earliest, latest] with guaranteed error bounds of <7ms. When a transaction commits, Spanner waits for TrueTime uncertainty to pass (commit-wait) before returning to the client. This ensures that any subsequent transaction (which starts after the commit returns) has a timestamp strictly greater than the committed transaction's timestamp, establishing a global causal order.

TrueTime relies on GPS receivers and atomic clocks in every Google data center, plus a carefully maintained time synchronization infrastructure. The bounded uncertainty (< 7ms) is the key: it limits commit-wait time to <7ms, making the external consistency overhead acceptable. No other cloud provider publicly offers an equivalent. CockroachDB approximates TrueTime with NTP-based hybrid logical clocks (HLC), accepting slightly weaker guarantees. Aurora DSQL (AWS 2024) uses a similar commit-wait approach.

examples.title: Google Chubby and Distributed Locking
examples.description: Google Chubby (described in the 2006 OSDI paper) is a distributed lock service built on Paxos consensus. It provides coarse-grained locks (held for minutes to hours, not microseconds) for leader election and file distribution across Google's services. The key design insight: Chubby is not designed for high throughput; it is designed for extremely high availability of a small service (5 replicas) that rarely changes. This tradeoff enables simple, correct implementation.

examples.title: Amazon DynamoDB Eventual Consistency
examples.description: DynamoDB's default read model is eventually consistent: reads may return data that is 1–2 seconds stale after a write. For use cases where this is acceptable (reading a user's preference settings), eventual consistency reads are cheaper and faster. DynamoDB also offers strongly consistent reads (read from the leader) at 2x the cost and with higher latency. This explicit trade-off exposure—letting the application choose consistency per read operation—is a model design pattern for user-facing consistency APIs.

keyTakeaways: Partial failure is the defining challenge of distributed systems; design for it explicitly
CAP theorem: since partitions are inevitable, you choose between consistency and availability
Consensus (Raft/Paxos) is the foundation for leader election, distributed locks, and replicated state
Idempotency keys + exponential backoff + circuit breakers form the standard retry safety stack
Linearizability is the strongest consistency model; it requires coordination overhead
Use etcd/ZooKeeper as consensus services; run them in odd numbers (3 or 5)
lessons.whyItMatters: Distributed systems fundamentals underpin every modern infrastructure component: databases, caches, message queues, and coordination services all implement variants of consensus, replication, and consistency models. Senior engineers are expected to understand CAP, consistency levels, and failure patterns—and to design systems that handle partial failures gracefully rather than catastrophically.
reflectionQuestions: Your service makes a payment API call that times out. What do you do next, and what must be true about the payment API for your retry to be safe?
A ZooKeeper-based leader election system is experiencing split-brain. Walk through the failure scenario and two mitigations.
Explain the trade-off you are making by choosing Cassandra (AP) over PostgreSQL (CP) for a user activity store.
Design a distributed counter that can be safely incremented from 100 servers simultaneously.

etcd write latency: 1–10ms within a data center; 100–300ms cross-region

sections.title: What Gossip & Membership is solving

sections.title: Core mechanics
paragraphs: Mechanically, Gossip & Membership involves a small set of moving parts: inputs, state, an algorithm or protocol, and outputs/side effects. Draw those parts explicitly. lessons.title: Raft Deep Dive
lessons.summary: Raft elects a leader and replicates a log for consensus. Understanding elections, terms, log matching, and commit rules is essential for etcd, Consul, and many coordination services.

sections.title: Roles and terms
paragraphs: Nodes are followers, candidates, or leaders. Terms are monotonically increasing eras. A leader for a term handles client writes and replicates log entries.
Heartbeats reset election timers. If followers time out, they become candidates and request votes. Majority wins; otherwise term increments and retry.

sections.title: Log replication
paragraphs: Clients write to the leader. Entries are appended locally then sent to followers. An entry is committed when stored on a majority; then applied to the state machine.
The log matching property ensures consistency: if two logs have the same index and term, prior entries match. Conflicts are resolved by overwriting follower suffixes.

sections.title: Safety and availability
paragraphs: Raft remains available with majority. A network partition that isolates the leader causes a new election on the majority side; the old leader steps down on seeing a higher term.
Membership changes need careful joint consensus. Mis-managed reconfiguration is a common outage class in real clusters.

sections.title: Using Raft in designs
paragraphs: Put Raft where you need strong leadership and a replicated log: metadata, configuration, small coordination state — not bulk data paths.
etcd uses Raft for Kubernetes state; if you embed Raft, budget for disk fsync latency on the log.

sections.title: What NCCL & Collective Communication is solving
paragraphs: NCCL & Collective Communication exists because naive designs around multi-GPU/multi-node training systems break under scale, partial failure, or changing requirements. Before choosing tools, name the problem: which resource is scarce, which invariant must hold, and which user-visible failures are unacceptable.

In interviews and production reviews, strong answers start with constraints (QPS, data size, latency budget, consistency needs) and only then map NCCL & Collective Communication onto those constraints.

A useful mental model separates the control plane (how you configure and observe NCCL & Collective Communication) from the data plane (the per-request/per-event path). Confusing the two leads to architectures that look neat and operate poorly.

sections.title: Core mechanics
paragraphs: Mechanically, NCCL & Collective Communication involves a small set of moving parts: inputs, state, an algorithm or protocol, and outputs/side effects. Draw those parts explicitly. If state is replicated, write down the replication/consistency rule. If work is asynchronous, write down delivery semantics.

Performance characteristics usually come from amplification (how much internal work per external request), locality (whether work stays on one node), and contention (locks, hot keys, leader bottlenecks).

Correctness characteristics usually come from failure handling: retries, timeouts, idempotency, and what clients observe during failover. If you cannot explain the failure story, you do not yet understand NCCL & Collective Communication.

sections.title: Designing with it
paragraphs: When incorporating NCCL & Collective Communication into a system, decide the API boundary first: what does a client call, what can fail, and what is retried. Keep the happy path boring and push complexity into well-tested libraries or platform components.

sections.title: Operations and failure modes

lessons.title: Continuous Batching & Paged Attention
lessons.summary: Continuous batching keeps GPUs busy by admitting new requests as others finish tokens. Paged attention makes the KV memory layout practical at high concurrency.

sections.title: From static to continuous batching
paragraphs: Static batching waits for an entire batch to finish before admitting new work — short requests pad behind long ones. Continuous (iteration-level) batching schedules at each decode step, so finished sequences free slots immediately.

The scheduler must account for KV memory, fairness, and latency SLOs. Without memory awareness, admitting too many sequences causes OOM; without fairness, long generations starve short interactive requests.

sections.title: Paged attention
paragraphs: Paged attention stores KV in non-contiguous blocks tracked by a block table, similar to OS virtual memory. This cuts waste from reserving max-context contiguous buffers per sequence and enables sharing blocks for identical prefixes.

lessons.title: Prefill/Decode Disaggregation
lessons.summary: LLM inference has two phases with different bottlenecks: prefill (compute-heavy prompt processing) and decode (memory-bandwidth heavy token generation). Disaggregating them onto specialized pools can raise utilization — at the cost of KV transfer complexity.

sections.title: Two phases, two bottlenecks
paragraphs: Prefill processes the prompt in parallel-friendly matmuls — often compute bound. Decode generates one token at a time while reading a growing KV cache — often memory-bandwidth bound.
A single mixed batch forces GPUs to compromise. Long prompts stall short interactive decodes and vice versa.

sections.title: Disaggregation idea
paragraphs: Run prefill on compute-optimized nodes; ship KV cache (or references) to decode nodes optimized for bandwidth and concurrency. Schedulers route based on phase.
The hard part is KV transfer latency, memory ownership, and failure handling mid-request.

sections.title: When it pays off
paragraphs: Workloads with long prompts and moderate output lengths, or highly variable mixes, benefit most. Short prompt/short output chat may not justify the complexity.
Measure GPU goodput, KV bytes moved, and p99 end-to-end — not just theoretical FLOPs.

sections.title: Design checklist
paragraphs: Define SLOs separately for time-to-first-token and inter-token latency. Autoscaling signals should include KV memory and queue time per phase.

paragraphs: Mechanically, Autoscaling Signals & Policies involves a small set of moving parts: inputs, state, an algorithm or protocol, and outputs/side effects. Draw those parts explicitly. If state is replicated, write down the replication/consistency rule. If work is asynchronous, write down delivery semantics.

Performance characteristics usually come from amplification (how much internal work per external request), locality (whether work stays on one node), and contention (locks, hot keys, leader bottlenecks).

Correctness characteristics usually come from failure handling: retries, timeouts, idempotency, and what clients observe during failover. If you cannot explain the failure story, you do not yet understand Autoscaling Signals & Policies.
bullets: Inputs → state/protocol → outputs/side effects
Name consistency and delivery guarantees
Identify the bottleneck resource early

core.title: Designing with it
paragraphs: When incorporating Autoscaling Signals & Policies into a system, decide the API boundary first: what does a client call, what can fail, and what is retried. Keep the happy path boring and push complexity into well-tested libraries or platform components.

Capacity plan with numbers: estimate peak load, working set, and headroom. Convert that into shard counts, cache sizes, thread/connection pools, or GPU/memory budgets as relevant to Autoscaling Signals & Policies.
Prefer reversible rollout: feature flags, dual-running, shadow traffic, and clear dashboards. New uses of Autoscaling Signals & Policies should be observable on day one.

core.title: Operations and failure modes
paragraphs: Operate Autoscaling Signals & Policies with SLIs that match user pain (availability, latency, lag, error rate, cost). Alert on burn rates and queue/lag growth, not only host CPU.
Common failures include overload without admission control, retry amplification, silent staleness, schema mismatches, and dependency brownouts. Write a runbook for the top three.
Chaos and game days should include slow dependencies and network delay, not only hard kills. Autoscaling Signals & Policies often fails in the gray area.

deepDive.title: Autoscaling Signals & Policies — deeper internals
paragraphs: Under the hood, Autoscaling Signals & Policies typically exposes knobs for batching, buffering, concurrency, retention, and timeouts. Each knob trades latency, throughput, and cost. Change one at a time and measure.

Instrumentation should include high-signal histograms and exemplars that jump to traces. For data systems, watch amplification and compaction/GC; for RPC systems, watch queue time and saturation; for ML systems, watch memory and tokens/s.
bullets: One knob at a time with a hypothesis
Histograms > averages
Tie dashboards to runbooks

deepDive.title: Autoscaling Signals & Policies — integration patterns
paragraphs: Integrate via stable contracts: schemas, idempotency keys, and versioned APIs. Dual-write carefully or prefer CDC/outbox patterns when crossing storage and messaging.
Boundary tests should prove behavior under duplicate delivery, reordering, and clock skew where relevant to Autoscaling Signals & Policies.

expert.title: Autoscaling Signals & Policies — multi-region and cost
paragraphs: Across regions, RTT and quorum placement dominate. Keep user-critical paths region-local when invariants allow; replicate asynchronously otherwise. Spell out the conflict/staleness model.
Track unit economics for Autoscaling Signals & Policies: cost per million requests, per GB stored, or per million tokens. Many scalability projects are cost projects — make the objective explicit.
