lessons.title: Schema Evolution & Contracts
lessons.summary: Schema Evolution & Contracts is a core topic in modern system design. This lesson builds a first-principles model around delivery semantics, ordering, and consumer lag, then connects that model to capacity, failure modes, and operational practice so you can use it in real architectures.

sections.title: What Schema Evolution & Contracts is solving
paragraphs: Schema Evolution & Contracts exists because naive designs around delivery semantics, ordering, and consumer lag break under scale, partial failure, or changing requirements. Before choosing tools, name the problem: which resource is scarce, which invariant must hold, and which user-visible failures are unacceptable.
In interviews and production reviews, strong answers start with constraints (QPS, data size, latency budget, consistency needs) and only then map Schema Evolution & Contracts onto those constraints.

A useful mental model separates the control plane (how you configure and observe Schema Evolution & Contracts) from the data plane (the per-request/per-event path). Confusing the two leads to architectures that look neat and operate poorly.

sections.title: Core mechanics
paragraphs: Mechanically, Schema Evolution & Contracts involves a small set of moving parts: inputs, state, an algorithm or protocol, and outputs/side effects. Draw those parts explicitly. If state is replicated, write down the replication/consistency rule. If work is asynchronous, write down delivery semantics.

Performance characteristics usually come from amplification (how much internal work per external request), locality (whether work stays on one node), and contention (locks, hot keys, leader bottlenecks).

Correctness characteristics usually come from failure handling: retries, timeouts, idempotency, and what clients observe during failover. If you cannot explain the failure story, you do not yet understand Schema Evolution & Contracts.
bullets: Inputs → state/protocol → outputs/side effects
Name consistency and delivery guarantees
Identify the bottleneck resource early

sections.title: Designing with it
paragraphs: When incorporating Schema Evolution & Contracts into a system, decide the API boundary first: what does a client call, what can fail, and what is retried. Keep the happy path boring and push complexity into well-tested libraries or platform components.

Capacity plan with numbers: estimate peak load, working set, and headroom. Convert that into shard counts, cache sizes, thread/connection pools, or GPU/memory budgets as relevant to Schema Evolution & Contracts.
Prefer reversible rollout: feature flags, dual-running, shadow traffic, and clear dashboards. New uses of Schema Evolution & Contracts should be observable on day one.

sections.title: Operations and failure modes
paragraphs: Operate Schema Evolution & Contracts with SLIs that match user pain (availability, latency, lag, error rate, cost). Alert on burn rates and queue/lag growth, not only host CPU.
Common failures include overload without admission control, retry amplification, silent staleness, schema mismatches, and dependency brownouts. Write a runbook for the top three.
Chaos and game days should include slow dependencies and network delay, not only hard kills. Schema Evolution & Contracts often fails in the gray area.

paragraphs: Under the hood, Schema Evolution & Contracts typically exposes knobs for batching, buffering, concurrency, retention, and timeouts. Each knob trades latency, throughput, and cost. Change one at a time and measure.

Instrumentation should include high-signal histograms and exemplars that jump to traces. For data systems, watch amplification and compaction/GC; for RPC systems, watch queue time and saturation; for ML systems, watch memory and tokens/s.

expert.title: Schema Evolution & Contracts — multi-region and cost
paragraphs: Across regions, RTT and quorum placement dominate. Keep user-critical paths region-local when invariants allow; replicate asynchronously otherwise. Spell out the conflict/staleness model.
Track unit economics for Schema Evolution & Contracts: cost per million requests, per GB stored, or per million tokens. Many scalability projects are cost projects — make the objective explicit.

lessons.title: Stream Processing
lessons.summary: Stream processing computes results over unbounded data streams in real time—or near-real time—as events arrive, rather than waiting to batch them. It enables fraud detection, real-time analytics, live dashboards, and event-driven microservices. Apache Flink, Kafka Streams, and Spark Structured Streaming are the dominant frameworks, each making different trade-offs between latency, throughput, and consistency.

sections.title: Stream Processing vs Batch Processing
paragraphs: Batch processing operates on a bounded, finite dataset: load yesterday's orders, compute revenue by category, write the result. It runs periodically (hourly, daily) and produces results with latency proportional to the batch interval. Stream processing operates on an unbounded, continuously arriving dataset: compute revenue by category over a sliding 1-hour window, updated every second. The result is always current, with latency measured in milliseconds to seconds rather than hours.

The fundamental shift is from pull (batch job reads all data, computes, finishes) to push (events arrive continuously; the stream processor maintains state and updates results as events arrive). This requires different primitives: windowing (how to group time-based streams into finite chunks for aggregation), state management (keeping running counts, averages, and aggregates between events), and time semantics (what does 'events in the last hour' mean when events arrive late due to network delays?).

Lambda Architecture (batch layer + speed layer + serving layer) was the original answer to needing both real-time and accurate historical results. Batch layer computes accurate results on historical data; speed layer computes approximate results on the latest data; serving layer merges both. The complexity of maintaining two separate codebases (batch and streaming) has led to the Kappa Architecture: a single streaming system that can reprocess historical data by replaying from Kafka. This is the current industry direction.
bullets: Batch: bounded data, periodic, latency in hours; Streaming: unbounded, continuous, latency in ms–s
Stream primitives: windowing, stateful operators, time semantics
Lambda: batch + speed layer; complex; largely superseded by Kappa (unified streaming)
Kappa: single Kafka-based streaming pipeline; reprocess by replaying from beginning

sections.title: Time Semantics: Event Time vs Processing Time
paragraphs: Event time is when the event actually occurred (embedded in the event's timestamp). Processing time is when the stream processor receives and processes the event. These differ because events travel over networks, may be buffered on mobile devices, and may arrive late due to retries. A mobile app that records user behavior offline may upload events hours after they occurred. If you window by processing time, offline events appear in the wrong window—your 'events in the last hour' query is actually 'events processed in the last hour,' which may include yesterday's offline events.

Flink, Kafka Streams, and Spark Structured Streaming all support event-time processing. The key mechanism is the watermark: a signal from the streaming system that says 'I believe all events with event_time before T have now arrived.' When the watermark passes T, windows closing at T can safely be computed and emitted. The watermark is typically derived from the maximum event timestamp seen minus a configurable delay (the allowed lateness). Setting allowed lateness too low drops late-arriving events; setting it too high delays window completion.

Late events are events that arrive after their window's watermark has passed. Options: (1) Drop them—simplest, some data loss. (2) Emit an updated result when late events arrive (Flink's side outputs; a correction message). (3) Extend the window's allowed lateness. For fraud detection (needs immediate results) or operational monitoring (latency over accuracy), processing time semantics may be acceptable. For billing, analytics, and anything where accuracy matters over long windows, event time with appropriate allowed lateness is correct.
bullets: Event time: when event occurred; embedded in event payload; correct for analytics
Processing time: when processor receives event; simpler; incorrect for late-arriving events
Watermark: signal that all events before timestamp T have arrived; enables window completion
Allowed lateness: how long to wait for late events; trade-off between accuracy and latency

sections.title: Windowing: Grouping Streams into Computations
paragraphs: Tumbling windows divide time into fixed, non-overlapping intervals: 1-minute windows from 00:00–01:00, 01:00–02:00, etc. Each event belongs to exactly one window. Use for metrics that should not overlap: 'requests per minute,' 'revenue per hour.' Sliding windows have a fixed length and slide at a fixed interval: a 10-minute window sliding every 1 minute creates windows that overlap by 9 minutes. Each event appears in multiple windows. Use for continuously updated metrics: 'average response time over the last 10 minutes, computed every minute.'

Session windows group events by user activity: a session window opens when the first event from a user arrives and closes after a configurable idle gap (e.g., 30 minutes of inactivity). Sessions have variable length. This is natural for user journey analytics: 'number of page views per user session.' Flink's session window implementation assigns events to sessions dynamically, merging sessions when new events bridge two previously separate sessions.

Global windows collect all events into a single window; a custom trigger defines when to fire. This is the most flexible but requires careful trigger design. For example: accumulate events until a watermark is reached (collect everything until the stream thinks it's complete) or trigger every N events. Flink's trigger API is a low-level but powerful mechanism for custom windowing semantics beyond the standard tumbling/sliding/session windows.
bullets: Tumbling: non-overlapping fixed intervals; each event in one window; for 'per period' metrics
Sliding: overlapping windows; each event in multiple windows; for 'over last N' metrics
Session: variable-length; idle gap closes window; for user journey analysis
Global window: custom trigger; most flexible; requires careful trigger design

sections.title: Apache Flink: Stateful Stream Processing
paragraphs: Apache Flink is the production standard for stateful stream processing. Flink operators maintain state (counts, aggregations, keyed windows) in managed state backends: RocksDB (spills to disk; handles terabytes of state) or memory (faster; limited by RAM). State is partitioned by key (same key always goes to the same operator instance), enabling parallel stateful computation without coordination. Flink's checkpointing mechanism periodically snapshots all operator state to durable storage (S3), enabling recovery from failure without data loss.

Flink's exactly-once semantics are achieved via two-phase commit with Kafka. Flink operators buffer output during checkpoint; when all operators complete a checkpoint, Flink commits the Kafka offsets and flushes output atomically. If a failure occurs between checkpoints, Flink restores the last checkpoint, replays events from Kafka from the saved offset, and recomputes—no duplicates because outputs after the last checkpoint are discarded. This transactional commitment model is what makes Flink's exactly-once semantics meaningful.

Flink's Job Manager (job coordination, checkpointing) and Task Managers (operator execution) are separate processes. A Flink cluster can run as a Kubernetes StatefulSet; task manager pods scale horizontally. For production, Flink's savepoints (manual checkpoints) enable version migrations: pause the job, take a savepoint, upgrade the code, restart from the savepoint. This upgrade mechanism is Flink's operational advantage over streaming systems that cannot be paused and resumed with state.
bullets: Flink state backends: RocksDB (disk; terabyte state) or heap memory (fast; RAM-limited)
Checkpointing: periodic state snapshot to S3; enables exactly-once fault recovery
Exactly-once via 2PC with Kafka: atomic offset commit + output flush on checkpoint completion
Savepoints: manual checkpoints for version migration; pause, upgrade, restart from state

sections.title: Kafka Streams and Spark Structured Streaming
paragraphs: Kafka Streams is a client library (not a separate cluster) for stream processing within Kafka. Stateful operators (joins, aggregations, windowed computations) store state in RocksDB on the application's local disk, backed by Kafka changelog topics. No external cluster is needed—it runs inside your existing Java application. Kafka Streams is excellent for microservice-local stream processing where you don't want to operate Flink or Spark, and for simple to medium complexity transformations. It lacks Flink's sophisticated event-time semantics and advanced windowing, but is simpler operationally.

Spark Structured Streaming is a micro-batch streaming model: Spark processes data in small batches (default 100ms trigger interval). Each micro-batch is a complete Spark SQL query on the latest arriving data. This gives you the full Spark SQL ecosystem (joins, aggregations, UDFs, ML model inference) with streaming semantics. Latency is higher than Flink (100ms–seconds vs milliseconds) but throughput per core is very high for wide-row transformations. The continuous processing mode (beta) reduces latency to <1ms per record.

Choosing between Flink, Kafka Streams, and Spark Structured Streaming: Kafka Streams for simple stateful in-process streaming; Spark for ML inference and complex SQL transformations where latency > 1 second is acceptable; Flink for sub-second latency, complex event-time semantics, or terabytes of operator state. All three integrate natively with Kafka as the input/output system and Iceberg/Delta Lake for batch output.
bullets: Kafka Streams: client library; runs in-process; no external cluster; simpler ops; good for microservices
Spark Structured Streaming: micro-batch; full Spark SQL; latency 100ms–seconds; great for ML + SQL
Flink: sub-second latency; sophisticated event-time; terabyte state; production standard for critical pipelines
All three integrate with Kafka as source/sink and Iceberg/Delta Lake for batch output

core.title: Stream vs Batch and Time Semantics
paragraphs: Stream processing: continuous, unbounded data, low latency. Batch: bounded, periodic, high latency. Kappa Architecture unifies both with a single streaming pipeline.
Event time vs processing time: event time is when it happened; processing time is when the system processes it. Event time is correct for analytics; requires watermarks.
Watermarks mark that all events before timestamp T have arrived; used to close windows safely. Allowed lateness handles stragglers.

core.title: Windowing
paragraphs: Tumbling windows: non-overlapping fixed intervals; each event in one window.
Sliding windows: overlapping; each event in multiple windows; for running averages.
Session windows: variable-length; idle gap closes window; for user sessions.

core.title: Flink vs Kafka Streams vs Spark
paragraphs: Flink: sub-second, event-time, exactly-once via 2PC, terabyte state, production standard.
Kafka Streams: in-process library, no external cluster, good for microservices, simpler operations.
Spark Structured Streaming: micro-batch, full SQL, ML integration, latency 100ms+.

deepDive.title: Stateful Processing and Exactly-Once Guarantees
paragraphs: Stateful stream processing maintains running state across events: counts, averages, keyed aggregations, join tables. State must be durable to survive failures. Flink's RocksDB backend spills to local SSD and backs up to S3 via incremental checkpoints. Incremental checkpointing only writes the state delta since the last checkpoint, dramatically reducing checkpoint size for large-state applications.

Exactly-once semantics require atomic commitment of consumer offset advancement + state update + output production. Flink achieves this by injecting Chandy-Lamport checkpoint barriers into the data stream. Each source injects a barrier; barriers flow through the operator DAG; when an operator receives a barrier from all its inputs, it snapshots its state and passes the barrier downstream. When all sinks have received the barrier, the checkpoint completes atomically.

Idempotent sinks are an alternative to true exactly-once: design the sink to handle duplicate writes safely. For Kafka sinks, idempotent producers deduplicate at the broker. For database sinks, upsert-on-primary-key handles duplicates. For HTTP sinks, idempotency keys ensure duplicate requests are ignored. At-least-once + idempotent sinks is operationally simpler than exactly-once and achieves the same correctness guarantee.

deepDive.title: Stream-Table Duality and Joins
paragraphs: In Kafka Streams and Flink, the stream-table duality is a core concept. A stream is an unbounded sequence of events; a table is the current state derived from a stream (the latest value per key). A KTable in Kafka Streams is a materialized view of a stream: for key K, the table holds the value from the most recent message with key K. Joining a stream with a table enriches each stream event with lookup data (like a hash join against a lookup table in SQL).

Stream-stream joins require both streams to be windowed: 'join order events with payment events where both have the same order_id and occurred within 10 minutes.' Flink maintains a time-bounded state for each stream (all order events in the last 10 minutes) and matches arriving events against the state. The window bounds must be large enough to tolerate event delivery latency. Unbounded stream joins would accumulate state forever—always use a window on stream-stream joins.

expert.title: Expert: Backfill and Historical Reprocessing
paragraphs: One of streaming's operational challenges is reprocessing: when you fix a bug in a streaming job, you need to recompute results for the past N days. With Kafka's configurable retention (up to years), you can replay from the beginning of history. The challenge is state: your stateful operators may accumulate state from the beginning of time, requiring memory/disk proportional to the full history.

Strategies for large-scale reprocessing: bounded reprocessing windows (reprocess only the last 90 days, then bootstrap from a snapshot), state bootstrapping from a batch source (precompute initial state from a data warehouse, then start the streaming job from that initialized state rather than from empty), and dual-writing (run old and new logic in parallel, compare outputs, switch over when new logic is validated). Flink's State Processor API allows reading and writing Flink savepoints from Spark or Flink batch jobs, enabling programmatic state initialization.

Flink checkpoint: periodic state snapshot to S3; enables exactly-once fault recovery

Set allowed lateness to cover the 99th percentile of event delivery latency for your data sources
Monitor Flink checkpoint duration; alert when checkpoints take longer than their interval

Watermarks too aggressive—late events dropped; results are silently incomplete
Unbounded stream-stream joins accumulating infinite state—always bound joins with time windows

Event ordering assumption with parallel consumers—parallel Kafka consumption destroys per-partition order

examples.title: Uber's Real-Time Surge Pricing
examples.description: Uber computes surge pricing using a Flink streaming pipeline. Driver location pings and ride requests flow through Kafka; Flink maintains a geo-keyed stateful operator computing supply/demand ratios over sliding 5-minute windows for each geographic hexbin. When demand exceeds supply by a threshold, the surge multiplier is updated and published to a serving layer. Event-time processing ensures that GPS pings that arrive late (poor cellular connectivity) land in the correct time window.

examples.title: LinkedIn's Kafka Streams for Notifications
examples.description: LinkedIn uses Kafka Streams to aggregate user activity events (views, likes, comments) and determine which users to notify with a 'You have new activity' email. The stream processes tens of billions of events per day in-process within the notification service, without a separate Flink cluster. Session windowing detects the end of a user's activity burst to trigger a summary notification rather than spamming one email per event.

keyTakeaways: Stream processing enables real-time analytics and fraud detection at millisecond-to-second latency
Event-time processing with watermarks is correct for analytics; processing-time is simpler but inaccurate
Flink's checkpointing enables exactly-once fault recovery; savepoints enable version migrations
Kafka Streams is the right choice for microservice-local streaming; Flink for complex cross-service pipelines
Windowing (tumbling/sliding/session) groups unbounded streams into finite computations
At-least-once + idempotent sinks achieves exactly-once correctness with simpler operational model
lessons.whyItMatters: Real-time processing is a distinguishing feature in competitive products. Fraud detection, live dashboards, recommendation updates, and event-driven microservices all require stream processing. Understanding the trade-offs between Flink, Kafka Streams, and Spark Structured Streaming—and when to use event time vs processing time—separates engineers who can design production streaming systems from those who can only operate batch pipelines.

lessons.title: Queues, Pub/Sub & Event Streaming
lessons.summary: Messaging decouples producers from consumers in time and space, enabling async processing, resilience, and event-driven architectures. Point-to-point queues, pub/sub fan-out, and durable event logs each solve different problems — with distinct delivery guarantees that your application must handle explicitly.

sections.title: Why Messaging Matters
paragraphs: Synchronous request-response ties the caller's fate to the callee's availability and latency. If the email service is slow, the signup API waits — or times out. Messaging introduces a buffer: the producer publishes a message and continues; the consumer processes it when ready.

Messaging enables load leveling (spiky traffic absorbed by a queue), service decoupling (producers do not know consumers), geographic distribution, and reliable retry without blocking users. Event-driven architectures treat state changes as facts that multiple services react to independently.
The cost is complexity: delivery semantics, ordering guarantees, poison messages, schema evolution, and observability across async boundaries are harder than synchronous calls.

sections.title: Point-to-Point Queues
paragraphs: A message queue delivers each message to exactly one consumer (competing consumers model). RabbitMQ, Amazon SQS, and Azure Service Bus implement this pattern. Ideal for task distribution: image processing, email sending, order fulfillment.

Queues provide natural load balancing — add more workers to drain faster. Messages persist until acknowledged (at-least-once) or until processed (with visibility timeouts in SQS). Dead Letter Queues (DLQ) capture messages that fail after max retries for manual inspection.
Ordering is generally per-queue, not global. FIFO queues (SQS FIFO) guarantee order within a message group at the cost of throughput. Design consumers to be idempotent because redelivery happens.

sections.title: Pub/Sub and Fan-Out
paragraphs: Publish/subscribe delivers one message to many subscribers. Google Pub/Sub, Amazon SNS, and Redis pub/sub fan out events to multiple interested services. A 'OrderPlaced' event might trigger inventory, shipping, analytics, and notification services simultaneously.

Pub/sub decouples event producers from the set of consumers — new subscribers can be added without changing the publisher. Message brokers handle subscription management and delivery retries per subscriber.
Ephemeral pub/sub (Redis) drops messages if no subscriber is listening. Durable pub/sub (Kafka, Google Pub/Sub) persists messages for later consumption — critical for reliability.

sections.title: Event Streaming with Kafka
paragraphs: Event streaming platforms (Apache Kafka, Apache Pulsar, Amazon Kinesis) store messages in an append-only, partitioned log. Consumers track their offset and can replay history — enabling event sourcing, audit trails, and reprocessing after bug fixes.

Kafka partitions provide ordering within a partition and parallel consumption across partitions. Partition key choice (e.g., user_id) ensures related events stay ordered. Retention is time- or size-based, not consumption-based — multiple consumer groups read independently.

Kafka suits high-throughput event pipelines: click streams, CDC, log aggregation, and microservice choreography. Operational complexity is higher than SQS — you manage brokers, partitions, and consumer lag.

sections.title: Delivery Semantics and Idempotency
paragraphs: At-most-once: messages may be lost but never duplicated — fire and forget. At-least-once: messages are redelivered on failure — duplicates possible, consumers must be idempotent. Exactly-once: the holy grail — achieved in practice via idempotent consumers plus transactional outbox or Kafka transactions, not by the broker alone.

Design every consumer to handle duplicate messages: idempotency keys, upsert operations, or deduplication tables. Retry policies use exponential backoff with jitter to avoid synchronized retry storms.
Poison messages — permanently failing payloads — must route to DLQ after N attempts. Alert on DLQ depth. Never infinite retry loops that block queue processing.

core.title: Why Messaging Matters
paragraphs: Synchronous request-response ties the caller's fate to the callee's availability and latency. If the email service is slow, the signup API waits — or times out. Messaging introduces a buffer: the producer publishes a message and continues; the consumer processes it when ready.

Messaging enables load leveling (spiky traffic absorbed by a queue), service decoupling (producers do not know consumers), geographic distribution, and reliable retry without blocking users. Event-driven architectures treat state changes as facts that multiple services react to independently.
The cost is complexity: delivery semantics, ordering guarantees, poison messages, schema evolution, and observability across async boundaries are harder than synchronous calls.

deepDive.title: Queues, Pub/Sub & Event Streaming — Operational deep dive
paragraphs: Operating Queues, Pub/Sub & Event Streaming well means defining the scarce resource (CPU, memory, disk, network, or tokens), the SLIs that reflect user pain, and the knobs that trade cost for latency.
Under load, measure amplification: how many bytes, RPCs, or disk writes you pay per user request. Prefetch and batch only when measurements show benefit — premature batching adds tail latency.
Failure drills should include dependency slowdown (not only hard down), clock skew, and disk full. Verify alerts, dashboards, and runbooks against those drills.

deepDive.title: Queues, Pub/Sub & Event Streaming — Correctness edges
paragraphs: Correctness edges around Queues, Pub/Sub & Event Streaming often appear at retries, partial writes, and schema evolution. Make handlers idempotent and state transitions explicit.

Document what clients may observe during failover: stale reads, duplicate messages, or delayed visibility. If the product cannot tolerate an anomaly, enforce a stronger consistency boundary — and pay for it knowingly.

expert.title: Queues, Pub/Sub & Event Streaming — Expert / multi-region notes
paragraphs: At multi-region scale, Queues, Pub/Sub & Event Streaming interacts with RTT, quorum placement, and cost of cross-region replication. Prefer region-local user paths with asynchronous global state when invariants allow.
Cost envelopes matter: chart unit cost vs QPS and vs data size. Many 'performance' projects are actually cost projects in disguise — make the objective explicit.

examples.description: Checkout API writes order to PostgreSQL and an outbox row in one transaction. An outbox relay publishes OrderCreated to Kafka. lessons.title: Dataset Curation & Dedup
lessons.summary: Dataset Curation & Dedup is a core topic in modern system design. This lesson builds a first-principles model around datasets, features, and quality gates, then connects that model to capacity, failure modes, and operational practice so you can use it in real architectures.

sections.title: What Dataset Curation & Dedup is solving
paragraphs: Dataset Curation & Dedup exists because naive designs around datasets, features, and quality gates break under scale, partial failure, or changing requirements. Before choosing tools, name the problem: which resource is scarce, which invariant must hold, and which user-visible failures are unacceptable.
In interviews and production reviews, strong answers start with constraints (QPS, data size, latency budget, consistency needs) and only then map Dataset Curation & Dedup onto those constraints.

A useful mental model separates the control plane (how you configure and observe Dataset Curation & Dedup) from the data plane (the per-request/per-event path). Confusing the two leads to architectures that look neat and operate poorly.

sections.title: Core mechanics
paragraphs: Mechanically, Dataset Curation & Dedup involves a small set of moving parts: inputs, state, an algorithm or protocol, and outputs/side effects. Draw those parts explicitly. If state is replicated, write down the replication/consistency rule. If work is asynchronous, write down delivery semantics.

Performance characteristics usually come from amplification (how much internal work per external request), locality (whether work stays on one node), and contention (locks, hot keys, leader bottlenecks).

Correctness characteristics usually come from failure handling: retries, timeouts, idempotency, and what clients observe during failover. If you cannot explain the failure story, you do not yet understand Dataset Curation & Dedup.

Name consistency and delivery guarantees
Identify the bottleneck resource early

sections.title: Designing with it
paragraphs: When incorporating Dataset Curation & Dedup into a system, decide the API boundary first: what does a client call, what can fail, and what is retried. Keep the happy path boring and push complexity into well-tested libraries or platform components.

Capacity plan with numbers: estimate peak load, working set, and headroom. Convert that into shard counts, cache sizes, thread/connection pools, or GPU/memory budgets as relevant to Dataset Curation & Dedup.
Prefer reversible rollout: feature flags, dual-running, shadow traffic, and clear dashboards. New uses of Dataset Curation & Dedup should be observable on day one.

sections.title: Operations and failure modes
paragraphs: Operate Dataset Curation & Dedup with SLIs that match user pain (availability, latency, lag, error rate, cost). Alert on burn rates and queue/lag growth, not only host CPU.
Common failures include overload without admission control, retry amplification, silent staleness, schema mismatches, and dependency brownouts. Write a runbook for the top three.
Chaos and game days should include slow dependencies and network delay, not only hard kills. Dataset Curation & Dedup often fails in the gray area.

Before choosing tools, name the problem: which resource is scarce, which invariant must hold, and which user-visible failures are unacceptable.

In interviews and production reviews, strong answers start with constraints (QPS, data size, latency budget, consistency needs) and only then map Feature Stores & Tokenization at Scale onto those constraints.

A useful mental model separates the control plane (how you configure and observe Feature Stores & Tokenization at Scale) from the data plane (the per-request/per-event path). Confusing the two leads to architectures that look neat and operate poorly.

core.title: Core mechanics
paragraphs: Mechanically, Feature Stores & Tokenization at Scale involves a small set of moving parts: inputs, state, an algorithm or protocol, and outputs/side effects. Draw those parts explicitly. If state is replicated, write down the replication/consistency rule. If work is asynchronous, write down delivery semantics.

Performance characteristics usually come from amplification (how much internal work per external request), locality (whether work stays on one node), and contention (locks, hot keys, leader bottlenecks).

Correctness characteristics usually come from failure handling: retries, timeouts, idempotency, and what clients observe during failover. If you cannot explain the failure story, you do not yet understand Feature Stores & Tokenization at Scale.

core.title: Designing with it
paragraphs: When incorporating Feature Stores & Tokenization at Scale into a system, decide the API boundary first: what does a client call, what can fail, and what is retried. Keep the happy path boring and push complexity into well-tested libraries or platform components.

Capacity plan with numbers: estimate peak load, working set, and headroom. Convert that into shard counts, cache sizes, thread/connection pools, or GPU/memory budgets as relevant to Feature Stores & Tokenization at Scale.
Prefer reversible rollout: feature flags, dual-running, shadow traffic, and clear dashboards. New uses of Feature Stores & Tokenization at Scale should be observable on day one.

core.title: Operations and failure modes
paragraphs: Operate Feature Stores & Tokenization at Scale with SLIs that match user pain (availability, latency, lag, error rate, cost). Alert on burn rates and queue/lag growth, not only host CPU.
Common failures include overload without admission control, retry amplification, silent staleness, schema mismatches, and dependency brownouts. Write a runbook for the top three.
Chaos and game days should include slow dependencies and network delay, not only hard kills. Feature Stores & Tokenization at Scale often fails in the gray area.

deepDive.title: Feature Stores & Tokenization at Scale — deeper internals
paragraphs: Under the hood, Feature Stores & Tokenization at Scale typically exposes knobs for batching, buffering, concurrency, retention, and timeouts. Each knob trades latency, throughput, and cost. Change one at a time and measure.

Instrumentation should include high-signal histograms and exemplars that jump to traces. For data systems, watch amplification and compaction/GC; for RPC systems, watch queue time and saturation; for ML systems, watch memory and tokens/s.
bullets: One knob at a time with a hypothesis

Tie dashboards to runbooks

deepDive.title: Feature Stores & Tokenization at Scale — integration patterns
paragraphs: Integrate via stable contracts: schemas, idempotency keys, and versioned APIs. Dual-write carefully or prefer CDC/outbox patterns when crossing storage and messaging.
Boundary tests should prove behavior under duplicate delivery, reordering, and clock skew where relevant to Feature Stores & Tokenization at Scale.

expert.title: Feature Stores & Tokenization at Scale — multi-region and cost
paragraphs: Across regions, RTT and quorum placement dominate. Keep user-critical paths region-local when invariants allow; replicate asynchronously otherwise. Spell out the conflict/staleness model.

Track unit economics for Feature Stores & Tokenization at Scale: cost per million requests, per GB stored, or per million tokens. Many scalability projects are cost projects — make the objective explicit.

lessons.title: GPU Memory Hierarchy & Roofline
lessons.summary: GPU performance is often memory-bound. Understanding HBM, caches, and the roofline model lets you predict whether a kernel or LLM phase is limited by FLOPs or bandwidth — essential for training and inference sizing.

sections.title: Hierarchy overview
paragraphs: Registers, shared memory/L1, L2, HBM. Latency and bandwidth differ by orders of magnitude. Tensor Cores thrive on tiles that fit the hierarchy.

sections.title: Roofline thinking
paragraphs: Arithmetic intensity (FLOPs/byte) determines whether you hit compute roof or bandwidth roof. Attention decode often sits on the bandwidth roof because of KV reads.

sections.title: Multi-GPU
paragraphs: NVLink/NVSwitch vs PCIe vs IB for collectives. Topology awareness prevents hidden bottlenecks in all-reduce and KV transfer.

sections.title: Sizing implications
paragraphs: Estimate bytes moved per token and per training step. Compare to HBM bandwidth × utilization. This predicts tokens/s better than peak TFLOPs marketing.

lessons.title: Attention Cost & KV Cache
lessons.summary: Transformers spend memory and compute on attention. The KV cache is the dominant serving-memory cost during decode — system designers must treat it as a first-class resource.

sections.title: Why attention dominates the systems budget
paragraphs: Self-attention lets every token attend to every earlier token. Naively, that is quadratic in sequence length for compute and memory. Training can often afford full attention; autoregressive inference cannot casually ignore the growing key/value tensors.

During decode, each new token reuses prior keys and values. Systems cache them (the KV cache) so they are not recomputed. Cache size grows with batch × layers × heads × sequence × dtype — frequently the binding constraint on GPU memory before FLOPs are exhausted.
bullets: Prefill: process the prompt (compute-heavy)
Decode: emit tokens one-by-one (memory-bandwidth heavy)
KV cache: stored keys/values per layer for prior tokens

sections.title: Design implications
paragraphs: Paged attention (as in vLLM) treats KV blocks like virtual memory pages to reduce fragmentation. Prefix caching reuses KV for shared prompt prefixes across requests. Separating prefill and decode onto different pools can improve utilization when traffic mixes long prompts with long generations.

When estimating capacity, start from concurrent sequences × expected context × bytes per KV element × layers — then compare to HBM. Quantization (FP8/INT8/INT4) and speculative decoding change the cost curve but do not remove the need for this estimate.

lessons.title: Context Length vs Memory
lessons.summary: Context Length vs Memory is a core topic in modern system design. This lesson builds a first-principles model around model compute/memory trade-offs, then connects that model to capacity, failure modes, and operational practice so you can use it in real architectures.

sections.title: What Context Length vs Memory is solving
paragraphs: Context Length vs Memory exists because naive designs around model compute/memory trade-offs break under scale, partial failure, or changing requirements. Before choosing tools, name the problem: which resource is scarce, which invariant must hold, and which user-visible failures are unacceptable.
In interviews and production reviews, strong answers start with constraints (QPS, data size, latency budget, consistency needs) and only then map Context Length vs Memory onto those constraints.

A useful mental model separates the control plane (how you configure and observe Context Length vs Memory) from the data plane (the per-request/per-event path). Confusing the two leads to architectures that look neat and operate poorly.

sections.title: Core mechanics
paragraphs: Mechanically, Context Length vs Memory involves a small set of moving parts: inputs, state, an algorithm or protocol, and outputs/side effects. Draw those parts explicitly. If state is replicated, write down the replication/consistency rule. If work is asynchronous, write down delivery semantics.

Performance characteristics usually come from amplification (how much internal work per external request), locality (whether work stays on one node), and contention (locks, hot keys, leader bottlenecks).

Correctness characteristics usually come from failure handling: retries, timeouts, idempotency, and what clients observe during failover. If you cannot explain the failure story, you do not yet understand Context Length vs Memory.

sections.title: Designing with it
paragraphs: When incorporating Context Length vs Memory into a system, decide the API boundary first: what does a client call, what can fail, and what is retried. Keep the happy path boring and push complexity into well-tested libraries or platform components.

Prefer reversible rollout: feature flags, dual-running, shadow traffic, and clear dashboards. New uses of Context Length vs Memory should be observable on day one.

sections.title: Operations and failure modes

lessons.title: BGP & Anycast
lessons.summary: BGP is how autonomous systems exchange reachability. Anycast announces the same prefix from many locations so users hit a nearby PoP. Together they power CDNs, DNS, and DDoS absorption — and create failure modes that look like 'random' routing flaps.

sections.title: Autonomous systems and BGP basics
paragraphs: The internet is a network of Autonomous Systems (AS). BGP advertises prefixes with AS paths. Policy — not pure shortest path — decides what you accept and export. That policy surface is why a single misconfiguration can blackhole traffic globally.
iBGP distributes routes inside an AS; eBGP speaks between ASes. Route reflectors and confederations scale iBGP. Attributes like LOCAL_PREF, MED, and AS path length influence selection.
For system designers, BGP matters when you run multi-homed services, anycast edges, or need to understand why traffic suddenly shifts regions.

sections.title: Anycast as a design tool
paragraphs: Anycast means many servers advertise the same IP prefix. Routers deliver packets to the 'nearest' announcement by routing metrics. DNS resolvers and CDN edges use this so clients land on a nearby PoP without an application-level directory.

Anycast is great for request/response UDP/TCP services that tolerate connection resets on route change. It is a poor fit for long-lived connections that must pin to one backend unless you terminate quickly at the PoP.
Health withdrawal is critical: if a PoP is sick but still announces, it becomes a blackhole. Couple BGP announcements with health-checked control planes.

sections.title: Failures and operational controls
paragraphs: Route leaks, hijacks, and RPKI invalid announcements are real. Monitoring control-plane (BMP, looking glasses) matters as much as data-plane latency.
Traffic engineering uses prepends, communities, and selective announcements. Overuse creates brittle topologies that break during maintenance.

sections.title: Design implications
paragraphs: When designing a global API, decide whether geo-DNS, anycast, or client-side region selection owns steering. Mixing all three without a clear source of truth causes oscillation.
State replication must match steering: if users flip PoPs, sticky server state will orphan sessions unless state is global or PoP-local with sticky routing.

lessons.title: TCP Congestion Control & BBR
lessons.summary: TCP congestion control governs how senders probe for available bandwidth while protecting the shared network from collapse. The classic algorithms—Reno, Cubic—react to packet loss as a congestion signal, which causes poor performance on modern high-bandwidth-delay-product and lossy wireless paths. BBR (Bottleneck Bandwidth and Round-trip time) replaces loss-based reaction with a model of the network's current state, achieving dramatically higher throughput on long-haul paths and better latency on bufferbloated networks. Understanding these mechanisms explains much of the latency and throughput behavior engineers observe in production.

sections.title: Why Congestion Control Exists
paragraphs: In 1986, the early internet experienced its first congestion collapse. Due to positive feedback loops—retransmissions increasing load further increasing loss further increasing retransmissions—throughput dropped by a factor of 1000 on affected paths. Van Jacobson's 1988 paper 'Congestion Avoidance and Control' introduced slow start and congestion avoidance to TCP, algorithms that remain at the core of TCP today. The fundamental insight: senders must self-regulate based on network feedback or the network degrades for everyone.

Congestion control addresses a collective action problem. No single sender owns the network; each sender can individually improve its throughput by sending faster, but doing so degrades throughput for all other senders. TCP's congestion control implements network-aware throttling: infer the network's current state from packet loss and RTT signals, stay close to the available bandwidth without pushing into collapse, and back off quickly when congestion is detected.

The congestion window (cwnd) is the sender's self-imposed limit on bytes in flight. The sender can have at most min(cwnd, rwnd) bytes unacknowledged at any time. Congestion control algorithms adjust cwnd in response to ACKs (increase) and loss events (decrease). The goal is for cwnd to converge to the bandwidth-delay product of the path: bytes_in_flight = bandwidth × RTT. Too small: underutilizes the path. Too large: overfills buffers, adds queuing delay (bufferbloat).

The bottleneck link is the slowest link on the path. When the sender's rate exceeds the bottleneck's capacity, packets queue in the bottleneck's buffer. Queue growth adds latency (queuing delay). When the buffer fills, packets are dropped. Loss-based algorithms interpret drops as congestion signals—which they are—but they only detect congestion after the buffer has already filled and latency has already spiked. This is the fundamental problem BBR addresses.
bullets: Bandwidth-delay product: BDP = bandwidth × RTT; optimal cwnd to fully utilize a link
Bufferbloat: oversized router buffers hide congestion; latency spikes before packet loss occurs
Congestion collapse: 1986 internet event; throughput dropped 1000× without congestion control

sections.title: Classic Algorithms: Reno and Cubic
paragraphs: TCP Reno introduced the four canonical phases: Slow Start, Congestion Avoidance, Fast Retransmit, and Fast Recovery. Slow Start: cwnd starts at 1 MSS, doubles each RTT (exponential growth) until it reaches ssthresh or experiences loss. Congestion Avoidance: cwnd grows by 1 MSS per RTT (additive increase), preventing overshoot. On loss (3 duplicate ACKs): Fast Retransmit resends the missing segment immediately; Fast Recovery halves cwnd and continues from there rather than restarting slow start. This additive increase / multiplicative decrease (AIMD) pattern converges to fair sharing between competing flows.

TCP Cubic (Linux default since 2.6.19, 2006) replaces Reno's linear congestion avoidance with a cubic function of time since the last loss event. The key difference: Cubic's growth rate is independent of RTT—it grows based on elapsed time, not RTT count. This makes Cubic much more aggressive on high-latency paths (inter-continental links, satellite) where Reno's RTT-counted linear growth is excessively slow. Cubic's cubic function also has a plateau near the previous cwnd maximum—it probes cautiously near the value where loss last occurred, then accelerates away from it.

Cubic's weaknesses are well-documented. First, it is loss-triggered: Cubic keeps increasing cwnd until it fills the bottleneck buffer and loses a packet, then halves. This means steady-state operation involves oscillating between filling buffers and backing off—causing periodic latency spikes (bufferbloat). Second, Cubic performs poorly on paths with high packet loss rates (wireless, mobile) where losses occur from channel errors (not congestion), causing unnecessary cwnd reductions. Third, Cubic does not distinguish between random packet loss and congestion-triggered loss.

SACK (Selective Acknowledgement) is a critical complement to any loss-based algorithm. Without SACK, TCP can retransmit only one lost segment per RTT (Go-Back-N style). With SACK, the receiver reports all received-but-out-of-order segments; the sender retransmits only the specific gaps. On a path with 5 lost packets in a window, SACK repairs all 5 in one round trip instead of 5. SACK is universally supported in modern TCP stacks and enabled by default.
bullets: AIMD: additive increase on ACK (+1 MSS/RTT), multiplicative decrease on loss (cwnd × 0.7)
Cubic cwnd growth: W = C × (t - K)^3 + W_max; cubic in time since last congestion event
SACK: receiver bitmaps received segments; sender retransmits only gaps; enabled by default

sections.title: BBR: Modeling the Network
paragraphs: BBR (Bottleneck Bandwidth and Round-trip time) was developed at Google and merged into Linux 4.9 (2016). Instead of inferring congestion from packet loss, BBR models two physical properties of the network path: the bottleneck bandwidth (BtlBw) and the minimum RTT (RTprop). These define the network's operating point—the maximum throughput at minimum latency. BBR continuously estimates both, pacing sends at BtlBw and maintaining a cwnd that keeps bytes in flight near BDP (BtlBw × RTprop).

BBR operates in four phases. Startup: like slow start, doubles the pacing rate each RTT to quickly find BtlBw. Drain: after finding the max, drains the queue that formed during startup by sending at a rate below BtlBw. ProbeBW: steady state; cycles through 8 RTTs: 1 RTT at 125% rate to probe for more bandwidth, then 1 RTT at 75% to drain any queue formed, then 6 RTTs at 100%. ProbeRTT: every 10 seconds, reduces cwnd to 4 packets for 200ms to drain queues and re-measure minimum RTT (which grows if buffers stay full).

BBR's key insight: on a bottleneck-bandwidth path, the bottleneck queue grows when you send faster than BtlBw, adding queuing delay. If you stop filling the queue (send at exactly BtlBw), RTT returns to its minimum (RTprop). BBR measures both by watching BtlBw (maximum ACK rate seen recently, filtered with an RTT-sized window) and RTprop (minimum RTT seen in the past 10 seconds). The algorithm avoids loss-based decisions entirely—it never reduces cwnd due to loss.

BBR has significant known problems in its v1 form. When multiple TCP flows compete, BBR flows can be unfair to Cubic flows: BBR probes aggressively during ProbeBW, while Cubic backs off on loss. At congested links where both BBR and Cubic flows compete, BBR can consume 90% of bandwidth while Cubic flows starve. BBR v2 (Linux 5.13+) adds loss-awareness: it respects packet loss signals partially, trading some throughput for fairness in mixed deployments.
bullets: BBR phases: Startup (probe BtlBw) → Drain → ProbeBW (steady state) → ProbeRTT (re-measure RTprop)
BBR ProbeRTT: drain to 4 packets every 10s to measure true minimum RTT; causes brief throughput dip
BBR fairness: v1 unfair to Cubic in shared bottlenecks; BBRv2 adds loss sensitivity to fix this

sections.title: Active Queue Management and ECN
paragraphs: Active Queue Management (AQM) algorithms control drop/marking behavior in router queues to signal congestion earlier—before buffers fill—preventing bufferbloat. Classic tail-drop queues drop packets only when full, allowing latency to spike. AQM algorithms drop or mark packets probabilistically as queue length grows, providing congestion signals earlier at the cost of some packet loss.

CoDel (Controlled Delay) is the most deployed AQM algorithm. CoDel's key observation: in an uncongested network, packets spend minimal time in queues; in a congested network, queuing delay is persistent. CoDel measures the minimum sojourn time (time a packet spends in the queue) over a sliding window. If the minimum exceeds the target delay (5ms by default) for longer than an interval (100ms), CoDel starts dropping packets. When minimum sojourn drops below target, CoDel stops dropping. CoDel reacts to chronic queuing rather than instantaneous queue length.

FQ-CoDel (Fair Queuing + CoDel) combines CoDel's delay-based dropping with per-flow fair queuing. Each active flow gets its own queue; flows are served round-robin. This prevents one flow (e.g., a bulk transfer) from filling the buffer and adding latency to other flows (e.g., DNS, interactive traffic). FQ-CoDel is the default qdisc in many Linux distributions and OpenWrt, dramatically improving latency for interactive traffic on shared links.

ECN (Explicit Congestion Notification) allows routers to signal congestion without dropping packets. The router sets the CE (Congestion Experienced) bit in the IP header of a packet it would otherwise drop (if ECN is negotiated). The receiver echoes this in the ECE bit of TCP ACKs; the sender reduces cwnd as if a loss occurred, but the packet was not actually lost. This eliminates one round trip of unnecessary packet loss. ECN is most beneficial for datacenter networks where packet loss rates should be near zero and any loss indicates real congestion.
bullets: CoDel target: 5ms default sojourn time; tune lower for latency-critical links (1ms for datacenter)
FQ-CoDel: default qdisc on Linux desktop; enabled on most OpenWrt deployments
ECN negotiation: TCP SYN with ECE+CWR bits; both endpoints must support ECN; router marks CE bit instead of dropping

sections.title: Congestion Control in Practice
paragraphs: Selecting the right congestion algorithm depends on the workload and network. For inter-datacenter replication and cross-region API traffic, BBR outperforms Cubic due to high BDP (10 Gbps × 50ms = 62.5 MB). For user-facing mobile clients on 4G/5G (variable bandwidth, 5–20% packet loss from channel errors), BBR v2 is preferred—BBR v1 ignores loss and can overshoot, while Cubic over-backs-off. For datacenter internal traffic (1–100μs RTT, near-zero loss), DCTCP (Data Center TCP) with ECN is optimal—it uses ECN to maintain near-zero queue depths, achieving optimal throughput at minimum latency.

Kernel configuration: on Linux, check the current default with 'sysctl net.ipv4.tcp_congestion_control'. Change globally with 'sysctl -w net.ipv4.tcp_congestion_control=bbr'. Applications can override per-socket with setsockopt(TCP_CONGESTION). BBR also requires the pacing scheduler: 'sysctl -w net.core.default_qdisc=fq' (FQ provides per-connection pacing; without it, BBR's pacing is emulated less accurately). Confirm available algorithms with 'sysctl net.ipv4.tcp_available_congestion_control'.

Measuring congestion control behavior in production: ss --info displays cwnd, ssthresh, and RTT per connection—essential for diagnosing whether congestion is limiting throughput. /proc/net/netstat (TcpExt:TCPCongestionRecovery, TCPSackRecovery, TCPLostRetransmit) provide system-wide counters. For long-haul transfers, iperf3 --logfile with --json output captures per-second throughput, RTT, and retransmit counts, allowing correlation with network events.
bullets: Linux BBR config: net.ipv4.tcp_congestion_control=bbr + net.core.default_qdisc=fq
ss --info: per-connection cwnd, ssthresh, rtt, retrans counters
DCTCP: requires ECN on all switches in path; reduces datacenter queuing to microseconds

core.title: Loss-Based Congestion Control Fundamentals
paragraphs: TCP Reno's AIMD: add 1 MSS/RTT during congestion avoidance; halve cwnd on loss (triple duplicate ACK). Slow Start doubles cwnd each RTT from 1 MSS until ssthresh or loss.
Cubic extends Reno with cubic time-based growth, performing better on high-BDP paths. It's the Linux default; loss-triggered, so it fills buffers before detecting congestion.
SACK enables selective retransmission of only lost segments, dramatically improving recovery speed on paths with multiple losses per window.
bullets: ssthresh: threshold where slow start transitions to congestion avoidance
Fast recovery: continue sending at reduced rate after loss; don't return to slow start
SACK: enabled by default; check with ss -i to verify sack negotiated

core.title: BBR: Model-Based Congestion Control
paragraphs: BBR estimates bottleneck bandwidth (BtlBw) and minimum RTT (RTprop) to operate at the network's physical capacity without filling queues. It paces sends at BtlBw and maintains cwnd ≈ BtlBw × RTprop.
BBR's four phases: Startup (exponential probe), Drain (queue drain), ProbeBW (steady-state cycling), ProbeRTT (re-measure minimum RTT every 10s).
BBR v1 is unfair to Cubic in mixed deployments; BBRv2 adds loss sensitivity for fairness while maintaining throughput advantages.
bullets: BBR does not reduce cwnd on loss events (v1); this is intentional, not a bug
BBR ProbeRTT reduces cwnd to 4 packets for 200ms every 10s; causes brief throughput dip
Linux 4.9+: BBR available; Linux 5.13+: BBRv2 available

core.title: AQM and ECN
paragraphs: CoDel drops packets when minimum sojourn time exceeds 5ms for >100ms, preventing bufferbloat without queue-length thresholds.
FQ-CoDel adds per-flow fairness: bulk transfers don't starve interactive flows. Default Linux qdisc on many distros.
ECN allows routers to signal congestion by marking packets (CE bit) rather than dropping them, reducing unnecessary retransmits.
bullets: FQ-CoDel: set with 'tc qdisc add dev eth0 root fq_codel'
ECN requires TCP SYN negotiation and router support; transparent to application
DCTCP: uses ECN fraction to scale cwnd reduction proportionally; optimal for datacenter

deepDive.title: BBR Internals and Measurement
paragraphs: BBR's BtlBw estimator uses a windowed max filter: the maximum ACK rate observed in the last 10 RTTs is the BtlBw estimate. ACK rate is computed as (bytes ACKed) / (time between ACKs). The 10-RTT window allows BBR to track changing bandwidth while filtering noise. During ProbeBW, the brief 125% rate probe allows BBR to discover if more bandwidth has become available.

RTprop estimation uses a windowed minimum: the minimum RTT observed in the past 10 seconds. RTT naturally increases when queues form (queuing delay); the 10-second window allows BBR to rediscover the true minimum after queues drain. The ProbeRTT phase actively reduces cwnd to 4 packets—below the BDP—forcing the queue to drain and revealing the true propagation delay.

BBR's pacing rate = BtlBw × pacing_gain. Without a pacing qdisc (FQ), the kernel sends the entire cwnd in a burst, then nothing. With FQ, sends are spread uniformly over the RTT—smoother traffic, fewer drops, more accurate RTT measurement. Without FQ, BBR works but is less efficient; always pair BBR with FQ qdisc.
bullets: BtlBw filter window: max over 10 RTTs; 10 × 100ms = 1s for 100ms RTT paths
pacing_gain cycle in ProbeBW: [5/4, 3/4, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1] × BtlBw
BBR inflight limit: 2 × BDP during ProbeBW; prevents excessive buffering

deepDive.title: Congestion Control in Datacenters and Cloud
paragraphs: Datacenter networks have RTTs of 10–500 μs and near-zero packet loss in normal operation. Loss-based algorithms (Cubic) perform poorly here: they target cwnd that fills router buffers before detecting congestion, adding hundreds of μs of queuing delay to what should be a 10 μs path. DCTCP uses ECN marking frequency (what fraction of packets are marked) to scale cwnd reduction proportionally—a small marking fraction causes a small reduction, maintaining high throughput while keeping queues nearly empty.

RDMA over Converged Ethernet (RoCE) used in GPU training clusters requires lossless Ethernet. Any packet drop in RDMA causes a catastrophic performance cliff—the entire RDMA queue pair stalls. Lossless behavior is achieved with PFC (Priority Flow Control): when a switch buffer exceeds a threshold, it sends a PAUSE frame to the upstream device, stopping transmission for that traffic class. Congestion Notification (CN) adds end-to-end congestion control on top of PFC to prevent PFC storms (where PAUSE frames cascade across the network).

QUIC's congestion control is per-path and pluggable. By default, most QUIC stacks use NewReno or Cubic. Google's production QUIC uses BBR. QUIC's ability to migrate paths means congestion state must be reset on migration (a migrated path may have completely different capacity). This is correctly handled in QUIC implementations by resetting cwnd to initial values after path validation on migration.
bullets: DCTCP: ECN fraction-based cwnd reduction; average queue depth <1 packet on well-tuned networks
PFC (Priority Flow Control): lossless Ethernet for RDMA; required for RoCE in GPU clusters
RoCEv2: RDMA over UDP; requires DCQCN (Data Center Quantized Congestion Notification) for congestion control

expert.title: Congestion Control at Hyperscale and Future Directions
paragraphs: At hyperscale, congestion control is a collective optimization problem across millions of concurrent flows. Google's B4 WAN uses a centralized SDN controller with global visibility to allocate bandwidth explicitly to flows via weighted max-min fairness, rather than relying on each flow's local congestion control. This eliminates the inefficiency of multiple competing flows probing the same bottleneck—the SDN controller knows the bottleneck capacity and assigns rates directly. For flows that can't be centrally managed (internet-facing traffic), BBR is the best available decentralized algorithm.

Practical Backpressure (PBP) and CCA variants for cellular networks (LTE, 5G) address the fundamental mismatch between TCP congestion control assumptions and cellular radio characteristics. Cellular links have highly variable capacity (1 Mbps to 100 Mbps within seconds), large per-hop queues in base stations, and loss patterns that reflect radio conditions, not congestion. Network-Assisted Dynamic Adaptation (NADA) and RMCAT (RTP Media Congestion Avoidance Techniques) are IETF-standardized algorithms for real-time media over cellular, used in WebRTC.

Prague (L4S-compatible Cubic) and Scalable TCP are emerging CCAs designed for the Low Latency, Low Loss, Scalable throughput (L4S) architecture. L4S uses a scalable congestion signal (ECN marking frequency increases with queue depth) rather than classic ECN's binary signal. Prague responds to this graded signal proportionally, maintaining cwnd near BDP without the AIMD oscillations of Cubic. L4S pilot deployments (Apple's Low Latency mode in iOS 16+, Comcast's L4S trial) show sub-millisecond queuing delay while saturating links—the theoretical ideal.

concepts: Congestion window (cwnd): sender's self-imposed limit on bytes in flight; adjusted by congestion control algorithm
Bandwidth-delay product (BDP): bytes_in_flight = bandwidth × RTT; optimal cwnd to fully utilize link without buffering
Slow start: cwnd doubles each RTT from 1 MSS; exponential probe of available bandwidth
AIMD: Additive Increase Multiplicative Decrease; +1 MSS/RTT on ACK, ×0.5 on loss; converges to fairness
Cubic: loss-based, time-driven cubic growth; Linux default; fills buffers before detecting congestion
BBR: model-based; estimates BtlBw and RTprop; paces at bandwidth without queue-filling loss signal
Bufferbloat: oversized router buffers add latency before loss; CoDel/FQ-CoDel prevent this
SACK: selective acknowledgement; sender retransmits only lost segments, not entire window
ECN: router marks CE bit instead of dropping; sender reduces cwnd without packet loss event
DCTCP: ECN-fraction-based cwnd reduction; optimal for datacenter near-lossless networks
practices: Deploy BBR + FQ qdisc for cross-region and internet-facing TCP flows; Cubic is suboptimal on high-BDP paths
Enable FQ qdisc (net.core.default_qdisc=fq) alongside BBR; pacing accuracy depends on it
Use DCTCP with ECN on datacenter-internal traffic for sub-millisecond queuing latency
Monitor ss --info cwnd and RTT per connection; sustained cwnd at ssthresh indicates chronic loss
Deploy FQ-CoDel on network egress to protect interactive flows from bulk transfer bufferbloat
On paths with >2% random loss (mobile, satellite), use BBRv2 not BBRv1 to avoid ignoring real signal
pitfalls: Using Cubic on high-BDP intercontinental links; Cubic grows too slowly and achieves a fraction of available bandwidth
Deploying BBRv1 in a mixed BBR+Cubic deployment without awareness of fairness issues; BBR flows can starve Cubic flows
Not pairing BBR with FQ qdisc; BBR without FQ bursts packets and measures RTT inaccurately
Ignoring bufferbloat on network devices; default tail-drop queues add hundreds of ms latency before signaling congestion
Treating all TCP packet loss as congestion; random loss from channel errors (Wi-Fi, 4G) should not trigger cwnd halving
Not validating ECN end-to-end before relying on it; a single middlebox that strips ECN bits breaks the whole mechanism

examples.title: Google BBR Deployment on YouTube
examples.description: Google deployed BBR on its global WAN in 2016, replacing Cubic for YouTube streaming. On paths with low RTT (< 30ms), improvement was modest. On paths with high RTT or moderate packet loss—the majority of YouTube's global user base—BBR achieved 4× higher throughput on average and reduced video rebuffering by 80%. The improvement was especially large for users in Africa and Southeast Asia accessing content across intercontinental links.

examples.title: FQ-CoDel on Home Routers
examples.description: OpenWrt enabled FQ-CoDel by default starting in 2015. Home routers running FQ-CoDel showed median RTT reductions of 10–50× under load compared to default tail-drop queues. A household running a torrent upload (bulk traffic) no longer experienced 300ms latency on video calls—the per-flow fairness of FQ-CoDel queued the torrent traffic separately and served interactive flows at near-zero queuing delay.

examples.title: DCTCP in AWS Enhanced Networking
examples.description: AWS's Enhanced Networking (ENA) uses DCTCP and ECN within availability zones to maintain sub-millisecond latency between instances. When ENA switch buffers start filling (signaled by ECN marking), instances reduce send rates proportionally before buffers overflow. This keeps inter-instance latency at 50–200μs even under heavy cross-rack traffic, compared to 1–5ms with tail-drop Cubic—critical for distributed databases and cache clusters.

keyTakeaways: Loss-based congestion control (Cubic) fills buffers before detecting congestion, causing latency spikes and poor behavior on high-BDP paths
BBR models bottleneck bandwidth and minimum RTT, pacing sends to match bandwidth without queue-filling; 4× throughput improvement on YouTube's WAN
FQ-CoDel prevents bufferbloat by measuring sojourn time and providing per-flow fairness; deploy it on all network egress
ECN allows congestion signals without packet drops; DCTCP uses ECN fraction for proportional congestion response in datacenters
BBRv1 is unfair to Cubic in shared bottlenecks; use BBRv2 in mixed deployments
Pair BBR with FQ qdisc (net.core.default_qdisc=fq) for accurate pacing; BBR without FQ is less effective
lessons.whyItMatters: Congestion control is why TCP throughput on a 100 Gbps link with 100ms RTT might achieve only 500 Mbps with default settings—and 95 Gbps after proper tuning. It explains why video calls lag when someone downloads a large file on the same network, and why Google's YouTube streaming improved 4× by switching algorithms. Engineers running cross-region replication, bulk data transfers, CDN origin pulls, or any workload sensitive to throughput or latency must understand congestion control to diagnose and fix the right knobs.
reflectionQuestions: Your cross-region database replication is achieving 200 Mbps on a 10 Gbps link with 80ms RTT. The connection has 0.01% packet loss. Walk through the diagnosis: which congestion control algorithm is likely running, what is the theoretical maximum, and what would you change?
Explain why BBRv1 is unfair when competing with Cubic flows at a shared bottleneck. What specific behavior in each algorithm causes this, and how does BBRv2 address it?

Design the congestion control strategy for a live video streaming CDN that serves users on mobile networks (1–50 Mbps, 1–5% loss), home broadband (100 Mbps–1 Gbps, <0.1% loss), and enterprise (10 Gbps, 0% loss). Would you use the same algorithm for all three?
numbersToKnow: 1986: internet congestion collapse that motivated Van Jacobson's congestion control paper
BDP for 10 Gbps × 100ms RTT = 1.25 GB in flight needed to saturate the link
4×: BBR throughput improvement over Cubic on YouTube's global WAN deployment
5ms: CoDel's default target sojourn time; packets queued longer trigger AQM drops
Linux 4.9 (2016): BBRv1 merged; Linux 5.13 (2021): BBRv2 merged

lessons.title: HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 & HTTP/3
lessons.summary: HTTP is the dominant application-layer protocol for web and API communication. Each major version solved specific performance bottlenecks—from connection overhead in HTTP/1.1 to head-of-line blocking in HTTP/2 to TCP-level blocking in HTTP/3. Understanding these evolutions is critical for API design, CDN configuration, and performance tuning.

sections.title: HTTP/1.1: The Foundation
paragraphs: HTTP/1.1, standardized in 1997 and refined over decades, is a text-based request-response protocol. A client sends a request with a method (GET, POST, etc.), path, headers, and optional body. The server responds with a status code, headers, and body. Each request is independent and semantically meaningful—GET should be safe and idempotent, POST creates resources, PUT replaces, PATCH partially updates, DELETE removes.

HTTP/1.1 introduced persistent connections (keep-alive), allowing multiple requests over a single TCP connection. Before this, each request required a new TCP handshake. Keep-alive dramatically reduced latency, but HTTP/1.1 still processes responses in order on each connection—if one request is slow, subsequent responses queue behind it (head-of-line blocking at the application layer). Browsers worked around this by opening 6–8 parallel connections per domain, which itself caused congestion.

Headers carry critical metadata: Content-Type defines the body format, Authorization carries credentials, Cache-Control directs caching behavior, and Set-Cookie establishes session state. Status codes communicate outcomes: 200 OK, 201 Created, 301 Moved Permanently, 400 Bad Request, 401 Unauthorized, 403 Forbidden, 404 Not Found, 429 Too Many Requests, 500 Internal Server Error, 503 Service Unavailable. Designing APIs with correct semantics—using the right status codes, methods, and cache headers—is a hallmark of production-quality engineering.
bullets: Idempotent methods: GET, PUT, DELETE — safe to retry without side effects
Conditional requests: If-None-Match (ETag) and If-Modified-Since enable efficient caching
Chunked transfer encoding: stream response bodies without knowing total size upfront

sections.title: HTTP/2: Multiplexing and Binary Framing
paragraphs: HTTP/2, published in 2015, addressed HTTP/1.1's performance limits while maintaining semantic compatibility. The key innovation is multiplexing: many request-response streams share a single TCP connection simultaneously. Streams are independent—slow Stream A doesn't block Stream B. Data is split into binary frames tagged with stream IDs, enabling efficient parsing and eliminating the need for multiple parallel connections.

HTTP/2 also introduced header compression (HPACK), server push (server proactively sends resources), and stream prioritization. In practice, server push saw limited adoption (browsers deprecated it) because preload hints and HTTP caching proved more effective. Header compression, however, is significant—API requests with large JWT tokens or cookie headers benefit substantially.

The critical limitation HTTP/2 didn't solve: TCP-level head-of-line blocking. TCP guarantees ordered byte delivery. If one packet is lost, all subsequent packets on that connection stall until retransmission completes—even if they belong to different HTTP/2 streams. On lossy networks (mobile, cross-continent), this can negate HTTP/2's multiplexing benefits. This limitation directly motivated HTTP/3.

Single TCP connection per origin reduces handshake overhead and memory

sections.title: HTTP/3: QUIC over UDP
paragraphs: HTTP/3 runs over QUIC, a transport protocol built on UDP. QUIC implements its own reliability, congestion control, and encryption (TLS 1.3 is integrated into the handshake, reducing setup to ~1 RTT or 0-RTT for resumed connections). Most importantly, QUIC multiplexes streams independently—packet loss on one stream doesn't block others, solving TCP's head-of-line blocking problem.

QUIC also enables connection migration: if a client's IP changes (switching from Wi-Fi to cellular), the connection persists via a connection ID rather than breaking on the 4-tuple change. For mobile users, this is transformative. Connection establishment is faster too—QUIC combines transport and TLS handshakes, and 0-RTT resumption allows sending data in the first packet for returning clients.

Adoption is accelerating: Cloudflare, Google, and major CDNs support HTTP/3. However, some corporate firewalls and middleboxes block or throttle UDP, causing fallback to HTTP/2. In system design, assume HTTP/3 at the edge (CDN to client) and HTTP/2 or gRPC internally (service to service), with graceful fallback mechanisms.

UDP port 443: QUIC uses the same port as HTTPS for firewall compatibility

sections.title: Caching, CDNs, and Performance
paragraphs: HTTP caching is one of the most impactful performance optimizations available. Cache-Control headers (max-age, s-maxage, no-cache, no-store, private, public) control how long responses are cached at browsers, CDNs, and reverse proxies. ETags enable conditional requests—clients send If-None-Match and receive 304 Not Modified instead of the full body. For read-heavy APIs serving relatively static data, aggressive caching can reduce origin load by 90%+.

Content Delivery Networks (CDNs) cache content at edge locations geographically close to users. A user in Tokyo hits a Tokyo edge server instead of your US-based origin. CDNs also terminate TLS, support HTTP/2 and HTTP/3, compress responses, and provide DDoS protection. Cache invalidation strategies—TTL-based expiry, purge APIs, stale-while-revalidate—are essential operational knowledge.

Performance best practices span all HTTP versions: minimize payload size (gzip/brotli compression), reduce round trips (bundle resources, use HTTP/2 push hints or preload), leverage caching aggressively, and use a CDN for static assets and cacheable API responses. Measure with tools like WebPageTest, Lighthouse, and server-side APM to identify whether latency is in DNS, connection setup, TTFB, or download.

sections.title: API Design with HTTP Semantics
paragraphs: RESTful API design maps domain concepts to HTTP resources and methods. Collections use plural nouns (/users, /orders), individual resources use IDs (/users/123). Nested resources express relationships (/users/123/orders). Use query parameters for filtering, sorting, and pagination (?status=active&page=2). Response bodies should be consistent—wrap collections in a standard envelope if your team agrees on a convention.

Versioning strategies include URL path (/v1/users), headers (Accept: application/vnd.api+json;version=1), or query parameters. URL versioning is simplest and most visible. Rate limiting via 429 status with Retry-After headers protects your service. CORS headers (Access-Control-Allow-Origin) are required for browser-based clients calling APIs on different domains—a common source of frontend integration bugs.

In microservices, HTTP is often the default inter-service protocol for its simplicity, debuggability (curl, browser dev tools), and universal support. However, for high-throughput internal communication, gRPC (covered in a later lesson) may be preferable. The choice depends on team familiarity, performance requirements, and whether you need browser compatibility.

Content negotiation: Accept header specifies preferred response format
Webhook callbacks: POST to client URLs for event-driven integration

core.title: HTTP/1.1: The Foundation
paragraphs: HTTP/1.1, standardized in 1997 and refined over decades, is a text-based request-response protocol. A client sends a request with a method (GET, POST, etc.), path, headers, and optional body. The server responds with a status code, headers, and body. Each request is independent and semantically meaningful—GET should be safe and idempotent, POST creates resources, PUT replaces, PATCH partially updates, DELETE removes.

HTTP/1.1 introduced persistent connections (keep-alive), allowing multiple requests over a single TCP connection. Before this, each request required a new TCP handshake. Keep-alive dramatically reduced latency, but HTTP/1.1 still processes responses in order on each connection—if one request is slow, subsequent responses queue behind it (head-of-line blocking at the application layer). Browsers worked around this by opening 6–8 parallel connections per domain, which itself caused congestion.

Headers carry critical metadata: Content-Type defines the body format, Authorization carries credentials, Cache-Control directs caching behavior, and Set-Cookie establishes session state. Status codes communicate outcomes: 200 OK, 201 Created, 301 Moved Permanently, 400 Bad Request, 401 Unauthorized, 403 Forbidden, 404 Not Found, 429 Too Many Requests, 500 Internal Server Error, 503 Service Unavailable. Designing APIs with correct semantics—using the right status codes, methods, and cache headers—is a hallmark of production-quality engineering.

Conditional requests: If-None-Match (ETag) and If-Modified-Since enable efficient caching
Chunked transfer encoding: stream response bodies without knowing total size upfront

core.title: HTTP/2: Multiplexing and Binary Framing
paragraphs: HTTP/2, published in 2015, addressed HTTP/1.1's performance limits while maintaining semantic compatibility. The key innovation is multiplexing: many request-response streams share a single TCP connection simultaneously. Streams are independent—slow Stream A doesn't block Stream B. Data is split into binary frames tagged with stream IDs, enabling efficient parsing and eliminating the need for multiple parallel connections.

HTTP/2 also introduced header compression (HPACK), server push (server proactively sends resources), and stream prioritization. In practice, server push saw limited adoption (browsers deprecated it) because preload hints and HTTP caching proved more effective. Header compression, however, is significant—API requests with large JWT tokens or cookie headers benefit substantially.

The critical limitation HTTP/2 didn't solve: TCP-level head-of-line blocking. TCP guarantees ordered byte delivery. If one packet is lost, all subsequent packets on that connection stall until retransmission completes—even if they belong to different HTTP/2 streams. On lossy networks (mobile, cross-continent), this can negate HTTP/2's multiplexing benefits. This limitation directly motivated HTTP/3.
