lessons.title: Back-of-Envelope Estimation
lessons.summary: Capacity estimation turns vague requirements into storage, QPS, bandwidth, and latency budgets. Good estimates are order-of-magnitude honest, explicit about assumptions, and revised when measurements arrive.

sections.title: Why estimate before drawing boxes
paragraphs: Estimates force requirements into numbers: daily active users, read/write ratio, object size, retention, peak-to-average. Without them, architectures are fashion.
Interview and production practice share the same skill: powers of ten, latency hierarchy, and stating assumptions out loud so others can challenge them.
An estimate that is 2× wrong is often useful; one that hides assumptions is dangerous.

sections.title: The latency and throughput vocabulary
paragraphs: Know approximate costs: L1/L2 cache nanoseconds, DRAM ~100ns, SSD tens to hundreds of µs, HDD ms, same-rack network ~100µs–1ms, cross-region 50–150ms+. These bound how many hops your p99 can afford.

QPS = concurrency / latency for a single server under saturation (Little's Law). If a handler averages 10ms and you want 10k QPS, you need ~100 concurrent in-flight requests — and enough CPU/IO to sustain them.
Bandwidth: 1 MB objects at 1000 writes/s is ~1 GB/s before replication and indexes. Replication factor and erasure coding multiply storage and sometimes network.

sections.title: Storage math
paragraphs: Rows × average size × indexes × retention × replication. Indexes often dominate. Compression helps sequential analytics more than point-lookup OLTP.
Time-series and logs: estimate ingest bytes/day and compaction overhead. 'Unlimited retention' is a cost decision, not a feature.

sections.title: Working the problem
paragraphs: Start from peak QPS and object size. Derive read QPS from write QPS × ratio. Check if a single shard fits; if not, partition. Check if cache can absorb reads given hit rate assumptions.
Always leave headroom (often 2–3×) for spikes, rebalancing, and incident recovery. Publish the assumptions next to the diagram.

lessons.title: Load Shedding & Overload Control
lessons.summary: When load exceeds capacity, systems must shed work intentionally — or they shed it randomly via timeouts and cascading failure. Good overload control protects latency for admitted traffic.

sections.title: Failure mode of uncontrolled overload
paragraphs: Queues grow, latency explodes, retries amplify load, thread pools saturate, and the service spends CPU on work that will be cancelled. Success rate collapses.

sections.title: Shedding strategies
paragraphs: Admit based on queue time, concurrency, or token buckets. Prefer shedding new low-priority work. Return explicit 503 with Retry-After.
Codel/adaptive LIFO approaches protect latency better than unbounded FIFO under overload.

sections.title: Client cooperation
paragraphs: Clients must backoff. Without coordinated retry budgets, shedding just moves the thundering herd.

sections.title: Place in the stack
paragraphs: Shed at edges and at each dependency boundary. Bulkheads prevent one capability from consuming all workers.

lessons.title: Sharding Strategies & Resharding
lessons.summary: Sharding Strategies & Resharding is a core topic in modern system design. This lesson builds a first-principles model around capacity, concurrency, and overload behavior, then connects that model to capacity, failure modes, and operational practice so you can use it in real architectures.

sections.title: What Sharding Strategies & Resharding is solving
paragraphs: Sharding Strategies & Resharding exists because naive designs around capacity, concurrency, and overload behavior break under scale, partial failure, or changing requirements. Before choosing tools, name the problem: which resource is scarce, which invariant must hold, and which user-visible failures are unacceptable.

In interviews and production reviews, strong answers start with constraints (QPS, data size, latency budget, consistency needs) and only then map Sharding Strategies & Resharding onto those constraints.

A useful mental model separates the control plane (how you configure and observe Sharding Strategies & Resharding) from the data plane (the per-request/per-event path). Confusing the two leads to architectures that look neat and operate poorly.

sections.title: Core mechanics
paragraphs: Mechanically, Sharding Strategies & Resharding involves a small set of moving parts: inputs, state, an algorithm or protocol, and outputs/side effects. Draw those parts explicitly. If state is replicated, write down the replication/consistency rule. If work is asynchronous, write down delivery semantics.

Performance characteristics usually come from amplification (how much internal work per external request), locality (whether work stays on one node), and contention (locks, hot keys, leader bottlenecks).

Correctness characteristics usually come from failure handling: retries, timeouts, idempotency, and what clients observe during failover. If you cannot explain the failure story, you do not yet understand Sharding Strategies & Resharding.
bullets: Inputs → state/protocol → outputs/side effects
Name consistency and delivery guarantees
Identify the bottleneck resource early

sections.title: Designing with it
paragraphs: When incorporating Sharding Strategies & Resharding into a system, decide the API boundary first: what does a client call, what can fail, and what is retried. Keep the happy path boring and push complexity into well-tested libraries or platform components.

Capacity plan with numbers: estimate peak load, working set, and headroom. Convert that into shard counts, cache sizes, thread/connection pools, or GPU/memory budgets as relevant to Sharding Strategies & Resharding.
Prefer reversible rollout: feature flags, dual-running, shadow traffic, and clear dashboards. New uses of Sharding Strategies & Resharding should be observable on day one.

sections.title: Operations and failure modes
paragraphs: Operate Sharding Strategies & Resharding with SLIs that match user pain (availability, latency, lag, error rate, cost). Alert on burn rates and queue/lag growth, not only host CPU.
Common failures include overload without admission control, retry amplification, silent staleness, schema mismatches, and dependency brownouts. Write a runbook for the top three.
Chaos and game days should include slow dependencies and network delay, not only hard kills. Sharding Strategies & Resharding often fails in the gray area.

lessons.title: Stateless Services & State Management
lessons.summary: Stateless services—where no instance holds request-specific state between calls—are the bedrock of modern scalable architecture. When any instance can handle any request, horizontal scaling becomes trivial, deployments become safe, and fault tolerance comes for free. The challenge is moving all necessary state to external stores while keeping latency and consistency guarantees acceptable.

sections.title: What Makes a Service Stateless?
paragraphs: A stateless service is one where every request contains all information needed to process it, and the server holds no memory of previous requests. HTTP is inherently stateless by design—each request is independent. When you log in to a website and your server records your session in a local in-memory dictionary, you've introduced statefulness: subsequent requests must go to the same server instance, breaking horizontal scaling.

Statefulness creeps in through several mechanisms: in-memory session stores, local file caches, connection state (TCP socket state, authenticated database connections held per-request), in-flight counters, and locally queued work. Each form of local state creates affinity between a client and a specific server instance. With affinity comes risk: if that instance crashes, state is lost. With risk comes complexity: load balancers must implement sticky sessions, deployments must drain connections carefully, and auto-scaling must account for inflight state.

The architectural principle is simple: push all state to external systems purpose-built to manage it. Sessions go to Redis or DynamoDB. Files go to S3. Database connections are pooled but stateless at the application level (each request acquires a connection, executes a query, and releases it). Rate limit counters go to a distributed counter store. When the application tier has no local state, every instance is identical and interchangeable—the ideal condition for horizontal scaling.
bullets: Stateless: every request is self-contained; any instance can handle any request
Statefulness sources: in-memory sessions, local caches, sticky connections, local queues
Session affinity: required for stateful tiers, but breaks auto-scaling and rolling deploys
Principle: externalize all state to stores designed for it (Redis, S3, DB)

sections.title: Session Management Patterns
paragraphs: HTTP sessions are the most common form of application statefulness. Classic session management stores a session object in server memory, keyed by a session ID cookie. This creates hard instance affinity. The upgrade path is externalizing sessions to a shared store: Redis is the industry standard for this. Every application instance reads and writes to the same Redis cluster; session ID in the cookie points to data in Redis rather than local memory. Any instance can handle any session, restoring statelessness.

JWT (JSON Web Tokens) take a different approach: encode session state inside the token itself, cryptographically signed so the server can verify authenticity without any external lookup. The client presents the token with each request; the server verifies the signature and reads the claims directly. This is truly stateless—no external call needed. The trade-off is that JWTs cannot be invalidated before expiry (there's no server-side state to delete), so short expiry times (15 minutes) combined with refresh token rotation are essential for security.

Choosing between Redis sessions and JWTs depends on your invalidation requirements. If you need to log out all sessions for a user immediately (e.g., after a security breach), Redis sessions support this trivially by deleting the session key. JWTs require a denylist (which re-introduces shared state) or accepting that issued tokens remain valid until expiry. Many systems use a hybrid: short-lived JWTs for most requests combined with a Redis-backed refresh token store that supports immediate revocation.
bullets: Redis sessions: external shared store; supports instant invalidation; adds network hop
JWTs: stateless tokens; no server lookup; cannot be revoked before expiry
Hybrid: short-lived JWT access tokens + Redis-backed refresh tokens for revocation
Session affinity in nginx: ip_hash or sticky cookie directives—avoid if possible

sections.title: External State Stores and Their Trade-offs
paragraphs: Moving state to external stores solves horizontal scaling but introduces new challenges: network latency, additional failure modes, and consistency semantics. Reading session state from Redis adds 0.5–2ms per request. For a service with a 10ms SLO, that's 5–20% of your budget on every call. Use in-process caching (e.g., cache the session object for the duration of a request to avoid multiple Redis hits) and Redis connection pooling to minimize overhead.

The CAP theorem applies to your external state stores. Redis Cluster (without strong consistency mode) may return stale data during network partitions—acceptable for session data but not for financial balances. PostgreSQL with synchronous replication provides strong consistency but higher write latency. Understand what consistency guarantee each store provides and match it to the consistency requirement of the state it holds. Session data: eventual consistency fine. User balances: strong consistency required.

Service mesh and sidecar patterns can make state externalization transparent. Envoy proxy can handle session affinity, circuit breaking to Redis, and retry logic without changing application code. But even with infrastructure abstractions, developers need to understand what state lives where, what happens if the external store is unavailable, and whether the application degrades gracefully (serve cached state) or fails hard.
bullets: Redis: sub-millisecond reads/writes; ideal for sessions, rate limits, feature flags
S3/blob storage: infinitely scalable object state; not for low-latency access patterns
PostgreSQL: strong consistency; appropriate for financial state and audit logs
Fail-open vs. fail-closed: decide in advance what happens if the state store is unavailable

sections.title: Twelve-Factor App and Stateless Principles
paragraphs: The Twelve-Factor App methodology (Heroku, 2011) codifies stateless service design. Factor VI ('Processes') states: 'Twelve-factor processes are stateless and share-nothing. Any data that needs to persist must be stored in a stateful backing service, typically a database.' This principle unlocks factors III ('Config in environment'), VIII ('Concurrency'), and IX ('Disposability'): when processes are stateless, they can be started and stopped instantly, scaled horizontally by running more copies, and deployed with zero downtime.

Disposability is the operational payoff of statelessness. A stateless process can be killed and replaced with no data loss—there's nothing to drain or migrate. Rolling deployments, blue-green deployments, and canary releases all depend on this property. When a Kubernetes pod restarts, in-memory state is gone; if your application relies on in-memory state accumulated over days (e.g., warming up an in-memory cache), restarts are expensive and disruptive.

Idempotency is the companion principle to statelessness. If a request is retried (due to network timeout, load balancer retry, or client retry), the second execution should produce the same result as the first. Idempotent handlers are safe to retry; non-idempotent handlers (e.g., 'charge credit card') need deduplication keys. Building idempotency into your service from day one makes the entire system more resilient to network failures and duplicate messages.
bullets: Twelve-Factor VI: processes are stateless and share-nothing
Disposability: stateless processes start/stop instantly; no drain needed
Idempotency: requests can be safely retried without duplicate side effects
Idempotency key: unique token per operation, stored in DB to detect duplicates

sections.title: Gradual Migration: Making Stateful Services Stateless
paragraphs: Legacy applications often have deeply embedded statefulness that cannot be removed in a single refactor. The incremental approach: first, audit all in-memory state to understand what it holds and how it's accessed. Categorize state by sensitivity (session vs. application cache vs. derived computed data) and access pattern (per-request vs. background aggregation). Start with the easiest wins: move session storage to Redis first since it's isolated, well-understood, and rarely has logic tied to the memory layout.

Application-level caches are the trickiest category. An in-memory cache of frequently-read config or reference data is tempting to leave in place because it's fast. The correct approach is to externalize it to Redis or Memcached with an appropriate TTL, accepting the small latency increase. If in-process caching is genuinely required for performance, use a two-level cache: a short-TTL in-process cache backed by Redis. Crucially, the in-process cache is now a performance optimization, not a correctness requirement—restarts are safe.

Background jobs and queued work introduce the hardest statefulness: in-flight tasks. A naive job processor that holds tasks in memory loses them on restart. The fix is a durable queue (Redis Streams, SQS, Kafka) that serves as the source of truth for pending work. Workers are stateless consumers: they claim a task from the queue, process it, and acknowledge completion. Failed workers simply let the queue redeliver the task to another worker. This pattern—competing consumers on a durable queue—is the standard solution for stateless background processing.
bullets: Audit: catalog all in-memory state before migrating
Start with sessions: isolated, well-understood, moves to Redis cleanly
Two-level cache: short-TTL in-process + Redis backing; in-process is optimization, not correctness
Background jobs: durable queue (Kafka, SQS) as source of truth; workers are stateless consumers

core.title: What Makes a Service Stateless?
paragraphs: A stateless service holds no memory of previous requests. Each call is self-contained. Statefulness creeps in through in-memory sessions, local caches, sticky connections, and locally queued work.
The architectural principle: push all state to external systems purpose-built to manage it—Redis for sessions, S3 for files, databases for persistent records.
When the application tier has no local state, every instance is identical and interchangeable—the ideal condition for horizontal scaling, rolling deploys, and auto-scaling.

core.title: Session Management Patterns
paragraphs: Redis sessions: externalize session objects; any instance can handle any session; supports instant invalidation; adds 0.5–2ms per lookup.
JWTs: encode session state in the token itself; no server lookup needed; cannot be revoked before expiry; use short expiry + refresh token rotation.
Hybrid: short-lived JWT access tokens + Redis-backed refresh tokens combines stateless performance with revocation capability.

core.title: Twelve-Factor App and Stateless Principles
paragraphs: Twelve-Factor VI: processes are stateless and share-nothing. Any persistent data lives in backing services.
Disposability follows: stateless processes start/stop instantly, enabling rolling deploys and auto-scaling without draining in-flight state.
Idempotency is the companion principle: retried requests produce the same result; use idempotency keys for non-idempotent operations.

deepDive.title: Consistency Semantics of External State Stores
paragraphs: Moving state to external stores introduces consistency questions. Redis with default configuration provides eventual consistency during network partitions—acceptable for sessions but not financial balances. Redis Cluster with WAIT command can achieve near-synchronous replication at the cost of write latency.

PostgreSQL with synchronous_commit=on provides strong consistency; every write is durable before the client receives acknowledgment. For financial state, inventory counters, or any state where loss would be catastrophic, pay the latency cost of strong consistency. Understand what guarantee each store offers and match it to the state's consistency requirement.

Distributed locking is sometimes needed for stateless services that must coordinate—e.g., ensuring only one worker processes a given job at a time. Redis SETNX (set if not exists) with TTL is the standard distributed lock primitive. Libraries like Redlock implement multi-node locking for higher safety guarantees. Be aware that distributed locks can fail in subtle ways under network partitions; prefer idempotent operations over locks where possible.
bullets: Redis: fast but eventual consistency; use WAIT for near-sync replication
PostgreSQL: strong consistency; appropriate for financial/critical state
Redlock: multi-node Redis locking; safer than single-node but still has edge cases
Prefer idempotency over distributed locks for resilience

deepDive.title: Stateless Architecture in Kubernetes
paragraphs: Kubernetes is built around the assumption of stateless workloads. Deployments (the most common workload type) treat pods as cattle: any pod can be scheduled on any node, killed and replaced, or migrated during node drains. This works perfectly for stateless services. StatefulSets exist specifically for applications that need stable network identity and persistent storage—databases, Kafka brokers—where each replica is unique.

Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA) scales stateless deployments based on CPU, memory, or custom metrics. Because pods are stateless, adding replicas is instantaneous and safe. Pod Disruption Budgets (PDB) ensure a minimum number of replicas remain available during voluntary disruptions (node upgrades, cluster maintenance), giving you rolling-upgrade safety without manual coordination.

Config and secrets in Kubernetes should be injected as environment variables or mounted volumes, never baked into container images—a direct application of Twelve-Factor III. This makes the same image deployable to dev/staging/prod by changing only the injected config, achieving environment parity without image rebuilds.

expert.title: Expert: Request Coalescing and In-Process State as Optimization
paragraphs: Truly stateless services still benefit from in-process state used as a performance optimization rather than a correctness dependency. Request coalescing (also called request deduplication) detects multiple concurrent requests for the same resource and serves them all from a single upstream call. The in-process state (the in-flight request map) is ephemeral: on restart it is empty, which means the first requests after a restart fan out normally. Libraries like singleflight (Go) and lock-based coalescing in Java implement this pattern.

Warm-up state—data loaded at startup that is expensive to fetch—is acceptable as long as the service degrades gracefully during the warm-up window and can function (perhaps with higher latency) while warming. Kubernetes readiness probes are the mechanism: the pod is not added to the load balancer endpoint list until the readiness check passes. This allows preloading config, ML model weights, or reference data before accepting traffic, while keeping the service architecturally stateless from the client perspective.

concepts: Stateless service: processes requests independently with no server-side memory between calls
Session affinity (sticky sessions): routing requests to the same server instance; anti-pattern for scaling
Redis session store: external shared session storage enabling stateless app tier
JWT (JSON Web Token): self-contained stateless token with cryptographic signature
Twelve-Factor App: methodology codifying stateless, disposable, horizontally scalable services
Disposability: processes that can start/stop instantly with no data loss
Idempotency: operations that produce the same result when executed multiple times
Idempotency key: unique token per operation used to detect and deduplicate retries
Two-level cache: in-process short-TTL cache backed by Redis; in-process is optimization only
Competing consumers: multiple stateless workers consuming from a shared durable queue
practices: Externalize all session state to Redis from day one—don't wait until scaling becomes painful
Use short-lived JWTs (15 min) with Redis-backed refresh tokens for revocable stateless auth
Make all handlers idempotent and test them by replaying the same request twice
Use Kubernetes readiness probes to gate traffic until warm-up state is loaded
Pool connections to external state stores; don't create a new connection per request
Set TTLs on all cached state; never rely on unbounded growth in an external store
Use durable queues (SQS, Kafka) as the source of truth for background job state
pitfalls: Embedding session state in-memory 'just for now'—it blocks horizontal scaling permanently until refactored
Long-lived JWTs without refresh rotation—a compromised token cannot be invalidated
Assuming Redis is always available—build graceful degradation for Redis unavailability
In-process cache as source of truth—a pod restart loses state that must be reconstructed from scratch
Background jobs that disappear on pod restart when backed only by in-memory queues
Session store becoming a hot-spot—all app instances funnel to one Redis; shard or use Redis Cluster

examples.title: Netflix API Gateway Statelessness
examples.description: Netflix's API gateway (Zuul) is fully stateless: every request carries a JWT that the gateway validates cryptographically without any external lookup. Session data for personalization and recommendation is fetched from dedicated microservices on demand. This allows the gateway tier to scale to thousands of instances and deploy dozens of times per day with zero downtime, since any instance can handle any request.

examples.title: Shopify's Redis Session Store
examples.description: Shopify hosts thousands of merchant storefronts from a shared Rails application fleet. All session state is stored in Redis, allowing any app server to serve any merchant. During flash sales where a single merchant drives 100x their normal traffic, Shopify auto-scales the app tier horizontally within minutes—possible only because the app tier is fully stateless.

keyTakeaways: Stateless application tiers enable horizontal scaling, rolling deploys, and auto-scaling without coordination
Externalize sessions to Redis; use JWTs for truly stateless auth with short expiry + refresh tokens
Idempotency is the companion to statelessness: safe retries require idempotent handlers
In-process cache is acceptable as a performance optimization, never as a correctness dependency
Kubernetes Deployments assume stateless workloads; StatefulSets exist for the exceptions
Background jobs need durable queues as state source of truth; workers should be stateless consumers
lessons.whyItMatters: Stateless services are the prerequisite for practically every horizontal scaling, deployment safety, and fault tolerance pattern used in modern distributed systems. Without stateless application tiers, you cannot reliably auto-scale, cannot do zero-downtime rolling deploys, and cannot recover gracefully from instance failures. It is the single architectural choice that unlocks the most operational capabilities.
reflectionQuestions: Your Rails app stores session data in an in-memory hash. What are the exact failure modes when you try to run two instances behind a load balancer?
What are the security implications of storing user permissions in a JWT that expires in 24 hours?
Design a background job processor for sending emails that is fully stateless and survives pod restarts.
An in-process LRU cache holds 10GB of frequently read data. How do you safely externalize it without hurting latency?
numbersToKnow: Redis round-trip: 0.5–2ms within same datacenter; 1–5ms cross-AZ
JWT typical expiry: 15 minutes (access token), 7–30 days (refresh token)
Redis Cluster: horizontal sharding across up to 1000 nodes; 16384 hash slots
Idempotency key storage: typically 7–30 days in DB to cover retry windows

lessons.title: Vertical vs Horizontal Scaling
lessons.summary: Every system eventually hits capacity limits. Understanding when to scale up (bigger machines) versus scale out (more machines) is one of the most consequential architectural decisions you will make. The two strategies have radically different cost curves, failure modes, operational complexity, and ceiling heights.

sections.title: Vertical Scaling: Bigger Machines
paragraphs: Vertical scaling (scale up) means adding more CPU, RAM, faster disks, or higher-bandwidth NICs to a single machine. When your database starts straining under query load, you move from a 4-core/16GB instance to a 32-core/256GB one. The appeal is simplicity: no code changes, no distributed coordination, no data partitioning. The same application binary runs on the larger machine and immediately benefits from all those extra resources.

Modern cloud providers let you vertically scale in minutes, making it an attractive first response to capacity pressure. AWS RDS, Azure SQL, and Google Cloud SQL all support live resizing with brief maintenance windows. Vertical scaling works exceptionally well for stateful systems like relational databases where distributing state is complex and expensive—a PostgreSQL instance on a 96-core machine with 384GB of RAM handles enormous workloads while remaining a single manageable system.

The ceiling, however, is real. Even the largest EC2 instance (u-24tb1.metal at 448 vCPUs, 24TB RAM) has limits, and cost grows super-linearly past a certain point. Commodity hardware scales linearly in price; high-end machines charge a premium for each increment. Beyond hardware limits, vertical scaling creates a single point of failure—when that one big machine goes down, everything stops. High availability requires redundancy, which means you need at least two machines anyway.
bullets: Zero code change: application runs on larger hardware with no modification
Operational simplicity: one machine to monitor, patch, and backup
Hard ceiling: no machine is infinitely large; costs grow super-linearly
SPOF: a single large machine is both the asset and the risk

sections.title: Horizontal Scaling: More Machines
paragraphs: Horizontal scaling (scale out) distributes load across a fleet of commodity machines. Instead of one 32-core database, you run eight 4-core nodes sharing the work. This model's ceiling is effectively unlimited—you can add nodes as traffic grows—and it naturally provides redundancy. When one node fails, the other seven continue serving traffic. This is why large-scale systems like Cassandra, Kafka, Elasticsearch, and stateless API services are all designed from the ground up for horizontal scaling.

The fundamental challenge is coordination. With one machine, you have a single address space, shared memory, and ACID transactions for free. With ten machines, you must decide how to partition data, how to route requests to the right partition, how to handle failures during distributed writes, and how to keep replicas consistent. These problems are non-trivial—the entire field of distributed systems research exists to address them. Technologies like consistent hashing, Raft consensus, two-phase commit, and eventual consistency are all responses to horizontal scaling's coordination challenges.

Stateless services scale horizontally most elegantly. If your API server holds no session state—all state lives in databases or caches—then any request can go to any server. Adding more API servers behind a load balancer is purely additive and risk-free. This is why the industry has converged on stateless application tiers: horizontal scaling of stateless components is cheap and reliable, while the complex state management is delegated to specialized storage systems designed to handle it.
bullets: Linear cost scaling: add commodity machines as needed
Natural fault tolerance: N-1 nodes handle one node failure
Requires load balancing, service discovery, and distributed coordination
Stateless services scale horizontally with near-zero overhead

sections.title: The Decision Framework: When to Choose Each
paragraphs: Start with vertical scaling for new systems. It's faster to implement, cheaper initially, and avoids premature complexity. A well-tuned single PostgreSQL instance handles millions of requests per day. Measure first—most systems never hit the limits of a vertical architecture within their operating lifetime, and over-engineering for horizontal scale adds years to your delivery timeline. The 'scale to millions of users' problem is a good problem to have; most products never get there.

Switch to horizontal scaling when you hit specific triggers: when the largest available instance of your database tier still can't keep up with read load (consider read replicas—a form of horizontal read scaling), when your application tier's CPU or memory requires more than the largest VM available, when you need zero-downtime deployments (rolling deploys across multiple instances), or when you need geographic distribution (data must live in multiple regions). These are concrete, measurable triggers, not speculative future needs.

Many production systems use a hybrid approach: vertically scale stateful components (databases, caches) up to a comfortable size, then add horizontal read replicas to distribute read load. For the stateless application tier, horizontal scaling is the default from day one because it's cheap and enables zero-downtime deployments. This combination gives you operational simplicity for the hard parts (stateful storage) and unlimited scale for the easy parts (stateless compute).
bullets: New systems: start vertical, avoid premature distributed system complexity
Read-heavy: add read replicas before rearchitecting to sharding
Stateless tiers: always horizontal (simple, cheap, zero-downtime deploys)
Trigger to shard: when primary write throughput exceeds largest available instance

sections.title: Practical Patterns: Auto-Scaling and Elasticity
paragraphs: Cloud-native systems combine both strategies through auto-scaling groups. Horizontal scaling handles the base load with a minimum fleet size, while auto-scaling policies add or remove instances in response to CPU, memory, or request-rate metrics. This elasticity means you provision for average load, not peak load, dramatically reducing costs for workloads with diurnal patterns (e.g., a consumer app seeing 10x traffic at 8pm versus 3am). AWS Auto Scaling, Kubernetes HPA, and GCP Managed Instance Groups all implement this pattern.

Scaling down is as important as scaling up. Systems that scale up for a traffic spike but never scale back down waste money and can mask performance regressions hidden by over-provisioning. Configure scale-in policies with appropriate cooldown periods to prevent thrashing (rapid scale-up/scale-down cycles that happen faster than your system stabilizes). Set minimum instance counts to handle cold-start latency—you don't want zero instances when the first request arrives after a quiet period.

Database scaling requires different mechanics. For writes, you eventually must shard—partition data across multiple primary nodes by key range or hash. For reads, add replicas and implement read-after-write consistency in your application (route reads that immediately follow writes to the primary, or use replication lag monitoring). Consider NewSQL databases like CockroachDB or Spanner that handle horizontal scaling transparently; they trade some performance for the operational simplicity of appearing as a single relational database.
bullets: Scale-out: add instances in response to load; scale-in: remove them to save cost
Cooldown periods prevent auto-scaling thrash on noisy metrics
Database sharding is the last resort; exhaust vertical and read-replica options first
NewSQL (CockroachDB, Spanner) offers horizontal scale with SQL semantics

sections.title: Cost Curves and Trade-offs
paragraphs: Vertical scaling costs are predictable but non-linear at the high end. Cloud providers typically charge 2–4x more per vCPU/GB for their largest instance families compared to mid-tier instances. A 96-core instance rarely provides 96x the performance of a 1-core instance due to contention, coordination overhead, and memory bus saturation. Beyond a certain size, you get diminishing returns per dollar, making horizontal scaling more cost-effective.

Horizontal scaling has fixed overhead costs that amortize across many instances: load balancers, service discovery infrastructure, monitoring per-node, and the engineering time to build and maintain a distributed system. For small-scale systems, these overhead costs make horizontal scaling more expensive than vertical. The crossover point depends on your engineering team size, operational maturity, and traffic patterns—but it generally occurs somewhere between 10,000 and 1,000,000 requests per day for typical web services.

Spot and preemptible instances are only viable in horizontal, stateless architectures. AWS Spot Instances provide up to 90% cost savings but can be reclaimed with two minutes notice. Stateless application tiers tolerate this because losing one node is handled gracefully by the load balancer. Stateful workloads on spot instances require careful checkpointing and restart logic. The combination of horizontal scaling and spot instances is one of the most powerful cost levers available to engineering teams running at scale.
bullets: Largest instances charge premium per vCPU; horizontal often cheaper above ~32 cores
Horizontal overhead (LB, service discovery) amortizes at ~10K+ RPS
Spot/preemptible instances: up to 90% savings, only safe for stateless or checkpointed workloads
Measure: profile before scaling; often the bottleneck is a slow query, not raw compute

core.title: Vertical Scaling: Bigger Machines

Modern cloud providers support live vertical resizing with brief maintenance windows. Vertical scaling works exceptionally well for stateful systems like relational databases where distributing state is complex and expensive.
The ceiling is real. Even the largest available cloud instance has limits, cost grows super-linearly at the high end, and a single large machine remains a single point of failure.
bullets: Zero code change: application runs on larger hardware with no modification
Operational simplicity: one machine to monitor, patch, and backup
Hard ceiling: costs grow super-linearly; largest instances are expensive
SPOF: a single large machine is both the asset and the risk

core.title: Horizontal Scaling: More Machines
paragraphs: Horizontal scaling distributes load across a fleet of commodity machines. This model's ceiling is effectively unlimited and naturally provides redundancy. Stateless services scale horizontally most elegantly.
The fundamental challenge is coordination. With multiple machines you must decide how to partition data, route requests, handle failures during distributed writes, and keep replicas consistent.
Technologies like consistent hashing, Raft consensus, two-phase commit, and eventual consistency are all responses to horizontal scaling's coordination challenges.
bullets: Linear cost scaling: add commodity machines as needed
Natural fault tolerance: N-1 nodes handle one node failure
Requires load balancing, service discovery, and distributed coordination

core.title: The Decision Framework
paragraphs: Start with vertical scaling for new systems—faster to implement, cheaper initially, avoids premature complexity. Measure first; most systems never hit limits of a vertical architecture within their operating lifetime.
Switch to horizontal when you hit specific triggers: read replicas needed, application tier exceeds largest VM, zero-downtime deployments required, or geographic distribution needed.
Many production systems use a hybrid: vertically scale stateful components, horizontally scale stateless tiers.

deepDive.title: Database Scaling Mechanics
paragraphs: Database scaling follows a well-worn progression: start with a single primary (vertical), add read replicas to offload read load, introduce connection pooling (PgBouncer, ProxySQL) to reduce connection overhead, then shard when write throughput exceeds what a single primary can handle. Each step is disruptive; plan transitions carefully.

Sharding strategies matter enormously. Range-based sharding (user_id 0–999999 on shard A, 1000000–1999999 on shard B) enables range queries but creates hotspots when IDs are sequential. Hash-based sharding distributes load evenly but makes range queries require scatter-gather across all shards. Consistent hashing with virtual nodes (Cassandra, Redis Cluster) minimizes data movement during rebalancing when shards are added or removed.

Cross-shard queries and transactions are the main pain points of sharding. A query joining users and orders becomes a multi-shard scatter-gather operation with significantly higher latency. Cross-shard transactions require two-phase commit or saga patterns—both complex and slow. The best mitigation is careful data modeling: colocate entities that are frequently joined (e.g., keep all data for a given tenant on the same shard in a multi-tenant system).
bullets: Scaling progression: single primary → read replicas → connection pooling → sharding
Range sharding: good for range queries, prone to hotspots
Hash sharding: even distribution, range queries require scatter-gather
Colocation: keep frequently-joined data on the same shard

deepDive.title: Auto-Scaling Design Patterns
paragraphs: Effective auto-scaling requires choosing the right signal. CPU utilization is the most common metric but often lags the actual problem—a request queue depth or response latency metric responds faster to load spikes. For web services, target tracking on request-per-second-per-instance gives more stable scaling behavior than reactive CPU thresholds.

Predictive scaling uses historical patterns to provision capacity ahead of expected load. If your traffic reliably doubles at 9am Monday, pre-scale five minutes before to avoid the lag between load increase, metric breach, instance launch, and warmup. AWS Predictive Scaling and KEDA (Kubernetes Event-Driven Autoscaling) both support time-series based proactive scaling.

Scale-to-zero architectures (AWS Lambda, Cloud Run, Knative) take horizontal scaling to its logical extreme: instances drop to zero when idle and spin up on demand. Cold-start latency (100ms–2s depending on runtime) is the main trade-off. Mitigate with minimum instance counts for latency-sensitive paths and use scale-to-zero only for infrequently-invoked functions.
bullets: Use request-queue depth or latency as scaling signal, not just CPU
Predictive scaling: pre-scale before expected load spikes using historical patterns
Scale-to-zero viable for infrequent, latency-tolerant workloads

expert.title: Expert: NUMA, Affinity, and Kernel-Level Vertical Scaling
paragraphs: On very large vertical machines (>8 sockets), Non-Uniform Memory Access (NUMA) topology means that memory latency varies by which socket owns the target memory bank. A thread on socket 0 accessing memory owned by socket 3 may pay 2–3x the latency of local access. High-performance databases like Oracle and SAP HANA expose NUMA binding; general-purpose workloads benefit from numactl binding and OS-level NUMA balancing. Ignoring NUMA on 100-core machines leaves significant performance on the table.

Kernel scheduling decisions—process affinity, cgroup CPU quotas, interrupt affinity—significantly affect throughput on large multi-core machines. Network interrupt processing (IRQ affinity) can be pinned to specific cores to avoid cross-NUMA traffic. CPU affinity masks for latency-sensitive threads prevent OS migration across NUMA nodes. These optimizations matter at the high-frequency trading and low-latency database tier level where microseconds count.

Horizontal scaling (scale out): distributing load across multiple commodity machines
Single point of failure (SPOF): risk inherent in any single-node architecture
Stateless services: application instances with no local state; can be freely replicated
Sharding: partitioning data across multiple database nodes by key range or hash
Read replicas: copies of a primary database that handle read-only queries
Auto-scaling: dynamically adding/removing instances based on load metrics
Consistent hashing: distributes keys across nodes; minimizes remapping when nodes change
Spot/preemptible instances: deeply discounted compute that can be reclaimed on short notice
NUMA: non-uniform memory access topology on multi-socket servers

pitfalls: Premature sharding: adds enormous complexity before exhausting vertical and read-replica options
Assuming more cores means proportionally more throughput—NUMA, coordination, and lock contention cap gains
Forgetting cold-start latency when scaling from zero—first request to a cold instance is slow
Using CPU as the sole auto-scaling metric—it lags behind user-visible latency
Stateful application tiers: session affinity requirements make horizontal scaling painful
Ignoring database connection limits when scaling application tier horizontally (N servers × M connections = overload)

examples.title: Instagram's Scaling Journey
examples.description: Instagram launched on a single EC2 machine. As traffic grew, they vertically scaled the database, then added read replicas, then moved to Django's stateless app tier running on hundreds of instances behind a load balancer. Only after reaching hundreds of millions of users did they introduce database sharding—and even then, they used PostgreSQL-based sharding rather than exotic distributed databases, keeping operational complexity manageable.

examples.title: Stack Overflow's Vertical Scaling
examples.description: Stack Overflow famously serves millions of requests per day from a small number of very large SQL Server instances. Their architecture is a deliberate counter-example to the 'everything must be distributed' orthodoxy. By using large vertical machines, aggressive caching, and read replicas, they maintain a tiny ops team while serving enormous traffic. The lesson: horizontal scaling is not always necessary or even optimal.

examples.title: AWS Aurora Auto Scaling
examples.description: An e-commerce platform uses Aurora with auto-scaling read replicas. The primary handles writes (vertically scaled to db.r6g.16xlarge for peak write throughput). Aurora automatically adds read replicas when average CPU on existing replicas exceeds 70%, and removes them when load drops below 30%. Combined with application-tier ECS auto-scaling, the system handles 100x holiday traffic without pre-provisioning.

Horizontal scaling is necessary for stateless tiers, geographic distribution, and beyond vertical limits
Stateless application tiers enable free horizontal scaling; push all state to dedicated storage systems
Database scaling progression: vertical → read replicas → connection pooling → sharding
Auto-scaling on latency/queue-depth signals is more responsive than CPU-only policies
Measure before scaling: the bottleneck is often a slow query or missing index, not raw compute
Spot instances + horizontal scaling = up to 90% compute cost reduction
lessons.whyItMatters: Vertical vs. horizontal scaling is one of the first questions every system design interview explores. Choosing wrong means either spending 10x on hardware or building distributed system complexity you don't need. The best engineers know when to scale up (stateful, early-stage, operationally simple) and when to scale out (stateless tiers, geographic distribution, beyond vertical limits), and they can defend the trade-offs clearly.

lessons.title: Stateless Services & State Management
lessons.summary: Stateless services can be added, removed, and replaced freely — they are the foundation of elastic, fault-tolerant systems. State must be deliberately placed in databases, caches, message queues, or object stores. Misplaced state is the most common reason scaling efforts fail.

sections.title: Stateless vs Stateful Services
paragraphs: A stateless service treats every request independently. It does not rely on data stored in local memory from a previous request on the same machine. Any instance can handle any request. This property enables horizontal scaling, rolling deployments, and instant recovery from node failure.

A stateful service remembers context across requests or over time — in-memory session stores, local file caches, embedded databases, or workflow state tied to a specific process. Stateful services require sticky routing, replication, or leader election to scale and survive failures.

Most production architectures push toward stateless application tiers while concentrating state in specialized, managed stores. The application becomes a thin orchestration layer: validate input, read/write state externally, return a response.

sections.title: Where State Should Live
paragraphs: User sessions belong in a distributed cache (Redis, Memcached) or a database — not in JVM heap or Node.js process memory. Redis offers TTL-based expiry, atomic operations, and sub-millisecond latency, making it the default session store for scaled web apps.

Long-lived domain data lives in the primary database with ACID guarantees. Caches hold derived or hot data with explicit invalidation policies. Workflow and job state goes to durable queues or workflow engines (Temporal, Step Functions). Uploaded files go to object storage (S3), not local disk.

Configuration and secrets belong in environment variables, config services, or secrets managers — injected at startup, not baked into images. Feature flags live in dedicated flag services so behavior can change without redeployment.
bullets: Session state → Redis / DynamoDB with TTL
Domain data → PostgreSQL / MySQL / distributed DB
Ephemeral hot data → in-memory cache with eviction policy
Async work state → message queues or workflow engines

sections.title: Sticky Sessions and Their Trade-offs
paragraphs: Sticky sessions (session affinity) route a user to the same server using cookies or load balancer rules. They allow in-memory session storage without immediate externalization — a tempting shortcut during early development.

The downsides are significant. Uneven load distribution occurs when some users are heavier than others. Node failure drops all sessions pinned to that node unless sessions are replicated (which reintroduces complexity). Rolling deployments require draining sticky connections carefully.

Sticky sessions are acceptable for WebSocket connections where connection state is inherently tied to a node — but even then, teams use pub/sub backplanes (Redis) to broadcast messages across a cluster. For HTTP APIs, prefer external session stores over stickiness.

sections.title: Shared-Nothing Architecture
paragraphs: Shared-nothing means each node is self-sufficient: own CPU, memory, and local disk, with no shared memory or filesystem between application servers. Nodes communicate only through the network via databases, caches, and queues.

This model maximizes fault isolation. One node's crash does not corrupt another's memory. Scaling is linear: add nodes, update load balancer, done. Google's Bigtable, Cassandra, and most microservice deployments follow shared-nothing principles.

The trade-off is network round-trips for every state access. Poorly designed systems chatter excessively with Redis and the database. Connection pooling, batching, and local caching (with short TTLs) mitigate latency while preserving statelessness at the service level.

deepDive.title: Stateless Services & State Management — Operational deep dive
paragraphs: Operating Stateless Services & State Management well means defining the scarce resource (CPU, memory, disk, network, or tokens), the SLIs that reflect user pain, and the knobs that trade cost for latency.
Under load, measure amplification: how many bytes, RPCs, or disk writes you pay per user request. Prefetch and batch only when measurements show benefit — premature batching adds tail latency.
Failure drills should include dependency slowdown (not only hard down), clock skew, and disk full. Verify alerts, dashboards, and runbooks against those drills.
bullets: Name the scarcest resource and budget it
Track p50/p99 and error rate for the user journey
Rehearse partial dependency failure

deepDive.title: Stateless Services & State Management — Correctness edges
paragraphs: Correctness edges around Stateless Services & State Management often appear at retries, partial writes, and schema evolution. Make handlers idempotent and state transitions explicit.

Document what clients may observe during failover: stale reads, duplicate messages, or delayed visibility. If the product cannot tolerate an anomaly, enforce a stronger consistency boundary — and pay for it knowingly.

expert.title: Stateless Services & State Management — Expert / multi-region notes
paragraphs: At multi-region scale, Stateless Services & State Management interacts with RTT, quorum placement, and cost of cross-region replication. Prefer region-local user paths with asynchronous global state when invariants allow.
Cost envelopes matter: chart unit cost vs QPS and vs data size. Many 'performance' projects are actually cost projects in disguise — make the objective explicit.

examples.title: JWT vs server-side sessions
examples.description: A mobile API uses signed JWTs for authentication — no server-side session store needed, enabling fully stateless API gateways. A web app with instant logout requirements uses Redis sessions instead, because JWTs cannot be revoked without a blocklist (which reintroduces state).

examples.title: Shopping cart during peak traffic
examples.description: Cart state lives in Redis keyed by user ID with a 7-day TTL. API servers are interchangeable. During a node failure, users retry and hit a different server — cart data is intact. Checkout transitions cart to an order in PostgreSQL atomically.

Kill nodes in testing to verify your state management actually works

lessons.title: Vertical vs Horizontal Scaling
lessons.summary: Scaling is how systems handle growth in traffic, data, and complexity. Vertical scaling adds power to a single machine; horizontal scaling adds more machines. Production architectures almost always combine both, but horizontal scaling — with stateless services and load balancing — is the path to massive, fault-tolerant scale.

sections.title: What Scaling Means in Practice
paragraphs: When users, requests, or data volume grow, every component in your stack faces pressure: CPU, memory, disk I/O, network bandwidth, and connection limits. Scaling is the set of strategies you use to increase capacity without rewriting the entire system.

The two fundamental approaches are vertical scaling (scale up) and horizontal scaling (scale out). Vertical scaling means upgrading the hardware or instance size of a single node — more cores, more RAM, faster SSDs. Horizontal scaling means running multiple copies of a service behind a load balancer and distributing work across them.

Early-stage products often scale vertically because it requires no architectural changes: you resize the database instance or upgrade the app server. But vertical scaling has hard ceilings — single-machine limits, diminishing returns on cost, and a single point of failure. Horizontal scaling removes those ceilings but demands that your application, data layer, and deployment pipeline support distribution from the start or through deliberate refactoring.

sections.title: Vertical Scaling: Strengths and Limits
paragraphs: Vertical scaling is operationally simple. You change an instance type, restart services, and capacity increases. Databases especially benefit early on: a larger PostgreSQL instance with more RAM holds more of the working set in memory, reducing disk reads dramatically.

The limits appear quickly at scale. Cloud providers cap instance sizes; beyond a certain point, doubling RAM costs more than doubling throughput. A single large database cannot survive zone failures without replication. Memory-bound workloads may not fit on any commercially available machine.

Vertical scaling also creates upgrade windows: migrating from db.r5.2xlarge to db.r5.4xlarge often requires downtime or complex failover. Teams that rely exclusively on vertical scaling eventually hit a wall where the only option is a painful horizontal split — sharding, read replicas, or service extraction.
bullets: Best for: early growth, stateful monoliths, workloads that resist distribution
Watch for: cost curves that outpace revenue, single points of failure, upgrade downtime

sections.title: Horizontal Scaling: Architecture Requirements
paragraphs: Horizontal scaling distributes load across N identical nodes. A load balancer — L4 (TCP) or L7 (HTTP) — routes incoming requests using algorithms like round-robin, least connections, or consistent hashing. Health checks remove unhealthy nodes automatically.

For horizontal scaling to work, application servers must be stateless or share state through external stores. Session data in local memory breaks horizontal scale: killing one node loses sessions for users pinned to it. Externalize sessions to Redis, use JWTs, or accept sticky sessions with their trade-offs.

Data layers scale horizontally through read replicas (scale reads), sharding (partition writes across nodes), or purpose-built distributed databases (Cassandra, DynamoDB). Each approach introduces consistency, query, and operational complexity that vertical scaling avoided.

sections.title: Auto-Scaling and Elastic Capacity
paragraphs: Modern cloud platforms offer auto-scaling groups that add or remove instances based on metrics — CPU utilization, request rate, queue depth, or custom CloudWatch/Prometheus signals. Elastic capacity matches cost to demand: fewer servers at 3 AM, more during peak events.

Auto-scaling requires warm-up time. New instances must pass health checks, load application code, and establish connection pools before accepting traffic. Scale-out policies should trigger before saturation; scale-in policies should be conservative to avoid flapping during variable load.

Design for scale-to-zero only when cold-start latency is acceptable (serverless functions). For latency-sensitive APIs, maintain a minimum fleet size and use predictive scaling for known traffic patterns like product launches or Black Friday.

sections.title: Choosing the Right Strategy
paragraphs: Start vertical when the team is small and traffic is predictable. Plan horizontal paths before you need them: stateless services, connection pooling, database read replicas, and clear service boundaries make future scale-out feasible.

Use vertical scaling for components that are inherently hard to distribute — single-leader databases, legacy monoliths, or licensed software with per-core pricing. Use horizontal scaling for stateless APIs, worker pools, CDN edges, and stream processors.

The best production systems combine both: vertically sized database primaries with horizontally scaled read replicas; horizontally scaled API tiers on moderately sized instances rather than one giant machine or hundreds of tiny ones.

examples.title: E-commerce checkout API
examples.description: An checkout service runs as 20 stateless containers behind an ALB. Session carts live in Redis; orders write to a PostgreSQL primary with two read replicas for order history. During flash sales, auto-scaling adds API containers from 20 to 80 based on request count, while the database scales vertically once before adding read replicas.

examples.title: Video transcoding pipeline
examples.description: Transcoding is embarrassingly parallel: each video chunk is independent. A job queue (SQS) feeds a horizontally scaled worker fleet. Workers scale from 5 to 500 based on queue depth. No vertical scaling needed — each worker is a modest CPU-optimized instance.

examples.title: Legacy monolith migration path
examples.description: A Rails monolith on a single 32 GB server hits memory limits. Phase 1: vertical upgrade to 64 GB. Phase 2: extract file uploads to S3 and sessions to Redis. Phase 3: run 4 stateless app servers behind Nginx. Phase 4: introduce read replicas for reporting queries.

lessons.title: AuthN, AuthZ, Encryption & Secrets
lessons.summary: Authentication establishes identity; authorization decides permissions; encryption protects data in transit and at rest; secrets management prevents credential sprawl. System designs that bolt these on late leak.

sections.title: AuthN patterns
paragraphs: Sessions, JWTs, mTLS for service identity, OAuth/OIDC for delegated user login. Know token lifetime, revocation, and audience restrictions.

sections.title: AuthZ models
paragraphs: RBAC, ABAC, ReBAC. Enforce on every data path — UI checks are not security. Central policy engines help, but local enforcement must fail closed.

sections.title: Encryption
paragraphs: TLS everywhere in transit. At rest: disk encryption plus field-level for sensitive columns. Key rotation and envelope encryption are part of the design.

sections.title: Secrets
paragraphs: No secrets in images or git. Use a vault/KMS with short-lived credentials. Audit access. Rotate on incident without redeploying everywhere.

sections.title: What Supply Chain Security is solving
paragraphs: Supply Chain Security exists because naive designs around identity, policy, and confidential data break under scale, partial failure, or changing requirements. sections.title: Core mechanics
paragraphs: Mechanically, Supply Chain Security involves a small set of moving parts: inputs, state, an algorithm or protocol, and outputs/side effects. Draw those parts explicitly. If state is replicated, write down the replication/consistency rule. If work is asynchronous, write down delivery semantics.

Performance characteristics usually come from amplification (how much internal work per external request), locality (whether work stays on one node), and contention (locks, hot keys, leader bottlenecks).

Correctness characteristics usually come from failure handling: retries, timeouts, idempotency, and what clients observe during failover. If you cannot explain the failure story, you do not yet understand Supply Chain Security.

lessons.title: Authentication, Authorization & Encryption
lessons.summary: Security is layered defense: verify identity (authentication), enforce permissions (authorization), protect data in transit and at rest (encryption), and manage secrets safely. Most breaches stem from misconfigured auth, leaked credentials, and missing encryption — not sophisticated zero-day exploits.

sections.title: Authentication: Proving Identity
paragraphs: Authentication answers 'who are you?' Common mechanisms include username/password (with bcrypt/argon2 hashing), multi-factor authentication (TOTP, WebAuthn), API keys, and federated identity via OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect (OIDC).

OAuth 2.0 delegates authorization to an identity provider (Google, Okta, Auth0) without sharing passwords. OIDC adds an identity layer — ID tokens (JWTs) containing user claims. The authorization code flow with PKCE is the standard for web and mobile apps.

JWTs (JSON Web Tokens) encode claims in a signed, base64 payload. Stateless verification is fast — no server-side session lookup. Downsides: revocation is hard (requires blocklists or short TTLs), tokens can be stolen if not stored securely, and payload is readable (not encrypted) unless using JWE.

sections.title: Authorization: Enforcing Permissions
paragraphs: Authorization answers 'what can you do?' Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) assigns permissions to roles (admin, editor, viewer) and roles to users. Simple and widely used for internal tools and SaaS products.

Attribute-Based Access Control (ABAC) evaluates policies against attributes — user department, resource owner, time of day, IP range. More flexible for complex enterprise policies. Policy engines (OPA, Cedar) evaluate ABAC rules at runtime.

Principle of least privilege: grant minimum permissions needed. Service accounts for machine-to-machine auth get scoped API keys or mTLS certificates — never root credentials. Regularly audit and rotate permissions.

sections.title: Encryption in Transit and at Rest
paragraphs: Encryption in transit protects data on the wire via TLS 1.2+ (HTTPS, mTLS for service-to-service). Terminate TLS at the load balancer or service mesh; enforce HSTS and modern cipher suites. Never transmit secrets or PII over unencrypted HTTP.

Encryption at rest protects stored data: database TDE (Transparent Data Encryption), S3 server-side encryption (SSE-S3, SSE-KMS), disk encryption on VMs. Keys managed by KMS (AWS KMS, HashiCorp Vault) with rotation policies.

Application-level encryption adds a layer for especially sensitive fields (SSN, credit card) — encrypt before storing so a database breach does not expose plaintext. Manage field-level keys separately from storage keys.

sections.title: Secrets Management
paragraphs: Secrets — API keys, database passwords, TLS private keys, encryption keys — must never appear in source code, Docker images, or git history. Use secrets managers: AWS Secrets Manager, HashiCorp Vault, GCP Secret Manager, Kubernetes Secrets (with encryption at rest enabled).
Inject secrets at runtime via environment variables or mounted volumes. Rotate secrets automatically where supported. Audit access to secrets — who read which secret when.
Development environments use separate secrets from production. .env files are for local dev only — add to .gitignore and use tools like git-secrets to prevent accidental commits.

sections.title: Security in System Design
paragraphs: Defense in depth: WAF at the edge, network segmentation (VPCs, security groups), auth at API gateway, authorization in services, encryption everywhere. No single layer is sufficient.

Input validation and parameterized queries prevent injection attacks. Rate limiting and CAPTCHA mitigate brute force. Security headers (CSP, X-Frame-Options) reduce browser-side attacks. Log and alert on auth failures and privilege escalation attempts.

Compliance frameworks (SOC 2, GDPR, PCI-DSS) mandate specific controls — understand which apply to your domain. Security is a continuous process: dependency scanning, penetration testing, and incident response plans.

paragraphs: Operating Authentication, Authorization & Encryption well means defining the scarce resource (CPU, memory, disk, network, or tokens), the SLIs that reflect user pain, and the knobs that trade cost for latency.

examples.title: SaaS multi-tenant authorization
examples.description: Users authenticate via Auth0 (OIDC). JWT contains user_id and org_id. API middleware extracts claims; each query filters by org_id for tenant isolation. Admin role checked via RBAC policy engine (OPA). Cross-tenant access returns 403.

examples.title: Microservice mTLS mesh
examples.description: Services in a Kubernetes cluster communicate via Istio service mesh with mutual TLS. Each service has a SPIFFE identity certificate. Unauthorized services cannot call internal APIs even if they reach the network — identity is verified on every request.

examples.title: PCI-compliant payment handling
examples.description: Credit card data never touches application servers — Stripe Elements tokenizes on the client. Tokens are sent to the backend, which calls Stripe API over TLS. Database stores only last-four digits. Secrets (Stripe API key) live in AWS Secrets Manager with 90-day rotation.
