lessons.title: Concurrency Patterns
lessons.summary: Concurrency patterns address the challenges of coordinating multiple execution paths—threads, goroutines, coroutines, or async tasks—that share resources or collaborate on work. From mutual exclusion and lock-free data structures to actor models and reactive streams, these patterns determine whether a system achieves its throughput and latency goals or suffers from races, deadlocks, and livelocks.

sections.title: Shared-State Concurrency: Locks and Their Problems
paragraphs: Shared-state concurrency allows multiple threads to access and modify common data, with mutual exclusion primitives (mutexes, semaphores, monitors) preventing simultaneous conflicting access. A mutex guards a critical section: only one thread executes it at a time. This model is intuitive and widely supported, but its correctness depends entirely on programmers remembering to acquire and release locks consistently—a discipline that breaks down at scale and under time pressure.

Deadlock occurs when two threads each hold a lock the other needs, and neither can progress. Thread A holds Lock 1 and waits for Lock 2; Thread B holds Lock 2 and waits for Lock 1. The system freezes without error. Prevention strategies: lock ordering (always acquire locks in a consistent global order), lock timeouts (tryLock with timeout; fail and retry), and lock hierarchy (establish an ownership hierarchy; lower-level code never acquires locks from higher levels). Detection requires monitoring thread states and finding cycles in the wait-for graph.

Livelock is the temporal counterpart to deadlock: threads keep executing but make no progress, each reacting to the other's actions. A retry-on-failure livelock: Thread A acquires Lock 1, tries Lock 2, finds it taken, releases Lock 1 and retries. Thread B does the same. Both keep releasing and retrying forever. The fix: introduce jitter in retry timing (randomized backoff) so the threads don't always conflict at exactly the same instant. Livelock is harder to detect than deadlock because threads appear busy.

Lock granularity is a critical performance lever. A single global lock is easy to implement but creates a bottleneck as thread count grows. Fine-grained locking (one lock per data item) maximizes parallelism but increases lock acquisition overhead and deadlock risk. Striped locking (ConcurrentHashMap's approach: 16 locks for 16 buckets, each covering 1/16 of the hash space) balances these concerns. Read-write locks allow concurrent reads but exclusive writes—use when reads vastly outnumber writes.
bullets: Mutex: mutual exclusion; one holder at a time; unacquired is blocking
Semaphore: count-based; allows up to N concurrent holders; use for resource pools
Read-write lock: concurrent readers OR exclusive writer; ideal for read-heavy data structures
Spinlock: busy-wait instead of sleep; only for very short critical sections on multi-core systems

sections.title: Lock-Free and Wait-Free Data Structures
paragraphs: Lock-free data structures use atomic hardware operations (Compare-And-Swap, Fetch-And-Add) instead of locks to coordinate access. CAS is the foundation: atomically compare a memory location to an expected value and swap in a new value only if the comparison succeeds. If another thread has modified the value, the CAS fails and the caller retries. This retry loop is the key property: some thread always makes progress (lock-free), even if individual threads may retry multiple times.

Wait-free is a stronger guarantee: every thread completes its operation in a bounded number of steps regardless of other threads. This is harder to achieve and not always necessary. Lock-free is sufficient for most practical concurrency needs. Java's AtomicLong, AtomicReference, and ConcurrentHashMap use CAS-based lock-free algorithms. Linux's futex uses a CAS fast path with kernel blocking as a fallback for high-contention cases—the best of both worlds for typical mutex usage patterns.

The ABA problem is a subtle hazard with CAS: Thread A reads value A, is preempted, Thread B changes the value to B and then back to A, Thread A's CAS succeeds because the value is 'A' again—but the data structure may have changed in a way the CAS doesn't detect. Solution: tagged pointers (pair the pointer with a version counter; CAS both; ABA becomes a valid change). Java's AtomicStampedReference implements this. In practice, ABA matters for pointer-based data structures (linked lists, trees); for simple counters and flags, it's not an issue.

Memory ordering is the other face of lock-free programming. CPUs and compilers reorder instructions for performance. Without explicit memory barriers, a lock-free algorithm that works correctly on a sequentially consistent model may fail on a relaxed-consistency architecture (ARM, POWER). Java's volatile and AtomicXxx classes provide the correct memory ordering guarantees. C++11's atomic library provides fine-grained ordering (relaxed, acquire, release, seq_cst). Using the wrong ordering produces races that only manifest on specific hardware, making them nearly impossible to debug.
bullets: CAS (Compare-And-Swap): atomic read-modify-write; foundation of lock-free algorithms
Lock-free: at least one thread always makes progress; no mutual exclusion
Wait-free: every thread makes progress in bounded steps; strongest guarantee
Memory barriers: prevent CPU/compiler reordering; required for correct lock-free code on relaxed-consistency CPUs

sections.title: Message Passing: CSP and the Actor Model
paragraphs: Message passing replaces shared state with communication: threads (or processes, or goroutines) communicate by sending messages rather than modifying shared data. The fundamental insight is that if data is owned by one thread at a time and transferred via messages, the need for locks disappears. Two prominent models: CSP (Communicating Sequential Processes), implemented by Go's goroutines and channels, and the Actor model, implemented by Erlang, Akka (Scala/Java), and Orleans (C#).

Go's goroutines and channels exemplify CSP. Goroutines are lightweight (4KB initial stack, multiplexed on OS threads) and cheap enough to create for each request or task. Channels are typed, synchronous (unbuffered) or buffered queues. The select statement multiplexes over multiple channels—wait for whichever channel has data first. The idiom 'do not communicate by sharing memory; instead, share memory by communicating' means data ownership transfers with the message rather than being guarded by locks.

The Actor model structures computation as a collection of actors: isolated units with private state that communicate only through asynchronous message passing. Each actor has a mailbox queue; it processes messages sequentially from its mailbox, eliminating concurrency within a single actor. Actors can create child actors, send messages to any actor by address, and define behavior changes in response to messages. Erlang's 'let it crash' philosophy builds fault tolerance on top of actors: if an actor fails, its supervisor restarts it.

Virtual threads (Java 21 Project Loom) bridge the gap between thread-per-request and async models. Virtual threads are user-space threads multiplexed onto carrier OS threads, costing ~1KB per thread vs. 1MB for OS threads. You can create millions of virtual threads, and blocking a virtual thread doesn't block an OS thread—the carrier thread is released for other virtual threads. This makes the synchronous, thread-per-request programming model (easy to understand and debug) work at the scale of async/reactive models without the callback hell.
bullets: CSP (Go): goroutines communicate via typed channels; select for multiplexing
Actor model (Erlang/Akka): isolated state, async message passing, supervision hierarchies
Virtual threads (Java Loom): millions of cheap threads; blocking is non-blocking at OS level
Backpressure: signal when a consumer is overwhelmed; prevents unbounded queue growth

sections.title: Async/Await and Reactive Streams
paragraphs: Async/await is syntactic sugar over callback-based async I/O that makes asynchronous code look synchronous. When an async function awaits a future/promise, the runtime suspends it without blocking a thread and schedules it for resumption when the awaited value is ready. Node.js (single-threaded event loop), Python asyncio, Rust's async/await, and C#'s Task are all variations of this model. The key insight: for I/O-bound workloads, a single OS thread can serve thousands of concurrent requests without context switching overhead.

Structured concurrency (Python 3.11 TaskGroup, Java Loom, Swift structured concurrency) addresses the 'lost tasks' problem in async code: when an async operation spawns sub-tasks and an exception occurs, all sub-tasks are properly cancelled and awaited before the exception propagates. Without structured concurrency, goroutine leaks, task escapes, and uncaught exceptions in background tasks are common bugs. The scope of a concurrent operation is bounded by the lexical scope of the structured concurrency construct.

Reactive Streams (RxJava, Project Reactor, Akka Streams) model data processing as a pipeline of operators (map, filter, flatMap, reduce) over asynchronous sequences. Backpressure is built in: downstream operators signal how many elements they can process; upstream operators respect this signal by buffering or dropping. This prevents the classic producer-faster-than-consumer problem that causes unbounded queue growth and OOM errors. Reactive streams excel for event processing pipelines and I/O-bound data transformations but add significant complexity for simple request/response patterns.

Thread pool sizing is deceptively important. A CPU-bound task thread pool should have N = CPU cores threads (avoid context switching overhead). An I/O-bound task thread pool can have many more threads (N = CPU cores × (1 + wait_time/compute_time))—Little's Law applied to thread sizing. For mixed workloads, use separate thread pools for CPU-bound and I/O-bound tasks to prevent I/O blocking from starving CPU tasks. Never use the common thread pool for both CPU-intensive tasks and I/O operations.
bullets: Event loop (Node.js, Python asyncio): single thread serves many I/O-bound requests via async callbacks
async/await: coroutine-based; suspends at await points without blocking OS threads
Structured concurrency: scope-bounded concurrent tasks with guaranteed cleanup on error
Backpressure: downstream signals capacity to upstream; prevents producer-consumer imbalance

sections.title: Concurrency Patterns in System Design
paragraphs: Thread-per-request vs. event-loop is a fundamental architectural choice for I/O-bound services. Thread-per-request (traditional Java EE, Go HTTP) is easy to understand, debuggable, and works naturally with blocking libraries. Event-loop (Node.js, Nginx, modern Netty) handles more concurrent connections with fewer threads but requires all I/O to be non-blocking and makes CPU-intensive work problematic. Java Loom's virtual threads make thread-per-request scale like event-loop, potentially ending this debate for JVM languages.

Work-stealing thread pools (Java ForkJoinPool, Go's goroutine scheduler) improve utilization by allowing idle threads to 'steal' work from busy threads' queues. This is especially valuable for recursive task decomposition (divide a problem into sub-problems, recursively until small enough to solve directly) and for work with variable execution time (a mix of fast and slow tasks). The Fork/Join pattern decomposes work: fork creates sub-tasks; join waits for sub-task results. Java's parallel streams and CompletableFuture.allOf use the common ForkJoinPool.

The producer-consumer pattern with bounded queues is the workhorse of concurrent system design. Producers add work items to a queue; consumers retrieve and process them. The bounded queue provides backpressure: when full, producers block (or drop/return error), preventing unbounded memory growth. Thread pool implementations are producer-consumer: HTTP handlers are producers (submitting tasks), worker threads are consumers. Kafka is a durable, distributed producer-consumer queue. The key operational concern: monitor queue depth as a primary health indicator.
bullets: Thread-per-request: one OS thread per connection; simple, debuggable, limited by thread count
Event loop: one thread serves many connections via async I/O; requires non-blocking everywhere
Work-stealing: idle threads steal from busy queues; high utilization for variable-duration tasks
Bounded queue: backpressure mechanism; monitor depth as a primary health metric

core.title: Shared-State Concurrency and Lock Patterns
paragraphs: Mutex, semaphore, and read-write locks guard shared state. Deadlock (circular wait), livelock (progress without advancement), and starvation are the main failure modes.
Lock ordering, timeouts, and hierarchy prevent deadlock. Randomized backoff fixes livelock. Fair locks prevent starvation.
Fine-grained locking maximizes parallelism; coarse-grained is simpler. Striped locking (ConcurrentHashMap) balances both.
bullets: Always acquire locks in a fixed global order to prevent deadlock
Read-write lock: concurrent reads, exclusive write—ideal for read-heavy structures
Lock-free alternatives are preferable when CAS operations suffice

core.title: Lock-Free Programming
paragraphs: CAS (Compare-And-Swap) is the hardware primitive for lock-free algorithms. CAS atomically checks-and-updates; retries on failure. At least one thread always makes progress.
ABA problem: value changes A→B→A fools CAS. Fix: tagged pointers / version counters (AtomicStampedReference).
Memory ordering (volatile, acquire/release semantics) is essential for correctness on relaxed-consistency CPUs (ARM).
bullets: Java AtomicLong, AtomicReference: CAS-based lock-free primitives
Memory barriers prevent CPU/compiler reordering
Lock-free ≠ wait-free; wait-free is strictly stronger

core.title: Message Passing and Modern Concurrency
paragraphs: Go CSP: goroutines + channels for safe concurrency. Data ownership transfers with message—no shared mutable state.
Actor model (Erlang/Akka): isolated actors process messages sequentially from mailboxes; supervision trees for fault tolerance.
Java virtual threads (Loom): millions of cheap user-space threads; blocking I/O doesn't block OS threads.
bullets: Go select: multiplex over multiple channels
Backpressure: downstream signals capacity; prevents unbounded queue growth
Structured concurrency: scope-bounded tasks with guaranteed cleanup

deepDive.title: Memory Models and Visibility
paragraphs: The Java Memory Model (JMM) defines when writes by one thread are visible to another. Without synchronization, there is no guarantee that a value written by Thread A will ever be seen by Thread B. The happens-before relationship is the formal guarantee: actions in Thread A that happen-before actions in Thread B are guaranteed to be visible. Acquiring a lock happens-before releasing it; a volatile write happens-before the subsequent volatile read; thread start happens-before all actions in the started thread.

Double-checked locking is a canonical example of JMM subtlety. The naïve implementation (check if null outside lock, acquire lock, check again, initialize) is broken without volatile: the JVM may publish a partially-constructed object to other threads. With volatile on the reference field, the write to the reference cannot be reordered before the write to the object's fields, making double-checked locking correct. This level of detail matters for high-performance singleton initialization and lazy loading patterns.

Cache coherence protocols (MESI) govern how CPU cores share memory. When Core A writes to a cache line, it must invalidate that cache line in all other cores before the write completes. This invalidation traffic is the hidden cost of sharing data across cores: false sharing (two unrelated variables on the same 64-byte cache line, modified by different cores) causes the same invalidation traffic as true sharing. Solution: pad data structures to align each frequently-modified variable to its own cache line. Java @Contended annotation does this automatically.
bullets: JMM happens-before: visibility guarantee; without it, write visibility is undefined
volatile: prevents reordering; ensures visibility; not sufficient for compound operations
False sharing: unrelated variables on same cache line; use padding or @Contended to separate
MESI protocol: cache coherence; writing to a shared cache line is expensive due to invalidation traffic

deepDive.title: Concurrency in Distributed Systems
paragraphs: Distributed concurrency extends single-node patterns to multiple machines. Distributed locks (Redis SETNX with TTL, ZooKeeper sequential ephemeral nodes, etcd leases) coordinate access to shared resources across nodes. The key difference from single-node locks: network failures and process crashes can leave locks in an inconsistent state. Always set TTLs on distributed locks; never use them without an expiry. Fencing tokens (a monotonically increasing sequence number issued with the lock) prevent stale lock holders from corrupting shared state after their lease expires.

Optimistic concurrency control (OCC) avoids distributed locking by detecting conflicts at commit time rather than preventing them at access time. Each record has a version number. The reader reads the version; the writer sends the version with the update; the database atomically updates only if the current version matches. On version mismatch, the client retries. OCC is efficient when conflicts are rare; it degrades under high contention as retries increase. Cassandra's lightweight transactions (IF EXISTS, IF NOT EXISTS) implement compare-and-set at the distributed level.

Eventual consistency models (Cassandra, DynamoDB with eventual consistency reads) exchange strict consistency for availability and partition tolerance. Concurrent writes to the same key may arrive at different replicas in different orders; last-write-wins (LWW) with client-side timestamps is the common conflict resolution strategy. CRDTs (Conflict-Free Replicated Data Types) provide stronger guarantees: specific data structures (counters, sets, registers) designed so concurrent updates can always be merged without conflict. Redis Cluster's CRDT-based modules enable multi-region active-active replication.
bullets: Distributed lock: Redis SETNX + TTL, ZooKeeper, etcd lease—always with expiry
Fencing token: monotonically increasing sequence issued with lock; prevents stale holder writes
Optimistic concurrency: version-based conflict detection at commit; efficient when conflicts are rare
CRDT: data structures with conflict-free merge semantics; enable active-active replication

expert.title: High-Performance Concurrent Data Structures
paragraphs: LMAX Disruptor is a high-performance ring buffer for inter-thread communication that eliminates CAS contention by using sequence numbers and memory barriers instead. Each producer and consumer tracks its own sequence; the ring buffer enforces ordering via happens-before relationships without locks or CAS. At 50+ million messages/second between threads (100x faster than LinkedBlockingQueue), Disruptor is used in financial systems (LMAX Exchange), network proxies, and real-time event processing where queue throughput is a bottleneck.

Skip lists are a probabilistic alternative to balanced trees for sorted concurrent data structures. Java's ConcurrentSkipListMap and ConcurrentSkipListSet use a lock-free skip list implementation. Unlike TreeMap (which requires external synchronization), ConcurrentSkipListMap provides O(log n) contains, get, and put operations in a lock-free, linearizable manner. For read-heavy workloads where sorted access is needed, ConcurrentSkipListMap outperforms ConcurrentHashMap despite higher constant factors.

Non-blocking I/O multiplexing (epoll on Linux, kqueue on BSD, IOCP on Windows) is the kernel mechanism underlying event loops. Rather than blocking one thread per socket, a single thread registers interest in many file descriptors and receives notifications when they're ready. This scales to millions of concurrent connections with a single OS thread for the I/O handling layer. The io_uring interface (Linux 5.1+) further reduces syscall overhead by batching submissions and completions via a shared ring buffer—Rust's tokio and Java's Netty are exploring io_uring backends for further performance gains.

concepts: Mutex: mutual exclusion primitive; one holder at a time; prevents data races on shared state
Deadlock: circular wait among threads, each holding a lock the next needs; no progress possible
Livelock: threads keep executing but make no progress, each reacting to the other
CAS (Compare-And-Swap): atomic hardware operation for lock-free algorithms
Lock-free: at least one thread always makes progress; no locks required
CSP (Communicating Sequential Processes): concurrency via channel-based message passing (Go)
Actor model: isolated actors with mailboxes, processing messages sequentially (Erlang, Akka)
Virtual threads (Loom): JVM user-space threads; blocking I/O doesn't block OS threads
Structured concurrency: scope-bounded concurrent operations with guaranteed cleanup on failure
Backpressure: downstream signals capacity to upstream to prevent producer-consumer imbalance
False sharing: performance degradation from unrelated variables sharing a CPU cache line
Disruptor: lock-free ring buffer for ultra-high-throughput inter-thread communication
practices: Prefer message passing over shared state; share memory by communicating, not communicate by sharing memory
Always acquire multiple locks in a consistent global order to prevent deadlock
Use virtual threads (Java 21) or goroutines for I/O-bound concurrency; avoid explicit thread management
Monitor thread pool queue depth as a primary health metric; set bounded queues with explicit rejection policies
Use @Contended or manual padding to prevent false sharing in performance-critical concurrent data structures
Instrument lock contention (Java Flight Recorder lock profiling, pprof mutex profile in Go) before optimizing
Prefer optimistic concurrency (versioned updates) over distributed locking when conflict rates are low
pitfalls: Using double-checked locking without volatile—partially-constructed objects are published to other threads
Holding locks across I/O operations—causes long lock hold times and cascading thread starvation
Thread pool starvation: a task submitted to a pool that itself submits tasks that must complete before the original task finishes (dependency cycle in a bounded pool)
Unbounded queues: thread pool with unlimited queue depth masks overload until OOM kills the process
Silent exception swallowing in thread pool tasks: RuntimeExceptions in Runnable are swallowed by default
Distributed lock without TTL: a crashed holder never releases the lock; system freezes permanently
Using synchronized on a class object (this) instead of a private final lock object—external callers can deadlock you

examples.title: Go Channel Pipeline
examples.description: A Go image processing pipeline uses goroutines and channels: a generator goroutine reads file paths from disk and sends to a paths channel, three worker goroutines receive paths, decode images, and send decoded images to a decode channel, and an output goroutine receives decoded images and writes thumbnails. When the generator closes the paths channel, workers drain and close the decode channel, and the output goroutine drains and exits. This fan-out pattern processes images concurrently with bounded memory—the buffered channels act as backpressure mechanisms.

examples.title: LMAX Disruptor in Financial Trading
examples.description: LMAX Exchange built their trading platform around the Disruptor ring buffer. The incoming order stream is a single Disruptor ring buffer; multiple independent consumers (journal writer, risk checker, order book updater) each maintain their own sequence position and read the same events without coordination. The Disruptor achieves 6 million orders/second on commodity hardware. The key insight: a ring buffer with sequence-based coordination is orders of magnitude faster than a queue with CAS-based head/tail pointers because it eliminates CAS contention on the queue metadata.

examples.title: Thread Pool Starvation Debug
examples.description: A Java microservice was experiencing intermittent hangs. Thread dump analysis revealed all 50 HTTP worker threads waiting on CompletableFuture.get() for async database calls, while the async calls were themselves submitted to the same thread pool. The pool was exhausted with the outer tasks waiting for inner tasks that couldn't execute because the pool was full—a classic thread pool deadlock. Fix: separate thread pools for HTTP handlers and async database calls, or use virtual threads (Loom) where blocking an HTTP thread doesn't exhaust the pool.

keyTakeaways: Shared mutable state is the root cause of most concurrency bugs; prefer immutability or message passing
Deadlock prevention requires consistent lock ordering; detection requires monitoring wait-for graphs
CAS-based lock-free algorithms eliminate blocking but require careful attention to memory ordering and ABA
Go's CSP model and Java Loom's virtual threads make concurrent I/O-bound code safe and scalable without explicit locking
Backpressure is essential—unbounded queues hide overload until OOM errors occur
False sharing can silently destroy performance on multi-core systems; profile before assuming cache behavior
Distributed concurrency requires TTL-based locks, fencing tokens, or optimistic concurrency—not just local primitives
lessons.whyItMatters: Concurrency is unavoidable in any system that must handle multiple users, process background work, or utilize modern multi-core hardware. The wrong concurrency model produces race conditions that corrupt data, deadlocks that freeze systems, and resource exhaustion that collapses under load. The right model—message passing for most cases, careful lock-free structures for hot paths, structured concurrency for safe composition—enables reliable high-throughput systems.
reflectionQuestions: Your Java service has intermittent hangs under load. The thread dump shows all threads waiting on a database connection. Walk through your diagnosis: what are the possible root causes and how do you investigate each?
Compare Go channels, Java virtual threads, and Akka actors for a high-throughput event processing system. What are the trade-offs and when would you choose each?

You need a distributed counter that increments on every web request across 100 servers. What are the trade-offs between: a central Redis INCR, an optimistic CAS-based approach in PostgreSQL, and a CRDT-based local counter with periodic sync?
How does the LMAX Disruptor achieve higher throughput than a BlockingQueue, and what sacrifices does it make?
numbersToKnow: OS thread cost: ~1MB stack, ~10μs context switch; virtual thread: ~1KB stack, ~1μs context switch
Lock acquisition (uncontended): ~25ns (mutex); CAS: ~10ns; volatile read: ~5ns
Cache line size: 64 bytes on x86; false sharing occurs when two threads modify variables on the same line
LMAX Disruptor throughput: ~50 million messages/second between threads vs ~5 million for ArrayBlockingQueue
Go goroutine initial stack: 2KB (scales dynamically); can run millions on modern hardware
Thread pool rule of thumb: CPU-bound = N_cpu threads; I/O-bound = N_cpu × (1 + wait/compute)

interviewQuestions: What is a deadlock? Give an example and explain two strategies to prevent it.
Explain CAS (Compare-And-Swap) and how it enables lock-free data structures. What is the ABA problem?
How does Go's channel-based concurrency model differ from Java's thread-based model? When would you prefer each?
Design a thread-safe LRU cache that supports high concurrent read throughput. What locking strategy would you use?
Explain backpressure and why it's important in a producer-consumer system. How does it manifest differently in a local thread pool vs. a Kafka consumer?
exercises: Implement a thread-safe bounded blocking queue in Java without using any existing concurrent collections. Support put() (blocks when full) and take() (blocks when empty) operations. Identify where you use locks, conditions, and what invariants your lock guards.
Design a concurrent rate limiter using the token bucket algorithm that is safe for use across multiple threads without using synchronized blocks. Use atomic operations to implement it.
Analyze this code for concurrency bugs: a Java singleton using double-checked locking without volatile. Explain what can go wrong, on what hardware, and fix it correctly.

lessons.title: Core Design Patterns
lessons.summary: Core Design Patterns is a core topic in modern system design. This lesson builds a first-principles model around reusable structure inside services, then connects that model to capacity, failure modes, and operational practice so you can use it in real architectures.

sections.title: What Core Design Patterns is solving
paragraphs: Core Design Patterns exists because naive designs around reusable structure inside services break under scale, partial failure, or changing requirements. Before choosing tools, name the problem: which resource is scarce, which invariant must hold, and which user-visible failures are unacceptable.
In interviews and production reviews, strong answers start with constraints (QPS, data size, latency budget, consistency needs) and only then map Core Design Patterns onto those constraints.

A useful mental model separates the control plane (how you configure and observe Core Design Patterns) from the data plane (the per-request/per-event path). Confusing the two leads to architectures that look neat and operate poorly.

sections.title: Core mechanics
paragraphs: Mechanically, Core Design Patterns involves a small set of moving parts: inputs, state, an algorithm or protocol, and outputs/side effects. Draw those parts explicitly. If state is replicated, write down the replication/consistency rule. If work is asynchronous, write down delivery semantics.

Performance characteristics usually come from amplification (how much internal work per external request), locality (whether work stays on one node), and contention (locks, hot keys, leader bottlenecks).

Correctness characteristics usually come from failure handling: retries, timeouts, idempotency, and what clients observe during failover. If you cannot explain the failure story, you do not yet understand Core Design Patterns.
bullets: Inputs → state/protocol → outputs/side effects
Name consistency and delivery guarantees
Identify the bottleneck resource early

sections.title: Designing with it
paragraphs: When incorporating Core Design Patterns into a system, decide the API boundary first: what does a client call, what can fail, and what is retried. Keep the happy path boring and push complexity into well-tested libraries or platform components.

Capacity plan with numbers: estimate peak load, working set, and headroom. Convert that into shard counts, cache sizes, thread/connection pools, or GPU/memory budgets as relevant to Core Design Patterns.
Prefer reversible rollout: feature flags, dual-running, shadow traffic, and clear dashboards. New uses of Core Design Patterns should be observable on day one.

sections.title: Operations and failure modes
paragraphs: Operate Core Design Patterns with SLIs that match user pain (availability, latency, lag, error rate, cost). Alert on burn rates and queue/lag growth, not only host CPU.
Common failures include overload without admission control, retry amplification, silent staleness, schema mismatches, and dependency brownouts. Write a runbook for the top three.
Chaos and game days should include slow dependencies and network delay, not only hard kills. Core Design Patterns often fails in the gray area.

deepDive.title: Core Design Patterns — deeper internals
paragraphs: Under the hood, Core Design Patterns typically exposes knobs for batching, buffering, concurrency, retention, and timeouts. Each knob trades latency, throughput, and cost. Change one at a time and measure.

Instrumentation should include high-signal histograms and exemplars that jump to traces. For data systems, watch amplification and compaction/GC; for RPC systems, watch queue time and saturation; for ML systems, watch memory and tokens/s.
bullets: One knob at a time with a hypothesis
Histograms > averages
Tie dashboards to runbooks

deepDive.title: Core Design Patterns — integration patterns
paragraphs: Integrate via stable contracts: schemas, idempotency keys, and versioned APIs. Dual-write carefully or prefer CDC/outbox patterns when crossing storage and messaging.
Boundary tests should prove behavior under duplicate delivery, reordering, and clock skew where relevant to Core Design Patterns.

expert.title: Core Design Patterns — multi-region and cost

lessons.title: Transactional Outbox
lessons.summary: Transactional Outbox is a core topic in modern system design. This lesson builds a first-principles model around reusable structure inside services, then connects that model to capacity, failure modes, and operational practice so you can use it in real architectures.

sections.title: What Transactional Outbox is solving
paragraphs: Transactional Outbox exists because naive designs around reusable structure inside services break under scale, partial failure, or changing requirements. Before choosing tools, name the problem: which resource is scarce, which invariant must hold, and which user-visible failures are unacceptable.
In interviews and production reviews, strong answers start with constraints (QPS, data size, latency budget, consistency needs) and only then map Transactional Outbox onto those constraints.

A useful mental model separates the control plane (how you configure and observe Transactional Outbox) from the data plane (the per-request/per-event path). Confusing the two leads to architectures that look neat and operate poorly.

sections.title: Core mechanics
paragraphs: Mechanically, Transactional Outbox involves a small set of moving parts: inputs, state, an algorithm or protocol, and outputs/side effects. Draw those parts explicitly. If state is replicated, write down the replication/consistency rule. If work is asynchronous, write down delivery semantics.

Performance characteristics usually come from amplification (how much internal work per external request), locality (whether work stays on one node), and contention (locks, hot keys, leader bottlenecks).

Correctness characteristics usually come from failure handling: retries, timeouts, idempotency, and what clients observe during failover. If you cannot explain the failure story, you do not yet understand Transactional Outbox.
bullets: Inputs → state/protocol → outputs/side effects
Name consistency and delivery guarantees
Identify the bottleneck resource early

sections.title: Designing with it
paragraphs: When incorporating Transactional Outbox into a system, decide the API boundary first: what does a client call, what can fail, and what is retried. Keep the happy path boring and push complexity into well-tested libraries or platform components.

Capacity plan with numbers: estimate peak load, working set, and headroom. Convert that into shard counts, cache sizes, thread/connection pools, or GPU/memory budgets as relevant to Transactional Outbox.
Prefer reversible rollout: feature flags, dual-running, shadow traffic, and clear dashboards. New uses of Transactional Outbox should be observable on day one.

sections.title: Operations and failure modes
paragraphs: Operate Transactional Outbox with SLIs that match user pain (availability, latency, lag, error rate, cost). Alert on burn rates and queue/lag growth, not only host CPU.
Common failures include overload without admission control, retry amplification, silent staleness, schema mismatches, and dependency brownouts. Write a runbook for the top three.
Chaos and game days should include slow dependencies and network delay, not only hard kills. Transactional Outbox often fails in the gray area.

lessons.title: Resilience Patterns
lessons.summary: Resilience patterns prevent failures in one component from cascading into system-wide outages. Circuit breakers, retries with backoff, bulkheads, timeouts, rate limiting, and fallbacks are the standard toolkit. These patterns transform fragile, tightly-coupled distributed systems into resilient ones that degrade gracefully under failure—a critical skill for designing systems that meet their availability SLOs.

sections.title: The Cascade Failure Problem
paragraphs: In a distributed system, services depend on other services. When a downstream service degrades—responding slowly rather than failing fast—callers accumulate threads waiting for responses. If the caller serves its own requests while waiting on the slow downstream, its thread pool fills with waiting threads. New incoming requests cannot be served. The caller's response time increases. Its callers start waiting. The slowdown cascades up the dependency chain until the entire system is unavailable, even though only one downstream service is degraded.

The fundamental insight behind resilience patterns is that in a distributed system, partial failure is the normal operating mode. Network calls will time out, services will occasionally return errors, and downstream systems will sometimes be overloaded. The question is not whether these failures will happen but whether your system handles them gracefully (degrading non-critical functionality while keeping critical paths healthy) or catastrophically (a single downstream failure brings everything down).

Failure taxonomy helps choose the right pattern. Fast failures (immediate error responses) are easiest to handle—detect quickly, retry or fallback. Slow failures (responses that take far longer than normal) are insidious—threads pile up waiting, resources are exhausted, and the system appears busy while making no progress. Intermittent failures (occasional errors under otherwise normal load) need retries. Persistent failures (a downstream service is completely down) need circuit breakers. Overload failures (the caller is sending more than the downstream can handle) need rate limiting and shedding.
bullets: Cascade failure: a slow downstream fills caller threads, which fills its callers' threads, up the chain
Fail fast: return an error immediately rather than waiting indefinitely—preserves thread capacity
Bulkhead: isolate failure domains so one failing dependency cannot exhaust all resources
Shed load: reject excess requests early (503) rather than queuing them until OOM

sections.title: Timeouts: The Most Fundamental Resilience Pattern
paragraphs: Every network call must have a timeout. Without a timeout, a thread waiting for a response from a failed downstream service will wait forever, consuming memory, file descriptors, and thread pool capacity. This is not theoretical—production incidents frequently trace to missing timeouts on HTTP clients, database connections, and gRPC calls. The fix is simple: always set connect timeout, read timeout, and total request timeout on every external call.

Setting timeout values is harder than setting them. Too tight and you generate false failures (the downstream is working, just slow on occasion). Too loose and you don't protect your thread pool fast enough when the downstream degrades. The rule of thumb: timeout at the p99.9 of normal healthy response time, not the p50. If your database normally responds in 5ms (p50) but can take 200ms under load (p99.9), set the timeout to 250–500ms, not 5ms. This allows for occasional slow responses without treating them as failures.

Deadline propagation extends timeouts across service chains. If the initial HTTP request has a 500ms deadline, every downstream call it makes should use a portion of the remaining deadline rather than a fixed timeout. gRPC Context deadlines propagate automatically. For REST HTTP, embed the deadline in a request header ('X-Request-Deadline') and check it at every hop. If the remaining deadline is insufficient for the downstream call, fail immediately with a 'deadline exceeded' error rather than making a call that will certainly time out.
bullets: Connect timeout: how long to wait for TCP connection establishment (typically 1-5s)
Read timeout: how long to wait for the first byte after connection (typically p99.9 of response time)
Total timeout: overall deadline for the full operation including retries
Deadline propagation: share remaining budget with downstream calls via context or headers

sections.title: Circuit Breaker Pattern
paragraphs: The circuit breaker protects a caller from a failing downstream by tracking error rates and 'opening the circuit' when failures exceed a threshold—immediately returning errors to callers without attempting the downstream call. The three states: Closed (normal operation, calls go through, errors counted), Open (circuit is open, all calls immediately fail without attempting the downstream, error counter exceeded threshold), and Half-Open (after a cooldown period, one probe request is allowed through; if it succeeds, circuit closes; if it fails, circuit reopens).

Circuit breaker configuration requires balancing sensitivity against false positives. A threshold that opens on 2 failures out of 10 requests trips on small transient blips. A threshold that requires 50% error rate over 60 seconds is slow to protect against a persistent outage. Modern implementations use a sliding window (count-based or time-based) with configurable minimum request count (don't open on 1/1 failures) and error rate threshold (open when error rate > 50%). Hystrix (deprecated), Resilience4j (Java), and Polly (.NET) are popular implementations.

The fallback is what happens when the circuit is open (or the call fails). Options: return a cached value (stale cache), return a default/empty response (graceful degradation), invoke a secondary/backup service (failover), or return a user-friendly error message. The fallback must be cheaper and more reliable than the primary call—otherwise it creates a secondary failure. A fallback that calls another potentially-failing service defeats the purpose of the circuit breaker.

Circuit breakers require careful health monitoring. When the circuit opens, an alert should fire: this means a downstream service is experiencing elevated error rates. The circuit breaker is protecting your service, but the downstream is degraded. Operations teams need to know to investigate. Track circuit state transitions as a time series metric: circuit_open{service='payment-api'} going from 0 to 1 is an actionable alert, not just a background metric.
bullets: Closed: normal; failures counted; Open: fast-fail all calls; Half-Open: probe request to test recovery
Sliding window: last N requests (count-based) or last N seconds (time-based)
Fallback: cached response, default value, backup service, or degraded-mode response
Alert on circuit open: it means a dependency is failing—don't treat it as silent auto-healing

sections.title: Retry with Backoff and Jitter
paragraphs: Retries are appropriate for transient failures: network blips, brief service overloads, and intermittent 500 errors. They are inappropriate for client errors (400 Bad Request won't succeed on retry), resource exhaustion (retrying into an overloaded service amplifies the problem), and non-idempotent operations (retrying a payment charge may double-charge). The idempotency key pattern—a client-generated unique ID included in the request—makes otherwise non-idempotent operations safe to retry: the server deduplicates by idempotency key.

Exponential backoff limits retry rate as failures accumulate: first retry after 1s, second after 2s, third after 4s, fourth after 8s. This gives the downstream time to recover without overwhelming it with retry traffic. The base interval, multiplier, and maximum interval are tunable. Backoff alone is insufficient when many clients all backed off simultaneously and retry at the same time (thundering herd). Jitter adds randomness to the backoff: each client retries after a random duration within [0, backoff_interval], spreading retry load across time.

Retry budgets prevent retry storms at the system level. Each service has a retry budget: for every 100 outgoing requests, at most 10 may be retries (10% retry budget). If the downstream error rate spikes and retries would exceed the budget, retries are stopped even if individual request timeouts haven't fired yet. This is an aggregate rate limit on retry traffic. Combined with circuit breakers, retry budgets prevent overloaded downstreams from being further overwhelmed by retry traffic from all their callers.
bullets: Retry only on transient, idempotent-safe failures (network errors, 429, 503)—never on 4xx
Exponential backoff: delay doubles with each retry; prevents retry storms
Jitter: randomize backoff interval; prevents synchronized thundering herd
Max retry count + max total time: both bounds needed; don't retry indefinitely

sections.title: Bulkheads and Rate Limiting
paragraphs: The bulkhead pattern, named after watertight compartments in ships, isolates failure domains by giving each dependency its own resource pool. If the payment service starts hanging, its dedicated thread pool fills up—but the inventory service, using a separate pool, is unaffected. Without bulkheads, a slow payment service exhausts the shared thread pool and brings down inventory and shipping along with it. Bulkheads are implemented as separate thread pools (ExecutorService per downstream), separate connection pools, or separate queue partitions per tenant (in multi-tenant systems).

Rate limiting protects a service from being overloaded by incoming requests. Token bucket rate limiting: a bucket holds tokens (max capacity = burst size); tokens are added at a fixed rate; each request consumes a token; requests are rejected (HTTP 429) when the bucket is empty. This smooths bursts while allowing short-term spikes up to the burst size. Leaky bucket is similar but smooths output at a fixed rate (no bursting). Rate limits can be applied per client, per endpoint, per user, or globally.

Adaptive rate limiting adjusts limits based on measured downstream health. If the payment service's error rate is rising, an adaptive rate limiter reduces the outgoing request rate to give the downstream time to recover—rather than waiting for the circuit breaker to fully open. Combined with circuit breakers, adaptive rate limiting provides a smoother degradation curve: request rate decreases gradually as health decreases, rather than a binary open/closed transition.

Load shedding is the last line of defense: when a service is genuinely overloaded beyond its capacity to process requests, it must reject excess requests (HTTP 503 Service Unavailable) to protect the requests it can process. Without load shedding, an overloaded service processes everything slowly—no request gets a timely response. With load shedding, a portion of requests fail fast (503) while the remaining requests are processed at normal speed. Priority-based shedding rejects low-priority requests (batch analytics, background sync) before high-priority requests (checkout, payment).
bullets: Bulkhead: separate resource pools per dependency; prevents failure isolation breach
Token bucket: fixed-rate token replenishment with burst capacity; most common rate limit algorithm
Leaky bucket: smooth output at constant rate; no bursting; strict rate enforcement
Load shedding: reject excess load with 503; better than slowing everything down equally

core.title: Cascade Failure Prevention
paragraphs: Cascade failures start with a slow downstream filling caller thread pools. The cure: timeouts (don't wait forever), circuit breakers (stop calling a failing service), bulkheads (isolate resource pools), and load shedding (reject excess load).
Partial failure is normal in distributed systems. Design for degradation: return cached/default data when non-critical dependencies fail; fail fast when critical ones do.
Failure taxonomy: fast (easy to handle), slow (dangerous—threads pile up), intermittent (retries), persistent (circuit break), overload (rate limit and shed).
bullets: Every network call must have a timeout—no exceptions
Fail fast beats fail slowly—a quick 503 is better than a 30s timeout
Degrade gracefully: continue serving critical functionality when non-critical dependencies fail

core.title: Circuit Breaker and Retry
paragraphs: Circuit breaker: Closed (count errors) → Open (fast-fail) → Half-Open (probe). Open after error rate > threshold over sliding window. Fallback returns cached/default response.
Retry: exponential backoff + jitter prevents thundering herd. Only retry idempotent operations on transient errors. Retry budget prevents overwhelming downstream.
Idempotency keys make non-idempotent operations safe to retry.
bullets: Circuit breaker protects caller from slow downstream—don't wait, fail immediately
Jitter: randomize backoff to prevent synchronized retries
Alert on circuit open—it's an indicator of downstream degradation

deepDive.title: Resilience4j Configuration Deep Dive
paragraphs: Resilience4j's CircuitBreaker supports count-based and time-based sliding windows. Count-based: track last N requests; open if error rate > threshold AND total calls >= minimumNumberOfCalls. Time-based: track requests in last N seconds; similar threshold logic. The minimum call count is critical: without it, 1 failure out of 1 attempt opens the circuit, causing massive false-positive tripping on startup or after long idle periods.

The RateLimiter in Resilience4j implements token bucket semantics with a configurable refresh period and permissions per period. For distributed rate limiting (limiting across multiple service instances), Resilience4j's RateLimiter is insufficient—it's local to one JVM. Distributed rate limiting requires a shared counter in Redis (INCR with TTL, Lua scripts for atomic token bucket), API Gateway rate limiting, or a service mesh policy.

Resilience4j's Bulkhead comes in two flavors: semaphore-based (limits concurrent calls to a dependency by blocking when semaphore is exhausted—simple, low overhead) and thread-pool-based (each dependency gets its own thread pool—full isolation, higher overhead). Use semaphore for short, non-blocking I/O calls; use thread-pool for calls that may block for significant durations. Compose with CircuitBreaker and Retry in the correct order: Retry(CircuitBreaker(Bulkhead(call)))—the bulkhead limits concurrency, the circuit breaker gates on error rate, and the retry wraps the whole thing.
bullets: minimumNumberOfCalls: prevents tripping on startup or idle periods with 1/1 false positives
Distributed rate limiting: Redis Lua scripts for atomic token bucket across multiple instances
Composition order: Retry → CircuitBreaker → Bulkhead → actual call
Resilience4j metrics: integrate with Micrometer for Prometheus/Grafana dashboards

deepDive.title: Service Mesh Resilience Policies
paragraphs: Service meshes (Istio, Linkerd) implement resilience patterns at the infrastructure layer, transparently to application code. Istio's DestinationRule configures connection pool settings (max connections, max pending requests, max retries), outlier detection (circuit breaker equivalent: eject hosts with >50% error rate from the load balancing pool for 30 seconds), and retry policies (retry on 503 responses, max 3 retries, per-try timeout 25s). These policies apply to all traffic flowing through the mesh proxy without application code changes.

Infrastructure-level resilience via service mesh is powerful but has limitations: it cannot implement business-logic-aware fallbacks (returning a cached product catalog when the catalog service is down requires application code), it's less flexible than application-level patterns (custom retry predicates, partial circuit breaking by endpoint), and it adds operational complexity. The pragmatic approach: use service mesh for baseline resilience (timeouts, basic retries, outlier detection) and application-level patterns (Resilience4j, Polly) for sophisticated business-logic-aware resilience.

Chaos engineering validates that resilience patterns actually work under real failure conditions. Chaos Monkey (Netflix), Gremlin, and AWS Fault Injection Service inject failures: kill random instances, inject latency into network calls, exhaust CPU, saturate disk, corrupt network packets. Without chaos testing, resilience patterns may be incorrectly configured (timeout too long, circuit breaker threshold too high) and provide false confidence. Run chaos experiments in production during low-traffic windows, with clear stop criteria, and instrument the blast radius carefully.
bullets: Istio outlier detection: eject unhealthy hosts from load balancer pool (circuit breaker at LB level)
Mesh retry policies: apply to all services without code changes; limited to transport-level logic
Application-level fallbacks still required for business-logic-aware degradation
Chaos engineering: the only way to verify resilience patterns actually work

expert.title: Resilience at Scale: Lessons from Netflix and Amazon
paragraphs: Netflix's Hystrix (now deprecated in favor of Resilience4j) pioneered bulkhead-based isolation in microservices. Each service dependency had its own thread pool. When recommendations failed, the UI could still display movies from cache; when billing failed, browsing was unaffected. The key insight was that most features are non-critical: 90% of a streaming service's features can degrade gracefully without preventing video playback. This hierarchy—critical vs. non-critical paths—is the foundation of resilience design: define what must stay up and isolate everything else.

Amazon's TimelineService paper documents the 'retry storm' pattern: a large service using a dependency experiences elevated errors, retries amplify the load on the dependency, the dependency becomes more overloaded, error rates increase further, more retries are added, until the dependency is completely overwhelmed. The solution: bounded retry budgets at both the client level (no more than 10% of requests can be retries) and the server level (shed excess load with 503 to prevent overload amplification). This requires coordination between client retry logic and server load shedding policies.

The 'defense in depth' principle applied to resilience: each layer of the stack should be independently resilient. Client-side: timeouts, retries with jitter, circuit breakers. Load balancer: health checks, connection draining, slow-start. Service mesh: outlier detection, retry policies, rate limits. Server-side: load shedding, priority queues, admission control. No single layer is sufficient; each layer catches what the layer below missed. The goal is defense in depth: multiple independent failure containment mechanisms, each incomplete on its own, together providing comprehensive protection.

concepts: Cascade failure: downstream slowness fills caller threads, propagating outage up the dependency chain
Circuit breaker: tracks error rates and stops calling failing services; Closed/Open/Half-Open states
Timeout: bounded waiting time for external calls; prevents thread exhaustion on slow downstreams
Retry: re-attempt failed requests; must be idempotent, bounded, with exponential backoff and jitter
Bulkhead: isolate dependencies into separate resource pools; prevent one failure from exhausting all resources
Rate limiter: control request rate into a service; token bucket (burst allowed) or leaky bucket (smooth rate)
Load shedding: reject excess requests (503) when overloaded rather than processing all slowly
Fallback: alternative response when primary call fails; cached value, default, backup service, or degraded mode
Idempotency key: client-generated unique ID enabling safe retries of non-idempotent operations
Jitter: randomized delay in backoff to prevent synchronized retry thundering herd
Deadline propagation: share total request deadline across all downstream calls in a chain
Retry budget: cap on what fraction of outgoing calls may be retries; prevents retry storms
practices: Set timeouts on every external call: connect timeout, read timeout, and total deadline
Use exponential backoff with jitter for all retries; cap max retry attempts and total retry duration
Implement circuit breakers for all downstream service dependencies; alert when circuit opens
Create separate thread/connection pools (bulkheads) for each downstream dependency
Design fallbacks for every circuit breaker: know what you return when the downstream is unavailable
Make all state-modifying operations idempotent or use idempotency keys to enable safe retries
Test resilience patterns with chaos engineering; don't assume they work without failure injection
pitfalls: Retrying non-idempotent operations (payment charges, email sends) without idempotency keys
Missing timeouts on database connections, HTTP clients, or gRPC calls
Circuit breaker with too-sensitive threshold that trips on normal traffic variance
Fallback that calls another potentially-failing service, creating a secondary cascade
Retrying on client errors (4xx)—these will never succeed; retry only on 5xx and network errors
No retry budget—a service with elevated errors triggers infinite retries that amplify the overload
Using synchronous retries in a request-serving thread—ties up the thread during backoff intervals; use async retries

examples.title: Netflix API Gateway Resilience
examples.description: Netflix's API Gateway uses circuit breakers and bulkheads for every microservice dependency. When the recommendations service degrades, the circuit opens after 50% error rate over a 10-second window. Callers immediately receive a fallback: a pre-computed popular movies list from cache. The recommendations service can recover without being overwhelmed by continued traffic, and the user experience degrades gracefully (less personalized recommendations rather than a broken page).

examples.title: Payment Service Retry with Idempotency
examples.description: An e-commerce checkout service calls a payment API that sometimes returns network errors. The payment API accepts idempotency keys: a unique key per checkout attempt. On network failure, the checkout service retries with the same idempotency key after exponential backoff (1s, 2s, 4s, max 3 retries). If the payment was actually processed on the first attempt but the response was lost, the retry receives the original successful response rather than charging twice. The idempotency key is stored client-side for 24 hours to handle edge cases.

examples.title: Database Bulkhead
examples.description: A microservice calls two databases: PostgreSQL for user data (high priority) and ClickHouse for analytics (low priority). Using separate connection pools (5 connections for ClickHouse, 20 for PostgreSQL), a slow ClickHouse query queue doesn't consume connections needed for user-facing PostgreSQL queries. When ClickHouse is degraded, analytics endpoints return 503 or stale cached data, while user authentication and profile endpoints continue operating normally—a classic bulkhead-based isolation.

keyTakeaways: Every network call needs a timeout—this is the most basic and most commonly missing resilience pattern
Circuit breakers prevent cascade failures by stopping calls to failing services and enabling recovery time
Retries must be idempotent, bounded, and use exponential backoff with jitter—unconstrained retries amplify outages
Bulkheads isolate failure domains by giving each dependency its own resource pool
Design for degradation: define which features are critical vs. non-critical and design fallbacks for each
Rate limiting and load shedding protect service stability when downstream is healthy but incoming load exceeds capacity
Chaos engineering is the only way to validate that resilience patterns actually work under real failure conditions
lessons.whyItMatters: The difference between a 99.9% available system and a 95% available one often comes down to resilience patterns. Without them, any single dependency failure can cascade into a full system outage. With them, the system degrades gracefully, maintains critical functionality, and recovers automatically. These patterns are tested in every system design interview that involves microservices, and they're the first things an experienced SRE checks when investigating a production outage.
reflectionQuestions: Your checkout service calls payment, inventory, and notification services. Design the resilience strategy for each: what timeout, retry, circuit breaker, and fallback policy would you apply, and why do they differ?

A payment service experiences a cascade failure during Black Friday: 10,000 checkout services are retrying simultaneously, amplifying load on the already-overloaded payment service. What patterns would have prevented this, and how do you recover now?
Explain the difference between a circuit breaker and a retry with max attempts. When does each one activate? Can they coexist, and in what order should they be composed?

Design a rate limiter for an API that allows 1,000 requests per second per user with a burst of 5,000. How does it work, where does it live, and how does it handle distributed deployments (multiple service instances)?
numbersToKnow: Circuit breaker typical settings: 50% error rate threshold, minimum 20 calls, 30-60s open state duration
Retry exponential backoff: base 100ms, multiplier 2x, max 30s, jitter ±50%, max 5 attempts
Thread pool bulkhead: 5-20 threads per downstream service; small enough to limit blast radius
Token bucket rate limiter: bucket capacity = desired burst; refill rate = desired steady-state rate
HTTP timeout typical values: connect 1-3s, read 5-30s (service-dependent), total 10-60s
Retry budget: allow at most 10% of outgoing calls to be retries to prevent amplification

lessons.title: Saga & Process Managers
lessons.summary: Process managers/sagas coordinate multi-step business workflows across services with explicit state machines, timeouts, and compensations — a pattern-level view of distributed transactions.

sections.title: Process manager role
paragraphs: A process manager listens to events, advances a workflow state machine, and commands participants. It owns the workflow state, not the domain aggregates' invariants.

sections.title: State and timeouts
paragraphs: Persist workflow state. Timeouts trigger probes or compensations. Humans may be in the loop for exceptional paths.

sections.title: Implementation tips
paragraphs: Use durable workflow engines (Temporal, Cadence) or carefully built state machines. Exactly-once side effects still need idempotency keys.

sections.title: Anti-patterns
paragraphs: God orchestrators that encode all business logic. Prefer managers that coordinate while domains keep invariants.

lessons.title: Essential Design Patterns
lessons.summary: Design patterns are reusable solutions to recurring problems in software architecture — not copy-paste recipes, but a shared vocabulary for discussing trade-offs. This lesson covers the patterns that appear most often in production systems and system design interviews: creational patterns for object lifecycle, structural patterns for composition, and behavioral patterns for communication and responsibility.

sections.title: Why Patterns Matter in System Design
paragraphs: A design pattern names a problem-solution pair that experienced engineers recognize instantly. When someone says 'we used a circuit breaker here' or 'this is a classic observer setup,' the entire team understands the constraints, failure modes, and alternatives without a whiteboard session from scratch.

Patterns sit at the intersection of code and architecture. Singleton and Factory appear in application code; Circuit Breaker, Bulkhead, and Saga span service boundaries. Learning patterns trains you to see structural similarities across domains — a payment retry queue and a notification dispatcher both implement variations of the same publish-subscribe and retry idioms.

Patterns are not goals. Applying every pattern from the Gang of Four catalog to a simple CRUD app is over-engineering. The skill is recognizing when a recurring force — varying object creation, decoupling senders from receivers, isolating failure domains — makes a named pattern the simplest correct solution.

In interviews, patterns demonstrate that you think in abstractions transferable across companies and stacks. In production, they give you proven starting points with documented pitfalls, so you spend design time on domain specifics rather than reinventing structural solutions.
bullets: Pattern = recurring problem + context + proven solution + consequences
GoF (1994): 23 classic OOP patterns — still relevant at architectural scale
Enterprise patterns (Fowler, Hohpe): messaging, integration, domain logic
Cloud-native patterns: sidecar, ambassador, anti-corruption layer

sections.title: Creational Patterns: Controlling Object Creation
paragraphs: Creational patterns manage how objects are instantiated — critical when construction is expensive, configuration varies, or you need to enforce a single shared instance. Factory Method and Abstract Factory delegate creation to subclasses or factory objects, letting you swap implementations (PostgreSQL vs. DynamoDB repository) without changing callers.

Builder separates construction of a complex object from its representation. You see this in fluent API clients (AWS SDK builders), SQL query builders, and HTTP request construction. It prevents telescoping constructors with twelve optional parameters and makes immutable objects practical.

Singleton guarantees one instance — useful for connection pool managers, configuration registries, and metric collectors. The danger is hidden global state: singletons make testing hard, create hidden coupling, and in distributed systems, 'singleton' is a lie unless backed by leader election. Prefer dependency injection with a scoped lifetime over static singletons in modern codebases.

Prototype clones existing objects instead of building from scratch — valuable when object creation requires parsing configs or deep copying is cheaper than re-fetching. Object pools (borrow/return instead of new/GC) are creational cousins common in database drivers and thread pools.
bullets: Factory Method: subclass decides which concrete type to instantiate
Abstract Factory: families of related objects (UI toolkit, storage backend)
Builder: step-by-step construction with validation at build() time
Singleton: one instance — use sparingly; prefer DI container scoping

sections.title: Structural Patterns: Composition and Adaptation
paragraphs: Structural patterns organize classes and objects into larger structures while keeping them flexible and efficient. Adapter wraps an incompatible interface so legacy code works with new APIs — the classic integration pattern when you cannot rewrite the vendor SDK or third-party service.

Decorator adds behavior dynamically without subclass explosion. Middleware stacks in Express, Koa, and gRPC interceptors are decorator chains: logging wraps auth wraps rate limiting wraps the handler. Each layer implements the same interface and delegates to the inner layer.

Facade provides a simplified interface to a complex subsystem. An API gateway is a distributed facade: clients call one endpoint; the gateway routes to dozens of internal services. Inside a monolith, a service layer facade hides repository, cache, and messaging details from controllers.

Proxy controls access to another object — lazy loading, access control, caching, or remote calls. Smart references in ORMs that lazy-load associations, caching proxies in Redis clients, and RPC stubs are all proxies. Composite treats individual objects and groups uniformly — useful for tree structures like org charts, file systems, and UI component trees.
bullets: Adapter: translate one interface to another (legacy integration)
Decorator: stack behaviors without modifying original class
Facade: single entry point hiding subsystem complexity
Proxy: indirection for lazy load, cache, security, or remote access

sections.title: Behavioral Patterns: Communication and Responsibility
paragraphs: Behavioral patterns govern how objects interact and distribute responsibility. Observer defines a one-to-many dependency: when one object changes state, dependents are notified. Event buses, WebSocket push, React state updates, and domain event publishing are observer variants at different scales.

Strategy encapsulates interchangeable algorithms. Payment processing (credit card vs. PayPal vs. crypto), compression codecs, and routing algorithms all use strategy so runtime configuration swaps behavior without conditional spaghetti. Dependency injection makes strategy trivial — inject the interface, not the implementation.

Command encapsulates a request as an object, enabling undo, queuing, logging, and retry. Job queues (Sidekiq, SQS consumers) process command objects. CQRS command handlers are named commands with idempotent execution. Template Method defines a skeleton algorithm with overridable steps — base class handles the flow, subclasses fill in specifics.

Chain of Responsibility passes a request along a handler chain until someone processes it — middleware pipelines, servlet filters, and approval workflows. State pattern lets an object alter behavior when its internal state changes — order lifecycle (pending → paid → shipped) without giant switch statements.
bullets: Observer: publish-subscribe within and across process boundaries
Strategy: swap algorithms at runtime via interface injection
Command: requests as first-class objects — queue, log, undo, retry
Chain of Responsibility: middleware and filter pipelines

sections.title: Patterns at Architectural Scale
paragraphs: Many 'microservice patterns' are behavioral and structural patterns scaled to the network. Circuit Breaker (from Release It!) stops calling a failing dependency after a threshold, failing fast instead of hanging threads. Bulkhead isolates thread pools or connection pools so one slow dependency cannot exhaust all resources.

Saga coordinates long-running distributed transactions through a sequence of local transactions with compensating actions — the distributed cousin of Command + undo. Outbox pattern combines Observer with transactional integrity: write events to a database table in the same transaction as business data, then a relay publishes to Kafka.

Anti-Corruption Layer (from DDD) is an Adapter at bounded-context boundaries — translate external models into your domain language so legacy systems do not leak their terminology into your core model. Sidecar and Ambassador (from cloud-native patterns) attach cross-cutting concerns (logging, TLS, retries) without polluting application code.

The meta-pattern: choose the pattern that minimizes the cost of the change you expect. If algorithms vary, use Strategy. If wiring varies, use Factory. If failure isolation matters, use Bulkhead and Circuit Breaker. Name your choices so the next engineer understands intent.

deepDive.title: Essential Design Patterns — Operational deep dive
paragraphs: Operating Essential Design Patterns well means defining the scarce resource (CPU, memory, disk, network, or tokens), the SLIs that reflect user pain, and the knobs that trade cost for latency.
Under load, measure amplification: how many bytes, RPCs, or disk writes you pay per user request. Prefetch and batch only when measurements show benefit — premature batching adds tail latency.
Failure drills should include dependency slowdown (not only hard down), clock skew, and disk full. Verify alerts, dashboards, and runbooks against those drills.
bullets: Name the scarcest resource and budget it
Track p50/p99 and error rate for the user journey
Rehearse partial dependency failure

deepDive.title: Essential Design Patterns — Correctness edges
paragraphs: Correctness edges around Essential Design Patterns often appear at retries, partial writes, and schema evolution. Make handlers idempotent and state transitions explicit.

Document what clients may observe during failover: stale reads, duplicate messages, or delayed visibility. If the product cannot tolerate an anomaly, enforce a stronger consistency boundary — and pay for it knowingly.

expert.title: Essential Design Patterns — Expert / multi-region notes
paragraphs: At multi-region scale, Essential Design Patterns interacts with RTT, quorum placement, and cost of cross-region replication. Prefer region-local user paths with asynchronous global state when invariants allow.
Cost envelopes matter: chart unit cost vs QPS and vs data size. Many 'performance' projects are actually cost projects in disguise — make the objective explicit.

concepts: Factory Method / Abstract Factory: delegate creation to swap implementations
Builder: construct complex objects step-by-step with validation
Singleton: single instance — global state risk in tests and distributed systems
Adapter: wrap incompatible interfaces for integration
Decorator: add behavior via composable wrapper chains (middleware)
Observer: one-to-many notification — events, pub/sub, reactive UI
Strategy: interchangeable algorithms selected at runtime
Command: encapsulate requests for queue, retry, undo, audit
Circuit Breaker: fail fast when a dependency is unhealthy
Saga: distributed transaction via compensating local steps
practices: Name patterns in design docs so reviewers instantly grasp structure and trade-offs
Prefer composition (Decorator, Strategy) over deep inheritance hierarchies
Use Factory or DI to swap implementations — never hard-code concrete types in business logic
Apply Circuit Breaker and Bulkhead on every synchronous cross-service call
Replace switch-on-type with Strategy or polymorphism when behavior varies by category
Use Command objects for async work — enables retry, idempotency keys, and dead letter queues
Avoid Singleton for testability; inject shared instances through your DI container
pitfalls: Pattern obsession: adding indirection when a simple function or module suffices
Singleton abuse: hidden global state, untestable code, false 'single instance' in distributed systems
Wrong pattern for the force: using Observer when polling or batch processing is simpler
Leaky abstraction: Decorator chains so deep that debugging requires tracing ten layers
Ignoring consequences: Saga compensations are hard — not every workflow fits choreographed events
Copy-paste from tutorials without adapting to domain constraints and failure modes

examples.title: Express middleware as Decorator chain
examples.description: An Express app stacks middleware functions — each implements (req, res, next), adds behavior (auth check, body parsing, logging), and calls next(). The final route handler sits at the innermost layer. Adding rate limiting means inserting a new decorator without touching existing handlers.

examples.title: Netflix Hystrix → Resilience4j Circuit Breaker
examples.description: When a downstream recommendation service latency spikes, the circuit breaker opens after error/latency thresholds. Callers receive fallback responses immediately instead of blocking threads. After a cooldown, half-open probes test recovery. This is the Circuit Breaker pattern applied at service mesh scale.

examples.title: E-commerce order Saga
examples.description: PlaceOrder → ReserveInventory → ChargePayment → ShipOrder. If payment fails after inventory reservation, a compensating ReleaseInventory command runs. Each step is a local transaction; the saga coordinator (or choreographed events) ensures the workflow completes or rolls back logically — not via a single distributed lock.

keyTakeaways: Patterns are a shared vocabulary for proven solutions to recurring design forces
Creational patterns control object lifecycle; structural patterns organize composition; behavioral patterns govern interaction
Middleware, event buses, and job queues are production-scale Command, Decorator, and Observer
Circuit Breaker, Bulkhead, and Saga are essential architectural patterns for distributed systems
Choose patterns based on expected change — not to fill a catalog checklist
Every pattern has consequences; name them in design reviews so trade-offs stay visible
Dependency injection makes Strategy, Factory, and test doubles natural in modern codebases
lessons.whyItMatters: Senior engineers communicate design intent in pattern names and apply proven structures instead of reinventing fragile ad-hoc solutions. In interviews and architecture reviews, recognizing patterns — and knowing when not to use them — signals maturity and saves teams months of debugging implicit design decisions.
reflectionQuestions: Identify three patterns in a codebase you know. For each, what problem force does it address, and what are its consequences?
When would you choose a Saga over a two-phase commit? What compensating actions would an order cancellation require?
Draw the middleware chain for an HTTP request in your stack. Which layers are Decorator, which are Chain of Responsibility?
Where have you seen Singleton cause testing or scaling problems? What would you use instead?
