lessons.title: Redis Internals
lessons.summary: Redis is an in-memory data structure store used as a cache, message broker, session store, and real-time leaderboard. Its single-threaded event loop, built-in data structures (strings, hashes, lists, sets, sorted sets, streams, probabilistic structures), and persistence mechanisms (RDB snapshots, AOF log) make it one of the most versatile components in distributed system architectures. Understanding its memory model, eviction policies, replication, and clustering is essential for using it effectively at scale.

sections.title: Architecture: Single-Threaded Event Loop
paragraphs: Redis processes commands in a single-threaded event loop using the I/O multiplexing primitives of the host OS (epoll on Linux, kqueue on BSD). Despite this single-threaded model, Redis achieves 100,000–1,000,000 operations/second on commodity hardware because all data lives in memory and operations are CPU-cheap—a GET is a hash table lookup; a ZADD is a skip list insertion. The event loop eliminates lock overhead entirely: there is no concurrent modification of shared data structures. This simplicity is a feature, not a limitation.

Redis 6.0 introduced I/O threads for network reads and writes: multiple threads handle the network layer (parsing requests, writing responses) while a single main thread still executes all commands. This threading model addresses the CPU bottleneck in high-connection-count workloads where the main thread was spending significant time on network I/O. With I/O threads, Redis can saturate 10GbE network interfaces. The command execution itself remains single-threaded, preserving the simplicity of the data model.

The command lifecycle: a client sends a command over TCP; the event loop's read handler receives it; the command is parsed (inline or RESP protocol); the main thread executes the command against the in-memory data structure; the response is buffered; the write handler sends it. For pipelining (multiple commands in one network round-trip), the client sends a batch of commands, the server processes them all, and sends responses in a single batch. Pipelining reduces round-trip overhead and can multiply throughput 10x for small-operation workloads.

Slow commands are Redis's Achilles' heel. Because the event loop is single-threaded, a single O(n) operation on a large key (KEYS *, SMEMBERS on a 10 million element set) blocks all other clients for the duration. KEYS * is documented as 'never use in production'. Use SCAN for iterating keys, SSCAN/HSCAN/ZSCAN for iterating large data structures—all use cursor-based pagination to process a small batch per call without blocking the event loop for extended periods.
bullets: Single-threaded main loop: no locks, no race conditions, 100K-1M ops/sec on commodity hardware
I/O threads (Redis 6+): separate threads for network read/write; main thread executes commands
Pipelining: batch multiple commands in one round-trip; 10x throughput improvement for small ops
KEYS *: O(n) over all keys—blocks all clients; use SCAN with count hint instead

sections.title: Data Structures and Their Use Cases
paragraphs: String is the most fundamental Redis type—a byte array up to 512MB. Redis stores integers in a compact binary representation, allowing INCR/DECR without deserialization. Strings are used for: simple caching (key=cache-key, value=JSON), counters (INCR for page views, rate limiting counters), feature flags, session tokens, and distributed locks. The SET command with NX (set if not exists) and EX (expiry seconds) is the atomic primitive for distributed locks: SET lock:resource token NX EX 30.

Hash stores field-value pairs under a single key: ideal for objects (user:1234 → {name: 'Alice', email: '...', age: 32}). More memory-efficient than storing each field as a separate key because Redis uses a compact ziplist encoding when the hash has fewer than 128 fields and all values are under 64 bytes. Use hashes for user sessions (avoid storing the entire session JSON as a string when you only need to update one field), configuration objects, and shopping carts (hset cart:user:1234 productId quantity).

Sorted Set (ZSET) is Redis's most powerful data structure: a set of unique members, each with a floating-point score, maintained in score order. Members are stored in both a hash table (O(1) member lookup) and a skip list (O(log n) rank operations). Use cases: leaderboards (ZADD scores user_id score, ZREVRANK scores user_id), rate limiting with sliding windows (each timestamp is a member, score is the timestamp), delayed queues (score = execution time, ZRANGEBYSCORE to find due jobs), and geospatial indexing (GEOADD encodes coordinates as ZSET scores).

List is a doubly linked list supporting O(1) LPUSH/RPUSH/LPOP/RPOP and O(n) random access. Use for: message queues (LPUSH + BRPOP for blocking queue), job queues, timeline feeds, and activity logs with fixed retention (LTRIM to maintain maximum length). BRPOP/BLPOP block the client until a list element is available—this is the primitive for a reliable Redis-based queue without polling. Stream (added in Redis 5.0) supersedes lists for most queue use cases with consumer groups, message acknowledgment, and persistent message IDs.
bullets: String: bytes, integers, JSON blobs; NX+EX for atomic distributed lock primitive
Hash: field-value object; ziplist encoding for small hashes saves significant memory
Sorted Set: members with scores in order; leaderboards, rate limiting, delayed queues
List: doubly linked; BRPOP for blocking queue; Stream for durable queue with consumer groups

sections.title: Memory Management and Eviction Policies
paragraphs: Redis stores all data in memory using an internal allocator (jemalloc by default). Every key-value pair has a Redis object header (robj: 16 bytes) plus the actual data. For small integers (0-9999), Redis maintains a shared integer pool—INCR counters to 9999 are free. For small strings, Redis may use an embedded string representation (string data stored inline in the robj, avoiding a malloc call and improving cache locality). These optimizations mean the same value stored differently can consume 10x more or less memory—memory profiling (DEBUG OBJECT key) reveals encoding.

maxmemory sets the memory ceiling. When Redis reaches maxmemory and must accept a new write, the eviction policy determines what to remove. Policy options: noeviction (return error—safe but causes writes to fail), allkeys-lru (evict least-recently-used key across all keys—good for general caching), volatile-lru (evict LRU only among keys with TTL—preserves keys without TTL), allkeys-lfu (evict least-frequently-used—better for Zipf-distributed access patterns), volatile-ttl (evict the key with shortest remaining TTL—prioritizes soon-to-expire keys).

Memory fragmentation occurs when Redis allocates and frees many different-sized objects, leaving gaps that are too small for new allocations. The mem_fragmentation_ratio in INFO memory should be close to 1.0–1.5; above 2.0 indicates significant fragmentation. Redis 4.0+ added MEMORY PURGE to trigger active defragmentation. Setting ACTIVE_DEFRAG_ENABLED yes enables background defragmentation. Restart with CONFIG REWRITE if fragmentation exceeds 3.0 and can't be resolved dynamically.

Key expiration is handled lazily (checked on access) and actively (periodic sampling). Redis samples 20 random keys with TTLs every 100ms and expires any that have exceeded their TTL. This means expired keys accumulate between sampling cycles—if you set 1 million keys with 10-second TTLs all at once, Redis may not clean them up for a few seconds. For exact expiration guarantees (e.g., sliding session windows), always use TTL-based cleanup and account for the sampling delay in your design.
bullets: jemalloc: Redis's memory allocator; use INFO memory for fragmentation ratio
Eviction policies: noeviction, allkeys-lru, volatile-lru, allkeys-lfu, volatile-ttl
LFU vs LRU: LFU better for skewed access patterns; LRU better for sequential scan patterns
Active defragmentation (Redis 4+): background compaction; enables ACTIVE_DEFRAG_ENABLED yes

sections.title: Persistence: RDB and AOF
paragraphs: Redis Persistence Database (RDB) creates point-in-time snapshots of the entire dataset via fork-based copy-on-write. Redis forks a child process; the child writes the full dataset to a temp file while the parent continues serving requests. When the child finishes, it atomically replaces the existing RDB file. RDB is compact (compressed binary format), fast to restore on restart, and has minimal overhead during normal operation. The downside: data since the last snapshot is lost on crash. Default snapshot schedule: save after 900 seconds if 1 key changed, 300 seconds if 10 keys changed, 60 seconds if 10,000 keys changed.

Append-Only File (AOF) logs every write command to an append-only file. On restart, Redis replays the AOF to reconstruct the dataset. AOF provides much better durability: with appendfsync everysec, at most 1 second of writes is lost on crash. With appendfsync always, every write is synced to disk before acknowledging—zero data loss but significant performance impact. AOF files grow unboundedly; BGREWRITEAOF compacts the log by replacing the full sequence with a minimal set of commands that produce the same state.

In practice, use RDB + AOF together: RDB for fast restarts (replaying a large AOF on startup takes minutes; loading an RDB takes seconds), AOF for durability between snapshots. Configure AOF with appendfsync everysec for most use cases. If Redis is used purely as a cache with no durability requirement, disable both RDB and AOF—the cache will be cold on restart but correct data comes from the source of truth.

Redis 7.0 introduced RDB-AOF hybrid persistence: the AOF file starts with an RDB snapshot followed by AOF increments since the snapshot. This combines fast load times (start from RDB) with per-second durability (AOF increments). Enable with aof-use-rdb-preamble yes. This is now the recommended persistence configuration for most production deployments that need both performance and durability.
bullets: RDB: fork + copy-on-write snapshot; compact; fast restore; up to N minutes of data loss
AOF: command log; appendfsync everysec = max 1s data loss; slower restart
Hybrid (RDB+AOF): RDB preamble + AOF increments; fast load + good durability
BGREWRITEAOF: compacts AOF file without blocking; run when AOF exceeds 2x original size

sections.title: Replication, Sentinel, and Cluster
paragraphs: Redis replication is asynchronous: the primary streams write commands to replicas; replicas apply them in order. Replicas can serve read traffic, offloading reads from the primary. Replication lag (the time between a write on primary and its visibility on a replica) is typically under 10ms on a healthy network but can grow to seconds under heavy write load or network congestion. Applications that read from replicas must tolerate stale data—never use replica reads for data that requires read-after-write consistency.

Redis Sentinel provides automatic failover for a primary-replica setup. Sentinels monitor the primary; when quorum (typically 2 of 3) agrees the primary is unreachable, they elect a replica as the new primary and reconfigure other replicas to follow the new primary. Clients use the Sentinel API to discover the current primary address. Sentinel failover typically takes 30-60 seconds and involves a brief window of unavailability. During failover, writes to the old primary may be lost (asynchronous replication lag).

Redis Cluster provides horizontal scalability by sharding data across multiple primary nodes. Keyspace is divided into 16,384 hash slots; each node is responsible for a range of slots. Keys hash to slots via CRC16(key) % 16,384. Clients route commands directly to the responsible node; if they hit the wrong node, they receive a MOVED redirection. Redis Cluster supports automatic resharding, online node addition/removal, and fault tolerance (each shard has its own replica for HA). Limitations: multi-key commands (MGET, pipeline) require all keys in the same slot (use hash tags {user}:profile and {user}:session to colocate related keys).

Redis 7.0 added Redis Functions (server-side Lua scripting replacement) and ACL v2 for fine-grained access control. Redis 7.4 introduced active-active geo-replication (Redis Stack Enterprise feature). For most use cases, Cluster (sharded, auto-failover) is the production-grade choice for scale, while Sentinel (single shard, auto-failover) is appropriate for datasets that fit in one node's memory.
bullets: Replication: async; replicas for read scaling; stale reads possible under lag
Sentinel: HA for single-shard setups; 30-60s failover; some write loss possible
Cluster: 16,384 slots sharded across N primaries; auto-failover per shard
Hash tags {tag}: colocate keys on same slot for multi-key commands across cluster

core.title: Event Loop and Data Structures
paragraphs: Redis's single-threaded event loop processes commands sequentially with no locks. This achieves 100K-1M ops/sec because all data is in memory and operations are O(1) or O(log n).
Data structures: String (cache, counters, locks), Hash (objects), List (queues), Set (membership), Sorted Set (leaderboards, rate limits), Stream (durable queues with consumer groups).
Avoid O(n) commands on large datasets: KEYS *, SMEMBERS on large sets, LRANGE 0 -1. Use SCAN for iteration.
bullets: Pipelining: batch commands in one round-trip for 10x throughput
SCAN: cursor-based iteration; O(1) per call, no blocking
Sorted Set: skip list + hash table; O(log n) for most operations

core.title: Memory, Eviction, and Persistence
paragraphs: maxmemory caps Redis memory. On reaching it, eviction policy (allkeys-lru, allkeys-lfu, volatile-lru, noeviction) determines what's removed.
RDB: periodic fork-based snapshot. AOF: command log with appendfsync everysec for 1s durability. Hybrid mode combines both for fast load + good durability.
Memory fragmentation (mem_fragmentation_ratio > 1.5): enable active defragmentation or restart.
bullets: LFU (allkeys-lfu): better than LRU for skewed/Zipf access distributions
Hybrid persistence: recommended for production; RDB preamble + AOF increments
BGREWRITEAOF: compacts AOF without blocking; run when ratio exceeds 2x

core.title: Replication, Sentinel, and Cluster
paragraphs: Replication is async: primary streams commands to replicas. Replica reads are stale by definition—never rely on them for read-after-write consistency.
Sentinel: quorum-based HA for single-shard; 30-60s failover. Cluster: 16,384 slots sharded across N nodes; per-shard HA.
Hash tags {tag} colocate keys on same slot for multi-key commands in Cluster.
bullets: Sentinel quorum: typically 2/3 required to agree primary is down before failover
Cluster MOVED redirection: client hits wrong node; server returns correct node address
Replication lag: typically <10ms healthy; can grow under heavy write load

deepDive.title: Redis Data Encoding Internals
paragraphs: Redis uses different internal encodings for the same data type depending on size and content. A Hash with ≤128 fields and all values ≤64 bytes uses listpack (formerly ziplist)—a contiguous memory block with no pointers, excellent cache locality, 10x more memory-efficient than hashtable encoding. When either threshold is exceeded, Redis automatically upgrades to hashtable encoding. Knowing these thresholds lets you tune configuration or key design to stay in compact encoding.

Sorted Sets use listpack for ≤128 members with ≤64-byte values, skiplist+hashtable otherwise. A leaderboard with 10,000 users always uses skiplist. But a sorted set used as a sliding window rate limiter (ZADD with timestamps as scores, usually <100 members per user) stays in listpack encoding for most users—significantly more memory-efficient. Use OBJECT ENCODING key to inspect the current encoding and DEBUG OBJECT key for detailed memory info.

Integer encoding: strings that look like integers (0-9999) are stored as actual integers (8 bytes in a shared pool, 0 bytes if in pool). A counter key INCR count stores an integer value, consuming the minimum memory. Keys themselves are stored as dynamically allocated strings in the main hash table. Redis 7.0 added listpack for Hash and List (replacing ziplist) with slightly different threshold handling but similar memory efficiency characteristics.
bullets: listpack (ziplist): compact encoding for small hashes/lists/zsets; 10x memory savings vs pointer-based
OBJECT ENCODING key: inspect current encoding (listpack, hashtable, skiplist, etc.)
Encoding upgrade: automatic when thresholds exceeded; never downgrade automatically
hash-max-listpack-entries 128: config knob to tune listpack→hashtable threshold

deepDive.title: Redis Patterns: Distributed Locks, Rate Limiting, and Pub/Sub
paragraphs: Redlock is the distributed lock algorithm for Redis: acquire a lock by running SET key token NX EX ttl against N/2+1 independent Redis nodes. The lock is considered acquired if a majority (N/2+1) of nodes succeed within a time window much shorter than the TTL. This handles single-node Redis failures. Controversy: Martin Kleppmann argued that clock drift and process pauses can cause Redlock to issue two concurrent lock holders even with a quorum. For safety-critical distributed locking, use etcd or ZooKeeper with their stronger consistency guarantees.

Sliding window rate limiting: use a Sorted Set per user with timestamps as both member and score. For each request: ZADD ratelimit:user:1234 now now, ZREMRANGEBYSCORE ratelimit:user:1234 0 (now - window_seconds), ZCARD ratelimit:user:1234. If ZCARD > limit, reject. EXPIRE ratelimit:user:1234 window_seconds to clean up idle users. Use a Lua script to make the three commands atomic. This provides exact sliding window semantics at the cost of storing one entry per request per user.

Pub/Sub and Redis Streams: Pub/Sub (PUBLISH/SUBSCRIBE) provides fire-and-forget message delivery—subscribers receive messages published after they subscribed; they miss messages published while offline. This makes it unsuitable for reliable message delivery. Redis Streams (XADD/XREAD/XGROUP) provide persistent, consumer-group-based message delivery with acknowledgments—closer to Kafka semantics. For task queues, use Streams with consumer groups. For broadcast notifications (live chat presence), Pub/Sub is appropriate. For durable task distribution, use Streams.
bullets: Redlock: multi-node distributed lock; controversial for safety-critical locks—prefer etcd for strong guarantees
Sliding window rate limit: ZADD + ZREMRANGEBYSCORE + ZCARD in Lua script for atomicity
Pub/Sub: fire-and-forget broadcast; no persistence; missed if offline
Streams: persistent consumer groups with ACK; use for reliable task queues

expert.title: Redis at Hyperscale: Cluster Sizing and Hotspot Mitigation
paragraphs: Redis Cluster sizing: target 70-80% memory utilization per node (leave headroom for replication buffers, AOF rewrite, and fork overhead). With 64GB RAM per node at 70% utilization, effective capacity is 44GB per node. Plan for 2x replication (each primary has one replica). A 1TB dataset needs ~24 nodes (12 primary + 12 replica). Cluster rebalancing (resharding) is online but CPU-intensive—schedule during low-traffic windows.

Hot keys are the primary scaling challenge in Redis Cluster. A 'celebrity' key (product:trending:12345) receiving 100,000 reads/second hits a single shard. Mitigation: local in-process caching for the hottest keys (small TTL, refreshed on miss), read replicas for the hot shard (Redis Cluster supports replica reads for read-heavy slots), and key splitting (product:trending:12345:{1} through product:trending:12345:{N} spread reads across N shards). Key splitting requires application-layer aggregation.

Memory optimization at scale: set max 50% of memory to keys without TTL when using volatile-lru—keys without TTL are never evicted, so your cache fills with 'permanent' keys that squeeze out cached data. Enforce TTLs on all cache keys without exception. Use WAIT command to synchronously replicate critical writes before acknowledging to the client—trading latency for durability in cases where write loss is unacceptable. Keyspace notifications enable event-driven patterns (notify subscribers when a key expires) but generate significant overhead at high key creation/expiration rates.

concepts: Single-threaded event loop: processes commands sequentially; no locks; O(1) and O(log n) operations
String: byte array up to 512MB; integers stored efficiently; NX+EX for distributed lock
Hash: field-value pairs; compact listpack encoding for small hashes
Sorted Set (ZSET): unique members with scores; skip list for rank operations; leaderboards, rate limiting
Stream: persistent, consumer-group-based message queue with acknowledgment
RDB: fork-based snapshot; compact; fast restore; periodic data loss
AOF: append-only command log; appendfsync everysec = 1s max data loss
Replication: async primary-replica; stale reads from replicas
Redis Sentinel: HA for single-shard; quorum-based automatic failover
Redis Cluster: horizontal sharding across 16,384 slots; per-shard HA
maxmemory + eviction: allkeys-lru/lfu for cache; volatile-lru for mixed TTL/persistent
Pipelining: batch multiple commands in one round-trip; major throughput improvement
practices: Always set maxmemory and an eviction policy—running without them causes OOM process kills
Use SCAN instead of KEYS for key enumeration; SSCAN/HSCAN/ZSCAN for large data structures
Set TTLs on all cache keys; volatile-lru eviction silently fails to evict keys without TTL
Use pipelining for bulk operations—reduces round-trip overhead by 10-100x
Monitor mem_fragmentation_ratio; enable active defragmentation or schedule restarts if >2.0
Use listpack-friendly sizing (< 128 fields in Hash, < 64 bytes per value) for memory-efficient storage
Use Lua scripts for atomic multi-command operations (rate limiting, distributed lock acquire)
pitfalls: Using KEYS * in production—O(n) over all keys; blocks the event loop for seconds on large datasets
Storing session data in Redis without TTLs—memory fills with dead sessions; eviction fails to clean them
Using Pub/Sub for reliable message delivery—subscribers miss messages published while offline
Missing connection pool on the client side—each request opens a new TCP connection, overwhelming Redis
Very large hash or sorted set values—single HGETALL or ZRANGE 0 -1 on a 1M member set blocks the event loop
Not accounting for fork overhead in memory planning—bgsave/bgrewriteaof can double memory usage briefly due to copy-on-write
Using Sorted Set as a durable queue without consumer groups—no acknowledgment, messages lost on crash

examples.title: Session Store with Rolling TTL
examples.description: An e-commerce site stores user sessions in Redis Hashes (session:token → {userId, cart, lastActivity}). On every request, HSET updates lastActivity and EXPIRE resets the TTL to 30 minutes. The rolling TTL ensures active sessions never expire, while idle sessions are automatically cleaned up. With 1 million active sessions at 500 bytes each (compact listpack encoding), memory consumption is ~500MB—well within Redis's sweet spot. Sentinel provides HA so session loss during failover is confined to the ~30s window.

examples.title: Leaderboard with Sorted Set
examples.description: A gaming platform maintains real-time leaderboards using Redis Sorted Sets: ZADD leaderboard:daily score userId, ZREVRANK leaderboard:daily userId for rank, ZREVRANGE leaderboard:daily 0 99 WITHSCORES for top 100. With 10 million users, the sorted set consumes ~800MB (skiplist encoding with 8-byte score + variable user ID). ZADD/ZREVRANK are O(log n) even at this scale—10ms p99. A weekly leaderboard caches the top 1000 as a separate key, reducing query load on the main sorted set during peak traffic.

examples.title: Rate Limiting with Sliding Window
examples.description: An API gateway limits each API key to 1,000 requests per minute using a sliding window algorithm: a Lua script atomically ZADDs the current timestamp, removes timestamps older than 60 seconds (ZREMRANGEBYSCORE), counts remaining members (ZCARD), and returns allow/deny. This provides exact per-minute rate limiting that doesn't reset at a fixed clock boundary (unlike fixed window algorithms). The Sorted Set TTL is set to 2 minutes to automatically clean up inactive keys without manual cleanup jobs.

keyTakeaways: Redis's single-threaded event loop achieves massive throughput because all data is in memory and operations are O(1)/O(log n)
Data structure selection is a first-class design decision—Sorted Sets for leaderboards, Streams for queues, Hashes for objects
Always set maxmemory + eviction policy; use TTLs on all cache keys; monitor fragmentation
Persistence: RDB for fast restart, AOF for durability, hybrid mode for both—or no persistence for pure caches
Avoid O(n) commands on large datasets; use SCAN and structure-specific SCAN variants for iteration
Cluster provides horizontal scale; Sentinel provides HA; async replication means replica reads can be stale
Pipelining and Lua scripts are essential for high-throughput workloads and atomic multi-step operations
lessons.whyItMatters: Redis appears in virtually every distributed system architecture as a cache, session store, rate limiter, leaderboard, or message queue. Understanding its data structures, memory model, and operational characteristics is essential for using it correctly and diagnosing production issues. Its single-threaded nature means a single misconfigured operation can degrade latency for all users—this knowledge is tested in every senior engineering interview that involves caching or distributed state.
reflectionQuestions: You're designing a rate limiter that must track 1,000 requests/minute per user across 100 service instances. How would you implement it with Redis, ensuring atomic operations and handling Redis cluster key distribution?

A Redis cache is using 90% memory and eviction rate is high, causing cache misses. Walk through your investigation: what metrics do you check, what data structure misuses might you find, and what configuration changes would you make?
Compare Redis Pub/Sub, Redis Streams, and Kafka for a notification system that must deliver notifications to 10,000 subscribers and cannot lose messages. Which would you choose?
How does Redis handle persistence during a fork() for BGSAVE? What are the memory implications on a 32GB Redis instance with active writes?
numbersToKnow: Redis throughput: 100K-1M simple ops/sec on commodity hardware with single-threaded model
listpack threshold: 128 entries, 64 bytes per value for Hash/List/ZSet compact encoding
Sentinel failover time: 30-60 seconds typical; tune down-after-milliseconds and failover-timeout
Redis Cluster: 16,384 hash slots; CRC16(key) % 16,384 determines slot assignment
AOF appendfsync everysec: at most 1 second of data loss on crash
Fork overhead: BGSAVE may temporarily require 2x memory due to copy-on-write during write-heavy periods
Cluster node capacity target: 70-80% memory utilization; leave 20-30% headroom for fork and replication

Compare Redis List, Pub/Sub, and Streams for implementing a job queue. Which would you use and why?
Design a leaderboard system for 10 million users using Redis. What data structure, what commands, and what are the scaling considerations?
Explain Redis eviction policies. When would you use allkeys-lru vs. allkeys-lfu vs. volatile-lru?

exercises: Design a Redis schema for a social media feed: users follow other users; each post appears in followers' feeds. Address: how to store the feed, how to fanout new posts, what to do with users who have 10 million followers (celebrity problem), and how to paginate the feed.

Implement a token bucket rate limiter using a Lua script in Redis. The script should: check if a token is available, consume it atomically, and return whether the request is allowed—all in a single atomic operation.

A Redis instance is consuming 50GB of a 64GB server and the OOM killer is occasionally killing the Redis process during BGSAVE. Diagnose the root cause and propose a solution without increasing server size.

lessons.title: Object Storage Internals
lessons.summary: Object Storage Internals is a core topic in modern system design. This lesson builds a first-principles model around how production systems are built inside, then connects that model to capacity, failure modes, and operational practice so you can use it in real architectures.

sections.title: What Object Storage Internals is solving
paragraphs: Object Storage Internals exists because naive designs around how production systems are built inside break under scale, partial failure, or changing requirements. Before choosing tools, name the problem: which resource is scarce, which invariant must hold, and which user-visible failures are unacceptable.
In interviews and production reviews, strong answers start with constraints (QPS, data size, latency budget, consistency needs) and only then map Object Storage Internals onto those constraints.

A useful mental model separates the control plane (how you configure and observe Object Storage Internals) from the data plane (the per-request/per-event path). Confusing the two leads to architectures that look neat and operate poorly.

sections.title: Core mechanics
paragraphs: Mechanically, Object Storage Internals involves a small set of moving parts: inputs, state, an algorithm or protocol, and outputs/side effects. Draw those parts explicitly. If state is replicated, write down the replication/consistency rule. If work is asynchronous, write down delivery semantics.

Performance characteristics usually come from amplification (how much internal work per external request), locality (whether work stays on one node), and contention (locks, hot keys, leader bottlenecks).

Correctness characteristics usually come from failure handling: retries, timeouts, idempotency, and what clients observe during failover. If you cannot explain the failure story, you do not yet understand Object Storage Internals.
bullets: Inputs → state/protocol → outputs/side effects
Name consistency and delivery guarantees
Identify the bottleneck resource early

sections.title: Designing with it
paragraphs: When incorporating Object Storage Internals into a system, decide the API boundary first: what does a client call, what can fail, and what is retried. Keep the happy path boring and push complexity into well-tested libraries or platform components.

Capacity plan with numbers: estimate peak load, working set, and headroom. Convert that into shard counts, cache sizes, thread/connection pools, or GPU/memory budgets as relevant to Object Storage Internals.
Prefer reversible rollout: feature flags, dual-running, shadow traffic, and clear dashboards. New uses of Object Storage Internals should be observable on day one.

sections.title: Operations and failure modes
paragraphs: Operate Object Storage Internals with SLIs that match user pain (availability, latency, lag, error rate, cost). Alert on burn rates and queue/lag growth, not only host CPU.
Common failures include overload without admission control, retry amplification, silent staleness, schema mismatches, and dependency brownouts. Write a runbook for the top three.
Chaos and game days should include slow dependencies and network delay, not only hard kills. Object Storage Internals often fails in the gray area.

expert.title: Object Storage Internals — multi-region and cost

lessons.title: Kafka & Nginx Internals
lessons.summary: Kafka and Nginx are infrastructure workhorses — one moves events at scale, the other terminates HTTP at the edge. Kafka's log-structured partitions and consumer groups enable durable, replayable event streams. Nginx's master/worker event-driven model serves millions of connections with minimal memory. Understanding both internals is essential for designing reliable pipelines and high-throughput web tiers.

sections.title: Kafka: Distributed Commit Log Architecture
paragraphs: Kafka is a distributed, partitioned, replicated commit log. Producers append records to topic partitions — ordered, immutable sequences identified by offset. Unlike traditional message queues that delete messages after consumption, Kafka retains records for a configurable period (or size), allowing replay and multiple independent consumer groups.

Each partition is an ordered log stored as segment files on disk (index + .log). Sequential disk writes achieve throughput comparable to memory when batching and page cache cooperate. Partitions are the unit of parallelism: more partitions mean more parallel consumers and producers, up to broker and cluster limits.

Brokers are Kafka server processes. A cluster has many brokers; each partition has one leader broker handling reads/writes and zero or more follower replicas syncing data. ISR (In-Sync Replicas) is the set of followers caught up within a configurable lag. If the leader dies, a follower from ISR is elected — availability and durability depend on replication factor and acks setting.

ZooKeeper (legacy) or KRaft (Kafka Raft metadata mode) manages cluster metadata: broker registration, partition leadership, consumer group offsets (offsets now stored in internal __consumer_offsets topic). KRaft removes the ZooKeeper dependency, simplifying operations in modern Kafka versions.
bullets: Topic → partitions → ordered, append-only log segments
Offset: monotonic position within a partition
Leader + followers; ISR = replicas eligible for leadership
Retention by time (log.retention.hours) or size — not consume-and-delete

sections.title: Kafka: Producers, Consumers, and Delivery Semantics
paragraphs: Producers choose a partition via key hash (same key → same partition → per-key ordering) or round-robin. Batching (linger.ms, batch.size) amortizes network overhead. acks=0 fire-and-forget; acks=1 leader ack; acks=all waits for all ISR — the durability vs latency trade-off.

Consumer groups distribute partitions among group members — each partition consumed by at most one consumer in the group. Rebalance occurs when members join or leave; during rebalance, consumption pauses (unless using cooperative sticky assignors). Scale consumers up to partition count; extra consumers sit idle.

Delivery semantics: at-most-once (commit offset before process — may lose messages), at-least-once (process then commit — may duplicate), exactly-once (Kafka transactions + idempotent producer — higher overhead, limited to Kafka Streams / specific flows). Production systems almost always implement at-least-once with idempotent consumers.

Log compaction retains the latest record per key — useful for changelog topics (KTables, config propagation). Tombstone records (null value) delete keys after delete.retention.ms. Compact + delete retention policies can coexist on different topics.
bullets: Partition key → consistent hashing → per-key ordering guarantee
Consumer group: one consumer per partition within a group
Rebalance: partition reassignment on membership change
Idempotent producer: dedup via PID + sequence number per partition

sections.title: Nginx: Master/Worker and the Event Loop
paragraphs: Nginx uses a master process (reads config, manages workers, binds ports) and one or more worker processes (handle connections). Workers are single-threaded with an event-driven loop — epoll on Linux, kqueue on BSD. Thousands of idle connections cost kilobytes each (connection state), not megabytes per thread.

The event loop: register socket events (readable, writable), wait via epoll_wait, dispatch handlers. Non-blocking I/O is mandatory — a blocking read in one worker stalls all connections that worker manages. Proxy upstream calls use the same non-blocking model with retry and timeout logic.

Accept mutex (older versions) or SO_REUSEPORT (modern) distributes incoming connections across workers. SO_REUSEPORT lets each worker bind the same port; the kernel load-balances accepts — better CPU utilization on multi-core hosts.

Static file serving uses sendfile (zero-copy from disk to socket, bypassing user-space buffer copies). gzip/brotli compression, caching headers, and open_file_cache reduce disk and CPU for repeat assets. These optimizations explain why Nginx dominates static content and reverse proxy roles.
bullets: Master/worker: workers are single-threaded event loops
epoll/kqueue: O(1) readiness notification for many connections
sendfile: zero-copy static file delivery
SO_REUSEPORT: kernel-level accept load balancing across workers

sections.title: Nginx: Reverse Proxy, Load Balancing, and TLS
paragraphs: As a reverse proxy, Nginx terminates client connections and opens separate upstream connections to backend servers. proxy_pass, upstream blocks, and keepalive connections to upstreams reduce TCP handshake overhead. Health checks (commercial Plus or open-source modules) remove failed backends from rotation.

Load balancing methods: round-robin (default), least_conn, ip_hash (session stickiness), hash (consistent hashing on URI or custom key). Weighted backends support heterogeneous capacity. For WebSocket and HTTP/2, proxy modules handle protocol upgrade and multiplexing.

TLS termination at Nginx offloads crypto from application servers. ssl_session_cache (shared across workers) and session tickets reduce handshake cost. HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 (QUIC) modules push protocol handling to the edge. Certificate management (Let's Encrypt, cert-manager sidecars) integrates at this layer.

Rate limiting (limit_req, limit_conn), WAF integration, and request buffering protect backends from abuse and slow clients. Large upload buffering to disk prevents memory exhaustion when clients send slowly — a classic slowloris mitigation combined with timeouts (client_body_timeout, proxy_read_timeout).
bullets: upstream keepalive: reuse backend TCP connections

sections.title: Kafka and Nginx in System Architecture
paragraphs: A common pattern: Nginx at the edge terminates TLS, serves static assets, load-balances to API servers, and enforces rate limits. API servers publish domain events to Kafka; downstream consumers (search indexer, analytics, email) process independently with at-least-once semantics and idempotent handlers.

Kafka absorbs write spikes in the log (disk-bound retention) but slow consumers fall behind (consumer lag metric). Monitor lag, rebalance frequency, and under-replicated partitions as Kafka SLOs.

core.title: Kafka: Distributed Commit Log Architecture
paragraphs: Kafka is a distributed, partitioned, replicated commit log. Producers append records to topic partitions — ordered, immutable sequences identified by offset. Unlike traditional message queues that delete messages after consumption, Kafka retains records for a configurable period (or size), allowing replay and multiple independent consumer groups.

Each partition is an ordered log stored as segment files on disk (index + .log). Sequential disk writes achieve throughput comparable to memory when batching and page cache cooperate. Partitions are the unit of parallelism: more partitions mean more parallel consumers and producers, up to broker and cluster limits.

Brokers are Kafka server processes. A cluster has many brokers; each partition has one leader broker handling reads/writes and zero or more follower replicas syncing data. ISR (In-Sync Replicas) is the set of followers caught up within a configurable lag. If the leader dies, a follower from ISR is elected — availability and durability depend on replication factor and acks setting.

ZooKeeper (legacy) or KRaft (Kafka Raft metadata mode) manages cluster metadata: broker registration, partition leadership, consumer group offsets (offsets now stored in internal __consumer_offsets topic). KRaft removes the ZooKeeper dependency, simplifying operations in modern Kafka versions.

Offset: monotonic position within a partition

core.title: Kafka: Producers, Consumers, and Delivery Semantics
paragraphs: Producers choose a partition via key hash (same key → same partition → per-key ordering) or round-robin. Batching (linger.ms, batch.size) amortizes network overhead. acks=0 fire-and-forget; acks=1 leader ack; acks=all waits for all ISR — the durability vs latency trade-off.

Consumer groups distribute partitions among group members — each partition consumed by at most one consumer in the group. Rebalance occurs when members join or leave; during rebalance, consumption pauses (unless using cooperative sticky assignors). Scale consumers up to partition count; extra consumers sit idle.

Delivery semantics: at-most-once (commit offset before process — may lose messages), at-least-once (process then commit — may duplicate), exactly-once (Kafka transactions + idempotent producer — higher overhead, limited to Kafka Streams / specific flows). Production systems almost always implement at-least-once with idempotent consumers.

Log compaction retains the latest record per key — useful for changelog topics (KTables, config propagation). Tombstone records (null value) delete keys after delete.retention.ms. Compact + delete retention policies can coexist on different topics.

core.title: Nginx: Master/Worker and the Event Loop
paragraphs: Nginx uses a master process (reads config, manages workers, binds ports) and one or more worker processes (handle connections). Workers are single-threaded with an event-driven loop — epoll on Linux, kqueue on BSD. Thousands of idle connections cost kilobytes each (connection state), not megabytes per thread.

The event loop: register socket events (readable, writable), wait via epoll_wait, dispatch handlers. Non-blocking I/O is mandatory — a blocking read in one worker stalls all connections that worker manages. Proxy upstream calls use the same non-blocking model with retry and timeout logic.

Accept mutex (older versions) or SO_REUSEPORT (modern) distributes incoming connections across workers. SO_REUSEPORT lets each worker bind the same port; the kernel load-balances accepts — better CPU utilization on multi-core hosts.

Static file serving uses sendfile (zero-copy from disk to socket, bypassing user-space buffer copies). gzip/brotli compression, caching headers, and open_file_cache reduce disk and CPU for repeat assets. These optimizations explain why Nginx dominates static content and reverse proxy roles.

epoll/kqueue: O(1) readiness notification for many connections

core.title: Nginx: Reverse Proxy, Load Balancing, and TLS
paragraphs: As a reverse proxy, Nginx terminates client connections and opens separate upstream connections to backend servers. proxy_pass, upstream blocks, and keepalive connections to upstreams reduce TCP handshake overhead. Health checks (commercial Plus or open-source modules) remove failed backends from rotation.

Load balancing methods: round-robin (default), least_conn, ip_hash (session stickiness), hash (consistent hashing on URI or custom key). Weighted backends support heterogeneous capacity. For WebSocket and HTTP/2, proxy modules handle protocol upgrade and multiplexing.

TLS termination at Nginx offloads crypto from application servers. ssl_session_cache (shared across workers) and session tickets reduce handshake cost. HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 (QUIC) modules push protocol handling to the edge. Certificate management (Let's Encrypt, cert-manager sidecars) integrates at this layer.

Rate limiting (limit_req, limit_conn), WAF integration, and request buffering protect backends from abuse and slow clients. Large upload buffering to disk prevents memory exhaustion when clients send slowly — a classic slowloris mitigation combined with timeouts (client_body_timeout, proxy_read_timeout).

deepDive.title: Kafka & Nginx Internals — Operational deep dive
paragraphs: Operating Kafka & Nginx Internals well means defining the scarce resource (CPU, memory, disk, network, or tokens), the SLIs that reflect user pain, and the knobs that trade cost for latency.
Under load, measure amplification: how many bytes, RPCs, or disk writes you pay per user request. Prefetch and batch only when measurements show benefit — premature batching adds tail latency.
Failure drills should include dependency slowdown (not only hard down), clock skew, and disk full. Verify alerts, dashboards, and runbooks against those drills.
bullets: Name the scarcest resource and budget it
Track p50/p99 and error rate for the user journey
Rehearse partial dependency failure

deepDive.title: Kafka & Nginx Internals — Correctness edges
paragraphs: Correctness edges around Kafka & Nginx Internals often appear at retries, partial writes, and schema evolution. Make handlers idempotent and state transitions explicit.

Document what clients may observe during failover: stale reads, duplicate messages, or delayed visibility. If the product cannot tolerate an anomaly, enforce a stronger consistency boundary — and pay for it knowingly.

expert.title: Kafka & Nginx Internals — Expert / multi-region notes
paragraphs: At multi-region scale, Kafka & Nginx Internals interacts with RTT, quorum placement, and cost of cross-region replication. Prefer region-local user paths with asynchronous global state when invariants allow.
Cost envelopes matter: chart unit cost vs QPS and vs data size. Many 'performance' projects are actually cost projects in disguise — make the objective explicit.

examples.title: Event-driven order pipeline
examples.description: Order API (behind Nginx) writes to Postgres and publishes OrderPlaced to Kafka partition keyed by order_id. Inventory, email, and analytics services each consume in separate consumer groups — all receive every event, process at their own pace, and commit offsets after successful handling. Nginx rate-limits checkout endpoints during flash sales.

examples.title: Nginx edge with microservices upstream
examples.description: Nginx terminates TLS, applies WAF rules, and routes /api/users to user-service, /api/orders to order-service via location blocks. Upstream keepalive pools 32 connections per backend. least_conn balances skewed request durations. Static assets served via sendfile with 1-year cache headers — 90% of bytes never hit application servers.

examples.title: Kafka replay for bug fix deployment
examples.description: A bug in the search indexer corrupted documents for 6 hours. Because Kafka retains 7 days of events, the team resets the consumer group offset to the incident start time and replays OrderPlaced events idempotently (upsert by document ID). Without log retention and idempotent writes, manual backfill would take days.

At-least-once with idempotent consumers is the production default for delivery semantics
Nginx scales via event-driven workers — non-blocking I/O and sendfile for efficiency
Edge proxy handles TLS, load balancing, rate limiting — protect and offload backends
Monitor Kafka consumer lag and Nginx upstream 5xx/latency as primary health signals
Partition key design determines ordering scope — choose keys aligned with business invariants
lessons.whyItMatters: Kafka and Nginx form the data plane and control edge of most modern backends. Interview questions about event ordering, consumer lag, and reverse proxy configuration assume you understand internals, not just configuration snippets. Production incidents in both systems trace directly to partition design, rebalance behavior, worker limits, and timeout mismatches.

Design partition count and consumer group topology for 100K events/sec with 5 downstream processors.
When would you bypass Nginx and expose a service directly behind a cloud load balancer?

lessons.title: Redis & PostgreSQL Internals
lessons.summary: Redis and PostgreSQL sit at opposite ends of the data store spectrum — in-memory structures vs. durable relational pages — yet both appear together in nearly every production stack. Understanding their internal architectures explains why Redis is fast (single-threaded event loop, O(1) structures) and why Postgres queries behave as they do (MVCC, buffer pool, WAL, query planner).

sections.title: Redis: In-Memory Data Structures and Single-Threaded Execution
paragraphs: Redis is primarily an in-memory key-value store with rich data structures: strings, lists, sets, sorted sets, hashes, streams, and more. Each type is implemented with optimized internal encodings — a small hash might use a ziplist (compact contiguous memory) and automatically upgrade to a hash table as it grows.

The core Redis server process is single-threaded for command execution. One event loop (epoll/kqueue) handles thousands of client connections; commands are processed sequentially, eliminating lock contention on data structures. This design is why Redis achieves sub-millisecond latency — no mutex overhead on the hot path.

Persistence is optional and configurable. RDB snapshots fork a child process (copy-on-write) to dump memory to disk periodically. AOF (Append-Only File) logs every write command and replays on restart — fsync policy (always, everysec, no) trades durability for throughput. Most production setups use both: RDB for fast restarts, AOF for minimal data loss.

Eviction policies (allkeys-lru, volatile-ttl, etc.) kick in when maxmemory is reached. Redis is not a cache by default — without maxmemory and eviction, it grows until OOM. Treat explicit TTLs and memory limits as mandatory operational configuration, not optional tuning.
bullets: Single-threaded command execution — no locks on data structures
Encodings upgrade automatically (ziplist → hashtable, intset → set)
RDB: point-in-time snapshot; AOF: command replay log
Streams: log-like structure with consumer groups (Kafka-lite)

sections.title: Redis: Replication, Cluster, and Common Pitfalls
paragraphs: Primary-replica replication is asynchronous by default. Replicas connect to the primary, receive a full sync (RDB transfer) or partial resync (backlog buffer), then stream incremental commands. Read-your-writes is not guaranteed on replicas — a write to primary may not appear on replica for milliseconds, causing stale reads if you route reads to replicas blindly.

Redis Cluster shards data across 16,384 hash slots. Each master owns a slot range; replicas failover via gossip and majority quorum. MOVED and ASK redirects tell clients the correct node. Cluster mode adds operational complexity — multi-key transactions only work within the same hash slot (use hash tags {user:123}.profile and {user:123}.sessions).

Lua scripts and MULTI/EXEC provide atomicity on a single node. There is no cross-slot distributed transaction in cluster mode. For distributed locks, Redlock is controversial — understand clock skew and fencing tokens before trusting Redis locks for financial correctness.

Memory fragmentation, big keys, and hot keys are production killers. A single 100 MB hash key blocks the event loop during deletion. MONITOR and KEYS commands block production — use SCAN instead. Pipeline batches commands to amortize round-trip latency without changing atomicity semantics.

Hash slots: 16384 slots partitioned across cluster masters
Hash tags {id} force related keys to same slot for multi-key ops
Pipeline: batch commands; Transaction (MULTI/EXEC): atomic batch on one node

sections.title: PostgreSQL: Pages, Buffer Pool, and MVCC
paragraphs: PostgreSQL stores data in 8 KB pages (blocks) organized in tables and indexes (B-tree default). The shared buffer pool caches hot pages in memory — identical in concept to an OS page cache but managed by Postgres. A sequential scan reads pages from buffer or disk; repeated access benefits from cache warmth.

MVCC (Multi-Version Concurrency Control) lets readers never block writers and writers never block readers. Each row has xmin (inserting transaction) and xmax (deleting/updating transaction) system columns. UPDATE creates a new row version; the old version becomes dead tuple until vacuum reclaims space.

Vacuum (autovacuum) is not optional housekeeping — it prevents transaction ID wraparound, reclaims dead tuple space, and updates visibility map bits for index-only scans. Bloat from long-running transactions holding old snapshots is a top Postgres performance incident: a forgotten open transaction blocks vacuum from cleaning millions of dead rows.

Indexes are separate B-tree structures pointing to heap tuples. A query may index scan + heap fetch (random I/O) or bitmap index scan for moderate selectivity. Covering indexes (INCLUDE columns) enable index-only scans when visibility map confirms tuples are visible — a major optimization for read-heavy workloads.

MVCC: row versions with xmin/xmax; UPDATE = insert new + mark old dead
VACUUM reclaims dead tuples; autovacuum must keep pace with write rate
B-tree index: default for equality and range; GIN/GiST for full-text, JSON, geo

sections.title: PostgreSQL: WAL, Checkpoints, and the Query Planner
paragraphs: Every change goes to the Write-Ahead Log (WAL) before data pages are flushed to disk. WAL is sequential append — fast on SSD and HDD. On crash recovery, Postgres replays WAL to bring data files to a consistent state. WAL also feeds logical replication and physical streaming replicas.

Checkpoints flush dirty buffer pool pages to data files and create a recovery starting point. Too frequent checkpoints increase I/O; too infrequent checkpoints lengthen crash recovery and increase WAL size. tuning checkpoint_completion_target spreads flush I/O to avoid latency spikes.

The query planner estimates cost using statistics (ANALYZE). It chooses nested loop (small inner), hash join (equi-joins, large tables), or merge join (pre-sorted inputs). Bad plans from stale statistics — a column went from uniform to skewed — cause catastrophic seq scans on billion-row tables. EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) is your primary diagnostic tool.

Connection model matters: Postgres uses one process per connection. Thousands of idle connections consume memory and hurt performance — use PgBouncer (transaction or session pooling) in front of the database. Long transactions hold locks and prevent vacuum — set statement_timeout and idle_in_transaction_session_timeout.
bullets: WAL: durability and replication source; sequential writes
Checkpoints: periodic flush of dirty pages to data files
Planner: cost-based; depends on pg_statistic from ANALYZE
PgBouncer: pool connections — essential at high client counts

sections.title: Using Redis and Postgres Together
paragraphs: The canonical pattern: Postgres is the source of truth; Redis is cache, session store, rate limiter, or pub/sub layer. Cache-aside: read Redis first, on miss query Postgres, populate Redis with TTL. Invalidate on write (delete cache key) rather than update-in-place to avoid race conditions.

Write-through and write-behind are alternatives when consistency requirements differ. Sessions and rate limits tolerate loss on Redis failure — rebuild from login or reset counters. Financial balances belong in Postgres with ACID guarantees; never rely on Redis alone for authoritative ledger state.

Hot key mitigation in Redis: local in-process cache (Caffeine) in front of Redis, read replicas for read-heavy keys, or application-level sharding of a hot counter into multiple keys summed at read time. In Postgres: partition large tables, partial indexes for active subsets, and read replicas for analytics (with lag awareness).

Understanding internals lets you tune intentionally: Redis maxmemory-policy and key design; Postgres shared_buffers (~25% RAM), effective_cache_size, work_mem for sorts, and index strategy matched to query patterns. Blind defaults work until scale proves otherwise.

Route critical reads to Postgres primary when replica lag is unacceptable
Monitor Postgres dead tuples, autovacuum lag, and long-running transactions
Run EXPLAIN ANALYZE on slow queries; keep statistics fresh with ANALYZE after bulk loads
Use PgBouncer when connection count exceeds a few hundred
Invalidate cache on write (delete key) rather than update cache synchronously
pitfalls: Treating Redis as durable primary storage without AOF fsync=always — data loss on crash
Reading from Redis replicas immediately after write to primary — stale data
Big keys and hot keys blocking Redis single thread — shard or local-cache mitigations
Neglecting Postgres vacuum — table bloat, XID wraparound emergencies
One process per connection at 5000 app instances — connection exhaustion without pooling
Missing indexes or stale stats causing seq scans on large tables under production load

examples.title: Session store in Redis, orders in Postgres
examples.description: User sessions (TTL 24h, JSON blob) live in Redis for fast lookup on every request. Order placement writes to Postgres in a transaction, then deletes the user's cart cache key in Redis. Session loss on Redis restart forces re-login — acceptable. Order loss would not be — Postgres WAL ensures durability.

examples.title: Postgres bloat from a long transaction
examples.description: A BI tool opens a read transaction at 9 AM and holds it until 5 PM. Autovacuum cannot reclaim dead tuples from millions of updates that day. Table bloat grows 40%; queries slow from seq scans and heap fetches. Fix: idle_in_transaction_session_timeout + read replica for analytics queries.

examples.title: Cache stampede on popular product page
examples.description: A flash sale product key expires simultaneously across 10,000 clients. All miss cache, hammer Postgres, and repopulate Redis at once. Mitigation: probabilistic early expiration, request coalescing (single-flight lock in Redis), or pre-warming cache before sale start.

keyTakeaways: Redis speed comes from in-memory structures and single-threaded execution — avoid blocking operations and big keys
Postgres durability and concurrency rest on MVCC, WAL, and vacuum — operational discipline required
Use Redis for ephemeral acceleration; Postgres for authoritative, transactional state
Replication in both systems is asynchronous — design for replica lag and stale reads
Postgres query performance depends on indexes, statistics, and connection pooling
Cache-aside with TTL and invalidation-on-write is the safest default caching pattern
EXPLAIN ANALYZE and Redis SLOWLOG are essential production diagnostics
lessons.whyItMatters: Redis and PostgreSQL appear in almost every backend architecture interview and production stack. Knowing their internals — not just their APIs — lets you explain latency spikes, design cache strategies that do not corrupt data, tune Postgres before incidents, and make credible storage choices under load.

What happens in Postgres when two transactions UPDATE the same row concurrently? Walk through MVCC step by step.
Your Redis latency p99 jumped from 1ms to 50ms. What internal Redis factors would you investigate?
When would you choose Redis Streams over Kafka for event delivery?

lessons.title: Colocation, Clocks & Fairness
lessons.summary: Colocation, Clocks & Fairness is a core topic in modern system design. This lesson builds a first-principles model around determinism, latency, and fairness, then connects that model to capacity, failure modes, and operational practice so you can use it in real architectures.

sections.title: What Colocation, Clocks & Fairness is solving
paragraphs: Colocation, Clocks & Fairness exists because naive designs around determinism, latency, and fairness break under scale, partial failure, or changing requirements. Before choosing tools, name the problem: which resource is scarce, which invariant must hold, and which user-visible failures are unacceptable.
In interviews and production reviews, strong answers start with constraints (QPS, data size, latency budget, consistency needs) and only then map Colocation, Clocks & Fairness onto those constraints.

A useful mental model separates the control plane (how you configure and observe Colocation, Clocks & Fairness) from the data plane (the per-request/per-event path). Confusing the two leads to architectures that look neat and operate poorly.

sections.title: Core mechanics
paragraphs: Mechanically, Colocation, Clocks & Fairness involves a small set of moving parts: inputs, state, an algorithm or protocol, and outputs/side effects. Draw those parts explicitly. If state is replicated, write down the replication/consistency rule. If work is asynchronous, write down delivery semantics.

Performance characteristics usually come from amplification (how much internal work per external request), locality (whether work stays on one node), and contention (locks, hot keys, leader bottlenecks).

Correctness characteristics usually come from failure handling: retries, timeouts, idempotency, and what clients observe during failover. If you cannot explain the failure story, you do not yet understand Colocation, Clocks & Fairness.
bullets: Inputs → state/protocol → outputs/side effects
Name consistency and delivery guarantees
Identify the bottleneck resource early

sections.title: Designing with it
paragraphs: When incorporating Colocation, Clocks & Fairness into a system, decide the API boundary first: what does a client call, what can fail, and what is retried. Keep the happy path boring and push complexity into well-tested libraries or platform components.

Capacity plan with numbers: estimate peak load, working set, and headroom. Convert that into shard counts, cache sizes, thread/connection pools, or GPU/memory budgets as relevant to Colocation, Clocks & Fairness.
Prefer reversible rollout: feature flags, dual-running, shadow traffic, and clear dashboards. New uses of Colocation, Clocks & Fairness should be observable on day one.

sections.title: Operations and failure modes
paragraphs: Operate Colocation, Clocks & Fairness with SLIs that match user pain (availability, latency, lag, error rate, cost). Alert on burn rates and queue/lag growth, not only host CPU.
Common failures include overload without admission control, retry amplification, silent staleness, schema mismatches, and dependency brownouts. Write a runbook for the top three.
Chaos and game days should include slow dependencies and network delay, not only hard kills. Colocation, Clocks & Fairness often fails in the gray area.

deepDive.title: Colocation, Clocks & Fairness — deeper internals
paragraphs: Under the hood, Colocation, Clocks & Fairness typically exposes knobs for batching, buffering, concurrency, retention, and timeouts. Each knob trades latency, throughput, and cost. Change one at a time and measure.

Instrumentation should include high-signal histograms and exemplars that jump to traces. For data systems, watch amplification and compaction/GC; for RPC systems, watch queue time and saturation; for ML systems, watch memory and tokens/s.
bullets: One knob at a time with a hypothesis
Histograms > averages
Tie dashboards to runbooks

deepDive.title: Colocation, Clocks & Fairness — integration patterns
paragraphs: Integrate via stable contracts: schemas, idempotency keys, and versioned APIs. Dual-write carefully or prefer CDC/outbox patterns when crossing storage and messaging.
Boundary tests should prove behavior under duplicate delivery, reordering, and clock skew where relevant to Colocation, Clocks & Fairness.

expert.title: Colocation, Clocks & Fairness — multi-region and cost
paragraphs: Across regions, RTT and quorum placement dominate. Keep user-critical paths region-local when invariants allow; replicate asynchronously otherwise. Spell out the conflict/staleness model.
Track unit economics for Colocation, Clocks & Fairness: cost per million requests, per GB stored, or per million tokens. Many scalability projects are cost projects — make the objective explicit.

lessons.title: Market Data Pipelines
lessons.summary: Market Data Pipelines is a core topic in modern system design. This lesson builds a first-principles model around determinism, latency, and fairness, then connects that model to capacity, failure modes, and operational practice so you can use it in real architectures.

sections.title: What Market Data Pipelines is solving
paragraphs: Market Data Pipelines exists because naive designs around determinism, latency, and fairness break under scale, partial failure, or changing requirements. Before choosing tools, name the problem: which resource is scarce, which invariant must hold, and which user-visible failures are unacceptable.
In interviews and production reviews, strong answers start with constraints (QPS, data size, latency budget, consistency needs) and only then map Market Data Pipelines onto those constraints.

A useful mental model separates the control plane (how you configure and observe Market Data Pipelines) from the data plane (the per-request/per-event path). Confusing the two leads to architectures that look neat and operate poorly.

sections.title: Core mechanics
paragraphs: Mechanically, Market Data Pipelines involves a small set of moving parts: inputs, state, an algorithm or protocol, and outputs/side effects. Draw those parts explicitly. If state is replicated, write down the replication/consistency rule. If work is asynchronous, write down delivery semantics.

Performance characteristics usually come from amplification (how much internal work per external request), locality (whether work stays on one node), and contention (locks, hot keys, leader bottlenecks).

Correctness characteristics usually come from failure handling: retries, timeouts, idempotency, and what clients observe during failover. If you cannot explain the failure story, you do not yet understand Market Data Pipelines.
bullets: Inputs → state/protocol → outputs/side effects

Identify the bottleneck resource early

sections.title: Designing with it
paragraphs: When incorporating Market Data Pipelines into a system, decide the API boundary first: what does a client call, what can fail, and what is retried. Keep the happy path boring and push complexity into well-tested libraries or platform components.

Capacity plan with numbers: estimate peak load, working set, and headroom. Convert that into shard counts, cache sizes, thread/connection pools, or GPU/memory budgets as relevant to Market Data Pipelines.
Prefer reversible rollout: feature flags, dual-running, shadow traffic, and clear dashboards. New uses of Market Data Pipelines should be observable on day one.

sections.title: Operations and failure modes
paragraphs: Operate Market Data Pipelines with SLIs that match user pain (availability, latency, lag, error rate, cost). Alert on burn rates and queue/lag growth, not only host CPU.
Common failures include overload without admission control, retry amplification, silent staleness, schema mismatches, and dependency brownouts. Write a runbook for the top three.
Chaos and game days should include slow dependencies and network delay, not only hard kills. Market Data Pipelines often fails in the gray area.

lessons.title: Matching Engines
lessons.summary: A matching engine applies deterministic rules to an order book under tight latency budgets. Correctness, fairness, and replayability dominate design.

sections.title: Deterministic core
paragraphs: The matching loop consumes a sequenced input log and produces trades and book updates. Determinism enables replay for audit, debugging, and state reconstruction after failure. Shared-nothing per-symbol shards are common; cross-symbol constraints need careful design.

sections.title: Latency path
paragraphs: Hot path techniques include preallocated structures, avoidance of syscalls on the match path, and careful cache locality for price levels. Market data fanout and persistence are adjacent systems with their own SLOs — do not block matching on slow consumers.

lessons.title: Order Books
lessons.summary: An order book stores bids and asks by price level and matches incoming orders by defined rules (price-time, pro-rata, etc.). Structure choice (trees, arrays of levels, intrusive lists) drives latency and determinism.

sections.title: Book mechanics
paragraphs: Limit orders rest; market orders aggress. Price-time priority is common: better price first, then earlier time. Partial fills and cancel/replace are first-class.

sections.title: Data structures
paragraphs: Price levels often in sorted maps or contiguous arrays for hot top-of-book. Orders in FIFO queues per level. Avoid allocations on the hot path — preallocate pools.

sections.title: Determinism and journaling
paragraphs: For audit and replay, apply a sequenced input log to a deterministic book. Same inputs → same trades. This is the backbone of exchange reliability.

sections.title: Market data
paragraphs: Publishing top-of-book vs full depth changes bandwidth. Conflate wisely; never block matching on slow consumers.

designChallenges.title: Notification System (Advanced)
designChallenges.description: Design a scalable, multi-channel notification system handling push, email, SMS, and in-app alerts for 500M+ users with per-user preferences, deduplication, and guaranteed delivery.
hints: Fan-out fan-in: publish one event, fan-out per channel, aggregate delivery receipts
Use priority queues to separate critical (OTP, security) from bulk (marketing) notifications
Store a notification inbox in Cassandra keyed by user_id for in-app retrieval
Deduplication window: check a Redis bloom filter before enqueuing to avoid duplicate sends
Respect per-user quiet hours by scheduling delivery into a future-time bucket
checklist: Define channel types: push (APNs/FCM), email (SES/SendGrid), SMS (Twilio), in-app

Event ingestion: single event bus (Kafka) fans out to per-channel workers
User preference service: opt-outs, frequency caps, quiet hours, language/locale
Delivery guarantee: at-least-once with idempotency tokens, dead-letter queue
Deduplication: bloom filter or Redis set keyed on (event_id, user_id, channel)
Status tracking: sent → delivered → opened pipeline, analytics aggregation
Rate limiting per third-party provider (APNs, Twilio) to avoid bans

Provider rate limits and backpressure are handled
